paragraphs.text: The present festival is for us the beginning of feasts. It is the first of those that border on the law and its shadows, and it is also the entrance to those that lead to grace and truth. It is at once beginning, middle and end. Its beginning is the completion of the law. Its middle is the link that joins the two extremes. Its end is the revealing of the truth. For Christ is the end of the law, and he leads us away from the letter as far as he leads us up to the spirit. This is the fulfilment. The Lawgiver himself brought all things to completion, carried the letter over into the spirit, summed up all things in himself, and settled the law by grace. He put the one under the yoke and joined the other to it in harmony, without confusing what belongs to each. In a manner fully worthy of God he channelled whatever was burdensome [?], servile and subject into what is light and free. So we are no longer enslaved under the elements of the world, as the Apostle says, nor held under the yoke of slavery to the letter of the law. This is the sum of Christ's benefits to us. This is the revealing of the mystery:

this is the nature that emptied itself, God and man, and the deification of what he assumed. But [?] so bright and so glorious a coming of God among men had to have some prelude of joy, through which the great gift of salvation would come forth to us. That prelude is the present festival. It opens with the birth of the Mother of God, and it concludes with the [?] of the union of the Word with flesh. In that union the newest of all the marvels ever heard of, though people always appeal to it, remains hard to grasp and hard to contemplate, since it is hidden even as it is revealed and revealed even as it is hidden. From here, then, the light of virginity, beyond [?] … bearing [?], and gathering its crown as if from the pure flowers of the spiritual meadows of Scripture, this grace-filled day, first of the feasts, sets out a gladness shared by all creation. "Take courage," it says. "This festival is a birthday, and the refashioning of our race. For a virgin is now born, nursed and formed, and a mother is being prepared for God, the King of the ages." From David, and with David, this spiritual spectacle has been assembled for us. She, as Mother of God, sets forth her own God-given birth. He shows the noble heritage [?] of our race and the utterly new kinship of God with humankind. What a wonder! She stands between the height of the Godhead and the lowliness of the flesh, and becomes mother of the one who formed her. He prophesies the future as though it were already present, and receives from God, under oath, the glorious continuance and preservation of his line from his loins. So it is right that we celebrate the mystery of this day, and bring words themselves as our gifts to the Mother of the Word, since nothing else is dear to her except the word and the honour that words give. And in doing this we shall gain something twofold:

one part leads us up to the truth, and the other leads us away from slavery to the letter and from life under the law. How, and in what way? Clearly, as the shadow gives way at the coming of the light, and grace brings in freedom in place of the letter. The present festival stands on the boundary between these. It sets the truth over against the symbolic types and brings in the new in place of the old. Paul, the divine trumpet of the Spirit, cried out about this, saying: "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; be renewed [?]. The old has passed away; behold, all things have become new." For the law made nothing perfect, but a better hope was brought in, through which we draw near to God. So the truth of grace has been plainly revealed. The Lawgiver himself, lowering himself beyond words into self-emptying, came forth as man according to the divine plan, to supply what was lacking and to give the better and more perfect in exchange for the worse. The sublime John, the theologian and thunder of the Word, means this when he says most clearly: "From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace." For when he emptied himself and was then formed from us, beyond nature, in what is ours, we received the fullness, and were enriched with the deification given in return to the human substance he assumed. So let the whole universe rejoice today, and let nature leap. Let heaven above be glad, and let the clouds rain down righteousness. Let the mountains drip sweetness and the hills gladness. For the Lord has visited his people and raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David: this utterly spotless virgin, who knew no man, from whom comes Christ, the salvation and the expectation of the nations. Let every grateful soul now dance, and let nature call creation to its own renewal and refashioning. Let barren women run eagerly, for a childless and barren woman has given birth to the Virgin, the child given by God. Let mothers leap, for a mother who could not conceive has borne the incorrupt mother and virgin. Let virgins rejoice, for the unsown earth has borne, beyond words, the One who is from the Father [?]. Let women clap their hands [?], for woman, who long ago brought about the occasion of sin, has now brought in the firstfruits of salvation. She who was once condemned has been shown to be chosen by God: a mother without a husband, elected by her Maker, and the restoration of our race. So let all creation sing and dance, and contribute something worthy of the day. Let there be today one common festival of the heavenly and the earthly, and let everything composed within the world and beyond it celebrate together. For today the created temple of the Creator of all things is built, and a creature is newly prepared as a divine dwelling for the Creator. Today the nature that had been turned to earth receives the beginning of deification, and the dust, raised aloft, hastens to run up to the highest glory. Today

Adam offers to God firstfruits from us and on our behalf, and offers Mary as those firstfruits. She is the part of the whole lump that was not kneaded with the rest, and through her bread is made for the refashioning of our race. Today the great treasure of virginity is uncovered, and the Church, as a bride, puts on the inviolable pearl of true incorruption. Today the pure nobility of humankind receives back the grace of its first fashioning by God and returns to itself. The comeliness of beauty had been darkened by the baseness of evil, but nature, turning to the newborn mother of the Beautiful One, receives it again as a most excellent and godlike fashioning. This fashioning becomes, in the proper sense, a recalling. The recalling becomes deification, and the deification becomes a likeness to the original. Today the barren woman is found, beyond all hope, to be a mother. And she who will be mother of a child without a father, springing from barren loins, sanctifies the births of nature. Today the comely dye of the divine purple has been applied, and the poor nature of humankind is clothed in royal dignity. Today, as was prophesied, the shoot of David has sprung up. She has become Aaron's ever-flourishing rod and has blossomed for us into the rod of power, Christ. Today a virgin maiden comes forth from Judah and David, bearing the stamp of both kingship and priesthood, for she bears the One who was priest after the order of Melchizedek, not after Aaron. Today grace has whitened the mystical ephod of the divine priesthood, which it had woven beforehand, as a type, from the seed of Levi. And God has dyed the royal robe purple with the blood of David. In short, today the reshaping of our nature begins. The aged world receives a most godlike restoration of its elements and takes up the opening of a second fashioning by God. For the first forming of humankind was made from pure and spotless earth, but [nature] obscured

its [?] … the original dignity [?], robbed of grace by the fall of disobedience. Through that fall we were cast out of the place of life, and nature exchanged life in paradise for a mortal life. That mortal life came down to us like an ancestral inheritance, and from it came death and the ruin of our race. Then, since all preferred the land below to the land above, every hope of salvation had been taken away, and nature needed help from on high [?]. No law was able [?] to heal the sickness: not the law implanted in us, not the written law, not the fiery and reconciling word of the prophets. No one knew how to restore human nature [?], by whom it might perhaps easily have been brought back to its former nobility. Now the [?] of all was pleased

[?] might be brought about, with a pure and untouched Virgin first serving the mystery and then carrying in her womb the One beyond being, by a law that overcomes the laws of nature. And who could she be understood to be, if not that woman alone who was chosen before all generations by the Begetter of all nature? She is Mary, the Mother of God, the name renowned [?], from whose womb the One beyond God came forth with flesh. He made her a temple for himself and joined [?] himself to her in a way beyond nature, for in being born he did not corrupt the womb that bore him, nor did what was born need seed. For he was God, even if he chose to be born in the body [?], without labour and without birth pangs [?]. And the mother [?], wondrously nursing with milk, bore a child without a husband. The virgin who brought forth an unsown offspring remains a virgin, chaste [?] even after the birth, bearing the seals of virginity. For this reason she is rightly proclaimed Mother of God, virginity is honoured, the birth is worshipped, and God, united to humankind and then revealed in the flesh, grants the dignity of his own glory [?]. [?] from that first curse, and at once the nature of woman receives its correction: as it began the sin, so it makes the beginning of salvation. Our discourse has now come to its main point. So today I come here [?] as speaker at this festival and as host of this sacred banquet for you, setting out a gladness for all to share. "Truly," I said, "the Redeemer of our race [willed] to show anew,

in place of the former, a new birth and refashioning. Long ago, at the beginning, he took clay from virgin and pure [?] earth and formed the first Adam. So now he carries out his own incarnation himself, and in place of other earth, so to speak, he has chosen this pure and utterly spotless virgin out of the whole of nature. In her he renewed what is ours, taken from us, and the Maker of Adam became a new Adam, so that the new One who is beyond time might save the old." But who was she, and who were her parents? Come, let us say it briefly, running through the story as best we can. She, the boast of all, is the daughter of David and the seed of Joachim, a descendant of Eve and the child of Anna. Joachim [?] was a meek and gentle man, brought up in the laws of God. He lived temperately and devoted himself to God, and as he went on this way he was growing old without children. His nature was still vigorous, but it had no offspring to show in return. Anna too loved God. She was chaste but barren, devoted to her husband but childless, and she had no other pursuit than honouring the law of the Lord. Every day she was pierced by the goads of her barrenness, and, as barren women are likely to suffer, she was distressed, grieved and vexed, unable to bear her childlessness. So Joachim and his wife were weighed down with grief, because they had no child to support their line. Yet for a time the wick of their hope was not wholly put out, and both of them prayed that a child might be granted them to raise up offspring [?]. Both of them followed the example of the famous Hannah. They gave themselves to the temple and with prayers appealed to God to give release from their childlessness and fruit to their barrenness, and they did not stop until they obtained what they longed for. And indeed they obtained it, for the Giver of the gift did not withhold the gift they hoped for. As they implored and pleaded with God, the power that does not delay came to them quickly. It strengthened him for begetting fruit and her for bearing a child. The passages of their generative organs had dried up, but he moistened them with the fluids of procreation and made them fruitful instead of sterile. So from fruitless and dry trees, as from green wood, this all-spotless Virgin sprang up for us as fruit [?]. The bonds of barrenness were loosed, and the prayer was shown to be fruitful [?]. The barren woman bore a child, and the childless woman became the mother of a beautiful child. When the ear of grain of incorruption came forth from the womb of the barren mother [?], her parents brought her, in the earliest years of her life, to the temple [?] and dedicated her there. The priest who was then serving his course in the priesthood saw the choirs of virgins going before her and following after. He was delighted and rejoiced greatly, as one who already saw the [fulfilment?] of what had been hoped for [?]

[?] … all the inner sanctuaries of the holy places, laying up there this great treasure of salvation. There the child, entering as if into bridal chambers [?], was fed with heavenly food until the time of her betrothal [?] came. That time had been set before every age by the One who would be born from her through his inexpressible compassion, by the One who, before all creation and time and interval, begot him in a divine manner, and by his co-natural, co-enthroned and worshipped Spirit. Just as theirs is one Godhead, so too their nature and kingship are undivided and not estranged, and do not differ from themselves in any way, except in the distinct properties of the [divine persons?]. Therefore I celebrate with dancing and pour out my offering, and I bring a festal gift to the Mother of the Word, because her childbearing has made known to me the [?] of faith in the Trinity. For when the Word and Son, who has no beginning, carried out his own incarnation, the Father who begot him is seen consenting, and the Holy Spirit is seen descending eagerly and sanctifying the womb of her who conceived the incomprehensible One [?]

[?] Now is the time to ask David: what did the God of all say to him under oath? Come then, hymn-writer; come, prophet; strike the lyre and move the strings; say it clearly: what did the Lord swear to you? "What did the Lord swear to me? 'One of the fruit of your loins I will set upon your throne.'" This he swore, and he did not go back on it. He swore, and he sealed his words with deeds. "Once I have sworn by my holiness; will I lie to David? His seed shall endure for ever, and his throne like the sun before me, and like the moon established for ever; and the witness in heaven is faithful." Having sworn this, he fulfilled it, for it is impossible for God to lie. "See then: Christ is proclaimed as my Son according to the flesh, and he is hymned as my Lord and worshipped as my Son, and all the nations worship him, for they see him enthroned upon a virgin's throne. See, this Virgin has now sprung from our loins. From her womb the One who was before the ages, made flesh at the end of the ages, has come forth and renewed the fabric of the ages." So much for that. But let us, the people of God, the holy nation, the sacred assembly, dance our ancestral dances and honour the power of the mystery. Let each, according to the gift received, contribute something worthy to the festival. Let fathers bring the good fortune of their line; mothers, their fine children; barren women, the [fruitfulness?] of sin [?]; virgins, their twofold incorruption, I mean of soul and of body; married couples, their harmony. If anyone among you is a father, let him imitate the Virgin's father. And if he is childless, let him reap his prayer as fruitful, gathering it from a life that loves God. If any mother is nursing, let her rejoice with [?] …

Anna, who nursed a child granted through prayer after barrenness. If any woman is barren and childless and has no fruit of blessing, let her approach in faith the God-given shoot of Anna and shear off her barrenness. If any virgin keeps herself chaste, let her become a mother of the Word, adorning the state of her soul with the Word. If anyone is married, let him bring a spiritual offering from what he has obtained through prayer. Rich and poor together, young men and maidens, old and young, priests and Levites, queens and noblewomen, all of us, men and women alike, let us keep bright festival for the maiden, the Mother of God and prophetess, from whom came to dwell among us the Prophet of whom Moses wrote, Christ our God, the Truth. Let us imitate [?] the virgins who run ahead; let us enter together into the very Holy of Holies. For there are the swaddling clothes, after the birth, after the breast, after infancy [?] …

On the Nativity of our all-holy [?] Lady, the Mother of God. With a demonstration that she descends from the seed of David. Let others set out other themes of feasts for those who want them. For us, let this one be laid before us now for praise. Its chief subject is the present festival, which has at its opening the Mother of the Word, through whom the Spirit comes upon all, and those who [?] receive [the gift] of speaking [?] …

[?] they have. From here I turn the reins of my discourse back toward the turning-post and go through what follows from what was said before. I am held back by fear of speaking unworthily of the theme before us, yet eager, out of longing, to present it as worthily as I can. But wherever I turn, I will let my discourse run boldly, since I bring the day with me as a good helper, whether for my timidity or for my boldness. In the previous discourse we already celebrated the birth of the Mother of God as was fitting: I, the leader of the feast, and you, and all that is [?] beyond the world. With Joachim we were visited. With the virgins we ran. With David we shone together [?], I mean the patriarch and king, who is in both respects an ancestor of God. With Mary the Mother of God we were brought to the temple, and dwelling in the inner sanctuaries of the holy places we shared in the mysteries themselves. Thanks be to him who glorified his own, so that he might gather to himself those who were once far off. Now I think it neither out of tune nor superfluous to turn my discourse, by way of a short digression, to the good fortune of the line from which the Virgin descends, and to go through what it is fitting to say and what the present festival delights in. It delights in whatever shows that the Virgin, from whom the One beyond God came, beyond being, into existence in time, is of the seed of David. It delights too in all that God, who spoke to us through the law and the prophets, clearly proclaimed about her beforehand throughout the whole of Scripture. So, having considered the matter as well as we can, let us go at once to the contest itself and cut out at the root the tongues growing against us of the Jews who, of old and now, rage drunkenly against Christ, so that no root of bitterness may spring up any longer and trouble the flock of the Church. And how could we most easily achieve this, except by careful examination and inquiry? For I think we must first show from the books of Moses that Christ, the Son of God and himself God, arose from Judah, as the Apostle says, and appeared as the Son of the Virgin, as the Gospel says. We must bring forward the voices of the prophets, and only then take up the chief and decisive points. In this way the discourse, through its precision, will be irrefutable and firm on every side, and the character of the ancient law will also be kept pure. So let Jacob be brought before us, that most clear-sighted beholder of the lofty ladder, and before him Abraham the patriarch, in whom and to whom the promises were given. For Matthew too, at the beginning of his Gospel narrative, placed him first, after setting David at the head [?] of his writing. Upon

[?] and tracing the genealogy downward, as each one stands in the line of descent, he brought each in turn to a close, and from there he again fittingly took up Joseph, the descendant of David. In this way he showed, at the proper point, that she who had sprung from David, and had then been prepared beforehand for God, was betrothed to Joseph, who was of David, as a member of the same tribe. In ancient times it was not lawful for tribe to mix with tribe, or for one sceptre to be grafted onto another.

In this way, then, the great one among the patriarchs was called by God to leave Haran [?], so that he would obtain the promises. He had already received in advance no small part of them as symbols, for the things performed of old are symbols of the things [?]. He was not deceived in the hope of the covenants, and he did not fail to obtain the inheritance of the land. For the God of all says to him: “To you and to your seed I will give this land; for in your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed.” As the divine Paul also holds: “When God made the promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater to swear by, he swore by himself, saying: Surely I will bless you with blessing, and multiply you with multiplying. And so,” he says, “having waited patiently, he obtained the promise.” How, and in what way, the promises made to him came to fulfilment, you may learn from what follows, if you examine it truthfully. God, who had spoken to him of old, said to him: “In Isaac your seed shall be called.” And being fully convinced that what he had promised he was also able to perform, Abraham considered his own body, already as good as dead since he was about a hundred years old, and the deadness of Sarah's womb. Yet he did not waver at the promise of God, but grew strong in faith, giving glory to God. So it is fitting that he obtained the promise and gained the promised son, the one who received what had been promised. Twin children were conceived to Isaac, yet he gave the blessing of the promise to the one who, at his mother's prompting, had stolen the inheritance of the covenants by a trick. From him the twelve tribes sprang up abundantly from different branches. Among these, God especially honoured and preferred two sceptres, those of Levi and of Judah. To the one, somewhat earlier [?], had been entrusted the long robe of the priesthood, the divine [?], the mitre, the plate of holiness and the breastpiece of the Urim, as a prefiguring of a greater priesthood. To the other had been shown the royal throne, the diadem of beauty [?], precedence over all the tribes, and also leadership of the people together with the anointing. [?] the Child of God, the [?]

On the Nativity of Mary II. [?] and the one who brought all the ages into being, having appeared to the world through flesh in a new way, did not live according to the law of a fleshly commandment, as the Apostle says. He received a twofold dignity, not in a human way, as one might say, by which I mean according to what is visible, so that he was merely regarded as priest and king. Rather, he is attested to hold both dignities by nature, according to the power of an indestructible life: the priesthood, I mean, and the kingship. For he remains high priest forever. As priest, he has a priesthood that does not pass on, because he remains forever; therefore he is able to save completely those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them. And as king, Prince of peace and ruler in Israel, he is not shown to have sat visibly on the throne of his father David. Rather, he reigned spiritually over the house of Jacob forever, and his kingdom never came to an end. Since this is so, who would not be astonished at those who wrote these things about him and at the same time bore witness to the opposite? For they neither present him as successor to David's kingdom nor report that he sat on David's throne. Nor do they say that he took up power to rule equal to that of Herod or of Pontius Pilate, unless one tries to take these things in the most mystical sense of anagogy, as in “My kingdom is not of this world.”

So now let Jacob, great among the patriarchs, come forward for me, who at the proper time set out the things concerning Christ. There, foretelling the future to his sons, he [?] Judah, and in him he somehow paints beforehand the image of Christ in a more mystical [?], so that Judah is seen as a kind of body, taken in the sensible sense, and David as a kind of colour, understood by contemplation. From this it will be fitting for us to reach our aim, as we find David to be of the tribe of Judah and Christ to be descended from David. Once this is clearly shown, we shall also find that the Virgin is of the race of David, who sprang from Judah, since an offspring is born of the same race and the same tribe. Come then, best and most fruitful of the patriarchs, tell us: what was the allotment in blessings that you left to your children? What was the portion of each? And what did you assign to them as you were dying, and of what kind? “Yes,” says the patriarch, “the Spirit distributed to each of them what was fitting, according to the nature and rank each one had. Nothing was devised by me [?] apart from the purpose of the providence that governs all things. Rather, as it was determined by that providence, it foretold prophetically what concerned each one.” And so let anyone who wishes

take the books of Moses in hand [?] and learn, from the very account of the world's creation, the lots of the tribes [?], which I set out, he says, in the blessings [?], as God spoke in me. For now, though, our concern will be with one tribe only. Through it, it is easy to show that Christ, born from the Virgin according to the flesh, was descended from the tribe of Judah, so that every [unjust?] mouth that does not confess that Christ came from the seed of David may be stopped. What then does the seer say? For this is what Scripture usually calls those who are clear-sighted in mind. “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hands shall be on the back of your enemies; your father's sons shall bow down to you. Judah is a lion's whelp; from a shoot, my son, you went up. You lay down and slept like a lion and like a whelp; who shall rouse him? A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until what is laid up for him comes; and he is the expectation of the nations. Binding his colt to a vine, and his donkey's colt to the tendril, he will wash his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape. His eyes are gladdened by wine, and his teeth are whiter than milk.” We must consider, then, [?] when the words of the prophecy were fulfilled [?]. Clearly I see them fulfilled in Christ himself, the Saviour of us all, through both the law and [?]. At the end of the ages, the God beyond God dwelt among us through flesh. Wishing to bring to completion the counsel determined for him before the ages, according to the ineffable good pleasure of the Father who begot him and of the Spirit who is of the same kind, he arose from Judah and came forth from the Virgin who was from David. At that time all his brothers praised him, that is, all who through kinship with him have shared in his communion. The multitudes that have believed in Christ are countless and beyond the power of number. Speaking of them, the lofty John [?] said: “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, but of [?]

On the Nativity of Blessed Mary II. And on whose enemies' backs were hands ever stretched out so mightily, except Christ's alone? As the great David again sings in the Spirit: “He struck his enemies in the hinder parts,” using “hinder parts” to mean the back. He made this clear elsewhere, saying: “Let your hand find all who hate you, for you will make them turn their back.” And again, speaking in the person of the Father, in the passage where, after the anointing, he speaks of Christ's elevation to kingship and his proclamation according to his humanity: “My hand,” he says, “shall help him, and my arm shall strengthen him. The enemy shall gain no advantage over him, and the son of lawlessness shall not harm him again.” And again: “I will cut down his enemies before his face and put to flight those who hate him.” And again: “Before him the Ethiopians shall fall down, and his enemies shall lick the dust.” And the words “You made my enemies turn their backs to me, and you destroyed those who hate me”: to whom could they fittingly refer, if not to Christ alone? He says to the One in heaven: “I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and they will not be able to stand; they will fall beneath my feet,” and so on. And to whom did his father's sons bow down, except to Christ alone, who came forth from a woman? The story of Joseph had by then reached its end, since his dreams had been fulfilled, as was fitting. But what concerned Christ was to be a prefiguring of the Church from the nations. In that Church, all of us who have been begotten through it [?] bow down to him forever, for kinship with him has come about for us through mystical rebirth. And we have been named his brothers according to deification by grace and the riches of his love for us, inasmuch as we have received him whole and made him dwell in us [?], never corrupting any of his [life-giving?] commandments. In the same way he too, having shared in what is ours, appeared as one of the same nature as us. He took on the whole of human lowliness just as we have it, and all the marks of our nature, yet he plainly escaped the stain of sin and the condemnation of the first fall. All the nations have bowed down to Christ and bow down to him even now. Who is bold enough to deny this, seeing the whole world under the sun and all the ends of the earth bowing down to him and revering him, and taking pride in the name of the one they worship, in being Christians and [?]? And what could one say against the prophetic voices that expressly [?]? In one place: “All the nations shall serve him”; and: “Let all the kings of the earth bow down to him”; and: “Let all the earth bow down to you and sing to you”; and: “All the nations that

you have made shall come and bow down before you, O Lord,” and so on. And again: “Rejoice, you nations, with his people”; and: “Let all the sons of God bow down to him.” Do you see how the sons of his father, those enriched with the gift of adoption, have bowed down to Christ? But let us go on to what follows in the prophecy. “Judah,” he says, “is a lion's whelp; from a shoot, my son, you went up. You lay down and slept like a lion and like a whelp; who shall rouse him?” Well done, prophecy! He says “a lion's whelp.” Who is this, if not clearly Christ, descended from royal seed, that is, from David? It is not unreasonable to understand the lion as David, since the lion is a mark of royal dignity, and the lion's whelp as Christ, born from him according to the flesh, as what follows in the prophecy also shows. For he says: “From a shoot, my son, you went up.” And whom would you properly understand by the shoot, beloved, given what follows, except clearly her alone, the [?] holier than all the saints, who appeared wholly pure in body and spirit to the one who dwelt wholly in her? I mean Mary, a truly great and venerable reality and name: the branch of David, the rod of Jesse, the ever-flourishing shoot of Judah. From her the Child of God, who is above the world, before the world and coeternal with the one who begot him, sprang forth in the flesh. One might marvel at the precision of the prophecy. Having clearly declared the kinship of descent by the names “lion” and “whelp,” he added: “From a shoot, my son, you went up,” so as to say what Isaiah expressed so well: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from his root.” This clearly refers to Christ and the Virgin. The shoot is properly David, the rod is plainly the Virgin herself, and the flower is understood as Christ. So he himself, in the [?] of the Song, symbolically perfuming his own fragrant name, says: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.” And the prophet himself does not [conceal?] that Christ is king, and the most [?] of all kings: “For you lay down,” he says, “and slept like a lion, like a whelp; who shall [rouse him]?” In these words he indicates at once the royal, the fearsome and the [?], that is, the boundless power of divine authority. Christ himself also cries out in the Gospels: “I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again.” For truly, by the Saviour's own authority, everything in his universal [variant reading: “saving dispensation's”]

way of life was chosen and extraordinary. That is why he himself says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” They could not have destroyed it unless he willed it and, as it were, bade the Hebrews do so. By “temple” he means his all-blameless flesh, which he built around himself, without hands, from the womb of this undefiled and pure ever-virgin. Referring to it his life-giving sleep, when he accepted for our sake the voluntary sleep of death, he speaks as a man through David: “I lay down and slept; I awoke, for the Lord will help me.” And the words “Who shall rouse him?” clearly indicate the Father, who together with the Son raises and awakens the temple of the body. This accords with what is said in the Psalms in the person of the Son to the Father: “You will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor let your holy one see corruption.” And again: “Lord, you brought up my soul from Hades; you saved me from those who go down into the pit.” While the Son himself was working the resurrection of his own body, it was necessary that the Father also be shown as his co-worker, as being of the same nature and will as he is, so that through this joint action, identical in power and operation, their oneness of nature might be preserved in every respect. [?] We must go on to what follows: “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until what is laid up for him comes; and he is the expectation of the nations.” Oh, the foreknowledge! Nothing that was declared proved false. It was shown earlier that the Virgin properly sprang from the loins of David. Her shoot is Christ, who is both leader and ruler, and who takes away the spirit of princes. He would be the one who reigns over the house of Jacob forever, whose kingdom has no end. The kingdom of the Jews had been [overthrown?] even before Christ's coming. Yes, it was plainly brought to an end in the time of Jeconiah, through the most bitter deportation to Babylon. Yet the line did not fail; it was honoured and esteemed until Christ, and it preserved the traces of royal nobility. It remains, then, to understand “until what is laid up for him comes; and he is the expectation of the nations” as referring to the Christ of God, who is God himself and Lord himself. This all-holy Virgin, the stem of David, bore him for us virginally, in virginal labour. For once the rule of the Jews had passed away, no other king according to the flesh [sat?] on the visible throne of David, since his kingdom had been swept away into utter ruin, according to the prophecy of Jeremiah, which runs as follows: “Jeconiah was dishonoured like a vessel for which there is no use. Why was he cast out and thrown into a land he did not know? Land, land, hear

the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord: Write this man down as a man disowned; for no man of his seed shall grow up to sit on the throne of David, as ruler still in Judah.” Since the prophet has said this, who else could be understood as the expectation of the nations, except Christ alone? The prophet and elder Simeon, who received God, had been divinely told that he would not see death until he had seen him come in the flesh. And the oracle was fulfilled, the outcome of the oracles coming about in deeds. Simeon saw him as a baby and received into an old man's arms, from his mother's arms, the one who is before the ages and older than his mother. At once he leapt up with an old man's leaps, for even old age leaps when it is invigorated by great joy. With words of praise he hymned the Lord who had become an infant. He called him Master, confessed him as Saviour, proclaimed him a light of the nations and heralded him as the glory of Israel, that is, the Lord who had come to dwell among us for the expectation of the [salvation?] of the nations. To these the Father revealed the Son, as one can also learn from another prophet, who says most clearly: “Behold, I have given him as a witness to the nations, a ruler and commander among the nations.” And again: “Behold, nations that do not know you shall call upon you, and peoples who do not know you shall flee to you.” And from another, who says: “I have set you as a light of the nations.” And from yet another: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance”; and: “All the nations shall call him blessed”; and: “In him all the nations shall be blessed.” “Binding,” he says, “his donkey's colt to a vine.” What is the vine? It is the one who cries out in the Gospels: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser.” And we would be his colt, we who have been united to him and joined to him as if by an unbreakable bond through the nature he assumed. In it the rich one, becoming poor with our poverty, gave what is his to us who are most poor. In this way we have become gods through him, and he for our sake has been called man. The colt of his donkey might also be understood, more mystically, as the all-venerable [Church?], which typifies the calling of the nations, to which we are led up. For we were once [?] brutish, held fast by irrationality, until the Word himself came to dwell among us, [the] Wisdom [?]

[?] removed the veil of irrationality. He covered our nakedness for our good and clothed us in the rational robe of the [?] that was about him, the robe woven from above throughout. He bound us ineffably, like a colt to the tendril of the saving [?], and joined earthly things to heavenly. This is why the children, brought up in innocence, cried out with one voice when they saw him making his way to Jerusalem, going toward that life-giving and blessed passion which he willingly gave up for the salvation of the whole world, and riding royally on a colt as on a throne: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes, the king of Israel.” Zechariah had proclaimed this earlier, saying: “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion. Behold, your king comes to you, meek and bringing salvation, sitting on a colt, the young of a beast of burden.” And what clearer proof of the truth could anyone find than these words? Then next: “He will wash his robe in wine,” he says; “his eyes are gladdened beyond wine, and his teeth are whiter than milk.” With what wine, then, will he wash his robe, he who cleanses the world of sin, the true and ripe cluster of grapes of the Church? Clearly with the blood of his all-blameless flesh, as he cleanses us and washes us like a soiled garment. For he truly clothed himself with us, for whose sake he also became man. With what blood of the grape will the undefiled one wash his whole garment, if not with the living and all-blameless stream from the spring of his divine side? For he was the most mystical cluster of the true vine, pressed out in the winepress of the [?] Church, because he was shamefully abused on the beam of the cross so that he might wash away our filth. He arrayed himself in a truly God-woven garment, the flesh like ours, taken from us. Dyed from undefiled virgin blood, he royally made it purple in the Spirit, and he put on our substance like royal purple [?]. Like a tunic, it was steeped in blood, as the stream of blood from his life-giving side then dripped upon it. Isaiah is a witness, bringing in the powers around him at the very moment of the passion [?] and having them say: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with crimson garments from Bozrah?” And again: “Why are your garments red, as if from a trodden winepress?” I think he himself shows this in the Song, where he says: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?”, using the part

to indicate the whole. Whose eyes are gladdened beyond wine, except Christ's alone? About him again, in the Songs, the soul betrothed to God says: “Bring me into the house of wine.” It is as if she were saying: “Bring me into the house of the Church, where the cup of gladness is set out, mixed for salvation in the blood of the Lamb.” When she has come inside, she says: “Show me your face, and let me hear your voice; for your voice is sweet, and your face is lovely.” As soon as she saw him, she says: “Behold, my brother is white and ruddy, and beautiful. His head is fine gold; his locks are like fir branches, black as a raven.” Of him the great David also sings: “The Lord awoke like one who sleeps, like a mighty man who has drunk deep of wine.” After his return to life from the dead, he greeted the women who were then bringing myrrh with “Rejoice,” offering a greeting that brings joy and dispelling the gloom of their earlier grief. To the foremost of the disciples he likewise spoke a word of joy, saying: “Take courage; I have overcome the world.” And again: “Peace be with you; it is I; do not be afraid.”

[?] …being of the family of David. From this it will be clear to you that she too must be taken to be of the family of David who, by an ineffable conception, became his mother according to the flesh — provided one does not carelessly pass over the saying, “The tree is known by its fruit.” But let us run back once more to the birthday feast, and strike up for Anne a little song, like a wedding song: now for her who carries a God-given child, the pledge of the promise; now for her who, after barrenness, gives birth to a fruitful answer to prayer, [the herald] of God’s coming to dwell among men, a coming most manifest and beyond understanding. For it is fitting that she who bore such a shoot should be praised, and be counted worthy of a truly divine acclamation. Before us, then, lies Anne’s bedchamber like a bridal chamber, portraying the face of childbearing and of virginity: the one belongs to the mother, the other to the daughter. The mother has just received release from childlessness; the daughter, a little later, will undergo in a manner beyond nature the childbirth of Jesus, God fashioned in our nature. Fittingly, then, the God-possessed Anne, radiant and glad in the state of her soul, cries aloud: “Rejoice with me,” she says, “for I have borne a shoot of promise from a fruitless womb, and I nurse at my breast a fruit of blessing granted in answer to prayer. I have stripped off the [garment] of barrenness and put on the bright veil of fair childbearing. Let Hannah, whose prayer was heard, rejoice with me today, she who was set against Peninnah, and by her own example let her applaud the marvel of what has happened to me. Let Sarah too dance, leaping in her old age, and depicting my conception after barrenness. Let the barren and childless together join in acclaiming the visitation from heaven that has been made wonderful in me. Let every mother [?] also say: Blessed is he who granted their prayer to those who pray, who opened the passages of a barren womb, and who gave a shoot from fruitless parents — his own most wondrous mother according to the flesh, whose womb is a heaven in which he dwelt whom nothing can contain.” In harmony with these words, let us too offer our praise to her who was once called barren but has now become mother of the virgin bridal chamber. Let us say to her with Scripture, let us say: “How blessed is the house of David, from which you have come forth, and the womb in which God fashioned the ark of holiness, she who conceived him [without seed?].” So you are blessed, thrice-blessed, you who carried the God-blessed child, Mary, that most precious name, from whom Christ came forth as the flower of life; whose coming forth is glorious, and whose birth-pang is beyond this world. We too rejoice with you, O all-blessed one; for you have borne the God-given offspring of promise, the hope of us all. Blessed are you truly, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. [?]

Through you, too, women are called blessed who have cast off childlessness and become fruitful after barrenness. The tongue of the faithful magnifies your shoot, and every joyful word praises your childbearing. For it is truly fitting, and fitting above all, that she should be praised who was counted worthy of an oracle of divine providence, and who bore for us a fruit of such kind and so great, from whom came forth sweet Jesus, who is wholly sweetness and wholly desire, the last and highest object of desire among all things desired. Of him let us say: under his shadow we shall live, and under his wings we shall find rest. He is truly the one proclaimed through the law and the prophets, Christ Jesus our God, the Grace and the Truth, who came to save sinners and to call all back to their ancient nobility. To him glory and honor and worship are offered by all of us, with the Father who is without beginning and his [all-holy?] Spirit, now and to the ages.

On the [birth]day [?] of our all-holy Lady, the Theotokos and ever-virgin Mary: [?] a demonstration from ancient history and from various testimonies that she is descended from the seed of David.

Again a feast, again a festival, and again I am the skillful host, celebrating my own salvation and calling all to the spiritual banquet. The Theotokos presides over it, [pouring out] a torrent of delight, and feasts her own guests. In it, you swarm of Christ’s bees, flying about in godly fashion as around hives dripping with sweetness, gather [?] of honey and go home. And who would choose to be left out of such delight, especially those who have already tasted its good things? For if some do not [readily] withdraw from a table richly abounding in dishes until they have enjoyed its delights even beyond their fill, how would it not seem utterly ridiculous to leap away from the table before tasting the mysteries set out here? For the banquet is royal, that of a queen descended from royal seed. Come, then, beloved, receive our discourse once again, as it leads you back to that aim which in the previous [discourses] we [?] well, in which I clearly showed you Christ [from the root?]. Once this is shown, she too who bore him according to the flesh will fittingly appear to be of the same root. And it seems quite superfluous to me to bring in a second solution, since the more [?] one has already been set out by us somewhat more elaborately and at greater length, to demonstrate the truth. But so that we may send the contentious objection that the raging Jews raise against the truth off on the breezes of falsehood,

come, let us, as far as we are able, show that the Virgin herself is from the very root of David, using the evangelists as our witnesses, and the idiom of Scripture. I think, then, that one must first examine the generations from David according to the genealogies of Luke and Matthew — the one going backward, the other proceeding in order — and join them together in the mind at their ends; then set out in sequence the confusion by which the kinship of Joseph’s parents became confused; and so demonstrate clearly the way in which the Virgin too descends from the family of David, so that nothing concerning her may remain unproven. For I know that this is the most brilliant praise of any encomium: to take up arms against God-fighting tongues and to stop every mouth that rages against her. I shall begin, then, from here. And let each of those present who has been nourished on learning pardon me, since I am inexperienced in secular training and distressed on that account, as I cannot find a short road suited to what is needed. Yet, trusting in the Spirit who teaches every man knowledge, I strip for the contest before me.

In ancient times, then, a law prevailed that no woman could be taken in marriage from another tribe, but only one who shared the man’s own tribe. That this is true, hear the very words of the law, which run verbatim thus: “And Moses commanded the sons of Israel by the command of the Lord, saying: An inheritance shall not pass among the sons of Israel from tribe to tribe, for the sons of Israel shall each cleave to the inheritance of the tribe of his father; and every daughter who inherits an inheritance from the tribes of the sons of Israel shall be wife to one from the clan of her father’s tribe, so that the sons of Israel may each inherit the inheritance of his fathers, as the Lord commanded Moses.” And this was indeed kept for a time. For while the affairs of the Jews flourished and the Mosaic ordinances were at their height, none of their customs failed to prevail according to statute. But once these began to move toward destruction and deserted wholly to the opposite, diminishing little by little, they no longer took any account of their ancestral prosperity [?], living a rather gentile kind of life and treating the matter as of no great importance — although the law decreed it, the prophets cried out, and God himself bore witness through almost the whole of Scripture that they should not be scattered, should not corrupt the [?]

[?] they had come to the extreme of misery [?], and God punished them in many ways: at one time by the siege of the city, the sacking of the sanctuaries, and the trampling of the holy things under accursed and profane feet; at another by the ravaging and plundering of the nation and the overthrow of their ancestral land, by which they were driven out and went into a foreign country, becoming a spectacle to those who saw and a byword to those who heard. Hemmed in on every side, they fell into incurable [evils], and the race could no longer keep itself distinct, weighed down by the burden of its calamities and the multitude of misfortunes that befell it daily. Then indeed each of the tribes was confounded, and they were stripped of the special distinction of noble birth. Yet this renowned dignity of the race had not been wholly obliterated. For like a remnant there remained, still prevailing by succession, the worth of this inheritance, down to the celebrated Virgin — I mean her who alone among women is [unwedded?] mother and ever-virgin, whom I now hasten to show is of the Davidic tribe. Directing the intent of my discourse to the [sense?] of Scripture, I set it loose, God above all granting me to speak worthily.

But come, tell me, blessed Matthew: what is the reason why those you list in your genealogy disagree with those of Luke, the sacred initiate? “Among us,” says Matthew, that most divinely writing mind, once a tax collector and now a guide to the hidden mysteries, “there is no appearance of disagreement at all. For he, tracing his account as it were backward, passed over the natural fathers and sometimes mentioned only the legal ones; while I have clearly made mention of the natural fathers — not without reason, nor in a way unworthy of the Spirit. For each of us, inspired by one and the same Spirit, honors the other’s account, differing from it in nothing.” We must examine with precision, beloved, the genealogies set out by both, and from there hunt out the [?] of what we are seeking.

[?] But he did not stop there; his account went on as far as the Virgin’s betrothed. Luke, however, after the Savior was revealed at his baptism, diverting his account a little, writes as follows: “And Jesus himself, when he began, was about thirty years old, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph, son of Heli, son of Matthat, son of Levi, son of Melchi,” and so on in ascending order as far as Seth, son of Adam, son of God. Now the diligent mind of those who examine these things is not unaware that Scripture customarily calls “fathers by law” those who died childless but had children assigned to them after their death through offspring of a brother’s seed; and “fathers by nature” those who above all begot children for themselves by their own seed for the succession of the family, and who sometimes also, if their brothers had died childless, secured the inheritance for their brother through [levirate?] seed. Of the evangelists, then, the one mentioned only the natural fathers and passed over the legal ones; the other, conversely, passed over the natural fathers and mentioned the legal ones specifically; and neither strayed from what is reasonable. I think it good also to recall an ancient testimony on this point, which we have received from a certain [?] man of wide learning, and which runs verbatim thus:

“Since the names of the families in the genealogies of the evangelists are such that some children succeeded their true fathers, while others were begotten by one man but were called after another, and mention was made of both — of those who begot and of those who were reckoned to have begotten — neither of the Gospels is false, since they count both nature and law. For the two families, the one descended from Solomon and the one from Nathan, were intertwined with each other by the raising up of children and by second marriages. To make what I am saying clear, I will relate how the persons were intertwined. If we count the generations from David through Solomon, the third from the end is found to be Matthan, who begot Jacob, the father of Joseph. [From] Nathan son of David, according to Luke, the third from the end is likewise Melchi. Since, then, Joseph is the object of our inquiry, we must show how each is recorded as his father — Jacob descending from Solomon and Heli from Nathan, each of them tracing a different line. Now Matthan and Melchi took the same woman in turn and had children who were brothers by the same mother, since the law did not forbid a woman who was widowed or divorced to marry another man. It is handed down, then, that first Matthan, who traced his family from Solomon, begot Jacob; and when

Matthan died, Melchi, who traced his family back to Nathan, being of the same tribe but of a different family, as I said before, took her as a widow and had a son, Heli. Thus we shall find Jacob and Heli, from two different families, to be brothers by the same mother. Of these, Jacob, when his brother Heli died childless, took his wife and begot from her a third, Joseph — by nature his own son (for which reason it is written, ‘And Jacob begot Joseph’ [?]), but by law he was the son of Heli. For Jacob, being his brother, raised up seed for him. Therefore the genealogy concerning him will not be invalidated [?], which [Matthew gives]: ‘And Jacob,’ he says, ‘begot Joseph’; whereas Luke, on the contrary, says: ‘Who was, as was supposed’ (for he adds this) ‘the son of Joseph, son of Heli, son of Melchi.’ For it was not possible to express legal descent more pointedly. And in recording this kind of fatherhood he kept silent about the word ‘begot’ to the very end, carrying his account back by way of ascent as far as Adam, son of God.”

And a little later: “Heli and Jacob were brothers by the same mother. For when Heli died childless, Jacob raised up seed for him, begetting Joseph, by nature his own son, but by law Heli’s. Thus Joseph was the son of both.”

So much for him. And with Joseph’s genealogy traced in this way, by implication the Virgin herself, the [all-holy?] Mary, is shown along with him to be of the same tribe, since according to the law of Moses it was not permitted for tribe to mingle with tribe. For [she was required] to be joined in the partnership of marriage to one of those known to be of the same clan and family, so that the inheritance should not pass from tribe to tribe. And if anyone should demand that the all-holy Virgin, who knew no husband, be given a genealogy in her own right, he does not seem to me to act rightly, since the law nowhere allows this, nor has [Scripture] recorded it. For where among the ancients is a woman ever shown to have been given a genealogy, when the male [?] was preferred for entry in the genealogical record? For it was held more honorable that the nobility of a family be known from the father rather than from the mother. For us, however, [?] nothing at all, except that we should not counterfeit our ancient boundaries or [?] empty bonds; for it is not right to move the eternal boundaries which our fathers set. Of the things set out a little before [?] … [?] … she herself then [?] … [?] … this [?] Mother of God, [being of the tribe] of the man who by dispensation

was betrothed to her — I mean Joseph, who appeared [?]. If we grant that he descends from the seed of David, it will necessarily follow that she who was betrothed to him is of the same tribe. For “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary your wife,” said the angel who stood by him in a vision when he was distressed at the paradox of the ineffable conception. So Moses was not proved false, and David did not err: the one decreeing that the families should not be mingled with one another, the other prophesying under oath that Christ would be raised up from his loins. Thus our discourse, running along with the current, has clearly presented Christ to us as being from Judah and David.

I will try, however, to set out the account of this in another way as well, from ancient writings, for all of you who have drunk the pure milk of the Church. For I take no account of the others, since prophecy has so rebuked their hardness of heart: “They shall grope [at noon?] like the blind along a wall, and as if they had no eyes they shall grope.” For us the divine Apostle will suffice, who says: “We speak wisdom among the mature, yet not a wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are passing away; but we speak the wisdom of God, hidden in a mystery,” which the natural man cannot know: “for it is foolishness to him, and he cannot know it, because it is spiritually discerned.” Of the things done by Christ, then, there are some that escaped the many, and that were profitably kept silent by the people of that time — for example, the things he did before his baptism, and the manner of life he led throughout thirty whole years, which no Scripture records anywhere. Now one of the things kept most silent was also the miracle of his birth, which escaped almost everyone during the time he lived as man, except a few, as a holy man named Ignatius says somewhere: “And the virginity of Mary and her childbearing escaped the ruler of this age, and likewise the death of Christ: three mysteries to be cried aloud, which were wrought in the silence of God.” Fittingly, then, at that time Christ’s birth from the Holy Spirit was kept silent among the many, and Joseph was accepted in the place of a father. And so, fittingly, the genealogy was traced through him as the child’s father. For if

this had not been done, he would have been thought fatherless, having no genealogy traced from a father. Therefore the wonderful evangelists necessarily traced Joseph’s genealogy at that time, since he was the very one everyone proclaimed to be the son’s father. For if they had set him aside and traced the genealogy through the mother, not only would this have been unseemly, it would also have been foreign to the custom of the divine Scriptures, since no one before had [been traced] from a woman [?] … And in tracing Joseph’s descent from David for the reason given, they at the same time establish that the Virgin Mary too came from David, since she was above all of the tribe of Judah and of the clan of David, from which Joseph also sprang. For the law [cited above] was plainly known, which prevented intermarriage with the other tribes and expressly laid down that marriages were to be made within the inheritance and clan of one’s own tribe. For it says: “An inheritance shall not pass among the sons of Israel from tribe to tribe, for the sons of Israel shall each cleave to the inheritance of the tribe of his father.” Accordingly, then, this renowned Virgin too was of the seed of David, from whom the Master was also traced. For if the husband is the head of the wife, according to the great Apostle, and the two shall become one flesh, according to the law of Moses; and if a betrothed woman who sins suffers the punishment for adultery according to the law, as having become the body of her betrothed and having the man as her head — [is it not fitting], when the head is given a genealogy, that the body should be counted along with the head? So here too the Virgin, joined to Joseph, had fittingly to be included with him in the genealogy, since she has been shown to be above all of his tribe, and indeed of the clan and [house] of David as well. For this reason Gabriel too, prophesying in his address to her, said among other things: “And the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father,” teaching by this that David was the forefather of the one who was to be born of her. For how else would it have been fitting for the angel to say this to the Virgin, [?]

[?] that she is clearly of David? For he would not have said to a woman who was not of David, “God will give him the throne of his father David.” What father could the Virgin reasonably have asked about, when she confessed that she did not know a man but learned that she would conceive by the Holy Spirit, unless the word was plainly spoken to a daughter of David? This is why Luke rightly says: “And Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the town of Nazareth, into Judea, to be enrolled, to the city of David which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and lineage of David, with Mary his betrothed, who was with child.” So we shall no longer read this passage ambiguously, as if Mary merely came along to be enrolled. We shall read it as saying that she too, with Joseph, was of the house and lineage of David, since what has been set out gives us the grounds for this interpretation. I think, then, it has been clearly shown that the divine evangelists do not trace Joseph's genealogy in vain. Through him the Virgin, who was also a descendant of David, is necessarily made known as well, and so is the one born of her by a surpassing miracle, Christ Jesus, the Child of God before the ages. Whoever tries to contradict this is rather trying to sharpen the [?] of his own tongue against himself; let him be cast out of the sacred doors of our court. But for us, to whom the Word of God was sent forth, the grace and the truth, let it not be permitted to search out anything beyond what has been said, since divine Scripture bars us from inquiring into deeper things. For it says, “Think on what has been commanded you, and do not seek what is higher than you.” You, then, O Jew, understand the force of what has been said, and do not fight against the truth. Lay aside your doubting mind, and, free of all division of thought, be schooled in grace, through which you will be loosed from the bonds of the yoke that bows you down to the letter. Take away the veil; receive the pure light of what is written; pass by the shadows and leave the types behind. Receive grace unveiled. Come to the truth without hesitation. Glorify and hymn the one who decreed these things so. Say with Moses: “This is my God, and I will glorify him; the God of my father, and I will exalt him.” Let it always be open to you, and to anyone who wishes, both to think these things and likewise to teach them. But we, in whom the light of truth has been firmly stamped, have no leisure to investigate further and draw the discourse out without end, since the truth has been shown very distinctly and as readily as could be. For it is not fitting for those who wish to keep a festival to stretch their words into disputations; that would be out of place. Let the discourse head for the turning-post, then, and let the mysteries of the day come forth, especially since the feast is standing within the doors

and calling out to us a refrain of joy. Rejoice, then, and leap for joy, for what was awaited is here. The recall stands before the gates, redemption at the doors, salvation in our hands. How, and in what manner? Let us hear the one who says: “God will come manifestly.” From where will he come, and how? From heaven, and in our likeness: from heaven without a body, and in our likeness in form, nature and appearance like ours. But how could this happen unless God became flesh? For God cannot be seen in naked divinity unless, joined to our lump by union, he becomes as we are, yet without sin. Clearly [?] for the sake of the whole creature the Master of the creature is united to the creature, that he may save the creature. Where, and when? In the virginal place, and at the end of the times, when David foretold that he would come. And this is what we celebrate today: the birthday of the Virgin, the prelude of the feasts, the preface of the mystery of Christ. For the palace had to be prepared for the king first, and then the king could come. The royal swaddling clothes had to be woven first, and then the royal babe could be born. And finally the clay had to be kneaded first, and then the potter could come. Fittingly, then, the wonderful Joachim and his wife Anna, called by God through divine [?oracles], obtained the fruit of their prayer — I mean the queen of nature, the firstfruits of our lump, whose birthday we keep, whose swaddling clothes we honour, and in whom we venerate the recall of our race that begins here. Now our kindred nature begins its deification. Now the bonds of the former barren infirmity are loosed. The childless woman becomes a mother, the one without offspring [?] is found with child, and Anna rejoices as she nurses a virgin babe. Now the passages of barrenness are closed, the veins of childbearing are released, and the conception of the childless woman runs ahead of the wonder of the Virgin. For if it is a great thing for a barren woman to give birth, how is it not greater for a virgin to bear a child? The one, once shown to be a mother, no longer remained barren; but the other, having given birth without a man, remained a virgin still, her womb not corrupted, nor [?] the lot of mothers. The one came later, the other first, for the first was a pattern of the second. It was fitting for him through whom and in whom are all things, as Master of nature, first to work a new wonder on the grandmother and show a barren woman to be a mother; and then in the mother to make new the laws of nature, to show a virgin as mother, and to set the seal on the seals of virginity. Such is the birthday of the Virgin; this is the sum of the feast: the remembrance of God's covenants with men, the demonstration of the [?promises],

the manifestation of the hidden mystery, and finally the visitation of the whole race, in which we were [?visited] and through which we were enlightened — we who once sat in darkness and the shadow of death, now flashed upon by the inaccessible light of Christ Jesus, who dawned on us from on high, the Master of us all and our Saviour God. To him be glory, honour and might, with the Father who is without beginning and his life-giving Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

If the earth is measured with a span and the sea marked out with a line; if heaven is gauged in cubits and the multitude of the stars counted; if the drops of rain, the clods of the earth, the mass of the winds and the quantity of sand can be grasped, perhaps the subject now in our hands might also somehow be grasped. But this is the festival of the Mother of God, and what we celebrate is the birth of an admirable child — an ever-virgin child, a child who knew no marriage, a queen, a prophetess, whose royal swaddling clothes David, great among prophets and kings, portrayed with royal gaze when he cried out: “All the glory of the king's daughter is within; she is clothed in golden fringes, adorned.” From afar, I think, he was hinting at the comeliness of beauty that God cast around her straight from her swaddling clothes [?]

signifying it through the varied gifts of the divine [?Spirit]. For it is by these, as I understand it, that the gold-woven raiment and the golden fringes — and I think also the royal swaddling clothes — are interpreted by fair-minded readers without partiality. Foreseeing their inner comeliness and the loveliness of beauty shining outwardly around the Virgin, he cried out beforehand with a bold voice: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father's house, and the king will desire your beauty.” Although these words clearly refer to the Church from the Gentiles, it is not hard to take them of her as well, since by the wonder of the incarnation she was made wholly a temple for the whole Bridegroom of the Church. Come, then, gathering together

[?] with David, let us applaud the daughter of David with praises such as befit the Mother of God. Let us revere the splendour of the feast; let us offer the Virgin the solemn praises of virginity. Let us bring the queen of our race the oracles of the prophets as gifts and precious perfumes. Let us greet her with Gabriel's greeting. Let us say to the mother of joy: “Hail, full of grace!” Hail, radiant one, through whom darkness was driven out and light brought in in its place. “Hail, full of grace,” through whom the law fell still and grace shone forth. Hail, prelude of joy and end of the curse. “Hail, truly full of grace, the Lord is with you” — he who was afterwards from you was before that with you: the earlier in power, the latter in act; now preparing your womb as a dwelling for himself, then building from you in the flesh the great mystery of the dispensation. Hail, you who alone took to your bosom the Lord, the blessing, so that our first mother might put off the first curse. Hail, God-receiving treasury of virginity, from which an incorrupt birth came forth while the [?seal] of virginity remained inviolate. Hail, chaste mother and Virgin [?]. Hail, diadem of beauty and [?] of our race, adorned on every side with royal [?] wonders. Hail, sacred precinct of God, of Christ, who alone entered as priest into the [?holy places] of heaven after the order of

Melchizedek. Hail, rod of Aaron, root of Jesse, sceptre of David, royal robe, crown of graces, unwritten type of virginity, plate of holiness, oracle of the Urim. Hail, mediatrix of law and grace, seal of the old and new covenants, most manifest fulfilment of all prophecy, acrostic of the God-inspired truth of the Scriptures, living and most pure volume of God the Word, in which God the Word himself, the writer, is read daily without sound and without writing. Hail, firstfruits of our refashioning, fulfilment of God's promises to us, sanctuary of divine glory proclaimed beforehand by the predictions, long-awaited salvation of the nations. Hail, true ladder of Jacob, smoking mountain, ark of the sanctuary, overlaid on every side with gold, with the Spirit shining through it; golden jar bearing Christ, the heavenly manna and pure food of all. Hail, you through whom “In sorrow you shall bear children” has no more place, but has been changed into bearing in gladness. “Blessed are you among women,” through whom the nations, believing, cry out in knowledge: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; God is the Lord, and he has appeared to us.” “Blessed are you among women,” mystical vine planted by God, which spreads its branches in the branches of the Churches and from the womb brings to bloom for us the ripe cluster of incorruption. “Blessed are you among women,” field tilled by God, who carried in your womb, as in a granary, the unsown and unwatered ear of grain that is our life. “Blessed are you among women,” truly desirable land, from which the potter of our dust took the clay and renewed the vessel

broken by sin. “Blessed are you among women,” new Shiloh, in which the spiritual ark of the incarnation of God the Word came to rest; and indeed in which “all the fullness of the Godhead dwelt bodily.” “Blessed are you among women,” truly divine Debir, in which the God-bearing initiators of the holy Church, having the oracle of divine revelations, foretold what was to come. “Blessed are you among women,” spiritual Bethlehem, by adoption and by nature the most spiritual house of the Bread of life, both in fact and in name. For having dwelt in you as he knows how, and mingled without confusion with our lump, he leavened the whole of Adam into himself, that he might become living and heavenly bread. “Blessed are you among women,” you who surpass the legal and shadowy tabernacle, from whom the great Bezalel, Christ God, the grace, built for himself without hands a temple, his ensouled flesh, by the master-building of the Spirit. And whatever we may say, beloved, we shall not complete the wedding hymn for her as she deserves unless we mystically gather for her the flowers from the meadows of Scripture and weave the crown of praises. For there is nowhere, nowhere at all, as one goes through the whole of God-inspired Scripture, where one would not see signs of her scattered in various ways; and if you diligently uncover them in the words for yourself, you will find more distinctly how great a glory she received from God. See how she is adorned with names of many meanings and expressly revealed in many places of Scripture: as when, for example, it calls her virgin, maiden, prophetess; then bridal chamber, house of God, holy temple, second [?tabernacle], holy table, altar, mercy seat, golden censer, Holy of Holies, cherubim of glory, golden [?jar], tablets of the covenant, priestly rod, sceptre of the kingdom, diadem of beauty, horn holding the oil of anointing, alabaster jar, lampstand, vapour, torch, wick, chariot, bush, rock, earth, paradise, land, field, spring, ewe-lamb, drop,

and all the other names that the renowned prophets of the Spirit give her prophetically, according to the mystical contemplation of symbols. For instance, a bush, as when Moses says: “I will cross over and see this great sight, why the bush is burning and is not consumed.” A rod, as when Isaiah says: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from the root.” She is called a root: “And there shall be the root of Jesse, and he who rises to rule the nations; in him the nations will hope.” Holy ground: “Moses, Moses, take the sandals off your feet, for the ground on which you stand is holy ground.” Desirable land: “And they despised the desirable land.” Land springing up [truth]: “Truth has sprung up from the earth.” Teman: “God will come from Teman.” Mountain: “And the Holy One from a shaded, thickly wooded mountain.” “A stone was cut from a mountain without hands.” “The mountain in which God was pleased to dwell.” Olive tree: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God.” Ark: “Arise, Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your holiness.” Throne: “I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, and the house was full of his glory.” Gate: “And the Lord said to me: This gate shall be shut; it shall not be opened, and no one shall pass through it, for the Lord God of Israel will enter and go out through it; and the gate shall be shut.” Zion: “The deliverer will come from Zion; he will turn away ungodliness from Jacob.” “The Lord has chosen Zion; he has preferred her as a dwelling for himself.” She is called Mother: “Mother Zion, a man will say, and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her.” And: “Why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” Litter: “King Solomon made himself a litter from the wood of Lebanon.” Bed: “Behold Solomon's bed; sixty mighty men surround it, of the mighty men of Israel.” Scroll: “And I looked, and behold, a hand stretched out to me, and in it the scroll of a book; and he unrolled it before me, and on it were written things on the front and on the back; and he said to me: Son of man, eat this scroll.” Book: “And these words shall be to you, says God, like the words of the sealed book, which, if they give it to a man who knows letters and say to him, Read this, he will say, I cannot read it, for it is sealed.” Volume: “And the Lord said to me: Take for yourself a large new volume and write in it with a man's pen, To make spoil of plunder swiftly; for it is at hand.” Tongs: “And one of the seraphim was sent to me, and in his hand he had a coal

which he had taken with the tongs from the altar, and he touched my mouth and said: Behold, this has touched your lips, and it will purge away your sins.” Virgin: “Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel.” Prophetess: “And I went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son, and the Lord said to me: Call his name, Spoil quickly, plunder swiftly; for before the child knows how to say father or mother, he will take the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria.” Queen: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in gold-woven raiment, adorned.” Beloved: “You are all fair, my beloved; all fair, and there is no blemish in you. Arise, come, my beloved, my bride; come from Lebanon; you shall come, and come from the beginning of faith. Your lips drip honeycomb, my bride; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the scent of your garments is like the scent of Lebanon.” Sister: “How beautiful your eyes have become, my sister, my bride.” Garden: “A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed.” Daughter: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father's house, and the king will desire your beauty.” And: “Many daughters have acquired wealth, many have done mighty things; but you surpass them and have excelled them all.” Betrothed: “The angel Gabriel was sent from God to a town of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man named Joseph, of the house and lineage of David; and the virgin's name was Mary.” Cloud: “Behold, the Lord sits on a light cloud and will come into Egypt, and the handmade idols of Egypt will be shaken.” Vision: “I saw a vision of fire, and its brightness round about, like the appearance of a bow when it is in the cloud on a day of rain; so was the brightness round about. This was the vision of the likeness of the glory of the Lord.” Amber: “And I saw as it were the look of amber, a vision of fire within it round about, from the appearance of the loins downward.” Day and night: “Day to day pours forth speech, and night to night proclaims knowledge.” Heaven: “From heaven the Lord looked down; he saw all the sons of men.” “The heaven of heaven is the Lord's.” East: “Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God, sing praises to the Lord who mounts upon the heaven of heaven toward the east.” West: “Make a way for the Lord who rides upon the west; the Lord is his name.” Sun: “In the sun he set his tabernacle, and he is like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber.” City: “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God.” “The streams of the river make glad the city of God; God is in her midst, and she will not be shaken.” Brick: “And you, son of man, take a brick and set it before your

face, and draw on it a city, [Jerusalem], and lay siege to it.” Place: “How awesome is this place!
