This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.” And: “And the spirit lifted me up, and I heard behind me the sound of a great earthquake: Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place.” And: “I will not give sleep to my eyes, nor slumber to my eyelids, nor rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob.” Fleece: “He will come down like rain upon a fleece, and like drops falling upon the earth.” Woman: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.” And: “God sent forth his Son, born of a woman, born under the law.” Blessed: “Blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfilment of what was spoken to her from the Lord.” And: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked.” Mary: “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favour with God”; and: “Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins. He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High; and the Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.” And Mary said to the angel: “How will this be, since I do not know a man?” And the angel said to her: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the Holy One to be born will be called the Son of God.” And Mary said: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Saviour.” Who would not admire her who was raised to such a height as to become the Mother of God — a thing truly most astonishing, both to see and to hear? Be persuaded by me, and let us run back to her who leads the feast, so that the discourse, having strayed a little, may return to where it set out. Come, then, let us take up the hymns of the day, and after speaking a little with those gathered here, let us give the course of the discourse a rest. Human nature, then, crushed by our forefather's fall, needed the one who had fashioned it to set it upright again; and with a silent voice it cried aloud to the Creator: “Why, Lord, do you stand far off?” And more audibly, through the prophets, it lamented and implored: “Where,” it said, “are your ancient mercies, Lord, which you swore to David in your truth?” What then did [?] do? He did not overlook it, he did not delay; he did not put off his promises for long. And what are these? “I will never leave you, nor will I forsake you.” This he also said afterwards to the disciples, as he ascended from earth to the heavens, from which he had never been parted: “I will not

"I will not leave you orphans; I am coming to you." This he clearly promised through the prophets even before his ineffable incarnation. Since this is so, and the time was now calling for the promise to be fulfilled, see what he does who works out our salvation [?] from our own lump of clay. He did not bring in an instrument from outside; he did not refashion a vessel from some other substance. From the same clay, and, as one might say, from the same dough, he drew off a portion [?] and built himself a precious temple, a compounding truly beyond all words. In it he himself, the first and only High Priest and King, performed by his dispensation the sacred rite of our reconciliation with his own Father. He who is beyond being took up our whole being, and took it up in its very substance, from the substance of man. So God remembered his own creatures, for all the nations are his creation. The Lord of the ages remembered his compassions that are from of old; he remembered the covenant he had made with men. He remembered, and having remembered he did not delay, but at once brought his benefaction. For he remembered David, and what he had once sworn to him, that he would raise up the Christ from his seed, in whom he rebuilt like a tent the fallen handiwork of our race. [?] a paradox upon a paradoxical wonder he brought in together [?]. The chaste Anna was weighed down by the heavy burden of childlessness, and her husband too was bitterly oppressed because they had no child. God then loosed the deprivation of both. Moved by their prayers, he gives the barren woman offspring, which prayer had sown beforehand, and to her husband fruit, which hope had made to sprout: an ever-blooming flower for those withered by the scorching heat of childlessness. She who before was barren becomes fruitful, a vine that had put forth no shoot now flourishing again. What could be more venerable than this childbearing? What more wondrous than to see the Mother of God [?] put forth as the fruit of purity from a newly sown womb, opened but not corrupted, a virgin sprouting from a barren and childless woman? Why did this happen? So that by the surpassing wonder of the daughter he might confirm the wonder of the mother who bore her. The daughter brought into nature, against nature, something never before known to human nature: a fatherless birth from a labor without pangs. By a power beyond nature she bore in her womb the very maker of nature. She became a mother while escaping what belongs to mothers, and the infant had no one on earth to call father, since he was conceived without the mediation of seed, and she who bore him gave birth without corruption intervening. The mother, though she had many examples of women who had gone before her in barrenness, won a verdict that prevails over them all. For if

and lived with the patriarchs as their wives, were rightly deemed worthy of a similar wonder, the loosing of the [?] bonds of barrenness; yes, they had been allotted to be foremothers of this holy-born child. But their kinship with the wonder of the divine dispensation was very far off and remote. Anna came later, at the due time, at the very end of the times, when he who was seeking the royal coin, I mean our image, was standing at the very doors. He sought it so that he might scour the dust in which it had long been hidden, cleansing it by the Spirit that perfects in God, and from there, out of his love for mankind, refashion human nature as in himself. What, then, is the dust in which our nobility had been hidden? Perhaps it is plain at once, even if we do not say it, that he who fashioned us searched the dust from which we were first formed and later re-formed, and found what he sought. What was that? The archetype of the image, which he who by nature cannot suffer saw buried under the passions. He searches the dust in Adam. And the dust in which the thing sought was found was earth of the same form as our body, having as its field the all-pure [?] virginal womb. For this is the field our ear of grain, the source of life, found, in which, without sowing and without tilling, it sprang up and grew beyond nature. This is the dust; this is the ear of grain; this is the field of earth in which we were refashioned in a new way, and through which our dust, reshaped, returned to its ancient dignity. You see how many mysteries Anna's childbirth contains: how by the surpassing wonder of her glorious childbearing she outshone the barren women before her, and with what a pregnancy the virgin girl, beloved of God, Mary herself, the all-blameless, was deemed worthy. What other woman has ever been admired for so many glories, and such glories? Since our weak speech cannot be lifted to so lofty a height of vision and can go no further, let us greet the Mother of joy once more and say a few words. For it is good to add the cry of joy to her: Hail, full of grace! Hail, glorified one! Hail, joy-bringing offering for the salvation of all! Hail, truly golden censer of spiritual spices, in which Christ, the spiritual incense compounded of divinity and humanity, showed in the fire of his divinity the fragrance of the ensouled and rational flesh united to him, without confusion and without division! Rejoice, tabernacle not made with hands but made by God, into which once, at the consummation of the ages, the only God and first High Priest entered, to perform within you, in hidden mystery, the sacred service for all! You are the second veil of the holy places, in which the mercy seat of the world and the most precious overshadowing of the Cherubim

and you covered within your womb, behind the veil, the very Only-begotten [?] himself, carrying him in your belly. You are the seven-branched and [?] lampstand of the seven gifts, flashing with the seven lamp-spouts of the Spirit; the unquenchable wick of the light that has enlightened all, which the oil of anointing [?] mystically feeds. Rejoice, altar on which Christ the Lamb, the living whole burnt offering, is mystically offered; divinely consecrated table of the sacred rite beyond understanding, on which Christ, the bread from heaven, the Lamb for all, is sacrificed as incense and as a living victim, giving life to those who partake! You are the treasure of all mystic worship, in which God is slain in the flesh and sanctifies all the saints, and, mystically coming to dwell among men, makes his home in them and is partaken of, and endures to be handled by the hands of sinners, to be brought to lips of clay and to rest in the dust of our flesh, mingled with it but not dissipated. O ineffable self-emptying! O goodness! That God has granted us these things, beyond nature and convention, through a woman [?] of our own kin; a woman whose beauty of soul [?] infinitely, countless times over, toward him, and drew Christ himself, the incomparable Beauty, to desire her beauty and to choose from her a second birth, and that without a father. So comely too was the condition of her body, and it reached such a degree of purity, that it contained the incorporeal and uncircumscribable majesty of the nature beyond being, through one of its three hypostases. This is Mary the Theotokos, the common refuge of all Christians; the first recall from our forebears' first fall; the return of our suffering race to freedom from suffering; the vision long ago sketched mystically in shadow at Moses' bush; the fleece of Gideon, which he [?] symbolically moistened in silence by drops from heaven, turning the event into a wonder and taking the rain, together with the sacrifice, as a sign; David's divinely embroidered purple, the flesh that was assumed, woven as it were into a purple robe for the God of David made flesh; the Cherubic throne, exceedingly great, fiery, lifted on high, bearing in her bosom the King, the Lord of Sabaoth; the lintel of the heavenly sanctuaries, where the Seraphim stood wrapped in their wings: with some they covered their faces, with some their feet, and with others they flew, crying aloud that fearful hymn, unable to bear the sight of the unbearable glory. She is the gate of heaven, through which the Master of heaven alone has passed, granting entry to no one after him or before him.

Rejoice over her, O heaven! For she imitated you, and without being cramped contained the Lord whom you cannot contain. Dance over her, O earth! For her pregnancy raised your station to heaven and made earthly beings heavenly. Clap your hands, O sea, at the wonder of the Virgin! For Christ, who submitted to being born of her, after taking a body sanctified the liquid substance of the waters by being baptized in them. Let all creation, then, rejoice and dance and clap [?] its hands. For today a maiden is born for us, from whom comes salvation, and through whom comes the redemption of the whole world, Christ Jesus, God and Word, who is and who was and who is to come, and who abides forever. In him [?] let us rest our discourse, now come into harbor from the great sea of words about the Virgin. To God, the Trinity, worshipped in the Father and in the Son himself with the Holy Spirit, let us offer one glory in three holinesses [?], honor and worship, now and always and to all the endless ages of ages. Amen.

On the [?] of our most holy Lady, the Theotokos. Today the joy of all has come, loosing the former curse. He who is everywhere has come, to fill all things with joy. And how has he come? Not with bodyguards, not bringing hosts of angels with him, not vaunting his approach, but quietly and calmly. He does this to escape the notice of the ruler of darkness, so that, having snared the serpent by the craft of wisdom and deceived the mind of the dragon, the Assyrian, who had enslaved under

himself all human nobility, he might seize the spoil. For his immeasurably great compassion toward us could not bear that so great a work should be lost: man, for whose sake he vaulted the heavens, made firm the earth, poured out the air, spread out the sea, and fashioned the whole visible creation. That is why God is from earth [?], God from heaven, God among men, God carried in the womb of a Virgin, he who is everywhere unseen [?]. From here human nature receives the first strains of joy and makes its beginning of deification. From here, shearing away the much-fancied wealth of sin [?], it is led as a bride to its Creator. From here our first formation receives a new re-formation, and the world puts off the oldness that came from sin. But "let the heaven rejoice from above, and let the clouds sprinkle righteousness; let the mountains drip sweetness, and the hills gladness," for God has had mercy on his people. For today the mystery hidden before the ages is made manifest, and all things are summed up in Christ. Today the sovereign power that created all things brings to completion the plan [?] it had predetermined in making all that exists, so that it might strike down the counsel devised against us from the beginning by the [?] ruler [?]. That is why angels dance, [?], and the whole world, renewed, returns to itself. What mind, what [tongue] can contain these things? Nor can speech express

[a] joyful [?], and the restoration of our race. So today there are good tidings of joy, messages of God's love for mankind, glad news of salvation for the whole world. From where have they come, and from whom, and to whom? From heaven, and from God, and to a virgin betrothed to a man. Who is the virgin? Who is the man? What are their names? Hers is Mary, his Joseph. Both were of the house of David. Who ministered these things, and where did he come from? The archangel Gabriel, sent from the Most High to minister the wonder. For it was fitting that the minister of the Most High should fly down from the heights to earth and arrange a mystery more paradoxical than any paradoxical event. What is this mystery? The Lord's condescension; the ineffable manifestation of his dispensation for us; the declaration and confirmation of the divine counsel and foreknowledge hidden from of old. But where did these things happen, and when, and why? In Nazareth, a city of Galilee, in the sixth month after John had been conceived, so that he might herald the One who was coming while he himself was still in the womb. So Gabriel flew down from the ethereal upper chambers to the earthly bridal chamber, arrived at Nazareth, approached the Virgin, and silently delivered the message of the ineffable dispensation. This is the mystery of God's reconciliation with men. This is what we celebrate today: God's union with men, the deification of what he assumed, the re-forming of our image, the change for the better, the [?] and ascent to heaven. Therefore all things rejoice with joy today, and the whole spiritual array of the powers above the world is eager for the divine reconciliation with us. For our restoration to God is dear to them, and so is our progress and ascent to a better state. Indeed they are full of sympathy and love for mankind, since they are sent forth to serve those who are to inherit salvation. So let all things exult today, and let nature leap for joy. For heaven is opened, and the earth invisibly receives the King of all. Nazareth, imitating Eden, embraces the planter of Eden. The Father of mercies betroths the lowliest estate of humanity to the only one [?] born of him. [?] the ineffable manifestation [?] for the divine reconciliation with us [?]

[And] Gabriel ministers to the mystery and calls out to the Virgin, "Hail!", so that the joy which the foremother lost, the daughter of Adam who sprang from David might recover through herself. Today the Father of glory, moved to pity for the human race, looks with a merciful eye on the nature corrupted in Adam. Today the giver of compassion opens the abyss of his all-good heart and channels mercy into nature, as abundant waters that cover the seas. For it was fitting that he from whom, through whom, and in whom all things hold together should exchange the condemnation of our ancient curse for mercy, should by his own glory glorify beyond all expectation the nature that had fallen into disgrace in Adam, and should by truth shake off the ruinous counsel of the father of lies, whose work was the first transgression, the [?] of Adam's formation

It was for this reason that David, the great among kings and the ancestor of God, sang beforehand: "Mercy and truth have met; righteousness and peace have kissed." What does he mean by saying this, if not perhaps the mercy of the Son toward us, by the good pleasure of the Father? In this mercy the giver of mercy had mercy on us and became like us, except only for the fall, so that the transgression might be undone, so that he might raise us who had fallen from our fall, and refashion what had stumbled without crushing it. And by truth he means the manifestation that took place for him among men not in mere appearance. For he did not assume our nature in some semblance, as one might say, but in very truth. With love for mankind, and at the same time in human fashion, he who is beyond being took being from the being of men. Having deified in himself the whole of what he assumed from us, he did not make the dispensation a phantom, and he confirmed the truth of the flesh, while his divinity remained unaltered by any change that would make it depart from itself. Since, then, according to the prophecy, "mercy and truth have met," it follows that "righteousness and peace have kissed." Righteousness is the verdict pronounced against the one who wronged the first-formed. When, and by whom? Today, and by the Most High Father. By this verdict he who by nature loves mankind judged it right that his only-begotten Son, appearing in the likeness of our

form, should condemn the adversary. Peace is what the choir of angels suddenly hymned with one voice at the birth in the flesh of the Son, the Prince of Peace, saying, "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will among men." Glory is that by which human nature was glorified by Christ, raised above the vaults of heaven and lifted above every principality and authority and power, as the great Apostle says. Peace is what he himself mediated, joining the heavenly to the earthly and granting the earth a strange new path of ascent to heaven. Good will is what the Father himself was well pleased with, sending his beloved Son to us the condemned, so that he might fulfill toward us the salvation the Father was pleased to work in him, since the Son is of one will with the Father. This is what we now celebrate. Today Gabriel too is entrusted with this command; he mediates between divinity and humanity, and is the first to announce to the Virgin the pledges of complete reconciliation. For the Father of mercies, pitying our race, already corrupted by the [?] of sin, remembered the works of his hands. Not bearing to see us perish utterly, he first entrusted to the hands of Moses the law in letters, written on tablets of stone. But since the written law made nothing perfect, he sent Spirit-bearing men, the seers, I mean the prophets, who pointed out all the straight paths of God. But when those to whom they were sent stopped up their senses and remained no less in the same condition [?], the Father [?] did not abandon his creature. From his all-good and all-blameless bosom he sent forth the Son, who shares his throne and is equal to him in might and honor [?], to us who are unworthy, "on whom the ends of the ages have come." He judged it better to work the salvation of those who had offended him than to abandon a creature so great, the noble achievement of his own workmanship. Then, having decreed that one of the foremost angels should minister to the mystery, he gave command, I think, with a nod of his own majesty, in words like these: "Come, I say, go, Gabriel, to Nazareth, a city of Galilee, where a young virgin lives, betrothed to a man named Joseph. The virgin's name is Mary." To Nazareth, he says. Why? So that the Almighty might pick the divinely graced beauty of virginity like a rose from a thorny land; and because of the

prophecy: "He shall be called a Nazarene." Who? He who was later proclaimed to Nathanael as Son of God and King of Israel. Indeed, it is Gabriel's custom to minister in the mysteries concerning God, as we learned in Daniel. "Go, then, to Nazareth, a city of Galilee, and when you arrive there, hasten to say this first to the Virgin: the good news of joy that Eve once lost [?]. And do not trouble her soul. For the message is one of joy, not of harm; the greeting is one of gladness, not of dejection." For what joy was there, or will there ever be, more gracious to the human race than to become a partaker of the divine nature, and through union with him to become one with him according to the principle of the one hypostasis [?]? And what is more wonderful than to see God's condescension reaching even to being carried in a woman's womb? O paradoxical events! God in a woman's body, he who has heaven for his throne and the earth for his footstool! God in the womb, he who is above the heavens and shares the throne of the Father's eternity! And what could be more paradoxical than this: to see God in human form without his departing from his own divinity, and to see human nature united to the one who fashioned it, so that the whole man, who first fell under sin, might be deified? What then did Gabriel do? When he heard these things and understood the plan, ratified by divine decree but surpassing his own power, he stood on the border between fear and [?]. He had no clear ground for confidence at once, and he did not think it safe to object. Yet, obeying the divine command, he flew down to the Virgin, reached Nazareth, and stood at her little room. Then he grew thoughtful, and, as if perplexed within himself, was torn between his reasonings, saying to himself, I think, something like this: "Where shall I begin to carry out God's will? Shall I rush into the chamber? But I will alarm the virgin's soul. Shall I come in more slowly? But the girl will think I have stolen in. Shall I knock at the door? And how? For it is not proper for angels [?]" [?] the principle of the hypostasis [?] first [?]

[?] this, nor can anything that holds or is held keep out what is bodiless. Shall I open the gate first? But I can be inside even while it is shut. Shall I call her by name? But I would alarm the maiden. So this is what I will do: I will direct my course by the will of the one who sent me, for his aim is to save. And his will, though it is somewhat [strange?], is full of compassion, a token of reconciliation. How then shall I approach the Virgin? What shall I tell her first? The good news of joy, or the indwelling of my Lord? The coming of the Spirit, or the overshadowing of the Most High? So I will greet the Virgin, make the wonder known, draw near, salute her, and softly say, "Hail." A greeting is a fine way to begin speaking freely. Let "Hail" serve me as I speak with her. The word "Hail" alone will cause the girl no fear, and it will also settle the state of her soul in advance. So I will begin with joy, and announce the tidings of joy to her first. For it is fitting to greet the queen this way, with good news of joy. The manner brings joy, the moment is glad, the command is one of delight, the will is one of salvation, and this is the prelude to a joy beyond understanding. When the archangel had settled these things within himself, he came to the bridal chamber. Reaching the room where the Virgin lived, he quietly approached the door, and once inside he spoke to her in a gentle voice: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you." He who was before you is with you today, and shortly will come from you: the first eternally, the second in time. Oh, his boundless love for humankind! Oh, his goodness! The archangel was not content with the message of joy until he had also proclaimed the very author of joy, conceived by the Virgin. For "The Lord is with you" plainly declares that the King himself is present, wholly taking a body in her without departing from his own glory. "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you." Hail, instrument of joy, through whom the sentence of the curse was undone and the decree of joy brought in instead. Hail, truly blessed one; hail, you who are made radiant; hail, adorned [palace?] of the divine [?]

palace of glory. Hail, sacred palace of the King. Hail, bridal chamber in which Christ took humanity as his bride. Hail, you who were chosen by God before you were born. Hail, God's means of reconciliation with humankind. Hail, treasury of undefiled life. Hail, heaven, the dwelling above the heavens of the Sun of glory. Hail, spacious place of God, who can be contained nowhere yet is contained in you alone. Hail, holy virgin earth, from which the new Adam came to be by an ineffable divine fashioning, so that he might save the old one. Hail, holy leaven made perfect by God, by which the whole lump of the human race was leavened; made into bread from the one body of Christ, this wondrous mixture came together into one. "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you": he who said, "Let there be light; let there be a firmament," and all the other works of his creative majesty in order. Hail, mother of a joy beyond understanding. Hail, new ark of glory, in which the Spirit of God has come to rest [?]. You are the ark in which is the sanctuary of the new glory. He who is holy by nature, in the [?] workshop of nature, wondrously joined it to himself through the incarnation. He did not change what he was, for he is unchangeable, but he took on what he was not, for he became man. Hail, golden jar holding the manna that sweetens, which also brought forth honey from the rock for ungrateful Israel. Hail, tongs [?] of the mystical coal. Hail, spiritual mirror of [?] prophetic foreknowledge, through which the renowned interpreters of the Spirit mystically [beheld?] the [?] almighty [?] of God toward us. Hail, far-seeing lens, through which those who were shadowed in the joyless darkness of [?] received the Sun of righteousness rising from above with glory, and were mightily illumined. Hail, the [crowning glory?] of all the prophets and patriarchs, and the most truthful proclamation of God's unsearchable foreknowledge. [Note: read "unsearchable."] [?] "The sanctuary of the new glory [joined] to himself" [?] foreknowledge [?]

"Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb." And rightly blessed. For God [made?] you his tabernacle when you carried in your womb, beyond understanding, the man Christ Jesus, overflowing with the Father's glory, who is also God, complete in the natures from which and in which he exists. "Blessed are you among women," for in the inviolate storehouse of your virginity you held, without any constraint, the heavenly treasure "in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." You are truly blessed, "whose womb is a heap from the threshing floor": without seed and without tilling you brought to ripeness the fruit of blessing, Christ, the ear of incorruption. He is an abundant harvest, ten thousandfold, bringing thousands of the righteous [?] to the husbandman of our salvation. You are truly blessed, the only mother of all mothers prepared to be mother of your Creator, and [?] mothers. For your unique virginity was not destroyed by a mother's pangs, since your virgin shoot kept the seals of your purity intact. You are truly blessed, for you alone conceived without a man the one who stretched out the heavens and [?] the earth of your virginity in a wondrous way. "Blessed are you among women," for you alone inherited the blessing that God promised to the nations through Abraham. You are truly blessed, for you alone became mother of the blessed child Jesus Christ our Savior, to whom the nations cry, "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord," and, "Blessed be his name forever, and the whole earth shall be filled with his glory. So be it, so be it." "Blessed are you among women," whom "generations call blessed," whom kings glorify, whom the powers worship; "whose face [the rich] among the people entreat; and virgins following after her" and going before her "are brought together into the temple of the King." "Blessed are you among women," whom Isaiah, seeing with prophetic eyes, named "prophetess" and "virgin," and also "brick" and "place" and

"vision" and "roll of a book," and openly called her "sanctified" [?]. You are truly blessed, whom Ezekiel foretold as the East, and as a gate that is shut, which God alone passes through and which is shut again. You alone are truly blessed, whom Daniel, the man of desires, saw as "a great mountain," and the wondrous Habakkuk as "a shaded mountain"; whom your forefather and king sang of prophetically as "the mountain of God, a fat mountain, a curdled mountain, the mountain in which God was pleased to dwell." "Blessed are you among women," whom Zechariah, who saw God most clearly, saw as "a golden lampstand" [with seven lamps and seven pipes] [?], that is, lit up by the seven gifts of the divine Spirit. You are truly blessed, the spiritual paradise of the living tree of salvation, holding within you the very planter of Eden, Christ, seen in figure in you. By ineffable power he goes forth like a river from your life-giving womb, and through the Gospel, in four heads, he waters the [face?] of the world. "Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb." This is the fruit by eating which the first-formed man vomited up that ancient meal by which he had swallowed the bait of deceit. This is the fruit from which flows a sweetness that [?] the bitterness of the tree, cleansing humanity [?]. He is the one who pooled springs of drinkable water in the desert for Israel in its wanderings, who sweetened Marah, and who rained down bread, a strange food that needed no ploughing. Blessed is the fruit, who through Elisha made the barren, bitter waters drinkable and fruitful by pouring in [salt?]. Blessed is the fruit, who blossomed forth from the undefiled shoot of a virgin womb like a cluster of grapes ripened [?] beyond nature. Blessed is the fruit from which gush springs "of water leaping up to eternal life" [?]. [?] the garden overflowing. [?] "A garden enclosed is my sister" [?] "all these words," as in "the words of the book" [?] "words" in place of "vision" [?]. (67) [?] "roll of a book": Isaiah, "a great new roll" [?]

[On the Blessed Mary] [?] eternal." This is the fruit from which the living bread, the Lord's body, is offered, and the cup of immortality is shown to be a saving drink. Blessed is the fruit that every tongue "of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth" hallows with the threefold "Holy" of the Godhead sanctified in Trinity. Each tongue includes him in the identity of the essence, but marks him off as a person by the distinct property of the hypostases that share one origin. "Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb."

"But she," it says, "was greatly troubled at the saying, and considered in herself what sort of greeting this might be." She was troubled, it says. Her mind was not struck by any unbelief, far from it! It was rather out of reverence at the strangeness of the address, since she supposed that what had appeared was perhaps an omen. Nor did she suffer what Zechariah suffered earlier, when he disbelieved in the sanctuary. For that he received a penalty that passed from the organs of generation to the organs of speech, and he exchanged childlessness for speechlessness. But she was pure of every blemish and free of any intercourse or familiarity with a man, and she had trained her mind to stay fixed in unwavering contemplation of heavenly things. So she received the trouble that the greeting stirred in her soul. Being unused to speaking boldly, she would naturally hesitate at first. But she weighed what was said with steady reasoning first, so as not to lend her ear to the speaker casually, as one might say, or carelessly. That is why the evangelist very wisely [?] [?] "With reverence at the strangeness of the address" [?]. "With the threefold [Holy] of the Godhead sanctified in Trinity": the threefold [repetition] introduced into the hymn [?] holiness, as we explain there [?] Andrew.

[indicated] this when he said, "But she considered." She tested what she was considering, as it were, by the judgment of a pure mind, so as not to accept what was said without discernment. "Saying, what sort of greeting this might be." She was well-born and a daughter of [David?], so it was natural that she should not be unacquainted with the divine narratives of the Scriptures. Her mind would at once turn to the fall of the [first mother?], as she recalled the slip that came from deception and all the other such things recorded in the ancient writings. So the evangelist did not write that she was [?] [?]. Rather, to show how much shrewdness she had, he set down how steady and firm her judgment was, as if unwavering. For once the judgment of what is good has been tested by examining the reasoning [?], one must not [hastily?] assent to the address. Yet she was eager to [hide?] the trouble in her soul, and she uttered no word. By her bearing, as she hesitated a little, she showed the state of her soul, offering the steadiness of her character in place of speech. "Saying, what sort of greeting this might be": Am I to be the only woman to make nature new? Am I alone to be able to conceive without having come together with a man? "What sort of greeting this might be": Who is it that [brings] this promise, and from where has he come in and brought it? Shall I take the speaker for a man? But he appears bodiless. Shall I think him an angel? But he speaks like a man. I do not know what I am seeing, and I am at a loss over what is being said. What then did Gabriel do? As soon as he perceived the girl's trouble, he gave no thought to anything else but at once let his voice ring out and said, "Do not fear, Mary, for you have found favor with God." First he removed her fear, and then [he encouraged her] to take courage, saying, "Do not fear, for you have found favor with God": the favor that Eve lost. By saying "favor" he resolved the ambiguity, and what had seemed until then [?]. By adding "You have found favor with God," he persuasively drove away the Virgin's fear. "Do not fear, Mary." My manner is not deceitful. I have not come to [deceive?] you. I am not the hissing serpent again [?]; I do not speak to you from the earth. I have come from the heights, bringing you good news, and not [?] news but the gospel of joy. "[Do not fear,] Mary." This greeting is not one of mockery, nor is the [message] one of grief: "The Lord is with you," the [giver] of joy and Savior of the whole world. With you [?] not separated from the Father's bosom, yet conceived in your womb. I called you "full of grace" so that

I might make known the joy of the mystery in you. I called you "full of grace" because you have received all joy itself in your womb, and you are a robe truly graced with the splendor of divine gifts. I addressed you with "The Lord is with you" to make known the authority of the one who has gone ahead into you. For he is "Lord and God, the Mighty One, the Prince of Peace, and the Father of the age to come," and he is your Son, O Virgin, and the Savior of all. "The Lord is with you": grace and truth are with you. He is Lord of the law, father of grace, and source of truth. "Do not fear, Mary; the Lord is with you": the ruler of every [?], the Son of the Father of lights, begotten from him without beginning and made flesh from you in time. Above, he is wholly with the Father, in his bosom; below, he is wholly with you, in your womb. He is with you and in you. For he came ahead, leapt in, and entered your womb, and he who by nature cannot be contained has come to be contained in you. "Do not fear, Mary, for you have found favor with God": favor that Sarah did not receive, that Rebecca did not know, and that Rachel did not come to know. "You have found favor" of which the renowned Hannah was not counted worthy, nor Peninnah, her rival. For they became mothers after being childless, casting off barrenness along with virginity [?]. But you will be a mother and still keep your virginity, which cannot be taken from you. "So do not fear, for you have found favor with God": favor such as no one from the beginning of time has found as you have. And what favor from God could be as exceptional

"You have found favor, then, with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus." Oh, the wonder! First he resolved the problem that perplexed her, and only then did he add his explanation. And see how much he does in a few words. He calms her fear, announces the favor, explains the conception, foretells the birth, and records the name of the one to be born. Yet his speech does not stop there. To show also how great the authority of the child she would conceive was, he at once added: "He will be great and will be called Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign [?]

over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end." Do you see how he took away the Virgin's fear? Do you see how far he emboldened her soul? By saying "Son of the Most High" and naming David as the father of the one to be born, he at once gave wings to her whole mind, as what follows shows. And see the Virgin's understanding. When she learned these things and recognized that the divine will, supreme in power, could not be changed, "she said to the angel, How shall this be for me, since I do not know a man?" You promise me strange things, she says; you announce things that go beyond nature. I have no experience of marriage, for I am betrothed but not wed. I know Joseph only as my betrothed, not as my husband. The one betrothed to me lives in the same house but does not share my bed. My womb is unsown, though not [unfit] for ploughing [?]. "How shall this be for me, since I do not know a man?" Will nature show me alone to be a mother without marriage? Am I alone to bring in a birth strange to nature, contrary to nature? No marriage has taken place; I have had no experience of a man. For I have not known Joseph [?]; no man has been known to me. "So how shall this be for me?" Gabriel answers swiftly. He refines the coarseness of her [thinking] by the loftiness of his reply, and says: Why do you say such things, O [?]? Why do you raise such words? I have come from heaven [to announce] to you the new manner of this conception. I do not speak to you from the earth: I said, "The Lord is with you," and do you still puzzle, "How shall this be for me?" I [?] [?] "I am betrothed, but not wed." [?]

[On the Blessed Mary] [?] has risen above. And if [she] is wholly lacking in what is natural, [let her accept] at least the supernatural word, which prevails over what is natural. So the passion that always attends conception did not attend this conception, nor did it follow upon the [?] birth. "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you." Here the mystery of the Trinity is revealed. By saying "Holy Spirit" he means none other than the Paraclete; by "power of the Most High" he clearly describes the [Son]; and with the word "Most High" the person of the Father is brought in as well. "Will overshadow you" seems to me to express what, I think, Habakkuk saw earlier with prophetic eyes when he called the Virgin "a shaded mountain." He was all but describing the power of the Spirit that overshadowed her. That power wrought in her an ineffable pitching of a tent through the incarnation, by which [he built] without hands the temple of his body in the Virgin's womb, which was [wholly free?] of passions and pure of every material passion [?], as is clear from what follows. For he says, "Therefore the holy one to be born will also be called Son of God." For the child who is before all ages, fashioned beyond understanding from the Holy Spirit through the holy [Father?], will rightly be holy and will be called Son of the Most High, since he has appeared as the coeternal Word of the Most High. So it has been shown clearly to the Virgin [what] it is that is conceived in her and from her, where it comes from, and what kind of thing it is, and that what will be born is the Son of God. Then, to make the power of his word more vivid and [more convincing?] to her, he brings in Elizabeth's conception, as if to say: He who was able to show a womb fruitful in old age beyond all hope [will also make] plain a virgin bearing a child beyond all reason. Therefore he adds, "For with God no word will be impossible." When the Virgin heard these things, or rather, when her mind was illumined by the light of the one dwelling in her, she gladly assented to the delight of the promise and wholly [?]

…came to pass. And just as Scripture describes David, she appeared gracious in soul, with beauty of eyes, for she was delighted at the wonder and welcomed the greeting. Indeed, what was spoken was full of joy beyond words. Very readily and quite clearly Gabriel persuaded the Virgin to welcome the wonder by adding: “For with God no word will be impossible.” What then does the Gospel say? “And Mary said: Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.” Do you see her understanding? Do you see how far her modest composure went? Once she had learned and grasped the conception of the child and the manner of his birth, whose son he would be and of whom, what he would be called, whose throne he would inherit and over whom he would reign, and in short that the one to be born would not be outside kingship, she uttered a word of joy in return: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.” She was plainly saying this: Here I am, ready, and nothing stands in the way. My soul is eager; my womb is fit for it, for it is untouched, kept for the Creator alone. “Behold the handmaid of the Lord”: willing to obey, eager to serve, ready to receive. “Let it be to me according to your word.” For since, she says, you have announced everything well, as far as that was possible, the whole thing now being accomplished is filled with joy and the highest glory. “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.” Bravo for the dispensation beyond words! Bravo for the grace! Highest praise for the counsel and foreknowledge that have no beginning! Truly the Holy Spirit dwelt in the Virgin, and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, according to the predetermined counsel and foreknowledge of God. [Note:] Perhaps “eager” (otrynēs).

[?] being contained. And the one proclaimed the one coming after [?], borne in the womb of a Virgin for the salvation of humankind; the other, our [nature?] [?]

[?] of our first parents he destroyed. And having raised him up, “he seated him with himself in the heavenly places, far above every rule and authority and power, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come.” To him be glory and might, honor and worship, together with the Father who is without beginning and the all-holy and life-giving Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

On the Circumcision of our Lord Jesus Christ, and on Saint Basil.

It is good and pleasing to glorify everything that our Savior Christ did for us as God and man together, for all of it is full of wonder and amazement. And how could it not be? God mingles with human beings and makes himself known; he submits in everything as a man, carries out the commands of the law and promises to fulfill them, so that in return he might give what is his own, full of grace and truth. What the present discourse sets before us to marvel at is this: the next stage after Christ's birth, a birth without the pains of labor, namely the circumcision of his flesh on the eighth day. For this too is full of wonders, so let it also be glorified. And how could it not hold the very greatest wonder, not only because it fulfills the law, but also because it brings salvation to me? God in a name! He who has no measure and admits no comparison, who cannot be searched out and has no name, having become what I am, is once again plainly made known through a name. He is not only called Son by his most proper name (just as the Father is called Father because he begot, and the Spirit is called Spirit because he proceeds, since the three, in whom the Godhead is, are one God). He is also named Son as the one truly believed to be the Son of a Virgin; and from this he appears entirely approachable and gentle. And I, the runaway, finding the door of salvation opened, approach the Master and Creator with confidence. Luke recounts this in the words of the Gospel, saying: “And it came to pass, when the angels had gone away from them into heaven, the shepherds said to one another: Let us go over to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us. And they came in haste” [Note on “promising to fulfill”:] This was the first [?] of the Jewish [?]

“and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in the manger. And when they saw it, they made known the saying that had been told them about this child. And all who heard it marveled at what the shepherds told them. But Mary kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart. And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, just as it had been told them. And when eight days were completed for his circumcision, he was named Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.” Great is Luke, and he expounds great mysteries to us. The Gospel he wrote is worthy of Paul, who points to it even with pride when he says, “According to my gospel.” For if we were not enriched with this new Gospel, how would we have been taught how the Virgin received the good news, how John was born, how the Savior was enrolled in the census, how he was born in a cave, how shepherds received the good news, and how the angels said, “Glory in the highest, and on earth peace”? The census under Augustus was a sign of that peace. And how would we know how Simeon proclaimed the good news and Anna gave thanks? And we learn about Joseph, the betrothed of Mary, because of the closeness of their kinship, since both descended from two brothers, [?] and Panther; from them came Barpanther [?], the father of Joachim, from whom came the Mother of God. For from Melchi in turn Heli is born, by the wife of Matthan, [who married?] Melchi after she was widowed. She already had a son, Jacob, from whom came Joseph the betrothed. Joseph was by nature the son of [Jacob?], but by law the son of Heli. For when Heli died childless, his brother on his mother's side [Jacob?] raised up offspring by Heli's wife, as the law required; [Luke?] traces the line from there back to Adam [?]. And he speaks of the timelessness of his birth, which is from God: “son of God.” There are also very many other things concerning the passion:

the things about Herod and Pilate and the two thieves, and further things that the other evangelists passed over in silence. And what does he mean by saying, “the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb”? He explains it himself, presenting the angel as saying to Mary: “You will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called Son of the Most High.” Matthew too affirms this very thing, confirming it through the angelic dream in the account of Joseph's disbelief. He writes: “For when his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. And Joseph her husband, being righteous and not wishing to expose her to disgrace, resolved to divorce her quietly. But as he was considering this, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying: Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife, for what is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.” And he goes on: “All this took place to fulfill what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet,” that is, Isaiah, “saying: Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Jesus, which translated means, God with us.” Do you see how the evangelist's words and the prophet's correspond? For “God with us,” when translated, is the salvation of the people: the Master gladly dwelling with his servants. The name Jesus is in harmony with the angel's word. For “Jesus” is interpreted [as “Savior”?], since in his dispensation he compassionately did everything for our salvation. This is what the present season grants, and what the power of the day [brings about?]: it makes grace dawn on me in addition to grace, joins it to knowledge, and flashes forth with its splendor an illumination that calls for thanksgiving. That he was born I have already celebrated; I know the one born through things beyond words, and I know that she who bore him did so without seed. But must I approach the one who was born? I fear and shrink from coming familiarly to one who came forth in a way no one can search out. I am still at a loss; like a wanderer who regards his master as fearsome because he has run away, I hide myself. How then shall I be freed from such fear? The working of the day will show it, depicting for me the one who calls me by a name fitted to me. And what is that name? Jesus, which is interpreted as salvation, just as Emmanuel means “God with us.” It signifies God's reconciliation and closeness with human beings, as Jesus is called Savior. The shepherds too received this good news first. And they would not have come to the infant had they not first been won over by the name, and so, taking courage in one like themselves,

ran to him boldly. For what does the angel say to them? “Do not be afraid.” And what was the fear? As soon as the angel appeared to them, “the glory of God shone around them, and they were greatly afraid.” So to encourage them he adds “do not fear,” and he dispels their fear by the name of the one who was born. “For behold,” he says, “I bring you good news of great joy, which will be for all the people: for today in the city of David a Savior has been born to you, who is Christ the Lord.” What are you saying, angel? Is such power contained in the name Jesus? Yes, he says. For “Jesus” is interpreted as “Savior,” “who is Christ the Lord”: God and man, the same one both sovereign and compassionate. That is why I urged the shepherds to take courage, and by commanding Joseph that he be named on the eighth day, I made him appear approachable to all people. [?] I was commanded by the one being born to draw them on, as it were, with words that lead them [?]. For Joseph would not have accompanied the infant's mother without fear and with affection had I not commanded him to care for her as a husband for his wife. In the same way I made the shepherds [note: perhaps “I am confident that the shepherds”] run to the Master as to a benefactor and Lord, and I gave assurance that, fulfilling these rites, the one born would by God's good pleasure be named Jesus at the circumcision on the eighth day. So, taking courage in one who shares your nature, you may dare to run to him. And recognizing how greatly he has condescended to you, glorify the grace of this day. What does the eighth-day circumcision mean, and what else does it signify? Let us indeed make it known. The eighth completes the seventh and begins what is to come. The seventh brings the infant to completion, the eighth perfects it, and through the name it is counted among the perfect. The eighth is the beginning of growing up, and the infant, completed over a period of sevens, will be counted among children through learning. The eighth changes everything that belongs to infancy, both the teeth and [?], and it strengthens eating, speech and understanding. The seventh brings growth, but the eighth perfection. Circumcision, again, was introduced [Note:] Perhaps “I am confident.”

together with the earlier naming, and was given to the infant on the eighth day. And not without purpose. For since from Terah, the father of Abraham, human nature was going to be corrupted, a people had to be set apart for the Creator from Abraham onward by a seal, until his coming, which humanity was bound to need for its renewal. Circumcision casts off what is superfluous in the flesh and gives the seal of the eighth day, which points to the things to come. Circumcision shows that the coming of Christ sets it aside and will give rebirth through the Spirit. The seal of circumcision was given because of idolatry, to mark off the people of God, and with the overthrow of the madness for idols it has ceased again. The old things are a symbol of the new. For Christ is the eighth lawgiver from Adam. Adam himself was the first to receive a law; Noah was second; Abraham third; Moses fourth; David, in the hymns of praise concerning Kings [?] and Tabernacles, was the fifth lawgiver. Ezra, after the captivity in Babylon, who repeated the law and handed down certain customs, appears as the sixth; John the Baptist, preaching a baptism of repentance to the people and cleansing with water, the seventh lawgiver. Jesus Christ is the eighth. Concerning this great lawgiver Moses says: “The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers; you shall listen to him. And every soul that does not listen to that prophet will be utterly destroyed.” Since he alone is able, he says, also to fulfill what was laid down as law through me, he will be filled with abundant spirit when he is anointed, and he will give laws as Lord and Creator, even though he comes from among you, laws both divine and [?] … [?] circumcision had no other benefit than this alone: that by this sign they were recognizable and separated from the other nations. [?]

[?] the words match the worth of the one being praised. And now that our discourse has delighted for a little in the feast, let us pay what we owe to the feasts of both and bring the course of our discourse to an end, as God by his goodness strengthens us in all things, offering [?] in these words. Man of God and faithful servant, steward of the mysteries of God, “and man of the Spirit's desires”: for this is what Scripture calls those who have passed beyond the visible and are lofty and above it. I also call you a god to Pharaoh and to every Egyptian and hostile power, a pillar and foundation of the Church, the will [?] of the Lord, a light in the world holding forth the word of life, a support of faith and a dwelling place of the Spirit. [?]

Why should I list all the titles that virtue has given you, each one claiming and bringing in another? But lead, prosper and reign, and shepherd us, you under whose wings everyone who comes finds rest, and whose company we thirst for more than those exhausted by thirst long for the purest spring, O divine and sacred head! You are the one engraved on the hands of the Lord, unmarried, owning nothing, without flesh and almost without blood; first in words after the Word, wise among philosophers, above the world among worldly people. The old things that some set down in the divine Scriptures are passed over in silence; the new things are proclaimed. And he is best for us in discourse who happens most of all to know his writings, carries them on his tongue and makes his hearers understand. For to those most serious about learning, one man has seemed to stand in place of all, and to him alone time grants second place after the apostles. But leaving aside everything in between, I shall mention only the end of Moses and of Basil. Each departed this life, but neither left behind any memorial of his own attachment to the flesh. For no tomb of Moses is to be found, and this man was not buried under any material wealth. When he passed from this life, everything by which human life is sustained passed with him. So no material memorial of the man was found in any wealth left behind that might bury his reputation for higher things, just as the history testifies in the case of Moses, saying: “No one has found his tomb to this day.” If, then, our discourse has shown the great Basil to be such a man, so that he is not far from the saints, since by his life he sets beside himself each of the great ones [?], the sequence of the feasts rightly brings the present festival around to him now. But through the gifts granted there [Note on “without flesh and almost without blood”:] [?] Scriptures [?] Louis [?]

to him, it would be fitting to bring them before his memory, so that the wonder is not diminished along with the meagerness of our discourse, and so that those who attempt to praise him do not lessen the glory each person now holds of him. It would be better to increase the wonder within ourselves in silence than to belittle the praise by speaking. For how, having said this much, shall we now call you blessed, father Basil? You prick and drive away error with the goad of your word. You wisely take flight with the bees, settle in the meadow of the divinely inspired Scriptures, and gather from there prophetic flowers and apostolic dew. You always alight on the symbols of the virtues and from them build a divine hive. You wisely worked the honey of the blameless faith in the Holy Spirit. You teach us to despise the wicked wasps and to fly to heaven itself. You cried out like David, “How sweet are your words to my throat, O Lord!” For you, faithful Basil, sharpening our longing, we have struck up this sweet song. We do not offer you anything of our own, for that would be presumptuous. Instead we have gathered this from those who praise you, and at this life-giving festival of the eight-day Circumcision we have assembled things fit for a hymn, celebrating them together with your memory. For it was on the eighth day, the day of the Circumcision, that you ended your life, having served God for [?] years and having guided the throne of your sacred see for eight full years. The great Gregory teaches us to consider this in his verses inscribed for you. Through him theology is sung to us and flashes forth, and it marks you out as a theologian, since you both breathed the one thing and looked to the one thing. One soul seemed to be in both of you, carrying two bodies. Together with him is Gregory of Nyssa, himself also an interpreter of divine things, who falls short neither of your glory nor of closeness to you by nature. With them is also Ephrem, who by the divine Spirit watered the hearts of the faithful with the hidden things of the divine oracles. He makes you known through a revelation and proclaims you to those who do not know you. For he urges that you appear to the Church of God [?] as one set forth like divine thoughts [?].

But you, Father Basil, now delight together with the divine praisers themselves in the tents of the patriarchs, in the mystagogies of apostles and prophets, in the crowns of martyrs, in the choirs of monks, and in the good delights of the divine hierarchs and of all the righteous. Remember us there, and gather all who share your dwelling to intercede with you. Implore the common Master always, and now too, for the salvation of all. Ask him to establish the emperor of the Christians in righteousness and piety, so that he may have God as the ally of his counsels: God, the King who has no successor, by whom he himself is ruled from above. May the emperor govern his officials and governors in piety as his subjects, with the army fighting at his side, and keep the rest of the people united in concord in the divine faith and at peace with one another. May he anoint high priests in theology, so that they may steer well the Church that God, and you, have wisely taught and that has been entrusted to them. May he keep the priests in reverence, so that, living lives pleasing to God, [?] the hymn [?] to him who has now received you and crowned you and made you illustrious to all the faithful people, [?] let us indeed weave it. He who, though [rich], became poor for our sake, came forth from the womb bearing flesh, being what he was [?]. He who sits on high with the Father is born in a cave and swaddled in a manger. He is hymned by angels and marveled at by shepherds. On this present eighth day he is circumcised and receives the name of Jesus. He offers the offerings of purification, is acknowledged by Symeon and Anna, and is escorted by the Magi. He flees to Egypt and shakes the idols that hands made in Egypt. He reaches the full stature of a man, is baptized by a servant, and drowns the sin of the world in the [water?]. He is made manifest to the world and hated by the Jews, among whom he also worked strange wonders. At last he is handed over and crucified, and then buried, so that he might take Hades captive and [proclaim?] the promise of the resurrection to those in Hades. He also rose on the third day and gave me the second eighth day to honor, the day of true rest, which leads to the coming eighth day of the world's perfect redemption. He then appears to the disciples as well, and while they watch he is taken up into the heavens, [bearing] my lowly [nature?]. And he is known as one Lord in two natures, worshipped together with the Father and the divine Spirit. He bears the two wills and [the two] operations, and so he can be grasped and cannot be grasped, can be depicted and cannot be circumscribed. He is portrayed for us in figures and images, and in them he is worshipped, as through the medium of flesh and spirit. He is depicted for his own theologians and for all the saints. He shares with us in all things alike, for through the veneration given here the glory is brought to the arch-

-etype, as we have been taught by you, most divine Father Basil, who wrote: "For the honor paid to the image passes over to the prototype." If we hold the orthodox faith in this way, we shall escape the fear of the nations. And the islands of the Church will receive redemption: they suffered disorder through pestilent men who removed the images, and they were endangered by the Hagarenes. For the islands bear the figure of the Church, as Isaiah says: "Be renewed toward God, O islands." For to Christ himself, our God, belong honor, glory and worship, with the all-good Father and the all-holy and life-giving Spirit, now and always, and to the endless ages of ages. Amen.

On the Transfiguration of Our Lord

All of you who, through the self-emptying of the Word, have had the veil of unreason taken away, whose minds have been [lifted] from the earth, and who have been taught to set your minds on things above: come now and trust me, for I am setting before you a spiritual feast of words. Let us go up together with the Word, who ascends today onto the lofty mountain of the transfiguration. Let us strip off the material and dark life, and put on the robe woven from above throughout, adorned on every side with the rays of the rational virtues. For once we are clothed in white in both life and word, and given wings by the Spirit through pure thoughts, Christ himself, the pure rite [?], the superessential Word of the Begetter, who came down from above for our sake and out of love for humankind became poor by taking our flesh, would wish us to make this ascent with him. This is clear from the fact that he takes with him the chosen ones among the apostles, as those already closer to him in intimacy, and leads them up the lofty mountain. To do what, or to teach what? To show the glory and splendor of his own divinity, flashing [?] beyond... [?]

[?] into which, a little earlier more mystically, and now more [plainly?] through his transfiguration, he brought into kinship the nature that had heard, "You are earth, and to earth you shall return." This, then, is what we celebrate today: the deification of nature, its [change] for the better, its rapture and ascent from what is natural to what is beyond nature. How and from where does such great and supernatural grace come forth to us? Clearly, because the divinity, which incomparably transcends all [being] and reason, [is united] to the human through the Word. Properly speaking, it makes that which is anointed to be, and to be called, the very thing that anoints, according to the unerring and indemonstrable tradition of the mystery, [without confusing] the unchanging difference, which is kept unchanged in the mystery because of the unconfused union, in which the superior prevails. Or, to put it more properly, the ineffable deification offers the truest proof of itself in this: the hypostatic oneness and identity of the things that came together, which we know, beyond [understanding?], came about from the supreme joining of the mystery itself. I mean, as far as it concerns us, the most pure [embodiment] and taking of being by the Word, [?] and for our sake, and his second birth, from a Virgin Mother and without a father. Hence, according to the truthful mystagogy of the theologians, the great gift comes forth to us as from an ever-flowing spring, through the boundlessly giving grace of [that] deification. The angels marvel at this; the archangels glorify this. The whole ordered company of the supramundane [minds] feasts on it and takes it as clear and most truthful evidence of the Word's love for humankind toward us. Unable to grasp the boundless and limitless sea of that love in contemplation, it makes the incomprehensibility of the divinity the starting point of a greater ascent [?]. We too now wish to hymn this, but we cannot do so worthily. For [a fitting manner?] of hymning it is out of reach even for the angels, who behold the first splendor and dance unceasingly around the divinity that is queen of all. How much more for the prisoners of the earth, as the divine Jeremiah says, and for those before whom the gloom of the wretched and lowly [?]...

...body that weighs us downward. Because of it we are often not even allowed to receive any image of the blessed and intelligible sights, since our minds are held by a prior attachment to visible things. And so even our desire for the ultimate object of desire is sluggish. Nevertheless, God also welcomes what is done according to one's ability. Even if we must necessarily fall short of what is worthy, because the mystery is inexpressible and [incomprehensible], we should not shrink from the undertaking, nor hesitate to honor in words, as far as we can, what surpasses words. For that would be neither reasonable nor holy. Indeed, the aim of this speech is to show that what is being praised is beyond speech. So speech, by showing its own weakness in comparison with what it honors, attains what it seeks. Though defeated, it would justly be crowned, having contended lawfully by the very means through which it conquered. But let us [return] to the matter at hand, or rather, let us eagerly go up the mountain. How long shall we linger at the foothills of the word, admiring the beauty that lies before the [summit]? We could go up with the others alongside the Word, be found worthy of greater things, and be illumined by the cloud. Our sight would then be dimmed, we would be carried out of the things we see and [?], and the surpassing light would initiate us into things beyond human nature, once we had first been cleansed of everything material. And beyond all this, we could also [hear] that blessed voice borne from above from the Father, which bears truthful witness to the divinity of the Only-begotten and [shows] us clearly that he is identical in essence with the one who begot him. So that this may happen, come, as far as possible, let us silently [contemplate], by the mystagogy of the Spirit, the things the many do not see. Only through the Spirit does the mind see what lies beyond the senses. With it, let us feast on the mystical contemplations of what took place at the transfiguration of the Lord. For, as I think, the purpose of the transfiguration also looks to this, and the mystery wants to be hymned by us in this way. It wants us to understand, through knowledge, the depth of what was done and said in it, and so to draw its grace upon ourselves more effectively by imitating the one who was transfigured. Then that grace can work this wondrous and strange mystery in us as well. What, then, does the Gospel [say]? For it is good, I think, to make the [beginning] for those lifted up by the word [?]...

[?] of the [feast?] or banquet, or whatever I ought to call it, since the greatness of the grace overwhelms my tongue and my mind, from this point. Matthew, then, presents the Lord saying to the disciples: "Truly I tell you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom. And after six days Jesus takes Peter and James and his brother John, and leads them up a high mountain by themselves, and he was transfigured before them. His face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as the light." Mark too speaks in the same way. For the most part he keeps close to Matthew in both words and thoughts, since he was inspired by the same Spirit from the beginning and shaped in mind by it. Even if he seems to differ a little in one of these respects or in both, this is no contradiction or conflict with Matthew or the others. The evangelists seem to disagree either because they describe [?] the events with a different turn of phrase (to sum up and reflect a little on these things), or because one or another of them, or several, hands on things that this or that evangelist left out. Yet they do not oppose one another in the least. For neither all of them together, one after another, nor any one of the four by himself, wrote down everything the Word did in the flesh in the ineffable economy, he who is called flesh and did not cease to be God. Yet the four have one aim, the truth, and through the part they express the whole in potency and in summary. This often happens because of the concord and harmony of the oracles of the Spirit with one another; like members in one body, they have a continuity that brings about an indissoluble fitting together and composition. Witness to the truth of what I am saying comes not only from what is found in all of them, or particularly in some of them. The [divine] John also bears witness, at the very end of his Gospel: "There are also many other things," he says, "that Jesus did; if every one of them were written down, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written." The same will be said of Luke, who recounts the grace of the transfiguration and says: "Now about eight days after these sayings, Jesus took Peter and James and John and went up on the mountain to pray." "About eight days after these sayings," he says. What are you doing, O initiate of the ineffable? Why do you say, "About eight days after these sayings"? And what would [you say] when Mark and Matthew speak together as if with one mouth, saying, "And after six days Jesus takes Peter and James and his brother John, and leads them up a high mountain by themselves, and he was transfigured before them"? "Yes,"

says the blessed Luke. "Nothing that I and they have said is [inconsistent with], or rather it is wholly akin to, anything at all in the other. What we and they say is truly in agreement and has the same force. They leave out the day on which the Word foretold to all the apostles together what he would accomplish before long. They also leave out the day on which the Word wondrously accomplished what had been foretold. So they plainly count the days between the two, the first and the last, or rather the one and the eighth, which come to six. If you add the two, fitting the beginning and the end to the middle, you will have what you are looking for beyond dispute. And you will see the agreement of our accounts with one another, flashing forth the unified beauty of the truth, brighter and purer than the sun." Now that [I have shown] you in words the evident seemliness and harmony of the Word, that is, the teaching of Luke, come: I will venture into the sanctuary and unveil the splendor of the mystical sights hidden in the Word. It outshines what appears to the eye, just as what is grasped by the mind is more hidden and more lasting than what appears. But first, dear initiates of the Word and fellow lovers of the beautiful, purify both your hearing and your minds by the Spirit, who purifies and illumines all things. Then the Word, who is akin to you, may speak with you as with his own, and through untaught mystagogies reveal to you the more perfect things. What do we say, then, brothers? What is the intelligible banquet and contemplation of words to which we invited you today, and on which we think it right to embark [with the help] of the Spirit? Those who are wise in these matters say that six is the only perfect number below ten, since it is composed and completed from its own parts. And Christ, "the power and wisdom of God," the supremely good Word, "the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father," created in six days everything visible, and also man, who is composed of an immaterial soul and the matter of the body. Six, too, are the kinds of love, which are clearly enumerated. Nothing good is higher than love or equal to it. In these kinds he takes to himself the love shown to those in need. For he weighs out mercy in return for mercy to the merciful, and bestows the reward as a great [portion] of the blessedness there. He says to those already found worthy to stand at his right hand: "Come, you who are blessed by my

Father; inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was a stranger and you welcomed me; I was naked and you clothed me; I was sick and you visited me; I was in prison and you came to me." So the kinds of love are this many, and of this sort, as the Truth itself clearly cries out in the Gospels. Love of God is strengthened through love of neighbor, and through it the one whose desire is genuinely directed toward God is shown worthy of the hoped-for blessedness. And "on these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets," as the Gospel puts it. Hence it is clear that love is the most comprehensive of all goods and the highest of all that holy Scripture reveals. There is no kind of virtue through which a human being is made kin to God, joined to him, and given the glory and kingdom above as an inheritance, that does not depend on love and is not embraced by it, held together and guarded by an ineffable principle. Therefore love alone, carried out perfectly through its six parts, constitutes the highest perfection and purity possible for human beings in practical philosophy. Its end, they say, is the good, which is God himself. After this, love also joins a person to God in a special way, kindling the fire of theology. But why have I said all this? I say it because someone may be about to be lifted up with the Word, like a disciple, onto the mountain of lofty contemplation, to see the inaccessible glory of that kingdom, and to be found worthy of his visible and intelligible theophany. When such a person hears Christ foretelling that his kingdom will come before long (for this is the transfiguration, in which the Unchangeable shone brighter than the sun in what is above us and in what is ours), he will feed Christ and give him drink as he hungers and thirsts for the salvation of all. Or, put another way, he will serve, through those in need, the one who has made his dwelling in all who received him through faith. He will welcome him as a stranger, clothe him when he is naked, and care for him when he is sick. He will not overlook him when he is shut up in prison, since he is strongly urged on by a longing to do good. And because of his praiseworthy insatiability for what is good, he will not stop at what is visible, nor limit his love for the Master, who loves humankind, to outward kindness. (I dare to say this because I look to the words, "Inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me.") He will go further inward than what is visible, take care of the passions of the soul, and devise a fitting cure. "He will make them dwell in a green pasture," rational flocks, well formed for piety, "and beside the waters of

rest" he will nourish them. Someone may have left his homeland and be living in a foreign land, having become a wanderer. Out of reverence for him who became a stranger for our sake, [he will respect that exile?] and gladly lead such a person by the hand to his own hearth, whatever it may be. He will take him out of the earthly and divided life and move him to the unified and heavenly festival of the saints, where the citizenship of Paul and of those who fear the Lord is found. And when he sees another stripped of his father's wealth, having put off the robe of incorruption that was his by choice, he will pity his nakedness and clothe him again by leading him into the godly and blessed life. And what of the one who is weak in faith and whose mind is still childish in discerning what ought to be done? Will he pass him by in silence? Not at all. He will very quickly call him back to the health he longs for and to his proper end. He will drive out the passions of unreason by the word of truth and restore the innate reason to its rightful rule. He will rightly subject temper and desire, the pair that makes up the passible part of the soul, to reason, give them wings toward their proper objects, and renew them by the Spirit. Besides this, there is the one shut up in the gloom of ignorance and prevented from seeing the light of unerring knowledge. He will providentially stand in that dark place, as if through an angel, that is, through the word that illumines the mind. He will break the bonds of ignorance and lead that person out into the light of the freedom and way of life that are in Christ. No longer will he be held by a yoke of slavery, nor kept from walking freely in mind toward the heavenly beauties. All these things, and others like them, he will display in two ways, in a fitting manner and measure, his soul lit up like a beacon by love. For since we are twofold, made of soul and body, care also takes two forms. All of us human beings need it, some more and some less, as long as our will is subject to change, and

…matter of itself brings disorder and unevenness, or else it falls prey to abuse and hardship from outside. That is why above all we must treat one another with love for humankind, so that in another way we benefit ourselves even more.
