For a kindness grows greater than itself in the one who receives it and returns more abundantly to the one who did it; and so in being benefited, benefiting comes back around. By this a human being plainly imitates God. Imitation brings kinship, kinship brings likeness, and likeness is the summit of all goods. Do you see how great is the fruit of love for humankind? In the same way, through the self-complete sixfold number of the commandments, a person thrusts aside all slavish fear and cleanses himself as far as possible from the evil burden of the passions. Made perfect in love, he will carry off the prize of virtue. Then, in the spirit of natural contemplation, he will gain unerring [?] knowledge of the things subject to time and nature. He will know that the world established in six days, material and visible, is a type of what transcends the senses, and through the visible he will rightly see the invisible, harmoniously transposing the beauties of what appears to the intelligible beauty full of light. In this way he will have creation leading his mind by the hand to its own cause. So through both, I mean action and contemplation, once he is perfect in both (a perfection shown by the sixfold number of the divine commandments, and indeed also of the days in which the visible world came into being), he will be able to understand purely what the mystery of the eighth day is. This mystery, as it seems to me, is hinted at in Luke's mystical teaching, and one of those given to contemplation, who have risen above the senses, might see it. And what is said [?] and of true knowledge. Having come outside the flesh and the world, as far as is possible here, they will be taught the forms of the future state from what they have experienced. But these things only prepare the way, for the more discerning, toward the glory and grace that will be revealed on the mountain. When they have gone up with Jesus and come within [?], then far more clearly and [?], through the garments of the Word, made white as [snow?] and shining like the light, they will be counted worthy of the mystical vision of what was spoken of before, now that the symbols have given way to the truth.

In spiritual contemplation, the garments of the Word would be the things by which he is covered and through which he is revealed, which is something of a paradox. According to one form of anagogical interpretation, as it seems to me, the garments are the things the Savior said and did in that life of his. [?] the undefiled and spotless one; the one shown to the world through the economy of the flesh, yet not comprehended; the one incomparably free of all [?], who became for us, in his very being [?], the cause and pattern of all purity and holiness. The one beyond being came into being [?] and was given being beyond being, and lived among us through the flesh. He shone out surpassingly on the mountain. He did not then become brighter or loftier than himself (far from it!), but was what he had been before, now truly beheld by those of the disciples who were being initiated and taught the loftier mysteries. So the words and deeds of which that life was made up, which also together reveal the boundless depth of the Word's economy toward us, might quite reasonably be taken as the Savior's garments. Or those things would be signified through them by [?] of the Spirit, both shining like light because of their complete purity and the highest [?]…

In another way, and not unworthily of the Spirit, I think, the garments of the Word might be understood as the magnificence and splendor of the things the Word himself put on [?] and brought into existence, and also as the holy Scriptures. Creation, concealing him undefiledly as its creator and cause, makes manifest in itself [?] the invisible and uncontainable one. Scripture, in which the Word mystically dwells and makes his home, shows him ineffably to those worthy of the Spirit. Both are [?] and made brilliant through the Spirit, and are shown in such purity to lovers of divine things and [?] contemplatives as no fuller on earth can whiten. "For the Spirit searches all things, [it says,] even the depths of God." So it is through the garments that the Word hidden within them [reveals] himself and sends out the light of his knowledge: to those, clearly, who like Peter, James and John have been perfected in the spirit. Of these, the one, as Peter, firmly set upon the rock, takes upon himself the foundation of the faith and the building up of the Church through the virtues. The others, as "sons of thunder," are entrusted by the Word with the mystical vision of lofty theology, having a solid and unshaken [footing?], the immovable rock. The one shows, I think, the depth of the faith, the others its breadth and height, which through the incomprehensibility of the mystery exceeds all infinity equally on every side. Such, then, are the Savior's garments, shining out in this way. But what of the face that is beyond…

[col. 949] On the Transfiguration [?]. …the unutterable beauty, highest and most precious of all things loved, which [?] becomes for those who see it the source of unceasing gladness, insofar as it seems to be grasped when it is revealed? But what is hidden and more divine and newest of all, what mind or word will see it or be able to express it? For if the garments are like this because of the radiance flooding out from within, what then must that be which the garments wrap and cover, since it lies beyond sight and knowledge? If it were to appear by itself, stripped of every covering — but why do I say this? Even through its holy robe alone, which he made from virgin blood and mystically wrapped about himself through the Spirit, as they saw it revealed, who could look upon it? There is nothing, nothing at all among the things seen in creation, that can contain the surpassing degree of its brilliance. For even though the good is withheld from none of all things, it is not contained whole, whatever it may be, but only as much and in the way that those who share in it are able to attain; and this through its supreme goodness, by illuminations of boundless generosity, as it travels to all things and is poured out upon them. Proof of what has been said would be that blessed and much-hymned experience which the apostles underwent on the mountain, when the unapproachable and timeless light transfigured its own flesh and made it brilliant, beyond all being, with the surpassing outpouring of its own light. They could not bear the ray of that spotless flesh, which gushed forth through it beyond nature from the divinity of the Word, united to the flesh in his hypostasis, and they fell on their faces. O the wonder! In the most perfect ecstasy of nature, overcome by heavy sleep and fear, their senses closed, every movement and perception of the mind wholly stilled in them, they were with God in that divine, more-than-luminous and invisible darkness. By not seeing at all they received true seeing; by undergoing without knowing, they gained knowledge by way of transcendence; and they were initiated into a wakefulness higher than all the mind's attention. And paradoxically, in this paradoxical event, wakefulness becomes sleep, or rather sleep becomes wakefulness, confirming by this absence of cognitive perceptions [?] the knowledge that lies beyond nature. O who would give me speech as great as I wish? Who can be lifted up worthily together with this mystery? What movement of the mind, merely by looking toward it, is not at once completely extinguished, yielding before the inexpressible wonder? David too, I think, the royal and prophetic instrument, foresaw this from afar in the spirit and cried out with [?] mouth to the God of all, saying: "Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in your name." And he foretold that they would rejoice. But what, of what kind and how great the mystery of the transfiguration will be, precisely,

for which Tabor and Hermon will surely rejoice, is ineffable and inconceivable, to be [honored?] with silence and [?] made known to the worthy through experience. Now that the discourse has reached this point, it seems good to me to examine the words of Peter and explain them, which, not knowing [?] what to say and possessed by the Spirit, he uttered out of overflowing joy. Peter was delighted and enchanted in his soul beyond nature by the manifestation of light and the vision of God that had taken place, and was wholly filled with God. He could not interpret the experience in words, yet he could not bear to let the grace drain away in silence. So the words he utters are not of folly or silliness, as some might suppose; rather he makes his words the offspring and shoots of that ineffable initiation and divine working. And what does he say? "Lord," he says, "it is good for us to be here." For what reason, Peter? "So that, freed from the troublesome harassment of people, and with soul and senses cleansed by separation from the crowds, who move and talk in whatever way they please, we may have here the unfailing enjoyment of your inexpressible manifestation, Master. What could be better than this? What more desirable or more lovely, to those at least who have sense? So then, 'If you wish, Lord, let us make three tents here, one for you, one for Moses and one for Elijah.' For it is good that the letter of the law, which has come to its end, signified by Moses, and the living law of nature, shown by the living prophet, should dwell here with you, the Word who became man and pitched his tent among men, the true rest, the Lord of life and death, to whom all the saints live, even if they have suffered natural death through the separation of the parts that make up the human compound; the King of all, who holds all together and causes all. So that they too, illuminated by the unapproachable outpouring of your light, may make you manifest to the world, the Word who dwelt and walked among them. Laying aside their former life, they will receive only yours: the grace that consists in your Spirit and the divine fire, according to the declaration of the gospel; lofty and immaterial, which neither ends nor grows old nor wastes away, but always, by the fervor of the spirit, advances and is lifted up toward what is greater and more divine, because grace is infinite." Let us also go within the cloud and consider what the cloud means, so that, having traced as far as we can the meaning hidden in the depths concerning those who appeared in the cloud and spoke with Jesus, we may not be far from the [?] signified through them. The cloud, then, according to our interpretation, is the luminous one from which the Father's voice also [came], [proclaiming] clearly who the one being transfigured is and whence he comes…

[?], the dove [that appeared] a little earlier at the Jordan [?]: the Holy Spirit, coming down from above in the form of a dove and remaining upon the very one who was being baptized and who, according to John's testimony, baptizes "in Spirit and fire"; in whom the Spirit has his abiding, if one may put it so, inseparably, according to the mutual indwelling of the hypostases in one another. We are led to understand these things about the cloud because we have the great Apostle as our teacher on this too. Writing to the Corinthians, he says: "I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea." By the cloud he signifies the Spirit, and by the sea the water, from which and through which comes the fountain of baptism, or rather the great and most beautiful gift of divine birth. For the Father cannot be mirrored in the Son, nor the Son in the Father, except in the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father but dwells and rests in the Son by essence, as consubstantial, sharing the same throne and the same honor. Here, then, as at the Jordan, the same mystery of the Trinity is revealed, held together and shown forth in the supremely united and wholly single nature of the Godhead that is beyond all beginning, through the same words. And I will add: through the same deeds as well, at least to one who contemplates divinely [?] and, under the guidance of the Spirit, has risen beyond all creation. This is why the chosen apostles, enveloped by the cloud and [?] deprived of the power of sight by the light of the Lord's face, when they were counted worthy to become eyewitnesses and witnesses of the transfiguration on the mountain, came to be outside the things they saw, and even outside themselves. So, through the manifestation of the Word, the overshadowing of the Spirit and the voice of the Begetter borne from above out of the cloud, they were taught by not-seeing [?] and unknowing the mystery of the One beyond being, who by way of transcendence lies beyond every affirmation and negation. Under this cloud Moses and Elijah appear; they were seen talking with Jesus, and they foretell his departure by way of the cross. Of these, as I have already said, the one signifies the written law and the other the natural law, so that the Word, who is read through both "in many parts and in many ways," to speak with the Apostle, may be known as the maker of the one and the fulfiller of the other; and that he may set himself as the blessed end for the one, while the other, already grown old and dissolved for rational beings under…

…[who] became subject to our senses for our sake, having received knowledge of the things mystically revealed, should outrage [?] the grace and show himself unworthy of the Spirit [?] … should consider [?], and should make himself [?] to the illumination of the Spirit, who lived among us in a new way, by divine and human law. For it was for us, for whose sake he also became man, that he lived as he did; and he brought into life the way of life that is above the world, [?] gift. Human life, having received this, has been shown [?] in the things of the spirit. [?] from sin [?] … and humans dance with angels, together singing hymns to God and saying: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will among men." You have, then, beloved, the account of the mystery, [?] … falling far short of what one might hope for, yet not falling short of what we are able to give. But the higher and more mystical account you would seek from the Word himself [?], who bore flesh for [?]…

…[when he] rises and raises the one put to death by sin, and works divinely in the spirit. "For there is a time," as Solomon and the truth would have it, "for every matter." Knowing this, then, O man, never prove yourself unworthy of grace, and do not through idleness in life suffer the loss of heavenly [?] things. But thrust aside every desire of the soul [for?] [?], shake off the [inclination?] toward material things, and become wholly [?] of the better and heavenly things. Accept the life in the spirit together with the Word, pure and blessed [?], whose work is deification and the enjoyment of ineffable [goods?]. So that in you too it may be shown, through [?] and through unerring contemplation, that the truth of the Trinity is revealed; and that through wisdom Wisdom may be known, [?] of virtue and contemplation; the One contemplated and worshiped in Trinity, the [end?] of virtue and contemplation…

[?] "[let the dead] bury their own dead," the Word commands. Plainly everything that decays and is dissolved is dead, and it makes dead those who cling to it. That is why the dead bury the dead: those who, through their attachment to things that decay, are deprived of true life, and receive as the wage for their disposition toward things that dissolve this very thing, to become dead and be called so. What could be more wretched than that? So strip yourself of everything that flows and passes away; or rather, of your own will thrust aside everything that is extinguished together with this life and this poor flesh, and follow the Word without turning back. For your sake he was emptied and took a form not his own, and he carries you wholly with all that is yours, so that he may consume in himself what is worse in you and free you completely from sin. Journey with Christ, who journeys through the world for your sake. Do not be left behind, and do not stop anywhere along the course with your mind held fast by something. Go up with him [to the mountain?]; transfer your soul and your life there. It is good for you to be with God, where the festival of the saints is, where the sound of those keeping the feast is most brilliant [?]. Above all, as you contend in the good contest, have both fear and longing: by the one you may be helped, so that you do not fall into conceit, priding yourself on the greatness and beauty of your virtues; by the other, being [?], you may be drawn upward, so that you do not, through some satiety, insult your longing and ascent toward what is truly beautiful, but may keep this divine and supra-cosmic love unflagging and spotless forever. For the object of love stretches out before you [?], without beginning, without end, infinite. May we be [counted worthy?] of him now, as the breeze grows ever stronger. And when we pass from this world, may we be [?] blended with the One we long for, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom be glory, honor and might to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

On Lazarus, Four Days Dead. Lazarus has gathered this present assembly, and he wishes to prepare a [banquet?] in honor of his return to life, worthy of those who love what is good and [?]. Or rather [?] … [the faith of Christ?] … [?] how what was done in him so marvelously [?]…
[?] … through the investigation that follows, as can be seen in what came before.

[?] … despising the shame, as [?] says. … [?] those who remained unmoved [?] by the great working of miracles: where would they ever be softened, seeing an equal wonder [?], a man four days dead returning to life? And [?]…

[?] …that a man already decaying should come forth from the tomb was no ordinary wonder, nor less than the others they had seen. But [?] the great deed did not shame them; it only gave matter for their envy. So by "glory" here he clearly means the glory that came to him through the cross, when he chose to undergo death for us. Before every age he had the Father's glory, as God and as the Son of God of one substance with him. Yet he also counts the blessed passion of his all-holy flesh as glory, since it became the salvation of the whole world. But let us come to the road that Christ, the true way of life, showed us when he said: "No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends." For he knew that once the miracle went forth, the Jews would stir up the crowds and were about to cause an uproar, Caiaphas would rage, and he himself would suffer death by the cross. That Lazarus was a friend, the facts show: "For Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus." And who is so blessed as to be loved by Christ, who is Love itself? It is no wonder if women too, made manly in mind, were loved by him who came to call all people to himself. So great was the abundance of his love toward them that the miracle done for their brother surpassed his other miracles in the magnificence of the deed. "When he heard that he was ill, he stayed two days in the place where he was." Why? He knew beforehand that Lazarus would certainly die. Wishing to remove the suspicions of those who were hunting him, he put off his departure for a while, so that Lazarus might breathe his last and be buried, and so that rushing off as soon as he heard the news to display the miracle might not be thought a kind of vulgarity. "Then after this he says to the disciples: Let us go into Judea again." Here is a boldness fitting for God, and a soul eager to choose suffering and to carry the thread of the divine plan through to its end. "The disciples say to him: Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?" These are words of faintheartedness, or rather of ignorance. They did not know what was being worked out. Otherwise they would not have been distressed, nor would they have used words that reveal the weakness and unmanliness of their minds. At the same time, since their faith was not yet firm, they were naturally afraid. So they thought it reasonable to say: "Just now the Jews were seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?" Jesus answered: "Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him."

This is a veiled reference to the hour of the passion, which was shortly to arrive. By "day" you should understand grace and truth. Whoever walks the road of the gospel is lit by them, and does not stumble on the stone over which the Jews stumbled, "because he sees the light of this world." The light of the world is Christ, who said, "I have come as light into the world," and, "I am the light of the world." You should also understand "light" as the preaching of the gospel, the rebirth through baptism, and a life lived in holiness, as in the saying: "Let your light shine before people." By "night" understand the blindness of the law. In that night, whoever walks the road of types and clings only to the shadow of the letter stumbles against Christ, the rock of offense, laid down for the one who is dim-sighted through unbelief. And how does he strike against it? He strikes against grace, by which the shadowy darkness was driven out and broken through when the letter was lit up by the radiance of the Spirit. By "day" you may perhaps also understand the brightness of the miracle, which like the sun lit up the unlit [?] and at once shone round the whole of Judea. For here, unlike his other miracles, he did not order them not to tell of it, since he had not done it in secret. And by "night" you should likewise understand the fog of the Jews, which blinded the eyes of their souls. They were sick with these two things, ignorance and blindness: "For they did not know," it says, "nor did they understand; they walk in darkness." They refused to see the light shining in the darkness, and even if nothing else moved them, they were not put to shame by the number of his signs. So they were rightly likened to night, and Christ rightly becomes a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense to those who refused to believe. "He said these things," it says, "and after this he says to them: Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep." This seems to have been said to the disciples somewhat obscurely [?], but what it meant is then made plain. That is why he goes on to give the reason for his journey to Lazarus: "But I am going to wake him." He does not say this to boast. He spoke so faintly that not even the disciples themselves understood the saying. He did not say, "I am going to bring him to life [?] and raise him from the dead," but, "to wake him," which for the moment was unlikely [?] to arouse suspicion. "So the disciples said: Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover," for they were expecting him to wake from sleep. "But Jesus had spoken of his death; they thought that he was speaking of rest in sleep." You see how his teaching avoids boasting, so that even those who questioned him could not grasp what was said, because of the [?] of the phrasing. That is why he did not even rebuke them [?] for not understanding what he was telling them. Instead, correcting their slowness [?] and drawing back the veil of obscurity, [?]

…then [?] Christ makes the matter plain, and "says to them openly: Lazarus has died." They had so misunderstood what was said, and all the more so because the answer they gave twisted his meaning. So the Lord, very fittingly and triumphing over the matter, at once adds: "Lazarus has died." It is as if he were saying: Learn from this disclosure what is about to happen, "for I am going to wake him." This too he says without boasting. He is not seeking honor, as one might put it, nor uttering words of weakness or ignorance. Instead he shows everything at once: wisdom, foreknowledge and power, which belonged to him by nature. For he foretold the outcome as though the things to come were already present. "Lazarus has died; and I rejoice for your sake that I was not there. But let us go to him." Do you see how restrained his speech is? And how, by revealing his purpose a little at a time, he heightens his eagerness to display the miracle? He did not pair it as he did with "he has fallen asleep," by saying here as well, "I am going to raise him." Instead he keeps silent about that and says: "I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe, that I was not there." For had I been present, death would perhaps not have prevailed, humanly speaking, that is. "But let us go to him." For what reason? So that you may believe that I can raise even the dead as Lord. "Lazarus has died." When he spoke obscurely of his having fallen asleep, he called him a friend, veiling his death under the name of friend. But when he says openly that he has died, he leaves out "friend," so that he might not be thought to be bound to him by emotion. For this was a display not only of the divine plan of salvation but also of sovereign authority. The plan granted the assumed nature the human things and whatever belongs to natural weakness. Authority displayed the divine things, and whatever of divine power [?] the assumed nature. "I rejoice, then," he says, "for your sake, so that you may believe, that I was not there." Do you see how everywhere he sows faith in them? He says this perhaps so that the death might not seem staged. That is: had he been there, he would have given death no room to overcome his friend; he would have driven off the illness or restored the sick man to health. "These things would have happened," he says, "had I been present." The words "I was not there, but let us go to him" seem in some way more human. For to outward appearance he was not present. A body, being three-dimensional, is by nature circumscribed and can pass from one place to another. That is its nature. Even though it was enriched with what is beyond nature through its union with the divine [?], it lost none of its natural properties [?]. But as the mind perceives it, what place is wholly without him?

[?] What place does not hold him? Or what place can contain him? "So I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe, that I was not there." What are you saying? You were not there, you who are present everywhere and fill all things with your divinity? You were not there? "Yes," he says, "I was there, though not according to [?the flesh], but according to the divine dignity of my glory." "But let us go to him." It is time to fulfill the laws of friendship. It is time to show the sovereignty of his power. It is time to bind death with a word, and with his voice to loose the grave-clothes of the dead man. "So Thomas, who was called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples: Let us also go, so that we may die with him." This is an eager saying, and it could point to two different states of mind. It could show ardent affection, since it urged the others to rush headlong to death with their teacher. Or it could show unmanly cowardice, as if he suspected some danger that was not yet present. But far be it from us to think that he sank so low in cowardice, he whose own unbelief tempered us like steel in the coals of faith. So let the words be credited to boldness, not cowardice. It is likely that he was roused and stirred with deep feeling, and wanted to suffer something worthy of his devotion to his teacher. "If we have received from him the grace of signs," he says, "and everything else by which we stand apart from the many, what would we deserve to suffer if we abandoned him as he hastens to his suffering? He raised us to such glory that we can even move mountains and do greater things than these. So let us follow him, so that we may live with him while he lives and die with him when he dies." The words are eager, the intent is bold. "Let us also go, so that we may die with him." What are you saying? You have not yet seen him betrayed, and you are already speaking of death? I look for the supper. Where is the basin? Where is the cohort with which the traitor comes, to betray his benefactor under a show of affection? And where are the crowds, the torches, the clubs, the swords with which they came out as if against a robber? Not yet the kiss, the condemnation before Caiaphas, the standing before Pilate's judgment seat, the mockery, the scarlet robe, the crown of thorns, the reed, the blows, the spitting, the floggings, the whips. Not yet Pilate washing his hands in water and being stained with blood. Not yet the spear [?]; not yet the nails. And you say, "Let us also go, so that we may die with him"? "Yes," he says. "I foresee what is to come as if it were present. He will raise Lazarus, I know. He will kindle the envy of the Jews, and then these things will happen." "Let us also go, so that we may die with him." He speaks not only for himself; he also stirs up the eager[ness] [?] of his companions.

So much for that. Lazarus was now dead and already stinking, and Jesus, the Christ and God, the giver of life, was there. For the vessel had to be shattered before the potter came. The house had to fall into ruin before the builder appeared. Come then: as Christ, God and Word, goes up today to Bethany, let us also bring our word up with him. For what does the Gospel say? "So when Jesus came…" Came where, and from where? To Bethany, where he was heading, from the place beyond the Jordan where he had been staying. Yet where is Christ not? What place will be left without him? But this must be taken in a human sense, not a divine one. For God is unbounded and cannot be contained, enclosed by no limit. "So when Jesus came, he found that he had already been in the tomb four days." This too was very wise. He held back his coming so that the elements of the body would, as it were, have already dissolved, and the miracle would be thought all the more extraordinary. For in so many days the one held in the coffin would have decayed. "He found him already four days in the tomb," so that the one who would rise on the third day might first raise the man four days dead. And so that the senseless Jews might learn, as they watched a man already rotting and oozing with fluids leap out of the tomb at a word. "He found him already four days in the tomb." For the longer he had been buried, the more Christ's power was marveled at. "Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away." That is why so many went out to console Mary and Martha. "For many of the Jews," it says, "had come to Martha and Mary to console them about their brother." And naturally so. Since the city was near, it was likely that many would go out to them, for one of two reasons. Either they delighted in the holy life of the two women, for their life was splendid and outstanding in virtue, or they were drawn by the poignancy of a grief so full of pain. In any case, the crowd that had gathered also bore witness to the miracle, and their gathering was not without profit. "So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went to meet him, but Mary stayed sitting in the house." For Mary did not know that Jesus had come; had she known, she would not have stayed. Or even if she did know, she probably sat at home out of reverence, receiving the consolations of those who were present. Martha was somehow warmer and simpler, with an unaffected character. That is why she "went out to meet him," to show the greatness of her [?] and to be the first to tell him of their friend's death. She told him as though he did not know, although she confessed that Lazarus could have been kept from death had he been present. "For if you had been here," she says, "my brother would not have died. And even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you." Do you see her faith? Do you see her unwavering mind? In two ways she presents him as God and giver of life, even if she errs somewhat

through the simplicity of her nature. "For if you had been here," she says. What are you saying, Martha? Your words are mistaken. He was there; he was present, and he is present everywhere. But so that the miracle might be the greater, he who fills all things with his divinity held back a little and gave death room. "If you had been here, my brother would not have died." Do you see how she believed him to be God, able to hold death back and to raise the dead by his authority? "I know," she says, "that if you had been present, death would have had no power. The lamp of our family would not have been put out. The limits of life would have stayed idle if you had been present, you who set the measure of life for all." "And even now I know," she says, "that whatever you ask of God, God will give you." She spoke according to appearances. Yet see that even here she was not ignorant of the truth. The woman had wisdom, even if her judgment was weak. Since she was convinced that Lazarus would not have died had he been present, she had no doubt about the future either. That is why she went to meet him and added the second statement, saying: "And even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you. If you had been here, my brother would not have died." "He did not die," she means, "because human beings are subject to death, but because you, the conqueror of death, were not there." Her faith was strong, even if her words were weak. And she was quietly reproaching him, in a way, for not being there when they had sent word to him, saying: "Look, the one you love is ill." "Jesus says to her: Your brother will rise again." These are words of great joy, and they bring a twofold healing: they correct her error and lull her violent grief to sleep. "Your brother will rise again." Because he shunned boasting, he did not say, "I will raise your brother," but, "Your brother will rise again." He said "will rise again" without saying when, testing how genuine her faith was. So she too says: "I know that he will rise again on the last day." "If you believe in that resurrection," he says, "do not doubt this one either. For I am the one who brings about both." "Your brother will rise again." He said this also to correct her for having said, "I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you." "Your brother will rise again": he was showing her his dignity as Lord and his authority, so that she might learn not to speak rashly about God. So he says: "Whoever believes in me, even if he dies, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never see death, for ever. Do you believe this?" This means something like the following: "Even if the one who believes in me does die," he says, "he dies only the natural death, not a death that holds him in its power, as is likely for the disobedient." "Do you believe this?" So very clearly and persuasively does he bring the woman's mind over to faith in himself, as her answer shows. For what does she say? "Yes, Lord; I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world." Do you see the strength of the Word?

Do you see what faith he drew her into, so that she grasped the precise truth of doctrine, though a little before she had been erring through simplicity? Everything that needed to be confessed about Christ, she stated briefly and in a roundabout way. "Yes," she says, "I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world." She proclaimed this plainly, and at the same time she summed up the whole teaching both about his divinity and about his saving plan. "And when she had said this," it says, "she went away and called her sister, saying to her privately: The Teacher is here and is calling you. When she heard this, she rose quickly and went to him." Her joy was equal to her grief for her brother. As soon as she heard that Jesus had come, she at once laid aside her mourning and showed the fervor of her faith. Martha too acts fittingly in not announcing Christ's promise publicly. She saw the crowds present, who were sitting with Mary to console her, and some of them envied Christ for working miracles. "The Teacher is here and is calling you." "From the fact that he is here," she means, "consider what is going to be done. He has not come to console or to comfort. If he had, he would have come before now. He has come to give life, to raise your brother." "And as soon as she heard, she rose quickly and went to him." She did not ask any questions or wait even a little. As though she already held her brother alive in her arms, she got up at a run and leapt toward the Life, caring little or nothing for those who were with her. "Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still at the place where Martha had met him." She hurried so much that she reached the Lord at that very spot. He was walking more slowly because of the quarrelsome suspicion of the Jews, so that he might not seem to rush at the miracle but to be called by the women's urging. He did not even wish to be present unless he was urged and called, so that the deed might not be thought a pretense. So when the Jews who were with Mary saw her get up quickly and run out of the house, they thought she was hurrying to the tomb, perhaps to tear at herself and mourn her brother with wailing. So they went out with her, as if they wanted to stop her from her lament over her brother. But the divine plan arranged for them too to be present, so that the miracle, done before their eyes, would not lack witnesses. "So when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet, saying: Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died." She had the same mind as her sister, and she agrees with her in the same words. Consider, then, how much Mary does in so short a time. She runs to him as to God, falls at his feet, speaks boldly, and shows that Lazarus has died. Not only that, but she shows that his death came before its time, because he was absent. She perhaps means that he has come when the time no longer allowed for healing, since death had, as it were, shut it out. And

[?] For one may gather from this that she knew him to be God as well, and was speaking to him as to God, even if the words [?] "If you had been here." "When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in spirit and troubled himself, and said, 'Where have you laid him?'" He did not say, "Let us go to where the tomb is," so that he would not seem to be hurrying on to the miracle; instead he asked, "Where have you laid him?" "I am asking you," he says, "because I want you as witnesses of the miracle. [?] Run ahead and show me the tomb." "Where have you laid him?" "I pretend not to know, so that I may expose your lack of understanding." "Where have you laid him?" He asked this not out of ignorance, but to stir up those present to attend to the miracle. For how could he not know where Lazarus had been buried, he who knows the Father as the Father himself knows himself, "in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge"? The only explanation is that he was showing what is human, modelling in himself what belongs to us. For ignorance and the impulses that come from it are ours, not his who knows all things before they come to be. He did display in himself all the passions of our nature that plainly escape the blemish of sin. But he did not take on the stains brought into that nature by irrational impulse or perversion. Far from it! He is spotless and not subject to the passions, and he took on the whole of our nature without departing from his unchangeable divinity. One might say, perhaps, that he took these things on by way of appropriation, since taking them on by way of essence is far removed from him. The question "Where have you laid him?" is not that of someone who does not know, as has surely been shown. Otherwise how could he have said from a great distance, "Lazarus has fallen asleep"? "Where have you laid him?" "I ask this," he says, "so that I may make the miracle certain." For it was likely that many, running ahead out of great joy, [?]. "They said to him, 'Come and see.' Jesus wept." He wept as a man, not for Lazarus but for the Jews. He had come to raise Lazarus, and there was no need to weep for one who was about to rise. But he had good reason to weep for the Jews, since he foresaw their unbelief even after the miracle. "Jesus wept." In this he gives us a pattern and model, and sets the measure of how far we should weep for the departed. He wept for the corruption of our nature and for the image made unlovely, as death makes it. "So the Jews said, 'See how he loved him.'" Notice here too their envy and their contentious frame of mind. "See how he loved him."

Being loved, he loved, and rightly so. "For I," he says, "love those who love me." [?] "See how he loved him." In a way these are the words of people who marvel, but also of the envious, so that some said, "Could not this man, who opened the eyes of the blind man, have kept this man from dying too?" And if he opened the eyes of the blind man, why did you refuse to believe him and assail him with blasphemous words? Why did you entangle the man who had been healed in so many snares, judging and cross-examining him about who he was, where he came from, what sort of man he was, and what he did to open your eyes? Yet now you admit, even if unwillingly, that he opened the blind man's eyes. On the strength of that you ought to marvel at this too, but instead you disparage both the one and the other. This is the work of the Jewish disposition. For when did you not provoke Christ to anger? When did you not disobey him, after seeing so many great wonders? "Then Jesus, again deeply moved, came to the tomb. It was a cave": the dark heart of the Jews. "And a stone lay upon it": the hardness and resistance of unbelief. "Jesus said, 'Take away the stone.'" Roll away the heavy stone of disobedience, so that I may bring up what is dead in the letter. "Take away the stone": the burdensome yoke of the law, so that you may receive the life-giving word of grace. "Take away the stone" that lies like a veil and weighs down the mind. "I could roll the stone away myself, but I want you to perceive the stench as well. That is why I leave it to you to lift the stone from the tomb." "Take away the stone," so that you may bear witness that you yourselves rolled the stone from the tomb. "Take away the stone." "You Jews, not my disciples, so that tomorrow you cannot say, as you did about the blind man, 'Is this the man? Is it that one?' and cannot claim that I raised one man in place of another." "Take away the stone," if you want to see how great the miracle is. "Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, 'Lord, he already stinks, for he has been dead four days.'" He had spent four days in the tomb, long enough for the dead man to have decayed. "[?], for he has been dead four days." These are words of unbelief and doubt. Yet in the greatest miracles unbelief usually runs on ahead. "He already stinks." Martha said this when the stone had been lifted and she noticed the smell. Her words were those of someone who disbelieved, yet they added to the miracle, since the body was shown to be all the more decomposed. "Lord, he already stinks." "Do not come near," she says, "or you will be disgusted." "He already stinks." "You are fragrant ointment; [do not] come near one who stinks." "[?], he already stinks." The woman's [?] heightens the miracle. "Jesus said to her, 'Did I not tell you that if you believe you will see the glory of God?'" He said this as though [?] her. For it is clear that she had not been wholly freed from doubt, and that was why she gave such mistaken answers.

"And Jesus lifted up his eyes to heaven and said, 'Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me, but I said this for the sake of the crowd standing around, so that they may believe that you sent me.'" He lifted his eyes upward, [from where] he has come down to us. And he thanks the Father, not as if he had received something from him, for he had not asked. "For I thank you," he says, "that you have heard me." Yet he had not asked anywhere or prayed anywhere, so the words "that you have heard me" seem, as it were, out of place in the sequence. But he says these things for the sake of the Jews. He shows that he came from above, that he is the Son of God and God, and that he does all things by the will of the Father, since he is of one and the same will and nature with him. And he shows that, being man, he spoke more [humbly], so as not to [?] one. "Having said this, he cried out with a loud voice, 'Lazarus, come out.' And at once the dead man came out, his hands and feet bound with grave-bands, and his face wrapped in a cloth." He does not pray now, nor does he say, "Father, raise him." Such things belong to those under authority and of lower rank. Instead he cries out, and not simply cries out, but with a loud voice. Why? To point to the trumpet that is to come, which will call with a loud voice those who are in the tombs. "Lazarus, come out." It is the voice of a master, the command of a king, the order of one who has authority. "Come out." You who have put off corruption, take up again the [?]. "Lazarus, come out." Let the Jews know that the hour is coming when those in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of Man, and those who hear will live. "Come out." The stone, the stumbling block, has been lifted; walk toward me, who am calling you. "Come out." "As a friend I call to you, but as Master I command you." "Come out." "Let the Jews learn that if I raise a man four days dead from the tomb, much more will I myself rise on the third day, if indeed I taste death." "Lazarus, come out." "Come out wrapped in your swaddling bands and wearing your grave clothes, so that the Jews do not think you a pretended corpse. Let them see the hands and feet bound and the face covered, and let the Jews not disbelieve the miracle." "Come out." "The foul smell of your body will confirm your return to life. Let them unbind your wrappings themselves

and recognize the man they shut up in the tomb." "Come out." "Receive life, receive a soul, and step out of the coffin. Teach how in the twinkling of an eye all creation [?], when the voice of the trumpet brings about the general resurrection of the dead." "Come out." Breath in the nostrils; the veins full of blood; the voice in the throat; [hearing] in the ears; sight in the eyes; smell in its place; walking as nature intends; and the whole tent of the body, given a soul again, was fitted out with all its organs. "Come out." "Lay aside your swaddling bands and sing the praises of [?] wonders. Lay aside the foulness of your stench and worship the sovereign power of my authority. I command you, 'Come out,' I who said, 'Let there be light, let there be a firmament.' I bid you, 'Come out,' so that you may see me betrayed by a disciple, sold to the Jews, judged at Pilate's tribunal, and led willingly to my passion; so that you may see the insolence of the Jews and my meekness." "Come out." "So that you may see me crucified with robbers, given vinegar and gall to drink, and pierced in the side with a lance; so that you may see the light overpowered at midday and night overshadowing the sun, the Jews blaspheming and a robber confessing God." "Lazarus, come out." "And at once the dead man came out, his hands and feet bound with grave-bands, and his face wrapped in a cloth." This was because of the unbelief of the Jews. If the grave clothes had not been on him, they would probably have said, "He was not dead; he slipped into the tomb pretending to be a corpse." That is why he leapt out bound with grave-bands, stinking, his face covered and his feet bound, so that no pretext of any kind would be left to them. "Jesus said to them, 'Unbind him and let him go.'" So that the ungrateful would have nothing to say, he orders them to unbind Lazarus themselves, as if to say, "Unbind him with your own hands, so that you may be witnesses of the miracle." "Unbind him and let him go." For coming out bound was no lesser wonder than rising, and he wanted to make sure that what was done would not be thought some kind of illusion. "Unbind him," he says, "so that by [sight] and touch you may know for certain that it was he." "And let him go." "Let us see whether death can prevail when I do not will it." "Let him go." For he has no need of anyone to lead him by the hand: he has just received new life and has been taught to walk upright, he who a little earlier had decayed. "Unbind him and let him go." "Let this be a foretaste," he says, "of the general resurrection, when corruption passes into incorruption and all will rise from the dust of the earth." "Many therefore of those who had come to Mary and had seen what Jesus did believed in him." Blessed is the one who has traded in this good merchandise, faith; who has not come out of Bethany empty-handed, with no trade done (I mean, of course, the Bethany of the fast); who has acquired its splendid and precious goods through self-control and humility; who, believing rightly in Christ, has bought the fine pearls of his teachings, giving faith and receiving

knowledge. Blessed is the one who through freedom from passion has woven for himself a wedding garment worthy of union with God, so that he can eat the Passover that is being sacrificed with a pure heart, meet the Master with glory as he returns from Bethany, and spread beneath his [feet] the white garments of a clear conscience, so that he can say: "On me, Lord, on me the foot of the beast you have mounted will tread." This beast is the all-holy flesh which he put on for us in a manner beyond being. Who is so shrewd a merchant as to have traded for his own salvation in the way I have described? Would that you too, people of Christ, the new inheritance, had done such trading in the days of fasting just past! For the trade they offer is the best of all for those who know how to conduct themselves well. There gold is abundant: self-control. There are pearls: tears; translucent stones: virtuous deeds; silver: chastity; clean clothing: dignified conduct; spices: the words of the Lord. There is a necklace: humility, which traces the outline of obedience; [?] and braided ornaments and gold-threaded collars: the many [?] fulfilments of the commandments. But why should I describe to you one by one the costly gifts of the fast, when nature itself teaches that everything [?] from it turns to the good of its possessor? Who is there who has come out of this festival well? Who has become like Martha? Who has emulated Mary, the sisters of Lazarus? Who has bought fine pearls as they did, that is, tears, and brought them to Christ, weeping over his own soul that has died, as they wept over Lazarus? Who has traded for the precious stone, Christ the cornerstone, who ordered the stone to be rolled away so that he might raise Lazarus? What soul so dear to God has bought the finest spices, [iris?] and amomum and cinnamon, so that she might prepare the fragrant ointment and anoint the Lord as he sat at supper? Who has stood at his feet like her and poured [the ointment] over his head, then wet his feet with ointment and with tears? Who has heard with her own ears that gentle voice saying, "Your sins are forgiven"? What soul is so much a seller of perfume and so ready to weep as to anoint Christ, the inexhaustible ointment [?]? But perhaps someone listening to this will say, "Look, I am imitating the [sinful woman] and offering, if not ointment, at least tears. But where is the [?]? Where is the [?] through which forgiveness of offences is given?" Come, I will show you plainly: in the church, in your inner room. Why do I say in the church? In your own

private place. Christ is there. Pour out your ointment upon him there. Shed your tears there. "But I have no ointment," someone says, "no alabaster jar." You have no ointment? Yes, you do have ointment: grace. You have an alabaster jar: your heart. Tears: confession. Hair: quiet sighs. Offer these, consecrate these, and you will receive forgiveness. Christ is everywhere. Everywhere he is present when he is called. Only let Judas not be there; only let him be invited in the right way; only let the supper be free of deceit. Become Simon, if you like, and invite the Master. But do not have doubts like the Pharisee. Call him who is present everywhere, but do not invite Judas along with him. Become Lazarus, if you like: dead to the world, stinking to the [passions], keeping silence like a stone over your mouth. Or rather, first become a friend of the Master. You too have sisters: first the soul, then the flesh. Make friends with Christ, so that when you fall asleep they may send to Jesus, as Mary and Martha did, the one in word and the other in deed, saying, "Lord, behold, he whom you love is ill." Then, when you have wholly died to the world and to the things of the world, Christ may come to you [?] and say to his angels, "Unbind him and let him go." Unbind him from what? From the bonds of sin. And let him go where? To the bosom of Abraham, to the eternal dwellings, to the ageless blessedness of the divine inheritance. May we all attain it, by the grace and love for humankind of him who calls us all to the knowledge of himself, Christ our true God, with whom be glory to the Father together with the Holy Spirit for ever. Amen.

On Palm Sunday. [Yesterday] Lazarus feasted us together with the Master, setting before us at the feast the miracle done for him. Today God the Word himself provides our discourse as a feast for you who love the festivals and love [what is good]. You have long struggled under the weight of misfortunes, but today you have been strengthened by joy at the Master's festival. And with good reason. For if he, as God, stood by and brought back to life from the depths of Hades a man already rotting and decayed, surely now too he will strengthen the feebleness of the speech that has grown old in us and show it full of vigour for the festival that has been raised up. It will rightly have something youthful and bold about it, leaping up and springing forth from the organs of the voice, called by God the Word himself, as Lazarus was called from the tomb. So he who yesterday nourished us with the miracle done for Lazarus may today, the same Word, nourish us more richly and abundantly,

[setting before us] words about his sufferings. But before my discourse bursts forth from the birth pangs of the mind, I want to ask those present: What is this great gathering? What is the [?]? What is this assembly of people? What is this noise? What is this chorus of acclamation? Crowds everywhere, children everywhere, some holding branches, others palms. There is no wrestling yet, and already they are running to the contest; no victory yet, and the prizes are already in hand. Before the procession come the good omens, before the acclamation the crowns. A hymn on the tongue, a song on the lips: some blessing, others acclaiming; some waving branches, others spreading their garments on the roads, and all, in a word, spreading out their own hearts. For whom? Coming from where? Hastening where? Surely for the conqueror of death, who had just called Lazarus out and was hastening to enter Jerusalem in order to suffer. For what reason? So that by his own passion he might crush our passions, he who is above suffering. [?] Was it the sound of the dancers, or the clapping of [hands], that raised the festival to such a shout? The sound of the dancers was bright and pleasing, for it was a victory song and full of [?] joy. But the din of those in a frenzy was harsh and ugly, and plainly unpleasant in itself, being full of envy and [breathing] murder. Of these, some [met him] from Bethany, others when he had come down to the Mount of Olives [?]; others met him as he was nearly at the city, others when he had come inside the gates and reached the temple. And a very great [crowd] and swarm of infants burst forth and shouted the victory [hymns] in acclamation, saying, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel!" At this unusual spectacle and the unceasing hymn, the whole city was at once thrown into confusion and split into many opinions about him. Some said, "Who is this?" while others called him son of David. Some brought forward the prophetic predictions; others [disputed them], others agreed; others [?]; and all, in a word, as he said earlier, were drawn this way and that into countless opinions and fancies. And he was the sign that is spoken against, proclaimed by the prophet [?]. Is it any wonder if Jerusalem is troubled, and the assemblies of the Jews [?] at God being glorified, when even earlier, at his birth, the Magi [?]? "When Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him." [?]

Consider, my friend, how closely related and how parallel these events are. There, Bethlehem; here, Bethany. Then, Mary and Salome; now, Mary and Martha. There, Christ in swaddling clothes; here, Lazarus wrapped in grave-bands. There, a manger; here, a tomb. Do you see the likeness of places and persons? When Christ was born, Herod was in an uproar and Jerusalem in confusion. In Bethany, when he worked wonders and raised Lazarus, Jerusalem was troubled and the Pharisees stirred up the crowds. There, shepherds marvelled; here, priests [questioned]. There, the Magi attended him like an escort and fell down before him; here, crowds who fought against God took offence at him. There, children slain beforehand for Christ's sake wailed, as if lamenting at their own funeral; here, children went before Christ, singing songs for his entry, not a song of peace but a victory song, crying out, "Hosanna to the Son of David," taught by the Spirit as their guide. But enough of these parallel comparisons, now that the madness of the Jews has been sufficiently exposed, both then, when Christ was revealed in the flesh, and now, when he is [acclaimed and crucified?]. It is now time for us to touch on the mysteries of the feast and to uncover for you the mystical wealth of the day at hand, in the hope that [?] I may provide you abundantly with the treasure hidden in it. But come, let us go up together to the Mount of Olives and meet Christ as he returns today from Bethany and goes willingly to that venerable and blessed passion, so that the mystery of our salvation may be brought to its fulfilment. He comes, then, setting out on the road to Jerusalem [willingly], he who came down from above for our sake, so that he might [raise] with himself us who lie below, as the revelation says, "far above every rule and authority and power and every name that is named." And he comes not [in pomp] or boasting: "He will not quarrel," it says, "nor cry out, nor will anyone hear his voice." Rather, he is meek and humble, and makes a lowly entry. For what is lowlier than a donkey, what humbler than a beast of burden? Yet he was not ashamed, though he is [?] and rides upon the backs of the Cherubim, to sit on a colt as on a throne. For he fulfilled the prophetic

[?] the voice, foretold long before in the Spirit. “Rejoice,” it says, “daughter of Zion: behold, your King comes to you, gentle, and mounted on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.” What humility greater than this has been shown to you [?], among those admired for their glory? Is there anything among men lower than this? Did you not shudder [?], seeing the one enthroned upon the Seraphim riding on a colt? But come, learn the interpretation too, and be assured of the divine plan, so that once you understand the power of the mystery [?]. He was about to take away our irrationality, lifting off sin [?]: he who did not disdain even a manger, who did not refuse to lie in swaddling clothes. And fittingly he also [mounts?] the calling of the gentiles, who were only now receiving him [?], the consolation of Israel and the long-awaited light of salvation, for a revelation to the gentiles. From among them, as many as bowed their necks to [his yoke?] and [received] the one who came, and set the whole Master upon themselves, hastened all the more eagerly to show plainly the truth hidden until then [?], in the hope that he, mounting them wholly, might free them from their former beastliness. By the garments, beloved, which the crowds spread beneath the Word, you are to understand the coverings that darken the mind through ignorance. The Jewish veil fittingly stands for these, which lies upon their heart and is not lifted, because it is abolished only in Christ. “Whenever,” says the divine Paul, “Moses is read, a veil lies upon their heart. But when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.” I think that they too then took these off and spread them beneath the Word, who through the symbolic mounting of the beast removed the ignorance of their irrationality. The disciples’ garments laid on the colt [signify?] [?] clearly by them [?] powers are signified: all those, plainly, which clothe our nakedness, we who come from the gentiles [?], and, weaving for us the knowledge of Christ, clothe us with him, so that we may be God-bearers, carrying him wholly within us, worn and robed by us. This could never be brought about unless we were ready to suffer for Christ and to bear [what] Christ suffered for us and in our stead at the hands of those beneath him: the grandeur of the mystery. Come then, let us too go toward the suffering, and imitate those who went out to meet him, [not with branches] of olive or [palm?], not strewing palm fronds in his way, but spreading ourselves beneath him

as far as we can. With humility of soul and uprightness of mind let us receive the Word who has come, so that God, whom nothing can contain, may be contained in us. For he who is gentle, and who “rides upon the west,” the far edge of our condition, rejoices in becoming gentle toward us in this way: in coming and conversing with us, and leading us up, or leading us back, to himself, because of the nature he shares with us. Though he is said, with the firstfruits of our lump, to “ride upon the heaven of heaven toward the east”—of his own glory, I think, and divinity—yet, being a lover of humankind, he will not rest until he has raised human nature from the ground, from glory to glory, and shown it exalted together with himself. So we must spread ourselves beneath Christ: not tunics, nor lifeless branches and shoots of plants, matter that withers and pleases the eye for only a few hours, but ourselves, having put on his grace, or rather him wholly. “For as many of us as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ”: let us spread ourselves out like tunics. And as people once crimson with sin, who later, through the washing of saving baptism, have reached the whiteness of wool, let us bring to the conqueror of death not fronds from palm trees but the prizes of victory. Let us too say today with the children that sacred cry, waving the spiritual branches of the soul: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.” Where is he coming, and from where? To us, and from the Father; to those on earth, from the highest; to the cross, from the miracle of Lazarus. The first belongs to his good pleasure, the second to his authority. When, and why? In the fullness of time, and for our salvation. “For once, at the consummation of the ages,” he [underwent] death for humankind willingly, in order to save man, he who out of overflowing love for humankind became man. For the cross was the last act of his sojourn among us. If then, as the course of this sermon has shown, we meet Christ today and spread ourselves beneath him, we too shall be able to receive wholly into ourselves him who is perpetually sacrificed for us without sacrifice (for he is sacrificed in antitypes [?]

offered as a holy sacrifice for us in symbols), and to make him dwell in us in very substance, eaten as bread and understood as a lamb; and to share the experience of those whom the Son of Thunder recalled in the Gospels. For he says: “On the next day” (clearly after the [supper] [?] given by him) “a great crowd that had come to the feast, hearing that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, and cried out, saying: Hosanna in the highest; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, [the King of] Israel.” Oh, what hymnody! Oh, what harmony! This is the voice of [the Spirit?]; this is the teaching of the wisdom from above, not of earthly learning. For where one might have expected some discord, with the voice of so great a multitude breaking away from harmony, there was none; instead there was prophecy, [purity of speech?] and concord. For the crowds, inspired by the Spirit into the fullness of one [body?], struck up a single-voiced song of theology, not raising one voice against another, but uttering equal words with equal voices and shouting out the acclamation: “Hosanna,” they said, “blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.” It was as if they were saying what Nathanael said earlier, when Philip pointed Christ out to him—not prophesying but speaking the truth: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel.” Do you see how much the Spirit gives? Do you see what gifts he bestows on infants, laying down the law and teaching them what they had not learned? See, too, how unlettered men are granted knowledge greater than orators possess, while old men who pride themselves on wisdom and great learning are shown to be inexperienced and to have no share in [?] the laws. So they came to question him himself. [?] that they drove themselves to such blindness that they could not be as sensible as an infant, nor see the light of truth as clearly as unlearned men. [?] O dull ones: from where did such wisdom [?], having been taught to articulate the tongue, [?] been given? From where were the mysteries of theology sown in the crowds [?], so that with the angels they recalled the things of the angels, with the Cherubim they glorified, with the Seraphim they praised, lifting up that hymn not with fiery but with lips of clay [?] to the one who came from above to us to undergo death for us and in our place? And what [do they say]? “Hosanna in the highest; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” Do you see

earthborn people made heavenly and speaking theology on a par with the Seraphim? And what is more wondrous than that the unlearned should sing that awe-inspiring revelation on earth together with the choir above, so that men on earth might join the dance of the angels? And what is more wretched than to be deaf to these things, and, besides refusing to change [their course?], to add blindness as well; and, worse still, to reach such shamelessness as to dare to silence those who hymned these things so divinely and so like the Seraphim? “For when the chief priests and the scribes saw,” it says, “the wonderful things that Jesus did, and the children crying out, Hosanna to the Son of David, they were indignant and said to him: Do you hear what these are saying? And Jesus says to them: Yes. Have you never read, Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babes you have perfected praise?” “But you,” he says, “have not shown even the understanding of infants, let alone of sensible men. [?] if nothing else, out of respect for gray hair [?], [you should have been ashamed before?] those who speak in the Spirit.” “And leaving them,” it says, “he went out of the city to Bethany, and lodged there.” For since, hearing the Most High hymned on earth by the mouths of infants as in the highest, they shut their ears and their heart so as not to hear or understand what had been written about him, therefore “leaving them, [he went] out of the city,” so that what Isaiah says might come to pass: “And the house was filled with smoke.” By their house he truly means the Synagogue. From the moment Christ, the light, left them and went out, its light was put out and it was filled with smoke, the darkness that obscures the eye of the soul. For that is what smoke becomes for those who are blind in mind. And smoke is the avenger of wrath, as the Psalmist says: “Smoke went up in his wrath.” And where did he go out to? “To Bethany,” which in a figurative sense is taken to mean “house of obedience.” For since the Jews, maimed in mind, were blinded, he left them and went out to the house of obedience, where we, the gentiles, were sojourning at that time. Strangers [?] to the city of true knowledge and its thoughts, we were then wanderers without a city, not yet citizens of the holy and God-built land, that is, of the new Jerusalem, whose name means “vision of peace,” which becomes [accessible?] to those who enter through baptism. For once cleansed of the stains of the soul by the washing of regeneration, we no longer have the sins that came from them fighting against us. But by [contemplation] in the mind

[directed] toward the [vision?] of peace [?], we both become and are called Jerusalemites in the proper sense. As for the children of the Jews, all who [refuse] to have their minds illumined by the light of Christ, let them [weep] and lament, filled with smoke and [tears]. For that is what usually happens to those who come near smoke in the body. But we, all of us who have been illumined by the light and have cast off the dimness of sight that sin brought in, let us go eagerly to the meeting. Let us go out of Sodom, flee the unspeakable deeds of Gomorrah, escape to the mountain, enter Zoar with the setting sun. Let the Lord’s humility become our Zoar: in it, though immeasurable in divinity, he became very small by sharing our humanity, and he who has the Cherubim for a throne, he whom the Seraphim cannot behold, sat upon a colt, the foal of a beast of burden. So let none of the things that steal away the senses halt our eagerness: not a newly wedded bride, not a field [newly bought?], not fear of the Pharisees, not the [envy?] of the scribes, not the rage of Caiaphas. Let nothing, small or great, cut short our [course?] of piety. Friends, initiates and followers of Christ, let us go to meet Christ. It is good to meet Christ and to follow him as he hastens to his suffering. [It is good] to see a gentle king enthroned on a colt as on a small [seat?], and escorted [?] by his subjects. Let pride fall, and every [?] of self-exaltation, at the sight of God humbled in the flesh and hastening to suffer. Hades saw him asking, “Where have you laid Lazarus?” and, thinking the questioner a mere man, it struck against the Godhead; and when it heard the voice of the one who gave the command, it at once, on command, vomited out the man it had tyrannically despoiled a little before [?]. For it was not strong enough to resist the Master’s voice. For as soon as [?] had plundered its spoils, it abandoned that booty and went toward the last [?], having nowhere [to turn], struck with fear, once
Do you see what the height of humility can do? So let us be humbled; let us become poor, that we may be made rich. Let us taste the cross, that we may enjoy the sweetness of life.

[?]. Let us too say to Christ [?]: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” [?] palms as farewell offerings on his way to the cross [?]. Let us acclaim him not with olive branches but with the [glories] of mercy [?] toward one another. Let us spread beneath his feet, like garments, the [thoughts?] of the heart [?], so that, walking within us, he may [?] receive us wholly into himself, and [we may have?] him wholly in us. Let us say to Zion the prophetic acclamation: “Take courage, daughter of Zion, do not fear. Behold, your King comes to you, gentle, and mounted on a donkey’s colt, the foal of a beast of burden.” He comes who is present everywhere and fills all things, to work salvation in all things through all things. He comes who came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance, to call back those who have wandered into sin. [Fear not] then: “God is in your midst, and you shall not be shaken.” Receive into your hands, [O creation?], the one who painted your walls upon his hands. Receive the one who laid your foundations upon his palms. Receive the one who took upon himself all that is ours, except sin, so that he might [make] what is his our own. Rejoice, mother city Zion, do not fear. “Celebrate your feasts.” [With ...] of mercy glorify the one who has come to us in you. “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Jerusalem”; sing hymns, leap for joy. “Shine, shine,” we cry to you with Isaiah, the sacred trumpet, “for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you.” What light? “The one that enlightens every man coming into the world.” The eternal light, the light [timeless?] yet shown forth in time; the light made manifest in the flesh yet hidden in its nature; the light that shone around the shepherds and guided the Magi. The light that was in the world from the beginning, and the world was made through it, and the world did not know it; the light that came to its own, and its own did not receive it. What glory? The cross, plainly, in which Christ was glorified, the radiance of the Father’s glory, as he himself says when he was on the threshold of his suffering: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him; [and God will glorify him] in himself, and will glorify him at once.” By glory he means being lifted up on the cross. For the cross is Christ’s glory, and plainly his exaltation; for [he says]: “When I am lifted up, then I will draw all to myself.” So let no one hesitate or shrink back from going along with Christ

as he enters. I do not mean this new city of ours, the antitype of the dwelling above, but the city grown old in monstrous impieties. The one is a debtor for the blood of the prophets; the other a servant of the Master’s miracles. The one is trampled by profane feet; the other worshipped where the Master’s feet have trodden. The one reeks of bloody sacrifices; the other is fragrant with the Master’s sacrifice. Into this city, then, as Christ enters it, let us enter with him. Let us run ahead with the crowds; let us acclaim with those who acclaim; let us sing hymns with the children. Let us meet him with good works as with branches; let us welcome him with holy lives as with palms. Let the Jews [rage?]; let Annas and [Caiaphas] be torn [?]; let the Pharisees be sawn through [with fury], and if they wish, let them tear apart not their garments but their bodily senses, of which the divine David sings: “They were torn apart, and were not pricked to compunction.” Let them say once more to their own, as they see the glory of the Lord and cannot bear the crowds’ acclaim of him: “You see that you are gaining nothing. Look, the whole world has gone after him.” Let them proclaim their own stupidity; let them noise abroad their own failure: “You see that you are gaining nothing?” Alas for such insensibility! Alas for such hardness of heart! They see him acclaimed with theology no one had taught, and, shutting their eyes, they blind themselves willingly. “You see,” it says, “that you are gaining nothing.” They do not say this to the crowds, nor to those who received him through knowledge and came by grace to share in his [?], but to themselves and to the chief priests who thought as they did, deceivers of the people, who were working on the crowds and shamelessly trying, as it were, to muzzle them. For indeed they had threatened in advance and given orders that anyone who called him Christ would be put out of the synagogue. “You see,” it says, “that you are gaining nothing?” This is what people say when they blame the chief priests because [?] they were not at rest.

did not kill him long before, or when he raised Lazarus. For if that had happened, perhaps the affairs of Judea would not have come to this pass. And how would the words of the prophets have been fulfilled? And indeed, though you often wanted to lay hands on him, you did not dare. “For his hour had not yet come.” “You see,” it says, “that you are gaining nothing? Look, the whole world has gone after him.” And if the whole world has gone after the light, why do you not also let go of the darkness of ignorance and run back after the light? Why do you not run with the shining Sun of righteousness, leaving behind the shadow found in the letter and in types? Why do you not lift the veil of blindness and hasten toward the light of truth? “Look,” it says, “the whole world has gone after him.” What then? Are you not of the world? And what [follows]? Tearing yourselves away from the whole world, will you not cease from the storm and run with the world toward the salvation of the world, so that you may not be condemned with the world? Which world? The world that did not recognize its maker, nor understand the one proclaimed beforehand by the prophets and, in a word, by all divinely inspired Scripture, who is the expectation of the nations and the consolation of Israel. “You see that you are gaining nothing? Look, the whole world has gone after him.” If they are gaining nothing, your madness is in vain, your zeal empty, your efforts fruitless. But if the whole world has gone after him, why do you not also keep in step with the world and [follow]? Unless perhaps you claim that you do not owe your origin to the world, nor have any share in the providence that governs the world, but come from some other cause and nature, one that covertly sketches in mere chance and openly brings in godlessness? But let them rave, stoned by their own blasphemous words, striking and being struck by their own wickedness. For such are the wages of such people. But we, the flock of Christ, whom the Father sanctified, whom the Son [?], and whom the Holy Spirit sealed through the divine washing of baptism—come, let us shake off the errors and opinions of the Jews and run back without straying to the one and only faith of the Church, which is truly secure and effective, believing in the one who comes, who is Christ, grace and truth, through whom we have come to know the Father and have gained access to him, and the Holy Spirit. For in this way, with our minds enlightened and our longing for him ever growing stronger, we shall be able everywhere and always to be with him and to follow him; wherever he whom nothing can contain wishes to go, to remain inseparable from him; and to suffer eagerly with him and for his sake whatever must be suffered. And if he rises from the dead, we shall rise with him, be glorified with him, and reign with him in the kingdom that cannot be shaken and has no end. This is the reward; this is the wealth that life in company with Christ bestows. This is the recompense Christ gives to those who cleave to him. Such are the gifts Christ wishes to lavish on those who are his disciples
[?] There is nothing like our adding some relish of our own to these good things, and toward [?]

Come then, beloved, strain your ears and learn the [?] power of the word. For if you desire it earnestly, you may take Christ's sufferings upon yourself by imitation, and travel through all Christ's mysteries and deeds, by which he cleansed the shameful things in us and consumed, through the sufferings he bore for us, the stains that cling to us from sin.
