Do you wish, then, beloved, to keep the feast joyfully, to meet him with shining [?], and to be seen with Christ as he hastens toward his passion? Take for yourself a spiritual image, a contemplation formed mystically in the heart, and paint for me once more a picture of what happened then. Imagine that you are there with Christ as he travels the road to Bethany. Join the crowd of the disciples. Consider how he stood at the tomb of his friend. Picture yourself seeing Lazarus too, and Lazarus's grieving sisters; and seeing, all together, everything that was done. Then, from there, follow Christ and escort the victor, waving the tokens of victory before him with the crowd. Become one of those who lead the way, and run along with those who follow. Instead of palm branches, display a life of virtue. Make your hands into olive branches by stretching them out in mercy. Do not spread garments of the flesh like coverings for him who veils heaven with clouds; rather, bind your whole self by faith to him who became wholly flesh for your sake, put on your whole self like a tunic, and receive him wholly, who comes to you for your sake and hastens to suffer. Become a colt, if you like, showing a colt's eagerness in an aged mind. Carry Christ as he comes into Jerusalem. But perhaps you will say, "How can I become a colt, when I was made a rational being?" Yes, you will become one if you are willing. Have you not heard David singing, "I became like a beast before you"? Imitate the colt; or rather, become a colt in simplicity of mind. And just as that colt followed those sent to Bethphage to untie and bring him, without objecting in any way, but only bowing to those who led him, so you too must submit to the word that trains you to choose the humility that is according to Christ, resisting in nothing, and being truly [?] of Christ, [?] of all beastly unreason: not walking on the ground of an earthly mind, nor bent under a load as though weighed down by the burden of unreasonable passions, but going upon the [?] of practical works and borne above the pleasures of the flesh, and moreover trampling the empty breath of all vainglory. This is how someone becomes a colt of Christ. In this way he will become the vehicle of him whose throne is the Cherubim. Likewise

[?] become like the children of the Hebrews. Be a child [?] in malice. Change the whiteness of your hair into the gentleness of an infant. Grey hair is no use if simplicity is not there with it. Run with the multitude; with the crowds, ahead of the crowds, go along with the Master. Open [?] your mouth [?]. Dance, sing hymns, glorify him who has led you up from glory to glory. Become Zion, the watchtower, I mean, of the contemplative life. Become a soul of Jerusalem, truly a city of God, a glorious city, so that you may receive Christ coming to dwell in you. "For behold, he comes to you gentle and bringing salvation," yet not boasting of his kindness. Throw open the gates of your lips. Sing with the children, saying, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel." Make your heart a furnished upper room, so that you may receive Christ to eat that supper with you: not the one at Lazarus's house, but the mystical one, which portrays the image of the spiritual sacrifice. This one is a mystery; that one is full of tears. There a woman pours ointment; here Christ sanctifies himself for us. There a woman cleanses great sins with small tears; here Christ washes the disciples' feet, to show his lofty humility. Here Christ grants the inexhaustible sharing of the bread and the new cup; there Judas tries to talk them out of pouring the ointment, and pockets the price of the Lamb. But take care that, while dining with Christ, you are not carried off with Judas as he drags you toward the price of the ointment. Do not be persuaded by him when he gives the bad advice of supposedly caring for the poor. He is a liar and a lover of money, and he thinks he can steal the suspicions of the onlookers, as he stole what was put into the money bag. That is why he pretends to feel compassion for the poor, playing the part of greed under the pretext of love for the poor. If he says, "Why this great waste of ointment? For this could have been sold for a great deal and given to the poor," leap away from him, or rather laugh at him, and lift your mind to the burial of him who became poor for our sake. And if you eat the mystical supper, do not dip your hand in the dish along with Christ, and do not be rash and despise the teacher. If you hear, "One of you will betray me," do not leap up, and do not join in the insolence.

Be humble with the humble. Practise silence with the silent. And if you are asked, answer gently to him who knows all things, and nothing more [?]. Is it good to think yourself above the others [?], so that you too hear, "You have said it," and what [?] says: "Let your own mouth convict you, and not I; your lips have testified against you"? But let the discourse move on to what remains. There was a supper, then: the one there was a Pharisee's, the one here mystical. Here a basin sketches the [?] of humility; there tears wash away [?] the stains of the soul. There hair wipes the Master's feet, by which Hades was trampled and thrown down together with death its gatekeeper; here a towel wipes feet that grace has accepted in readiness for the gospel of peace. There a Pharisee; here [?] a man carrying a jar of water. Who is the man? The soul of each person. What is the jar? The rotten vessel of sin, by which I mean the body. What is the water? Cleansing through faith. What is the upper room? The heavenly mind. What does "furnished" mean? Rest from the turmoil outside, the repose of a gentle spirit. What is the Passover? The crossing over from things perceived by the senses to things perceived by the mind. Who is the one who sent them? Christ. Who are those sent? Two of the disciples. And who are these two? The Old and the New Testament; or, as it is not hard to say, perfection in knowledge and perfection in practice, in which and through which Christ celebrates the Passover. Where, and in whose house? In the soul prepared in this way. What kind of Passover? The Passover of the Law and the mystical one, if you like: the one by knowledge, the other by practice; the one as a lamb [?] the words [?]. Who is so ardent in faith as to be eager to suffer with Christ that desirable and blessed passion, so that when he hears him foretelling to the disciples, "Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man is handed over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles, and they will mock him and kill him, and on the third day he will rise," he may at once throw behind him all his attachment to the world and emulate his own Master, resolving to suffer everything

for his sake that he eagerly suffered for us? For he did not suffer for his own sake, but to set us a pattern and rules of courage and humility, so that we might not give way in any hardship. In what way? Lend me your ears, so that you may grasp the force of what is said. Have you been reviled by someone? Do not be indignant. For Christ too, who is Master and God and above suffering, was not only reviled but also scourged. Have you been insulted by your neighbour? But Christ too was struck. Have you been reproached? But he was even spat upon, and wore a cloak in mockery. Have you been seized by the hair? But Christ was crowned with thorns. Have you been dishonoured? But Christ too was mocked, and as Isaiah says, "He was dishonoured and not esteemed." Have you been struck with the hand? But Christ too was slapped, and struck on the head with a reed. Have you been whipped? But Christ too was scourged. Have you been beaten with fists? But Christ was even crucified, his hands and feet pierced with nails [?]. And not only this: even when crucified, he prayed for those who were crucifying him. How much heavier these things are than those! How much more unbearable and bitter are Christ's sufferings than ours! There is nothing that has ever happened, nothing at all, that can be compared with Christ's sufferings. For ours, being very paltry, are nothing, since they belong only to sinful and mortal human beings, who are subject to change, to coming into being, and to [?]. But how incomparably Christ's surpass ours no word could ever reach. For they are the sufferings of the God over whom no one reigns, the sinless God, the God who cannot fall, the immortal one, "with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning." And indeed, though he "takes away our sins and suffers pain for us," yet "he himself committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth." He is wholly "righteousness and sanctification and redemption," and the one who drives out all sin. See, then, how greatly Christ's sufferings surpass ours and differ from them; and do not look at the magnitude of the suffering, but stand in awe of the dignity of the sufferer. Send your mind there. Consider what it is to see a mere man hanging on a cross, and what it is to behold God being crucified, and that with robbers. Consider which human being would ever have chosen to endure such things as Christ then willingly came here to suffer. And when did this happen? After the divine signs, after the healings, after those unspeakable banishings of diseases, after the handing on of the mysteries, after

the acts of kindness by which he never ceased making better those who came to him, drawing up writs of release from sins for those who needed them, decreeing forgiveness for some and removing condemnation from others. Why should I not tell what came next, the evils he underwent? I mean the trials before the cross: the sale, the betrayal, the treacherous kiss of one who was a disciple but a faithless one, a sheep but in truth a wolf; the attack with swords and clubs, the leading away to Caiaphas, the false testimonies, the examination before the tribunal, the cry that the Jews raised, shouting, "Crucify, crucify him!"; the scourgings, the mockeries, the spitting, the blows, the crown of thorns, the scarlet cloak, the leading away to the Place of the Skull. And then the things on the cross: the nails, the bonds, the crucifixion on the wood, the vinegar, the gall, the spear, the lots cast for his garments, the dividing of them, the insults on the cross, as some abused him outrageously there, shaking their heads and saying, "He saved others; himself he cannot save"; others, "If he is King of Israel, let him save himself"; others, "Aha! You who destroy the temple and build it in three days, you cannot save yourself"; others, "Wait, let us see whether Elijah comes to save him"; and others, "If he is the Son of God, let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him." Do these things seem small to you as a model of humility? Have you ever come anywhere near the measure of even one of the sufferings that befell Christ, and kept silent? No indeed, I would say. Yet Christ, having suffered things of such a kind and such magnitude, kept silent. And what came after the cross, how fearful and astonishing it was! For instance: heaven above was darkened, the air turned gloomy, the sun was [?], the moon grew black, the earth quaked, the deep shrank back, the mountains split, the tombs sent up the dead, and all the other extraordinary things of that time. Though they were refuted by these things and taught that the one who suffered was God, and though they ought to have been converted and to have recognized what was right from the wonders taking place, they did not turn away from their wickedness any more readily; the wretches did not yield, but went on to worse. I leave aside the evil deeds after the burial that they practised: the guard at the tomb, the seal on the stone, the plot after the resurrection, the widely spread [?] [?]

[?] the passion, after the passion, from the day of his manifestation to Israel? At one time they said, "You have a demon"; at another, "A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners"; sometimes, "He breaks the law and profanes the Sabbath"; at other times, "A Samaritan" and "the carpenter's son," and all the rest that is contained in the books of the Gospels. Where shall we put the ambush on the brow of the hill, the mockeries, the trials, the questions with hidden intent? From one side came "Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar?"; from another, the question about the one woman married to seven husbands, so as to trap Christ; there, "By what authority do you do these things?"; here, "What sign do you show us, so that we may believe you?"; elsewhere, "How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Son of God, tell us plainly." How many things did these bold fighters against Christ insolently contrive against the gentle and humble one who decreed forbearance, while he was turning water into wine for them, lodging with them, eating with them, comforting them, calling Samaritans to himself, justifying tax collectors, leading harlots to chastity, drying up flows of blood, driving out demons, cleansing lepers, [healing] the lame here and the bent there, straightening the woman bowed to the ground, strengthening paralytics, healing a withered hand, granting hearing to the deaf, sight to the blind, speech to the mute, some by himself, others through the disciples; walking on the sea, feeding thousands with a few loaves, raising the dead with a word. Thus he was to make us too, who were dead in trespasses and deceitful desires, alive together in himself, by the grace and compassion of his love for humankind; through whom and with whom be glory, honour and worship to the Father, with his all-holy, good and life-giving Spirit, now and always, and to all the endless ages of ages. Amen.

On the Universal Exaltation of the Precious and Life-giving Cross.

We keep the feast of the Cross, and the whole fullness of the Church flashes with light. We keep the feast of the Cross, and the face of the world is lit up with the sparkle of joy. We keep the feast of the Cross, through which darkness was driven away and light was brought [...] in its place. [?] to improvise a [?] discourse, as the title indicates.

[...] in its place. We keep the feast of the Cross, and we are lifted up with the Crucified, leaving the earth below together with sin, so that we may gain the things above. The Cross is exalted, and it raises up with it humanity lying on the ground, and strikes the insolence of the demons with terror. The Cross is exalted, and the hostile power of Satan falls, retreats and shrinks away. The Cross is exalted, and the whole fullness of the Church runs together. The Cross is exalted, and cities celebrate and peoples pour out libations of joy. For even to remember the Cross is plainly a cause of joy and a check on gloom. And to see even the figure of the Cross, how great a thing that is! For it becomes a source of courage and a release from fear for the one who looks at it. So great a possession has the Cross become; and whoever has acquired it has acquired a treasure. Perhaps you think I mean a treasure of gold, or of pearls and costly Indian stones, in which lovers of the body delight, haggling over things of no worth. But I would rightly call that the treasure which is the most beautiful and precious of all good things, both in fact and in name, in which, through which and for which the whole sum of our salvation, once lost, was restored. For if there had been no Cross, Christ would not have been crucified. If there had been no Cross, Life would not have been nailed to the wood; and if it had not been nailed, the springs of immortality, blood and water, the cleansing of the world, would not have gushed from his side; the bond of sin would not have been torn up; we would not have won our freedom; we would not have enjoyed the tree of life; paradise would not have been opened; the turning sword would not have yielded the way to Eden; the thief would not [have entered] paradise

Why do I say these things? If there had been no Cross, Christ would not have come on earth; and if Christ had not come on earth, there would have been no [?], no second birth of Christ, no God in man [?], no [?], no manger, no swaddling clothes, no circumcision on the eighth day, no subjection to parents, no growing up, no bodily growth, no manifestation, no sharing in baptism, no display of miracles, no Judas the traitor, no Pilate [?], no daring of the Jews crying out that the [?] be crucified. And if there had been no Cross, death would not have been [?], Hades would not have been despoiled, the bitter serpent would not have been put to death. That is why the Cross is a great and precious thing. Great, because many good things were achieved through it, as many as are the miracles and sufferings of Christ, the trophies of victory over everything [?]. Precious, because the Cross is both the suffering of God and a trophy: a suffering, because of the death [?] of the passion on it; a trophy, because on it the devil was wounded and death was [?] along with him, the bars of Hades were shattered, and the Cross became the common salvation of the whole world. The Cross is the hope of Christians, [?] of those who have come to know it [?], a harbour for the storm-tossed, [?] of the sick

[?] physician, giver of health, life of the dead, proclamation of true religion, muzzle of blasphemy. The Cross is a weapon against enemies, the sceptre of kingship, a diadem of beauty, an unwritten figure, a rod of power, a support of faith, a staff for old age, a guide for the blind, a light for those in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, the destruction of sin, the sign of repentance, the outline of righteousness. The Cross is a ladder leading to heaven, a road guiding to virtue, a bringer of life, [?] of death, estrangement from corruption, a quencher of fire, boldness before God, the key of the kingdom of heaven. The Cross is a guard by night, a tower by day, a hand to lead us in darkness, a bridle in good cheer, a comforter in despondency, a reconciler, a propitiator, a friend, an advocate, a defender, a helper. The Cross is a helper in temptations, a saviour in dangers, a consoler in despondency, a helper in hardships, a pilot at sea, relief in misfortunes. The Cross keeps watch at night over those who sleep, keeps vigil with those who are awake, and helps defend the weary [?]. The Cross is strength for the feeble, rest for those who toil, food for the hungry, strength for those who fast, trainer of athletes, covering of the naked, fellow traveller [?] of strangers. The Cross is the corrector of the rich, the provider of the poor, the protector of widows, the support and nurturer of orphans. The Cross is the honour of rulers, the might of kings, the victory of generals, the seal of purity, the bond of marriage. The Cross is the guardian of [?], the security of homes, the joiner of friendship, a defence against enemies, an opponent of foes, the [?] of the nations, a thorn to the barbarians, the arbiter of peace. The Cross is the president of love, the reconciliation of the world, the cancelling of [?], the height of heaven, the depth of the earth, the framework of creation, the length of the visible world, the breadth of the inhabited world; and, to put it briefly, the Cross is the sum of Christ's sufferings, of the miracles toward us [?]

This is also called the glory of Christ, and it is named the exaltation of Christ. It is also understood as the desired cup, and the culmination of Christ's sufferings for us. To see that the Cross is the glory of Christ, hear him saying: "Now the Son of Man is glorified, and God is glorified in him, and he will glorify him at once." And again: "Glorify me, Father, with the glory that I had with you before the world existed." And again: "Father, glorify your name." Then a voice came from heaven: "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again." By "glory" here he means the change in the elements and their suffering in sympathy that took place then at the Cross. For the creatures had to suffer together with the Creator. [?] and [?] of Christ, the figure freeing [?] leading [?]. [?]

[?] …the cross. Hear what he himself says: “When I am lifted up, then I will draw all people to myself”; as he also says elsewhere: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.” Why? “So that everyone who believes in him may not perish, but have eternal life.” Do you see that the cross is Christ’s glory and exaltation? Do you want to know that where there is exaltation, glory follows? Hear David saying: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth.” And Isaiah again, speaking as if in the person of Christ: “Now I will arise, says the Lord, now I will be exalted, now I will be glorified.” If exaltation is glory, and the cross is exalted today, then clearly Christ too is glorified. For if the cross is Christ’s glory, the cross is exalted today so that Christ may be glorified. Christ is not exalted so that the cross may be glorified; the cross is exalted so that Christ may be glorified. And Christ is glorified so that he may lift us up with himself. So the cross is exalted, and it lifts up with it the minds of the devout. Christ is glorified, and he glorifies with himself those who glorify him. The cross is exalted, and it pulls down the haughty brow of the demons. Christ is glorified, and he puts to shame the serpent, the author of evil. The cross is exalted, and it sets upright those who are falling. Christ is glorified, and he dims the shame of those who have [?] through sin. The cross is exalted, and idols fall. Christ is glorified, and the devil is struck down. The cross is exalted, not only because Christ was lifted up on it, but because, once it was brought to light, it exposed the madness of the Jews. How was it brought to light? Under the emperors who believed in Christ: not in the way some have supposedly fabricated such things, beguiling the many with plausible tales, but by a divine and simple power, and truly by the working and firmness of faith; for the treasure was God’s. For after his death on the cross the Lord of life and death came back to life in three days; and the Jews, pricked by the goads of envy and gripped by fear that something used in that venerable and blessed Passion might be preserved and become a weapon against the Jews and a safeguard for those who serve Christ as Master, [?]

had buried it in the recesses of the earth, hiding away the treasure: I mean the cross and everything connected with the cross, that is, the nails, and the spear, and what Pilate wrote [and] fixed on the cross.

Then, when God had placed the royal scepters and the whole Roman dominion in the hands of the Christians, it pleased him at that very time to act through a pious woman, an empress, a woman of royal mind, while her son was then reigning as emperor of the Christians. Without toil, and with what one might call divine delights, he made the woman wise, so that she brought to bear, sometimes with weighty authority and sometimes with ordinary flattery, but always in royal fashion, everything that could bend the unbending heart of the Jews. And indeed, as the empress searched, the common treasure quickly appeared, God swiftly holding out the gift to the woman: this, I mean, the Lord’s cross, which today is exalted throughout the whole world, together with all the things by which that blessed Passion, the salvation of the world, was accomplished. This, then, is why we keep festival today, this is why we celebrate: because the holy thing once hidden has today been revealed; because the treasure in hiding has shone forth like gold from the mines of the earth; because the most glorious [?] of the Christian empire, once buried, has been uncovered; because the storm of the demons has been stilled now that the cross has been revealed; because the sword forged by itself against the enemies has been brought to light from the earth; because the Church has recovered its own adornment; because the drachma she had lost the emperor’s rule has found. This is the cross of Christ, the Master’s sign, the saving weapon, the royal might, the trophy of victory, the boundary between things above and things below, the bond of those firm in faith, the summit of the apostles and the lens of the prophets, the crown of the martyrs, the pledge of those who worship Christ. For since the cross, Christ is worshipped; since the cross, the Son of God has been recognized; since the cross, we worship the Son together with the Father; since the cross, the ways of the Jews have ceased, those of the Greeks have been extinguished, those of the Christians have risen up; the air has been sanctified; we have been freed from the blood of the altars; of the bloodless [?]

worship we have tasted. Since the cross, we have been rid of the reek of demonic sacrifice and share in the spiritual fragrance of the ointment poured out; since the cross, the mythical genealogies of the gods have vanished; since the cross, we have come to know the mystery of the divine birth of Jesus in our nature; since the cross, we have learned [?] from the beginning that is without beginning [?]; since the cross, we have been taught faith in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and have shaken off the polytheistic idle myth-making of the Greeks; since the cross, we have set aside the shadows of the typological symbols and have [?] to the light of truth in grace. Since the cross, death is despised, demons are struck dumb, wooden idols are smashed, animal sacrifices have ceased, idol temples are overthrown. Everywhere there are churches, altars, psalmody, all-night vigils, theology, baptisms, communions of the faithful, knowledge of the Scriptures, [?] from earth, the gaining of heaven, participation in God. Why say more? Since the cross, human beings share citizenship with the angels, and heaven itself is open to those on earth, and God is contained among human beings and dwells with them. But, O cross, the precious boast of Christ and of us! O glorious wood, on which Christ was stretched out! Plant of immortality, from which Christ, the cluster of grapes, poured out for us the life-giving drink! O cross, through which the bond of sin was torn up and the covenant of freedom was written! O treasure of countless goods, [?] agent of paradise, [?] heir of the kingdom, redeemer from sins, giver of righteous deeds! Christ, crucified on you, revealed you as the tree of immortality. Christ, [?] on you, [made you] the ladder of the road leading to heaven [?]. Christ, hanging on you, showed you forth as the agent of blessing. Christ, stretched out on you, appointed you to loose the bonds of those in chains. On you Christ, willingly lifted up, lifted up the world with himself. On you Christ, lifted up for our sake, held up to public shame the arrogant

serpent. No longer does the biting serpent lie in wait for the heel by the road. No longer does a bronze serpent, by being looked upon, put an end to the bites of biting serpents. No longer is “cursed everyone who hangs on a tree.” How, and in what way? Because the blessed child Jesus, the Son of God, has changed the curse into blessing for us. The cross is no longer accursed, since the curse was nailed to the cross, and Christ took the curse away and brought in blessing for us in its place. This cross of Christ has become for us the bringer of all good things. This cross of the Master has been called by many names. The cross is called a rod: of uprightness, of kingship, of power, of inheritance. “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; a rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom.” “With your rod you redeemed your inheritance.” “The Lord will send forth for you a rod of power from Zion.” A staff: “Your staff and your rod, they have comforted me.” A tree of life: “She is a tree of life to all who lay hold of her, and safe for those who lean on her as on the Lord.” A tree: “He shall be like the tree that is planted.” Where? David says: “By the streams of water.” What waters? The divinely inspired Scriptures. A footstool: “Exalt the Lord our God, and worship at the footstool of his feet, for he is holy.” A place: “Let us enter into his dwellings, let us worship at the place where his feet stood.” “I will not give sleep to my eyes, nor slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob.” Hinting at this cross, Jacob the patriarch, once laying his hands crosswise on his grandsons, foretold it symbolically. Prefiguring this same cross, he “bowed down” to Joseph “over the top of his staff.” The staff of [?] bore the type of the cross — “the scepter of your inheritance” [?] [?] On the Exaltation of the Holy Cross [?]

of the patriarch Jacob, when he crossed the Jordan; for he says: “With my staff I crossed this Jordan.” And a little before these events, the sign of the cross was shown to Abraham, figured between the horns of the ram, when through the sheep he mystically performed the sacrifice in type, a foreshadowing of the Crucified. Isaac too fulfilled the type of the cross, taking up the wood for the sacrifice and readily following his father as he led him to be sacrificed. The rod of Moses had the power of the cross when it was changed into a serpent, [?] transforming the rods of the Egyptians: swallowing them up, turning the river’s stream to blood for them so that they could not drink, making frogs creep out of the waters at one time, and at another producing locusts and gnats and a darkness that could be felt, and all that brought about the calamities of the Egyptians. Moses’ rod bore the type of the cross when, as he split the Red Sea this way and that, the waters congealed into a wall for him and the people. The pillar of fire and of cloud, by which God guided wandering Israel as it fled from Egypt, bore the sign of the cross. Moses himself also kept the shape of the cross, holding his hands up high on the mountain when Joshua’s men were fighting the foreign Amalek; he was supported by Aaron and Hur, and Israel, strengthened, prevailed. The rod that struck the rock in the wilderness and showed it pregnant and bearing also fulfilled the type of the cross. And Isaiah, sawn in two with a wooden saw, did he not form a figure of the cross? I pass over the crucifixion of [?] and the nailing of Sisera with a tent peg, which plainly point to the cross. But I would also say that Elijah’s mantle revealed the power of the cross, when he parted the stream of the Jordan in two and crossed over as on dry land. And where shall we place Elisha’s miracle, when he put the wood into the water and [?] the iron from the depths of the river, raising the heavy by means of the light? And the rod that sprouted nuts — does it not clearly sketch the cross?

Truly great is the cross: attested and prefigured in many places of Scripture, it sketched in advance the patterns of the miracles that are performed through it every day. Venerate the cross, because through it we have come to know the Lord. The cross is to be venerated, because on it we bless the one who was crucified. The cross is to be venerated, because through it we have received the blessing and been freed from the curse. The cross is to be venerated, because through it we have vomited up the bitter taste of the tree of disobedience and tasted the sweetness of salvation. Blessed is the wood through which the nations were blessed. Blessed is the wood on which God was bodily stretched out. And what is more astonishing than this: to see God crucified, and that among thieves? Blessed is the wood through which a thief came to dwell in paradise, and the taste of this wood drove out the bitter taste of the other. What is more wonderful than this? That what Adam closed when he was caught, the thief opened when he recognized the Lord; and from the place where that one became an exile, this one was enrolled as an invited citizen. Bravo for this fitting exchange! A thief went out, and a thief went back in: the one through transgression, the other through recognition; the one led astray by him who tripped him by the heel, the other crucified together with the

Blessed is the wood from which the ark was built, symbolically saving the world from the flood. Blessed is the wood which father Adam did not taste first, and so exchanged life for death through the rashness of his tasting, laying hold of the tree of knowledge; then, partaking of it afterward, he perceived its quality and found his recall. Blessed is the wood through which the proud arm is bent, the necks of enemies bow down, the barbarian turns his back, and the Scythian flees with no one pursuing. Therefore lift up your voices with me today, and with Scripture let us offer words of worship [?] to the treasure of the cross. By the treasure of the cross I mean the Son of God, Christ, to whom it is all the more fitting that the words
be lifted up by us, as we say: “All the nations you have made will come and worship before you, O Lord, and will glorify your name; for you are great and do wonders; you [?].”

On the Exaltation of the Precious Cross. Let us move our lips today, beloved, like a lyre. “Awake, psaltery and harp.” “Sing praises to God, sing with understanding.” Let us sing the glories of the [?]. Let us show how often in Scripture the figure of exaltation appears, so that from this we may perhaps show that the exaltation of the cross is great and beyond this world, and that its finding is not celebrated in vain in the churches of God throughout the earth. The cross, then, is exalted, brought to light from the earth, though a short while ago it was hidden through envy. The cross is exalted, not to receive glory (for what greater glory could it attain than Christ, who was nailed to it?), but so that God may be glorified, who is worshipped on it and proclaimed through it. The cross is exalted so that it may lift up our horn with itself. The cross is exalted to humble the proud one. The cross is exalted to bind the strong man and through us to plunder his goods. The cross is exalted to show the envy of the Jews to be empty; so that the treasure of life might not lie buried in the earth unnoticed; so that we might recover the pearl which the crucifiers, even against their will, [?]. For it was not [?] for them to take away the treasure of life for ever; and the wretches, examined in many ways and convicted by their own wickedness, were not going to escape for ever the [?] eye. What

does God do, he who on it and through it accomplished salvation for the whole world in the midst of the earth? Into the empress, as we said a little earlier, he puts a burning longing; into them he casts a fear that throws their whole life into turmoil. And they, when they saw that the search could not be avoided, made a willing act of what they did not wish, and revealed the precious sign of the Master. And it came forth from the depths beneath the earth as if from some other firmament, like the sun, flashing out the Master’s rays. So the Master’s sign came forth from the inner sanctuaries of the earth, the sign by which the depths of Hades were shaken and set free the souls held there. The Lord’s cross came forth from its earthen chambers like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber, the cross through which the Church of the nations, wedded to Christ, put away the many-begotten godlessness of the Greeks. The spiritual pearl of the faithful came forth, set like a lychnite gem in the crown of Christ, to flash its light over the whole inhabited world. The adornment of the Church came forth, the Lord’s cross, to adorn the whole of creation on earth. The innocent one came forth as from prison, to call back the guilty; from bonds came forth the one who cannot be held, to set the prisoners free; from dark places came forth the lampstand of light, so that, dispelling the night of ignorance, it might shine forth the light of knowledge. Fittingly, then, the Church, rejoicing with the Lord’s cross, arrays herself in her robe, and, unveiling her bridal beauty, gives dignity to the face of the day. Fittingly too this great people has gathered today, to behold the cross revealed today and, beholding it, to worship Christ exalted together with it. For it was revealed in order to be exalted; and it is exalted in order to be revealed. What is it? That which a little while ago lay hidden in the Place of the Skull, but is now worshipped everywhere. This we celebrate today; this we honor with festivity; this is the chief point of the present feast, this the revelation of the mystery. But it is now time to confirm the exaltation of the cross itself with the testimonies of Scripture. For this is what we promised a little earlier, even if the discourse ran ahead and passed over what lay between. For it was necessary, it was necessary that [?] become manifest; [?] the spiritual pearl of the faithful

that hidden and [?] wood, to be shown to all on high, like a city set on a mountain or a lamp raised on a lampstand. For this reason the first among the Christians who first took up the scepters of empire, in a triumph of the whole Church together, gave orders that it be raised aloft as from some lofty watchtower and displayed to the whole congregation. And this is what those who now hold the helm of the high priesthood do: going up to the raised place in the church, and holding up on high this most glorious and greatly venerated cross, they exalt it, and, stretching it up aloft in many directions, show it to the peoples, all but crying out: Behold, the hidden treasure of salvation has been found! Behold the seal with which we were sealed! Behold the cross through which we became known to the Crucified! Behold the horn “with which we will gore our enemies”; by which we pass unharmed over the snares of the enemy; trusting in which we [?] the blows of the demons as “the arrows of children.” Behold, today we see “our life hanging before us.” Let us hear, then, the prophet saying: “Exalt the Lord our God, and worship at the footstool of his feet, for it is holy.” Let us say with David the songs of David: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth.” “Be exalted, you who judge the earth.” “Let your hand be exalted.” “Let your hand be strong; let your right hand be exalted.” “Do not forget your poor for ever.” “But in your good pleasure let our horn be exalted.” Let us enter the very paradise of Scripture. Let us gather, like flowers, what is most useful for the occasion. Let us take as our guides the prophets, who point to the exaltation of the cross.

And let Moses be brought before us first, God’s servant and lawgiver, who lifted up that bronze serpent — not that it might be glorified, but that it might be held up to shame, and that, setting the rust of the bronze against the venom of wickedness, he might show by comparison the [?] of the bronze. So that bronze serpent was lifted up, not as a prefiguration or type of the cross, but as an antitype of the type, or a type understood figuratively. Moses himself also once lifted up his hands as a type of the

crucified Christ and of the cross now being exalted. “Let the sun stand still over Gibeon, and the moon over the valley of Aijalon,” Joshua once prayed as he was destroying Amalek — not only to point to the day of the cross, on which darkness spread over the whole earth, nor only to confirm on that day the height of God’s power and the arm lifted up against the enemies, but also to foretell the exaltation of the cross and to prefigure the ascent on it of the Sun of glory. Abraham too offers the sacrifice as a type of the mystical victim; but, obeying at once the voice from on high, he symbolically sacrificed the ram that appeared in the thicket of Sabek, on the lofty summit of the mountain, prefiguring the raising of the cross on high. Azariah and his companions once raised their hands on high in the fire of the Babylonian furnace as they prayed, and quenched the flame of the furnace that had risen on high, forming by the stretching out of their hands the figure of the exalted cross. Jonah once lifted up his voice, lifting his hands in the shape of a cross, and at once drew down power from on high, and was cast out by the sea beast unharmed. The renowned Judith once lifted up the scimitar against the head of Holofernes as he slept, prefiguring the exaltation of the cross, and won salvation for Israel. Daniel once lifted up his voice in the lions’ den to the Most High, prefiguring the exaltation of the cross, when the prophet Habakkuk, snatched up in an instant, brought him his meal. And what does Jeremiah mean, speaking in the person of the murderers of the Lord: “Come, they say, let us put wood into his bread, and wipe out his life from the earth”? And what does Isaiah intend by saying similar things, at one point: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer”; and, “In his humiliation his judgment was taken away, for his life is taken from the earth”; and at another: “And he bore the sins of many”? Where, if not on the wood of the cross? To which they nailed the bread and would not let go until they had raised it on high, as a testimony to those who saw it and as a type of the exaltation that lay ahead. What could we say this is, if not the exaltation and display of the cross? Just as the slaughter of the sheep too — the sheep that was carried up on the cross and nailed the sins of the world to it — clearly shows the exaltation of the cross itself. And [?] to bring forward the scriptural testimonies that proclaimed the exaltation of the cross in advance, but so that the discourse may not become tedious to the
But let us, worshipping Christ on it, consider the greatness of his power and all the wonders worked for us through him, just as

…as the most divine David says: “God, our King before the ages, has worked salvation in the midst of the earth.” Let no one doubt that the Place of the Skull is set firm in the midst of the earth. For it was necessary that, just as when a circle is drawn on a flat surface, the saving wood should be planted at the centre of the whole earth, so that, like another sun shining in heaven, the Sun of righteousness, standing at mid-heaven as if from a firmament of the cross, might send out his rays of light and, having set, might by the cross shine also upon those held beneath the mound of earth. This cross is both a visible wood and is called a sign in many places in Scripture. For what does David mean when he says: “Show me a sign for good”? And: “Let the light of your countenance be marked upon us, O Lord”? And: “You have given those who fear you a sign, so that they may flee from before the bow”? Or what the Lord himself cries out in the Gospels: “And then they will see the sign of God”? And before this: “This generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah the prophet,” which itself is also shown forth through the cross? And when Simeon, who received God, blessed the Virgin as he took into his arms the Lord who had appeared as an infant, what does he mean by saying: “This child is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be spoken against”? Did he not clearly hint at the cross through the sign? But the cross is also called power. For what does David say? “You have made your power known among the peoples.” And also arm: “With your arm you redeemed your people.” And that the cross is also the power of Christ, hear Paul saying: “The word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.” Hear also Christ himself saying to Moses: “I will surely harden Pharaoh’s heart, so that I may show all my power in him.” Here he speaks of power, meaning the all-powerful demonstration shown in advance through the rod of Moses as a type of the cross, by which he displayed his astonishing wonders [?]. This is how we have been taught to think and understand about the cross. This is how we urge the faithful people of God to honour the cross and revere it always. For through it the nations were gathered in the net; the faith was sown everywhere. For by it the disciples of Christ,

tilling barren human nature as with a plough and making the crops of the Church ever-flourishing, gathered an abundant harvest of those who had believed in Christ. Strengthened by it, the martyrs, even as they fell, struck down those who struck them. Through it Christ was made known, and the Church of the faithful, continually unrolling the Scripture, brings forward the same Christ, the Son of God, himself God and himself Lord, crying out with a loud voice: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” Through it the cause of the Christians flourishes and spreads everywhere. Through it kingship is strengthened, the commonwealth is made firm, enemies fall, the pride of the barbarians is taken captive, Israel is slaughtered, demons are struck as by lightning; for in it and through it we believe that we are saved, and it is “the sign of the Son of Man”; and, as it is written, “in it all flesh will see the salvation of our God.” And: “The Jews will look [and mourn] on him whom they pierced.” But we, all who have walked in its light, will be glorified with it and will reign with God, dancing with the angels around the Trinity, worshipped in Father, Son and Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

All of you who have come to this venerable sanctuary of the Mother of God, come here, I beg you, and help me today as I labour over my discourse and stand helpless before the height and depth of the wonder. Then, climbing together to the very summit, as the saying goes, let us peer into the mysteries of God and listen to words spoken over a tomb.

The saving and supremely good Word, then, who is both personal and beyond being, having lived out in the flesh on earth the whole economy of salvation on our behalf, and having fulfilled what had been foretold of him long ago, showing us in himself and himself wholly in us, has filled heaven and earth with glory and has enriched the whole creation with his holiness. Grappling with the author of evil through the cross, he conquered him; wrestling with death, he broke its tyranny over us; and he overthrew the lightless region of Hades and the kingdom there, its all-devouring [?], yet, I think, without entirely removing the boundaries set by the ancient curse. For it was the word of God that those once brought forth from the earth should be brought back to the earth, since [our nature], once made earthy, had not yet been set free from the slavery of generation and corruption [?]. And it was necessary that he who “was made like his brothers in every respect, without sin,” should display in himself all the marks of our nature. For this reason he, being God, became man out of love for mankind, and tasted sufferings to show his kinship with us, so that through the sufferings of the one who cannot suffer we might perhaps come to be beyond sufferings. For this reason too he consented to undergo the experience of corruption, to keep company with death, and to enter the joyless land of Hades, so that we, escaping from the bonds there, might pass over into incorruption. Yet we shall not on that account escape natural death, since it was by grace alone, and not by nature, that we received our being and were fashioned immortal. Why, then, do I say these things, brothers, and for what reason have I now been led into these words? Because if we are to touch the mysteries of her supernatural passing, the discourse must be led back a little to the Master, Lord and God of us all, Jesus Christ, and then, in due order, yoked back to the subject before us. For since it was laid up by necessity for human beings to die once, and this was altogether inescapable for our nature, [death having come] chiefly through the disobedience [?], he set us free from the bitter slavery of death, and, as the Hierophant says, [delivered] “all those who through fear of death were throughout

their whole life subject to slavery.” Someone might object: “Why then shall we not now die that death?” Yes, we shall die. But not [?] as before, when we were held fast by death through the bond of sin [?]; if so, this could not rightly even be called dying. For there are, there are some who will escape even this, but will be changed, according to the sacred revelation. That, truly, is the tyranny of death and death indeed: when, having died, we are no longer allowed to return to life. But when we die and after dying live again, and a better life at that, this is plainly not death but sleep, a return to the second life, which, through the complete cessation of earthly things, leads and escorts those who depart from here to there. This is what the author of Proverbs clearly indicates: “Death,” he says, “is rest for a man.” For God has shut up [?] … [?] of no longer, it may be, being active in what it naturally does. And what else could death be understood to be than the separation of the soul from the body, [?] summoning us, on the one hand, to the hope of the resurrection [?] of such a disjunction of the parts and then to their joining together again, and on the other assuring us through hope of a passage to incorruption and to a better lot, so that we no longer serve sin, according to [?], that is, the things of sense, most prone to passion [?]. If, then, the very Lord of life and death, the life of all, the resurrection of the dead, the light of the world, he who “by his own death destroyed him who has the power of death,” did not think it right, bent by his love for mankind, to pass by even this law unfulfilled, but, so that he might be made like us in all things, showed that this descent into the earth had necessarily to be made, and himself chose the same bond as ours, “walking in the midst of the shadow of death,” as it is written, and spending three days in the lowest parts of the earth, where the souls of those already dead were held captive, bound by inescapable chains, to whom the good news was also proclaimed, according to blessed Peter: “For he went and preached also to the spirits in prison,” how could it not be clear and wholly beyond dispute that now too the souls of all human beings, and indeed of the saints, pass through that unseen place, but are not

held there, except those who through laxity in life have drawn upon themselves the death that comes through sin? For all those who have submitted themselves to the divine laws and have shown forth in the Spirit, through the flesh, the citizenship of heaven, are clearly escorted on and transferred to places of light befitting such a holy state of the saints, over which the Lord watches, and, according to the oracle, his eyes continually look upon them. Their beauty and greatness and their unending state of blessedness, and, I will add, their loveliness beyond understanding, would rightly be seen more clearly and more loftily by those who are nearer to God than we are, who have finished their course here and received their rest, and for whom these things have been prepared all the more by the Providence that governs all things wisely. So the souls of the saints will pass, as has been shown, through the gates of Hades, “for the disciple is not above his teacher”; yet they will not, I think, be held there as before, when, as it is written, “sin reigned together with death.” They will pass through (listen with understanding) not so as to perish, but so as to explore and to be initiated there too into the strange mystery of the divine economy (I mean the descent into Hades, which Jesus, the source of life, made willingly for our sake, enduring death through the cross, he who cannot suffer or perish), and further to be taught the supernatural account of what was accomplished there, and how great and of what kind was the victory won by the Saviour through [?], when he broke down the everlasting bars. These things, then, we have recalled from the sacred oracles, and they have been examined in advance not without bearing on what we are about to say. Therefore I think it entirely consistent and fitting, having handled with care the matters concerning the hidden and glorious falling asleep of this holy-born Ever-Virgin, to set them before those who love what is good and love to behold it. For, if the truth must be told, the natural death of human beings came even as far as her; not [?] imprisoning her, as it does us, or harshly overpowering her, but only so far that she experienced its sleep, that sleep which escorts us to the things hoped for beyond this world, as though by a kind of [?] movement, so to speak, transforming us into a godlike state; as, for example, with that first sleep which the first man slept, when [?] the side for the completion of our kind, and he received back what was lacking from the part taken away. In this way, I think, she too, having fallen asleep according to nature,

tasted death, but did not remain in its grip, except so far as to yield to the laws of nature and to fulfil the economy which Providence, pervading all things, established for us from the beginning; and indeed to show clearly the manner in which she underwent the movement that passes from corruptible things to incorruptible ones. For it was not otherwise lawful to put off this flowing life, except by such a separation of the parts taking place according to nature. For if, according to the oracle, “there is no man who shall live and not see death,” and she who is now hymned is a human being, though also beyond human beings, it has surely been clearly shown that she too fulfilled the same law of nature as we do, even if perhaps not as we do but beyond us, and [?] the cause for which we are compelled to undergo this at all. This is how you are to understand her descent into Hades: in her case, by my definition and reckoning, the separation of the parts prevailed for as long a time as the course of natural movement required for her to gain knowledge by experience of the unknown regions, setting foot on them for the first time and passing through them as on a foreign and untrodden journey. Be gracious to us, O Virgin who received God and bore life, as we venture upon what cannot be attained, search out the depth of the hidden mysteries concerning you, and attempt to contemplate the divine works wrought in you in the incomprehensible abyss of God’s judgments. Merely to gaze on them in the mind’s contemplation instils fear even in those whose understanding is lofty, to say nothing of us who are more fleshly and who cover the beast with a fleece. Only so far as to show that you shared with us in the laws of nature have these things been set out beforehand by us with great fear. But the loftier of the mighty works accomplished in you, since you yourself experienced communion with them, you would know better, O all-blessed one, more divinely and purely than our discourse relates; and above all your only-begotten Son himself, who established the ages and clothed you with fitting glory and splendour, because of the flesh lent to him, which he assumed and gave being to; glory so great that none of us, nor perhaps even the most exalted angels, could grasp it with the mind. But let these things always be honoured and kept in divine and mystical secrecy, holding their own account of the truth until the final restoration of all that exists. Yet do not send us away without a share in your divine narratives; give us a word, as Mother of the Word, and make known to us the manner of what was accomplished in you [?]. For every hearer of divine things is still [?] bending toward you to hear your voice, as

she says, having transgressed none of the laws of human nature, but having accomplished everything both in a new way and in accordance with nature: “With my soul I magnify the Lord,” and I rejoice in my spirit, while in my body I am changed and formed into deification by grace, making that deification both beginning and end which the God beyond God, ineffably made flesh in my womb, displayed when he refashioned the human, deified in himself, and which he bestowed on us by participation in the Spirit, ascending with his body from the regions of earth into the heavens, which he never left. He, bent by his care for humanity, “looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid,” intending at once to lift the first curse of Eve; and by his appearing in the flesh he visited “those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death,” rising as the Dayspring from on high, and directed our feet into the way of peace. For being truly God, he was called man, born of me supernaturally from virginal blood, bringing into nature a strange conception and birth, so that through this innovation in the natures the old things might be taken away and new things brought in in their place, things that do not grow old, and all things might become new, and there might be a truly new creation through this new and most praiseworthy incarnation of the Word. For where among those before us was it ever heard that a woman became the Mother of God? Or that God was called the son of a woman? Or that a human form was above the Cherubim, appearing through a divine birth [?] and governing the universe? Who taught the worshippers above and below to worship the deified clay and the exalted dust as one Lord, the one object of reverence in both, without division? Who raised to heaven the lowly and earthbound lowest rank of humanity, which by its godlike [nature] swam beyond the bounds of nature, and showed the untrodden places to be trodden, opening a new path unknown to those on earth, so that human beings might be shown to be fellow citizens with the angels? These great things, then, have clearly come to pass in me, and through them I have received as my portion such great glory and splendour. Therefore rightly “from now on all generations will call me blessed, [for] he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name.” And what is greater than to be called, and to be, the Mother of God? As for the departure I have made from among human beings, you may gather knowledge of it more clearly from this very place, from which the substance of my earthly tabernacle was translated and departed—I mean of the virginal and God-receiving body from which the simple Jesus was composed. For anyone who wishes may infer what has been said from what is seen. Indeed, set before the eyes of those who faithfully contemplate divine things are certain vivid images and speaking imprints of my translation: this is that tomb, hewn in the rock, which has stood unharmed to this day, showing through the outline of the burial,

with a voice that makes no proclamation, the tokens of what happened. The most truthful witnesses of the laying of the body in it are the hollows in the rock, which inscribe as in sacred writing the seemly impressions of the limbs. And first of all that torrent of the Kidron, within which all these things are enclosed, trumpets the wonders aloud. I mean the Valley of Weeping, where the tomb of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, stands, in which that blessed passion of the one who cannot suffer had its beginnings. For there the Saviour often lodged with his disciples. There he prayed on bended knee to the Father in heaven, asking, by an ineffable economy, to be spared the cup he desired. There, stripped bare by the traitor [?], he was handed over to the God-slayers. And those who come to the place may learn these things more truly by experience. Let the unbeliever, then, go and learn the force of what is said by seeing it for himself; let the believer be content with what is said, and perceive through the things that appear the things that are not seen, and marvel at what is worthy of marvel. Such, then, is the burial, and so it stands. But the manner of the translation, though common to all, yet has a dignity peculiar to it, surpassing that of each individual. This translation is beyond word and hearing, yet it has its likeness in ancient examples. And what is the place of rest? Is it grasped by the senses, or contained by thought? Not at all. For how could it be seen, and by whom could it be understood, not being of such a nature, except by those who through freedom from passion, by infinitely generous grace, have already reached the place there and been counted worthy of the delight of the godlike state there? As my forefather David says: “In the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God, with the voice of rejoicing and thanksgiving, the sound of those keeping festival.” Such are the words of the Mother of God, from whose tongue the sweetness of the Spirit drips, “and grace is poured upon her lips.” But what should we say to these things, brothers, except to marvel at the infinitely great Providence that governs all things, saying: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how inscrutable his ways!” and the rest of the passage. For

these are truly the works of a divine hand and beyond human comprehension. Merely to fix the mind on them instils fear even in one whose mind is very lofty and [?]; how much more in me, who am [?] and grovelling, able to understand nothing but clay and matter and all that flows and passes away, and who therefore tremble and grow dizzy, lest the greatness of the day be outraged by the filth of my presumption and weakness [?]. One of the very [?] might reasonably wonder why we know of none of the theologians who has written about the undefiled and [?] translation of the Mother of God, or [?] composed any treatise for us, as they composed the divine book of the Gospels and handed down the theological histories. And we answer: because the falling asleep of the God-receiving one took place [many] years later [?]. For it is said that she reached extreme old age before departing from here. Or because the times did not yet allow an account of these things, since it was not yet timely, according to the very writing of the Gospel, for the word of the economy, newly sown, to speak [?] about these things, this being, as [?] specific, a matter for another occasion and treatment than at that time. But if it was for these reasons, we do not know what we should say. If, however, it was because the Spirit-bearing men carried the account of the economy only as far as the sojourn of the Word with us in the flesh, and set forth nothing beyond his ascent from the earth, and this is why they kept silent, I too am persuaded. Yet, lest, after all we have said, some should think that the mystery of the day has been handed down in complete silence, I think it good to add to the discourse what has been found, as far as we are able, for the understanding and confirmation of the subject before us. For it is not entirely [?] unpublished in the sacred oracles, even if it has been seen somewhat more dimly. It has been said, then, by one of the theologians [?] … wisely and knowledgeably [?], as he says, and of the mystical [?] of the supercelestial minds [?] in a manner befitting angels [?] to have been revealed. And further, the ineffable [?] revealed to the divine Paul through an excess of [?] to have been dictated, of which the [?]

[?] the world cannot hold the naming of God, since it lies beyond all hiddenness and all speech. Who is this, if you wish to know? Or shall I set his name aside and make him known to you by the marks that belong to the man, as one knows the lion by its claws? Yet I think that those who are not unacquainted with his [?] are not wholly ignorant of the man. His name, then, must be stated, in case the argument may also gain credibility through it. This is Dionysius, great in divine things, great in the teachings he heard of heaven, and in all that are images and likenesses of the unnameable naming of God. In his most holy treatise On the Divine Names, in the third chapter, which deals with this, that is, with the power of prayer, and with the blessed Hierotheus, and with reverence and theological writing, he reaches this point in his discourse and, recounting in a digression the things concerning that divine man, says the following in his letter to Timothy: "And indeed we have taken great care in this as well: where our divine guide himself has set things out clearly, we have attempted nothing at all that would merely repeat him in explaining the same passage of Scripture that was before him. For even among our God-inspired hierarchs themselves, when we too, as you know, and you yourself, and many of our holy brothers had come together to view the life-originating and God-receiving body, and James the brother of God was also present, and Peter, the chief and most venerable summit of the theologians, it then seemed good after the viewing that all the hierarchs should praise in hymns, as each was able, the infinitely powerful goodness of the divine weakness. After the theologians, as you know, he surpassed all the other sacred initiates. He was wholly carried away, wholly outside himself, and he experienced communion with the things he was hymning. By all who heard and saw him, whether they knew him or did not, he was judged to be possessed by God and a divine singer of hymns." O truly blessed soul and tongue, that were initiated into these things and uttered them! O, who would give to me

to my ears the echoes of what was hymned in a manner worthy of God! For if among those men, though they had been allotted so exalted a life and a contemplation of the mind untouched by things below, the one who sang the hymn was so admired, how great must have been the things he hymned, or rather the One he hymned? But let the discourse go on to what follows. "And what," he says, "should I tell you of the theology spoken there? For unless I have forgotten myself, I know that I often heard from you parts of those inspired hymns, so eager are you not to pursue divine things as a side matter. But I pass over the mysteries there, since they are unspeakable to the many and already known to you." This is what Dionysius tells us, that lofty guide in theology, the high-flying eagle of the heavens, the most [?] mind. I think it right not to pass hastily over these words, but to dwell on them as far as I can and to enter into the depth of their meaning, so that what we long for may be shown in sharper relief and now more plainly. And you, I pray, consider reverently the force of what is about to be said, so that you may understand where these mysteries lead and learn who and of what kind were those gathered in that assembly, [?] and the wonder of the sacred revealer himself [?]. Come then, let us set out from the stations of ever-memorable Zion (for the discourse brought us there a little earlier [?], since the Mother of God had it as her dwelling), and from there let us now fittingly escort the virginal body in procession. For it was there that the Mother of God committed her own soul into the hands of him in whose hand are the souls of us all, and brought her life in the flesh to its end. Then, having duly made the funeral procession, let us join [?] praise to the escort of hymns. In this way our discourse will run in proper order, and what has been said will be clearly unfolded. That this may happen, beloved, come, set out, and go with the brightest and most delightful keenness of mind to holy Gethsemane, and form in yourself a clear image, judging what has been said by the course of the events. For you will not need [?] words for the [?] of knowledge, [?] by deeds. "All things are plain to those who understand, and right to those who find knowledge." There, then, you will find a very beautiful [?], adorned and bright [?] [?]

adornment set around it. Beneath this surpassing and sacredly built house, observe the virginal shrine of the Theotokos, the bridal chamber. Look around with the eyes of faith at the place where the Queen's limbs, inscribed with holiness, were laid. Not long after the burial, when her holy tabernacle had been taken away, the hollows carved into the rock itself received their imprint, not made by hands. There too you will find the gathering of the sacred initiates who arrived so fittingly, if you search it out mystically by the contemplation of the mind. For the hierophant says that by an unspeakable good pleasure there was present at that time a throng of holy men not easily counted. So that we may be judged worthy to understand what has been said, come, let us be led by the hand by the mystical guidance of the divine Spirit, and let us take the Mother of the Word as the helper of our word. For she will be present as a giver of good things, teaching us and granting us understanding beyond anything we ask. But may you yourself also be present, our guide, initiate and beholder of things beyond grasp, priest who offers sacrifice in the true tabernacle. Lead by the hand one who longs to linger in your writings, and guide my mind unerringly toward the force of what we are seeking, through the vision of mystical apprehension. The inspired man, then, shows us through his own words that almost the whole company of the holy apostles had gathered around that venerable and great spectacle of the Mother of God, and that the disciples who were scattered through the whole earth were brought together at that time, among whom was he himself, along with Timothy and Hierotheus, those wise in God. "For when," he says, "we too, as you know, and you yourself, and many of our holy brothers came together to view the life-originating and God-receiving body." By "life-originating body" we can understand nothing else than the God-receiving and virginal tabernacle, from which the one beyond being deified the nature he assumed and, truly coming into being, took on being beyond being. For it is not the Lord's body that is meant, since those who came to believe after the Passion were not present before the Passion. And by "God-possessed hierarchs" I think he clearly indicates here the members of the company of the disciples, as the leaders of the word. Nor is it any wonder if the Spirit that once lifted up Elijah and took him up as the fiery charioteer of heaven should then suddenly have gathered these men too in the spirit by means of a cloud. For all things are very easy for God, as we have learned from Habakkuk and Daniel. And how many others, beloved, do you suppose were brought together there as followers from one place and another? For that is what "and many of our holy brothers" shows. So it is clear that not even the seventy, who were later appointed disciples of Christ, were missing from that council chosen by God. For it was fitting that the first should be brought there as the first workers of the mystery and lovers of the spectacle, and certain others immediately after them, as holding second place in theology, driven together by the divine Spirit,

[?] be brought. This he shows by what he adds: "And James the brother of God was also present, and Peter, the chief and most venerable summit of the theologians." One might well marvel when one considers how suddenly they assembled. When they had all come together in Jerusalem (and there was a countless throng around them), what follows will show what happened and what was done. "Then it seemed good," he says, "after the viewing, that all the hierarchs should praise in hymns, as each was able, the infinitely powerful goodness of the divine weakness." But what was that sight, how great its beauty, and what the hymned theology of [?] loveliness? Come, let us see, if indeed it can be seen with the eyes of the mind. In my view, the radiant and seemly sight that then appeared to the God-possessed would have been the all-shining divine radiance of the virginal tabernacle. In it was seen the life-originating and wholly luminous body of the Theotokos, which is beyond us and yet ours. Through it Jesus, the Author of life, granted us the beginning of a more divine life, making our firstfruits the beginning of life, the firstfruits he fashioned for himself beyond nature from a virginal womb. "If the firstfruits are holy," says the Apostle, "so clearly is the whole lump; and if the root is holy, so surely are the branches." Life-originating, then, is the body of the Theotokos, which received into itself the whole life-originating fullness of the Godhead. It is the precious treasure of virginity, the surpassing heaven, the earth tilled by God, the firstfruits of the Adamic lump deified in Christ, the image wholly like the original beauty, the treasurer sealed by God who keeps God's unspeakable judgments, the dwelling place of the virtues, the spiritual tablet on which are written the divine purposes of God's dispensation toward us, the inexpressible depth of the inexhaustible fullness "of him who fills all in all," the unbreakable tower of hidden hopes, the treasure-house of an incorruption beyond understanding, the royal robe of the Word made man, the earthly palace of the heavenly King, the renowned workshop of the divine exchanges [?], the all-harmonious material of the divine embodiment, the clay brought to perfection by God of the [?] master-craftsman, from which he who is beyond being, wholly and truly coming into being, took on being. [?] Truly blessed eyes, and lips [?] [?] the most radiant vehicle? She is the lamp [?] [?] the sun of righteousness, nature beyond [?]. She is the spiritual mirror of [?]; by her brightness [?]

[?] God, we were illumined. She is the throne, high and lifted up, on which the Lord of Sabaoth was seen seated by Isaiah, the most clear-sighted of the prophets. She is the royal dignity of the heavenly race, the sanctuary of all holy worship, the spiritual incense of the divine whole burnt offerings, the tongs that held the purifying coal, the Levitical rod, the root of Jesse, the scepter of David, the mother of the Creator, the nurse of the one who nourishes all, the gate of Christ the Dayspring, who rose as the dawn from on high, the small bosom of him who contains all things, the spotless garment of the Lamb and Shepherd, the heifer that never bore the yoke, mother of the fatted calf, the purest fleece that received the heavenly dew, the virgin earth of him who refashioned Adam, the heaven of him who made the earth heaven, the great vision of the prophets. In many parts and in many ways the saints saw her in visions, and through her they were taught in symbols the mystical works of divine fashioning and the great mystery of the dispensation [?]. She is the great world in a small one, belonging to him who brought the world from nothing into being, [bearer of] the angel of his greatness. But how could those who saw her, so honored and made glorious by God, the author of all creation and sustainer of the universe, lying on a bier, her bodily powers then at rest, not be struck with wonder? This, I think, is what the hierophant means when he says, "the infinitely powerful goodness of the divine weakness." For the sight was full of awe: she who bore Life was borne as one dead; she who conversed with God was voiceless; she who received Life in her womb [?] lay dead and breathless on a bier. These things are foreign to nature, but not without wonder. For there were mysteries there for the mind, for anyone able to see divine things spiritually: childbirth and virginity, the principles of providence and judgment, of exaltation and lowering, of greatness and humility. There something bodily dimmed the rays of the sun. There an ever-living mortality shone around the eyes of those who beheld it. There a wealth filled the whole of heaven and the things of earth. It was a new sight, the most remarkable of all sights. What is this maternal tabernacle lying on a pallet, from which God came forth as man, bearing our image, and, to sum it up, in which the lump of our nature that had become earthbound was refashioned and deified? Such was the sight, and so it stood; and perhaps it was greater than we have managed to describe in our modest way. But as for what the hymn was, and of what kind were the things hymned, let Christ be present and give us speech, since he is Word and Wisdom and Power, and let him guide our mind to the bright radiance of the divine hymns, by which [?]

may our understanding always be [?], and by which may we be illumined and held fast in Christ himself, our Lord, to whom be glory and might, with the almighty Father and the life-giving Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. [?]

[?] The present festival is a mystery. Its subject is the falling asleep of the Theotokos, and it surpasses the power of words. It is a mystery not already celebrated among [?], but now honored and cherished by all. And this is our festival: the manifestation, or rather the unfolding, of the mystery. Though it would prefer silence to words, it is compelled by longing, and yields a little to words and allows them to speak. Yet although words have [?] confidence, they are not ignorant of their own weakness, nor of how modestly they can render what is due to the secret of the long silence. The gift, then, must be celebrated, and not buried, not because it was recently discovered, but because it has returned to its proper [?]. For since it was not [?] by some of those before us [?] to be kept silent already [?], but because it did not escape notice, it is a holy duty to proclaim it. So let there be one common festival today for those in heaven and those on earth; let men rejoice together with angels, and let every tongue dance and sing "Hail" to the Theotokos. For Gabriel too first [?] this as the prelude to the mystery, when the most illustrious work of all theology, the divine fashioning of Jesus in our nature, was being newly formed in the virginal workshop of nature according to an ineffable dispensation. And we in turn must offer this greeting to the Queen of our race as a special prize and thank-offering, since it is fitting to say "Hail" to her at her departure as well. For she alone brought joy to dwell among us, [and banished] the grief of our first mother. "Let us sound the trumpet [?]; let us take up the psaltery and the harp." Let us sing to the Mother of God; let us sing, striking up not a wedding song but a funeral song. But someone who has considered these things very carefully might reasonably want to learn: for what reason

[?] did you call Zion to mind, you who speak of the brightness of this sacred hymnody? I would answer him that it was not without purpose [?]. This man called the all-holy [?] to mind [?], for there this great mystery of the Theotokos was revealed to the initiated. In that place the slabs laid on the ground where the holy knees of her all-pure body knelt cry aloud [?]. For she had this as her dwelling throughout the whole time of her sojourn on earth. There, after she had submitted to the laws of nature, she reached the end of her life, escaping the notice of the ruler of darkness here too, just as in giving birth she escaped the lot of mothers: she of the holy name, called by God, utterly blameless, who filled heaven and earth with glory and grace by the greatness of her departure, so worthy of God. If I wished to go through her story in order, her origin, her conception and her birth, I would find neither time enough for the discourse nor power of speech equal to the facts.
