For it is not possible to compress into [?] all the things for which she is honored: I mean the good fortune of her family, the distinction of both her parents, with the priestly dignity on one side and the royal on the other vying in splendor; the childlessness, the barrenness, their prayers, the frequent sacrifices with which they besought God, pleading and imploring, that he would loose the bonds of barrenness, that the childless might be shown fruitful instead of barren, [?] bearing fruit out of fruitlessness. Then the end of the barrenness, the fulfilment of the promise, and a little before these, the visions in dreams and the voices heard while awake, all that the holy ones, both together and individually, called by God through [?] higher than sight, received as oracles by divine illumination. In addition to these, her [?] coming forth into the world, the swaddling clothes, her [entry] into the divine temple, how the fair offering was dedicated to God, how she dwelt in the inner sanctuary as in golden chambers, [and] of food
Constant[inople?]: Whence also Nestorius, having arrived in the city of the Ephesians, where John the Theologian and the Virgin Theotokos, holy Mary, [had lived?]. [?] Nestorius, when [?]

[of ambrosia?], no common food, she partook. Then [?] her upbringing, her growth from childhood, her coming of age, and all the signs of complete maturity, through which, as was right, as she grew to youth she was raised in due measure to things beyond nature. I pass over the mysteries hidden in her pregnancy, which is utterly beyond knowing, and those that followed the supernatural and ineffable birth of Jesus, God made manifest: for example, her incorruption, the birth without the pangs of childbed, her spotlessness, the inviolate state of her virginal treasure, the strange nursing amid wonders, the purification under the law, the prophecies in the temple, in which the future was foretold through Simeon, the prophet who received the law and received God; then next the persecutions, the flight into Egypt, the return from Egypt, the wanderings, the sojourns in [?], the insults before the cross, the sorrows at the cross, the signs after the cross, and finally all that she did and all that was revealed in that life of hers. That life was unblemished and undefiled, and overflowing beyond measure with the purest chastity. The world could not contain it, nor was it strong enough to express it in words, and so it has kept it unspoken to the end, like the mystery of a king. It has made known traces of this mystery only to those taught to compare divine things in a divine way. To them, as people thoroughly purified by nearness to the Divine, the all-holy one, through speechlessness and unknowing beyond all utterance, lifted the spiritual veil and showed some part of the hidden, mystic splendor within. May it be granted to us too, all who have been illumined by this present festival of light, to be counted worthy of that surpassingly lovely manifestation of light and to see purely, or at least to receive in some measure a ray of the mystic vision, and to be clearly initiated into these things: not into the things of that ineffable life, for they are unknown, but to be taught, as far as possible, the meaning of the things over which we preside today. Come, then, my friends, initiates of the word, fellow lovers of beauty and lovers of the spectacle. For I summon you with a great and lofty proclamation: let us unfold the vision of the word, still veiled in symbolic fabrics, and show you the beauty within,

which outshines the rays of the sun in the beauty of its splendor. Now that the discourse has reached this point, I think it good first to forewarn some of those present, lest perhaps we approach the holy things with unwashed feet, as the saying goes, or impure ones. For the place of the holy things is not equally open or accessible to all, but only to those who through purity of mind have risen above all material things and passed beyond everything that falls under the senses. To them above all the all-holy tabernacle of God throws open its passages, generously grants them entry, and lavishly supplies the dishes of the spiritual banquet to which we have been invited. On those who boldly and unworthily presumed to approach Mount Sinai, lightnings and thunders and terrors, the sounds of trumpets and dreadful threats came crashing down. To the many it was not safe even to touch the walls of the temple, and for this reason there was need of second walls outside. It was a matter of great earnestness to purify oneself beforehand from contact with the holy things and to keep apart from the sacred rites. All this was so for those who still worshipped the shadow and clung to the veils of the types. How much more zeal, then, must those show who have the light of truth ringing in their ears, as they hasten to approach this magnificent and immeasurably great tabernacle of God's gifts! To her, beyond knowing, beyond understanding, beyond utterance, he came to dwell, lowering himself to self-emptying; and he whom nothing can contain dwelt without constraint in a virginal womb, which in its purity surpassed the whole of nature subject to generation. From there, as from a holy inner sanctuary, he initiated his own flesh. Who did this? He who needs nothing, and who took upon himself the whole of human lowliness. In this tabernacle shaped by God, the whole law and the prophets were fulfilled in deed, and in her the shadowy outlines of the prefiguring types grew dim, as the mirrors gave way to the truth. Now that the discourse has prepared these things well enough, come, let us leave the types behind and hasten up to the truth itself, or rather, let us approach the inner sanctuary. For how long shall we linger in the forecourts of the discourse, admiring the beauty before the entrance, when we may go in together with the Mother of the Word, part the veil, peer into the Holy of Holies, and be initiated into greater things [?]? For if the forecourts [of the holy things are such, and the vestibules] [?]

…of the temple are so august and immense that their surpassing beauty dazzles the eyes of the mind. How great, then, must be the space of the inner sanctuary, and the innermost parts of what is unseen and untrodden! These can be seen and spoken of only by eyes and lips that reflect the glory of the Lord most clearly, that have been cleansed by the coal from the Seraph's tongs, and that have reached the summit of dispassion. So trust me as a good counselor. Bid farewell to the passions of the flesh, and cleanse yourselves as far as you can of every material attachment and of the confusion here below. Then clothe yourselves in the light of the divine and blessed illumination that comes from above, and run together to the Theotokos. For when we have already been made bright in deed and in word, and shine on every side with the beauty of the virtues, Christ himself wishes to gather us together and feast us mystically. He is the pure rite, the ever-living light, who shines forth from the Sun of the [?] without beginning and without departing from it, as a sun shines out as a ray from light. He shows this clearly by what he does today. His ever-virgin mother, from whose womb he, being God, was ineffably formed in our likeness, he now transfers from the regions of earth as the queen of human nature. He leaves the power of the mystery unproclaimed, as it were, yet by no means wholly unshared. For the all-holy one was not brought to birth beyond the bounds that have been fixed for us from above, nor did she live by some law foreign to nature, for as long as she sojourned with us in the regions above the earth. Yet in this, as in other things, she had in some way a principle that was different and beyond nature. She lived and gave birth in a manner higher than ours; and in the end she departed from the things of this world; and truly, by the greatness of her nature, she surpassed all who are subject to generation. But let us now go on, and celebrate together what befits the occasion; for everything runs together and rejoices together for good at this festival. See, every one of you who hears my words, what is now before our eyes! The queen of the tribes, the church of the faithful, today goes in procession for the queen of our race, who is being royally taken up by God, the King and ruler of all, to the palaces of heaven; and she brings as gifts from herself all that is most beautiful and delightful. She who made dust heavenly puts off the dust; she lays aside the covering she had from birth, and gives back to the earth what is akin to it. She who procured life hastens back to a passing into life again, and takes up her dwelling in a place that is the source of life and cannot be taken, removed from every material and passion-bound position and relation. And finally the visible itself rises above visible things, and in an intelligible way joins what is intelligible, by reasons known to him who first bound together, then loosed, and then bound together again — if I am not being bold in touching things beyond reach. [Note: another reading has "in the others … in some way different"; [?] has instead "as in the inner sanctuaries, so in this too."]

Let no one disbelieve these things, remembering Elijah and Enoch. When they were shown to be above the things of this world, they closed their senses and went out of the flesh and the world; the one was snatched away in a chariot, the other carried aloft. Their parts were not separated from one another, nor dissolved; rather, the bounds of life [?] were set for them, which Providence, wisely determining all things, fixed around them. By Providence the things of old and the things of now alike are shaped and carried out. And if these are small things to set as a parallel for the one we are hymning, she will at any rate be sufficient for herself, comparing and likening her own case to itself. But we must consider whether any greater wonder will be found than what was so strangely accomplished in her. The law of nature has been conquered; it weakened late and fell with difficulty. The bitter sentence of death goes off into complete idleness and ruin. The power of the curse has been broken. Yet no one could have overcome what God decreed of old, unless the one who transforms and refashions all things by the nod of his own goodness were God by nature. It would be fully fitting for him to make things new now in the case of his Mother as well. For in this way he will show not only that she is his Mother by nature, but will also confirm the economy that came about through her. It is in this economy above all that we raise our more mystical discourses to the way of eminence. In it the life-originating Word leapt in and entered her womb, which nothing can contain, and taking up human nature in a manner beyond being, held it out to us. For this reason the things accomplished in her long ago, and those praised by us now, even if they seem somewhat paradoxical and removed from the bonds of nature, may still reasonably be referred to her with ease, in keeping with the supernatural principle of her ineffable childbearing. Clearly, then, the Word was present at that time too, and by his law put an end to the inexorable law of death. It was a truly new sight, beyond the reach of reasoning: a woman who surpassed the nature of the heavens in purity, entering the holiest places of the heavenly sanctuary; a Virgin who surpassed the very nature of the Seraphim by the wonder of bearing God, drawing near to the first nature, God the creator of all; a Mother who bore Life itself, putting forth an end of life to match her childbirth, a wonder worthy of God and of faith. For as her womb was not corrupted when she gave birth, so her flesh did not perish when she died. O the wonders! Her childbearing escaped corruption, and her tomb did not admit decay; for decay does not touch the holy ones. Do you want me to tell you the proof? And let none of you here mock me that the tomb is somehow empty. For I will ask you: How did the dead body disappear? How is it that the grave-clothes are not in the coffin — unless what was buried escaped…

…decay, unless the treasure was transferred? And if so, how can the transfer not be true, since everything else concurred as well: the separation of soul from body, the laying aside of the flesh, the dissolving of the composite, the parting of its members, dissolution, rejoining, reconstitution, and withdrawal into the invisible? For the tomb has stood empty right up to the present, both attested and attesting to the transfer. I do not know whether the parts were once more [joined] into the single compound of a body — for I will say [?] a little about these things — the Creator perhaps having devised this by his ineffable good pleasure to honor the one who bore him; or whether one part surpassed the other, so that after their separation from each other the one received a place beyond the bounds, the other a place on the border, and [?] restoration; or whether some strange and altered sequence of events came about supernaturally in her case, so that everything concerning her might be truly new, fittingly admitting an account beyond nature, since it lies beyond all reason and knowledge. To this spiritual banquet of words the Mother of the Word made flesh calls us together. She herself is set before us today as a richly laden table and the theme of our words, abounding and overflowing with mysteries perfected by God. The great splendor of those who love the feast, shining around their [?], surpasses the power of speech and adorns the face of the day. Today I too, a stranger and newcomer, am host of this feast, and, beyond my deserving, guide to these lofty sights. And let no one, looking at the lowliness of my insignificance, refuse the banquet because it is not from us [?] … the mystical narratives of these mystical contemplations. Since the table is full of them and invites the [?] guests, let us go, as befits the Spirit, into the depths of the Spirit. For now she who bore Wisdom according to the flesh, fittingly imitating Wisdom, kindly sets out her whole self as a mystical and heavenly table, prepared for those being initiated intelligibly into divine things. She does not slaughter victims or pour drinks into a mixing bowl, like those [?] victims of old and that bowl which held the [?] nectar; but she plainly sets out the supernatural and truly divine sights of the mysteries concerning her. To these above all she urges those who have gathered… [Note: "Decay does not touch the holy ones" refers to the saying, "You will not give…"]

…[?] of creation, she who by the economy carried in her womb the one who was made bread from the leaven of Adam's lump. He leads those who approach him in holiness to a newer life and makes them perfected in God; and in this way he purifies them and makes them immortal, those who are made his own by sharing in the truly new communion with him. And what she plainly feasts her lovers with is this: the things that made up that life, transcendent and ineffable, than which nothing seen in creation is higher. In that life he who is beyond all theology, through an ineffable self-emptying, moved by compassion and care for humankind, as the leader of all, chose a second time to come down even to our poverty, to be intertwined with our lump, and to share in blood and flesh just as we do — he who lacks nothing, who is more than full, who is rich. He chose an existence within [?], not by departing from his Godhead beyond being, but keeping for himself, even after the ineffable union, the principles of the natures that came together unimpaired, with no confusion or division finding any room between them. He did not make known even to the angels themselves, nor to the supramundane commanders of the heavenly ranks, what it was that was being accomplished, except to one of the foremost angels, who ministered to the saving advance of the new mystery. For in this way the bodiless one, made bodily, conversed with us through the medium of mind and flesh, so that, wholly mingled with our whole lump, he might wholly renew what he had assumed from us. This, then, as far as my knowledge goes and as it lies to hand, is the intellectual table of God-initiated wisdom. Such too are the God-given rites mystically celebrated in her. With these it is fitting also to mark the mysteries of the present day, on which the Mother of God, transgressing none of the laws of nature, was subject to the law that governs us, and brought her life in the flesh to its end within the same bounds as we do, leaving to the world both a birth and a departure full of wonder. If, then, something beyond us was arranged in her case by the divine nature, let no one be amazed, but look to the ineffability of the mystery so newly accomplished, which is infinitely, infinitely removed beyond all infinity. And let these things remain wholly folded up and unspoken, keeping their own principle unshaken. [Note: another reading: "mysteries."]

Let us, bright ones, brightly celebrate the memory of the burial of the all-holy, life-originating tabernacle. At this feast, together with the visible, all that is intelligible, all that is heavenly and all that is earthly, is gathered into one, and honors the Queen and goes in procession before our race. From her the common mercy seat was obtained — that is, the Lord's saving body, built as a temple from her without hands — of him who shared with us every natural and intellectual movement, sin alone excepted. O the wonder! She who, in a manner beyond being, contained in the small space of her womb God, infinite in greatness and set apart from all circumscription, today is carried on a bier of limited size and given burial by the hands of the holy. She who enthroned in her own bosom the one who rides on the backs of the Cherubim is entombed in the bosom of a rock hewn out beneath. And she whose childbearing the angels marveled at — today apostolic choirs lead and escort her tabernacle. Who could interpret the principles of what was accomplished there? Who could rise worthily with the mystery? Who will give wings to the mind, so that it may fly up with the wonder and come into communion with it? Who — to speak of the more modest matter, perhaps even of the secondary ones — could describe the flowing together and flowing apart of our own compound? Before this nature is at a loss; astonished at the incomprehensibility of its own constitution, it turns its impulse into wonder, and in the inspired words of David says to the God of all: "Your knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is too mighty, I cannot attain it." It is all but marveling at our composition, or constitution, or, conversely, our separation into parts. But now it also holds as divine the wonder, so hard to trace, concerning this Queen, his immaculate and renowned Mother — a wonder made known both to us in common and to her in particular, but known before the ages to him alone, as the maker of all and worker of such things. This is our formation; this our composition; the dissolution that we celebrate today. Hence I, shrinking back and honoring the mystery with fear, join my voice to that of Isaiah, the loudest-voiced of the prophets, saying: "Woe is me, for I am stricken; for being a man and having unclean lips," I dare to say something about the pure and undefiled one, overflowing with all holiness, and I attempt to praise her with funeral words — she whose divine ascent clouds encircle, while a kind of intellectual mist is poured round the… [Note: [?] that is, among those secondary matters. "Perhaps even of the secondary ones": [?] namely the theologians; compare Suidas under "to celebrate."]

…rational unfoldings concerning her, not allowing the folded-up comprehension of the mystery to shine forth clearly. To praise her worthily belongs to God alone, who, by principles he alone knows, wrought the mighty works concerning her. Surely not, then, to me, who lie on the ground and know nothing beyond what is at my feet, for want of a will directed toward the good? Never, then, shall I be ashamed to speak unworthily, even if it is not possible to speak worthily. But since what is offered according to one's ability is not to be rejected, I will break the silence by speaking, dedicating the discourse to God. To him be glory and might to all the ages of ages.

Once again the thread of the discourse brings us back to the festival; and we must certainly add what is lacking to what follows, so that the discourse may be complete and unbroken, with no part disjointed. In what has gone before, as far as possible and briefly, we have described the sight of the life-originating body — I mean the virginal tabernacle of the Mother of God. It remains to say what the hymn was, and what kind of things were hymned. And let no one now cast on me the reproach of presumption or boldness for daring to approach things so lofty. For I set out not on the strength of eloquence but only to fulfill a vow when I composed the discourse in hand, and I took care everywhere, as far as I could, to keep it humble and moderate. Yet the discourse does not on that account wish to belittle the mystery, as though [?], being inexperienced and untrained, it had first set out from presumption. And if the present discourse perhaps contains something not contemplated by many, let no one be surprised. For these things have been contemplated by us by way of conjecture, and as far as the mind could reach — for exactness even the angels could hardly attain. Already, then, that host of God-bearers, ten thousand strong, had gathered together, as we said earlier. And perhaps the whole intelligible order of the supramundane powers, flying invisibly from above, was joining in the extraordinary spectacle. And the God-possessed souls of the saints, I think, were present too, dancing around the bier…

…whom the Song of Songs, in its mystical vision, calls maidens. For it was fitting that the godlike souls of those who had lived [well] should attend the Queen of nature, preparing the way for her departure, leading and escorting her, and singing the hymns of departure over her. There lay in the midst that body of the Theotokos, three cubits long and full of light, which had contained the whole [?] of the thearchic Word. Seen upon the bier, it filled all creation with the fragrance of the myrrh of [?]. What mind, what tongue could trace out the principles of what was seen there? For everything lay infinitely beyond all [knowing] and all [seeing]. Hence the chosen ones among the God-wise, possessed by the divine Spirit, out of overflowing joy at that God-delighting splendor, and carried into ecstasy by the [?] of the illumination, took up those inspired hymns — I mean the inspired figurative speech — each as he was able, one answering another. These were not such as we ourselves are led to understand, or as someone might perhaps [?], but such as the Spirit shaped them to speak and permitted them to hear. This hymn itself, and the things hymned, were spoken and heard by the hymnists, infinitely surpassing the harmony and concord here below among us, and falling little or not at all short of the sound of the angels keeping festival in heaven. Their height and depth and infinite beauty are not for us to improvise about, who have never in any way tasted such sweetness; they are rather to be honored by silence. [Note: for "incomprehensible," another reading has "unutterable."] It is safe for us to attempt only those things in which success is delightful and failure carries no danger — things that neither grieve the learned nor vex the simple. But the hymn and the things hymned, even if they escape our comprehension, let them be as follows, so far as we can grasp them in outline: "This is the treasure of the covenant God made with us. This is the manifestation of the hidden depths of divine incomprehensibility. This is the goal conceived before the ages; this the crown of the divine oracles; this the ineffable and more-than-unknowable counsel of the care for humankind that was before all beginning; this the first-fruits of the communion and union of God, the begetter of all, with his own creature; this the pledge, with its own substance, of divine reconciliation; the surpassing beauty; the statue carved by God; the finely drawn image of the divine archetype; the foundation of all contemplation and ascent; the all-holy tabernacle of the creator of all; the God-receiving bowl of inexhaustible wisdom; the inviolable treasury of life; the unfailing spring of divine radiance; the unshakeable strength. Inasmuch as she was [?] from the passions, raised above all by [?], through her the things of salvation were given to us as pledges; and that she, so greatly marveled at, came down to the measure of our condition, and [?] what is common to nature, was her own; but that the characteristics of her life were not wholly as they are with us…

…was proper to her nearness to the Divine. Yet it is a clear proof of her perfect dispassion. For which of the very greatest things did not come to her together with a great abundance of virtue? Which extraordinary wonder was not brought forth in her as a sign, to show that she was the dwelling place of all the wonders ever brought forth or being accomplished now? The last part of these is the present one, even though it was determined before all time, since the divine counsel above perhaps thus determined the completion of the life of each of us. O the providence, to whose depths no one born has ever come, nor been able to find its trace! Its work is the mystery of the Virgin now being accomplished. For it is a mystery, even if it is seen in our own end; and this is the portion allotted to human nature from the beginning. But how was the barrier, bound together by sin, broken down? How was the bond twisted together by [?] torn apart? Why is death despised like a daydream? Fear is gone, no longer frightening [?] those who are infants in Christ. Or would corruption, sown by disobedience, not have been dissolved unless the dwelling place of God had perhaps died? Yes, it was dissolved, for Christ died first. For nature itself was called out of its condemnation to corruption, having taken up a state of incorruption. O new exchanges! O divine transactions! Nature sprouted a will overgrown with thorns; she in turn brought forth the one who fulfilled the Father's will. Nature travailed with a self-chosen death through disobedience; she in turn travailed with the one who through obedience destroyed death. For she alone, she alone was chosen, beyond nature, for the renewal of nature; she alone served the maker of all nature. Since, then, this divinely appointed coffin of the God-possessed tabernacle now lies before us, inviting the lovers of beauty like a generous giver of good things, let no one fall short of the [?]. For the gift needs no toil, only the will. So let everyone who has undoubting faith come eagerly; let him come to the [?] of the Virgin… [Note: [?] … the manuscript had: "Since, then, this divinely appointed coffin now lies before us."]

…place of oracles, and let him learn by experience how to find what he longs for. This common place of reconciliation lies before us: be reconciled to God, all of you. Here is the inexhaustible spring of immortality: come, you who have been put to death, and draw from it. Behold the ever-flowing rivers of life: come, all of you, and be made immortal. O daughter of Adam and Mother of God! O Mother without a husband, and virgin who bore a child! O creature of the One who was made in you in time, yet did not depart from his own eternity! The spokesmen of the Spirit proclaimed you beforehand. Moses was the first to foretell you, when he saw you as the bush: “I will turn aside and see this great sight.” The divine forefather David entreated Christ about you, saying: “Arise, O Lord, you and the ark of your holiness.” The same David, prefiguring your [?], sang beforehand about you: “The rich among the people will entreat your face.” “For behold,” he says, “all the glory of the king’s daughter is within; she is clothed and adorned with golden fringes.” The holy book of the Songs described you beforehand and hinted at you more mystically: “Who is this that comes up from the wilderness like pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all the powders of the perfumer?” Again the same book wrote beforehand about you, saying: “Behold the bed of Solomon: its pillars he made of silver, and its back of gold, its steps of purple; within it is a pavement of stones, love from the daughters of Jerusalem.” And again: “Go forth, daughters of Zion, [and behold] King Solomon in the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding, on the day of the gladness of his heart.” “Behold her, daughters of Zion, and call her blessed; queens and concubines, praise her, for the fragrance of her garments is above all spices.” Isaiah, foreseeing you, cried out under divine inspiration: “Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb.” And: “There shall be the root of Jesse.” And: “Blessed is the root of Jesse.” And: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall come up from the root.” For your sake the great Ezekiel proclaimed beforehand, saying: “Behold the gate facing east; and the gate shall be shut, and no one shall pass through it; the Lord God alone shall go in and come out, and the gate shall be shut.” [?] (Dan. 2:[?])

…[dispensation], “into which the angels long to look.” You are the most beautiful dwelling of the divine condescension, the truly desirable land. For “the King of glory desired your beauty” and loved the wealth of your virginity; he dwelt in you, “and dwelt among us,” and reconciled us through you to God the Father. You are the treasure of “the mystery hidden before the ages.” You are truly the living book of the spiritual Word, written in you without a sound by the living pen of the Spirit. You alone are [?] the God-written volume of the new covenant, which God of old had covenanted with mankind. You are “the chariot of God, ten thousandfold,” bringing “thousands of those who prosper” to him when he was made flesh. You are Mount Zion, “the fat mountain, the curdled mountain, in which God was pleased to dwell,” from which the One beyond being took flesh and was “curdled” into a body like ours, animated by a rational soul. O divine temple, and earthly human being! O pillar [?] and life-giving column, lighting the way not for the fleshly Israel in its flight, but for the spiritual Israel, guided straight toward the unerring light of knowledge, for which you blaze as a beacon! O cloud full of light, and “shady mountain,” overshadowing not the ungrateful people of the Jews, but the chosen [people] of God, the holy nation, signaling to it with your motherly torches! O you who are purer than all gold and than all creation, both sensible and immaterial! O virgin earth, from which came forth the second Adam, who is more ancient than the old one! What tomb will cover you? What earth will receive you, who have surpassed heaven and the nature of heaven in holiness? What will your grave-clothes be? What your swaddling bands? What your adornments? What perfumes will embalm your body—fragrant, undefiled, full of good, teeming with forgiveness, gushing with incorruption, from which comes deification, in which is perfection, through which is salvation? For you are truly and really “fair, and there is no blemish in you.” Let the most divine Solomon too sing a little to you once more: “Beautiful as Jerusalem, and the fragrance of your garments like the fragrance of frankincense.” You are the new casket of the inexhaustible ointment; you are the gladness of the oil of [?]. You are the [?] of the spiritual spices,

the incense. You are the flower of incorruption, the [?]-bearing earth, the life-bearing casket, the radiant lampstand, the God-woven purple, the royal garment, the [?]-embroidered robe, the golden double cloak, the unnameable [?] of the spiritual royal purple of the [Word?], the high-priestly woven diadem of the kingdom, the lofty throne, the uplifted gate of the heaven of heavens, the queen of all human nature, she whose title is unadulterated and matches its reality, she who is higher than all except God alone. What hands will bury you? In what arms shall we carry her who carried the One who cannot be contained? What prayer shall we make over you at the tomb? [?] shall we send you forth? With what lips shall we sing the hymn of your departure? With what [?]? With what words shall we eloquently set forth your great deeds? [?] we offer you these words instead: “Blessed are you among women, and in generations of generations. Blessed in heaven and glorified on earth. For every tongue gratefully glorifies you, proclaiming you Mother of [Life?]. All creation is filled with your glory; the universe is sanctified with the ointment of your fragrance; through you the occasion of sin has been abolished; the curse of the first mother has been changed into joy. All [?] sing through you together with us: ‘Glory in heaven, peace on earth.’ A tomb cannot hold you, for corruptible things do not darken the Master’s body. Hades has no strength to hold you, for fellow servants cannot touch a [?] soul. Depart, then, depart in peace. Leave the dwellings of creation; propitiate the Lord on behalf of our common race. For while you lived among things on earth, a small part of the earth held you; but since you were translated from the earth, the whole world holds you as a common propitiation. Be magnified above Enoch, in gladness, in unspeakable joy, in everlasting light, where the true [?] is, the all-luminous kingdom, the incomprehensible choir of the angels. Besides these, enjoy the beauty of your Son, [?] the inexhaustible joy and unaging blessedness, there where the torrent of eternal delight flows; where the meadows of incorruption are, the springs of ever-flowing life, the streams of divine light, the rivers of ever-living [?]. There is the goal of all things hoped for and still hoped for now; the sum of all good things, the [enjoyment?] of things hidden and only then beheld; the final end, beyond which there is nothing at all.”

[?] the strokes of the lyre; call the virgins; gather the choirs of singers; arrange the dances; let them run behind the bier, let them lead the way before the bier and after it; let them dance around the coffin. For behold the new ark of God’s glory, in which are “the all-golden jar, and Aaron’s rod that budded, and the tablets of the covenant.” Behold the sum of all that the oracles of the prophets cried out. Behold the ladder that Jacob saw when he was initiated into divine things, on which he saw the angels of God ascending and descending—whatever such a descent or ascent once was. This is the gate of heaven, of which he said: “How fearful is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.” Behold the mercy seat set up above the Holy of Holies of the God-revealed tabernacle and its inner sanctuary: once overshadowed by the wings of the seraphim, but now making propitiation for our sins through the mystical oversight of Jesus. No longer is the yoke of legal slavery laid on the true Israel, since Christ has signed our freedom through worship in the spirit, as in grace, by the body he took from the Theotokos. No longer is the yearly course of the high priests trodden into the holy place; for the great high priest himself, Christ Jesus, who has passed through the heavens in the flesh he assumed, flesh with a rational and intellectual soul, enters continually on our behalf, mystically, into the virginal temple as into a sanctuary. He offers incense, and sacrifices, and is sacrificed; offering whole burnt offerings, he is himself offered; and sanctifying himself for us, he sanctifies those who sanctify him. Such, Theotokos, are the mysteries of your falling asleep, which is beyond this world; these are the funeral songs of the sacred procession of your tabernacle, laid to rest by God; this is the hymn of departure, the memorials before the burial and after it, the farewell songs of your all-unknowable translation. These are likenesses, in riddles, of the divine mysteries and blessed illuminations that concern you. For our mind cannot reach to conjecture anything more than what has been said. This short discourse has been earnestly composed by us for you, as both thanksgiving and supplication. If it has anything worthy of your greatness, the thanks for it are yours, since you both give zeal and gladly accept it. But if—as all who attempt to say anything about you must suffer—it should appear to fall short of what is due, you will surely forgive, for you are compassionate by nature, through your nearness to your Son,

our protector, a nearness wholly your own. And you will accept this, I know, as a most beautiful gift, though composed from my poor labors. For I had nothing greater to offer the Mother of the Word, who surpasses all, than a word poured forth from the self-flowing springs of the grace that is in you, O you who are graced by God. Yet let your awesome and all-unknowable state in the divine life of unaging blessedness be honored with silence, since it is wholly undiscernible and unspeakable. For it is right that we should not lay hands on things beyond us, which wall off every inquiry by their incomprehensibility. To you, then, O all-blessed, thrice-royal Mother of God, what we owed—we who have been instructed by you [?] and by your prayers, which have free access to the Divine, in the hidden truths about you—has now been sketched modestly, according to our ability. But who will supply us with a voice proportionate to the height and greatness of the most glorious thoughts about you, and the power to speak them? But, O Lady of all mankind, container of the self-existent Wisdom and hypostatic Word, the first and principal Cause of all! O provider of life, life of the living, and co-cause of life! O holy one, holier than the holy, super-holy treasure of all holiness! O portion that united humanity to God indissolubly and without division! O queen of those born of earth, holding invincible power from the highest glory! O bulwark of the Christians’ faith, and champion of those who have set their hopes on you! Receive from us, who have received the light of truth through you, these solemn words, which we have beheld mystically, so far as we could, from faint images. And to us who take pride in you, Mother of God, grant in return for this small offering this reward: that we may have, more precious and more splendid than all treasures and costly wealth, your suppliant entreaty to your Son and our Master, King, God and Lord—through which, when we sin, we propitiate the Divine, and when we do right, we draw it to ourselves more graciously; through which we count the weapons of [barbarians?] as the arrows of infants, and spear and helmet and the shot of the bow remain ineffective and idle; through which, finally, every good thing is achieved for Christians, including likeness to God. Here, beloved, you have the discourse on the mystery, which, even if it falls far short of what was hoped, is at least not inferior to our eagerness. The more mystical and lofty discourse you may seek from the Word himself, who for your sake was emptied and took on the thickness of flesh, and out of his love for mankind united you wholly to himself—it is not amiss to say, and became man—so that he might deify you wholly in the spirit, consume the worse in the better, raise you up with himself from the ground, and seat you on the Father’s thrones. Be led up to him always by your life and by pure contemplation, living by divine words and ways, seeing God as far as is attainable, and being seen by him. Hasten to have him ever made clearer to you by the illuminations of contemplation and the ascents of virtue, so that from both—I mean action and contemplation—you may be complete and steadfast, attaining to the full-grown man…

Discourse 15. On the Beheading of John the Forerunner. Even old age often leaps when it is braced by the sinews of eagerness, and a weak discourse gains strength, empowered by the presence of its hearers. This is what our discourse now experiences: it is urged toward the subject of praise by those gathered here, yet it shrinks from pitting its own power against the eminence of the one praised. For the discourse, to speak with the Apostle, is “weak,” and uttered through ailing instruments; but the subject of the praises holds victory over every discourse, to the same degree that he gained preeminence, by comparison, among those born of women. So it needs only, and first of all, that voice of the One who alone and first is by nature the very Word, and the wisdom of God, and his power. Such is the subject, and so it stands; how weak our discourse is has surely been shown. The subject sets before us the great John, greatest among those born of women, than whom the saving word declared that no one from the beginning of the ages—patriarch, prophet or righteous man—was greater; while our discourse attempts to praise the voice of the Word who was before the ages. Looking at its own power, it all but embraces that silence which Zechariah underwent in the sanctuary because of his unbelief, until [?], coming first, loosens the silence of our discourse, since it is truly the voice of the One who is by nature the Word. And he will certainly grant this, as the voice of the Word: not so that he himself may be glorified the more (for what glory could be added to one who has woven from the Lord such a crown as no one born of earth has ever worn?), but so that through his praises we may be led to imitate him. For this is what God wills, who glorifies those who glorify him and exalts those who exalt him.

There the Father is worshiped, [the Son] is glorified, and the Holy Spirit is hymned: the single nature of the one Godhead in Trinity. Such things, I think, those God-possessed men then said and sang, and things still higher than these; for I do not know what more I could say, being earth and ashes, utter rottenness, crawling on my belly like the snakes. The debt of my discourse has now been sufficiently discharged according to my ability, and nothing, I think, has been overlooked of what bears on the present feast. And if anyone can contribute something loftier, that too will be gathered in for us and will add to the festival. When I have said a little more, I will rest the oars of my discourse somewhere here. In speaking worthily we all fall short alike; but in displaying our own power, the eagerness of each is equal. She who bore the Word will accept, I know well, this very brief word of ours, and will grant not perhaps as much as we ask, but surely as much as we are worthy to receive. For the all-holy one, being generous in gifts, is wont to return greater things even for the smallest. So let these things be. But we, O bright and most illustrious assembly (for I call you once more to the conclusion of the discourse), come, let us go out ahead in the sacred procession of the virginal body, let us sing the funeral songs, and let us crown the leader of the feast with honors as far as we are able. And that this may be the more splendid, let the whole assembly of heavenly and earthly beings be present today and join me in completing the hymn of departure, which is composed in these words: “The camp of God has departed, departed from the tents of Kedar, to the immaterial tents of life renewed. The tabernacle, the archetype of the tabernacle of the Law, has received the ark that is above the world, of which the ark of the Law was a type. The lintel of the doors above has been lifted up, so that the royal palace of heaven may royally embrace the gate of the God who is above all. Receive her, you angels robed in white; sing hymns, you heavens; give glory, you born of earth; exalt the city of God, the great King. Earth, clap your hands, acclaim, recount the glories of the Virgin, the swaddling clothes of her childbearing, the wonders of her tomb: how she was buried, how she was translated, how the tomb is seen empty and is venerated. Judea, gather your sons; proclaim the queen sprung from Judah. Take courage, do not fear; keep your feasts, Jerusalem; cry aloud, shout for joy, escort the mother-city of God, [?] David [?], say clearly: ‘When Israel went out of Eg-

-ypt.’ Mother Zion, whom the Lord chose, whom he [?], call your daughters, the churches from among the nations. Sing something mournful, but not tragic; [lamenting], but not complaining. For the present festival is heartwarming, not [mournful]. Gethsemane, receive the new queen; make ready the tomb; [prepare] the grave-clothes; adorn the coffin with perfumes. Let the casket be your guardian of the treasure; let the holy thing be guarded securely. If indeed it is kept and remains in it, it will be a common possession of angels and men, an object of veneration. But if something [unexpected] should happen, and the undefiled one should be translated, remain [?], proclaiming it. Recount the translation to the generations to come: to the spirits above, [?] the spirit of the Mother of God; to us, pouring forth the [sanctification?] of her body like myrrh from an ever-flowing spring. Let us all run together to the Theotokos: [souls of the forefathers?] and patriarchs, spirits of prophets and companies of priests, the assembly of apostles, the throngs of martyrs, the gatherings of teachers, the souls of the righteous, the ranks of the holy, every rank and age, kings and potentates, rulers and ruled, “young men and maidens, elders with the younger,” [?]. Make supplication; say to the Mother of God, [?]: “How blessed is the house of David, from whose loins you sprang, Mother of God!” Mothers and virgins, glorify her who alone is both mother and ever-virgin; and brides, [?] her who is unwedded and incorrupt among maidens, who alone without birth pangs brought forth the [Uncontainable?]. Barren women and widows, applaud her who, [without] knowing a man, exchanged the [reproaches] of childlessness. Daughters, leap for joy as you escort the [child-bearing] incorruption. Bless her, you nations; call her blessed, you tongues; sing to the Mother of [God …]; tribes of the earth, sing; strike up with [timbrels] and cymbals; shout aloud, magnify her, [?]. Take up, take up the timbrel, Miriam, and go out before the virgins. Strike the lyre, David; lift up your voice; hymn your queen; dance. We append: [?] “Israel went out of Egypt” [?] … [?] cloud, alleluia, etc. Whatever, however, truly [?] the songs of departure precede, and more mystical [?] [?]

[?] of those great and extraordinary marks [?]. So I decided that, for you who love the feasts, I should add something like a small relish: an exposition of the [?] that was read just now. The Baptist is content to be adorned with what is his own. Come then, [?], let us set out, as on a platter, the much-hymned contest of the Forerunner, which he fought to the end for the sake of the good.

“At that time,” it says, “Herod the tetrarch heard the report about Jesus, and said to his servants [?]: ‘This is John the Baptist; he has been raised from the dead, and that is why these powers are at work in him.’”

That came later. But what happened before it? Herod was committing adultery with the wife of his brother Philip, and John, by rebuking Herod, was trying to stop him from breaking the law. How, and in what way? By saying: “It is not lawful for you to have the wife of your brother Philip.” This drove Herod mad; this prepared him for murder. [?] That great one, so mighty among the prophets, did not shrink back in fear or stop rebuking him. For he knew that the law destroys such lust. “It is not lawful for you to have the wife of your brother Philip.” “You are setting yourself against the law of God,” he says, “against the tablets inscribed by God; you [?] in opposition to the statutes of Moses.” “It is not lawful for you to have the wife of your brother Philip.” Herod, buried in the ease of his unreasonable mingling in pleasures, could not even lift his head, nor did he look toward the light of truth; he stayed heavy-headed under the weight of his love of pleasure. John kept on admonishing, teaching and advising him, as befits a prophet of God. Yet Herod, although, as the [Gospel] says, “he knew him to be a righteous and holy man, and when he heard him he did many things, and [heard] him [gladly],” understood none of this then, or would not choose to understand it. He did not honor the prophet with the honors due to him; he did not [?] the weight of the law even in the slightest; and, if nothing else, he did not even respect the penalty that the law imposes on such things. Shall I say something even better known? He did not even imitate that Ahab, who was himself a slave to a woman, and who had Jezebel as his teacher in polytheism then, as this man now has Herodias. For when Ahab heard from Elijah the Tishbite of the wrath kindled against him by the Lord, and of the evils that were [?] to come upon him and his house, and was openly struck by the rebukes for the wicked deeds and lawless sacrileges he had committed, he did not grow angry; he did not

rebel. He did not consider the prophet's rebuke an insult. Instead, he held him in honor as a prophet of God who spoke divine words, and embraced his words with reverence and fear as commands of God. What, then, does he do? Listen to the Book of Kings: “And the Lord,” it says, “spoke to Elijah the Tishbite, saying: ‘Arise and go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, and speak to him, saying: Thus says the Lord: Because you have murdered Naboth and taken his inheritance, therefore, says the Lord, I will bring evils upon you, and I will burn up those after you, and I will cut off from Ahab every male [literally, one who urinates against the wall]’”; and the rest, in which he aimed [the threat] in anger not at him alone but also at Jezebel: “For he [sold himself],” it says, “[to do] evil in the sight of the Lord, and Jezebel his wife led him astray.” What does he do when he hears this? [?] He does not rise up in anger; instead he becomes downcast and takes on a gloomy look [?]. He becomes aware of his own [?]; he did not rebel against the prophetic rebukes. “For at the word, Ahab was pierced to the heart before the Lord, and [went about weeping], and tore his tunic, and [fasted], and [put on] sackcloth.” What then of [God], who waits for the conversion of us all, who is slow to strike and [quick] to [show mercy]? Listen to the Scripture: “And the Lord said,” it says: “‘Have you seen, Elijah, how Ahab was pierced to the heart before me? So I will not bring evils in his days.’” [?] the excess of wrath? Have you seen a swift repentance [?]? [?] Herod [?] ... to come round in this way? If not this, should he not at least have respected his own testimony, the testimony he gave to [John]? No, he did not go that way. [What] then? He turned his love of pleasure into murder, carrying [?] from matters of marriage over to matters of bloodshed. An evil way; [?]. For even if he wanted to give in somewhat to his passion, he ought not to have [?] the prophet, knowing him to be a righteous and holy man, and having often [?] heard him, and gladly [?] by him. But what was [?] of his [birthday], and to what [?] of folly did the pleasure-loving [?] that commanded him spur him on to murder [?]? Listen to the evangelists: “And an opportune day came,” it says, “when Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles and military commanders and the leading men

[?] a guide, entirely, by close kinship [?] this [?] ... I know that it is a most beautiful gift, though put together from my meager labors. For I had nothing greater to offer to the Mother of the Word, who surpasses all, than a word poured out from the self-flowing springs of the grace that is in you, O you who are graced by God. As for your awe-inspiring and utterly unknowable state in the divine life of ageless [splendor?], since it is wholly beyond discerning and beyond speech, let it be honored by silence. For it is right that we should not lay hands on things that are beyond us, things that wall off every inquiry with what cannot be grasped. To you, then, O all-blessed, thrice-royal Mother of God, this is what we owed, we who under you, and through your prayers to God, offered with great boldness, have been taught the hidden words about you: these things have now been modestly improvised [?]. But who will supply us with a voice that matches the height and greatness of the most glorious thoughts about you, and with the strength to speak them? O Lady of all people, who contained Wisdom itself and the subsistent Word, the first and original cause of all things! O giver of life, life of the living and cause of life! O holy one, holier than the saints, and all-holy treasury of all holiness! O portion, who indissolubly and [indivisibly] united humanity to God! O kingdom of those made of earthly dust, holding invincible power from the highest glory! O [bulwark?] of the faith of Christians, and champion of those who have set their hopes on you! Accept from us, who through you have received the light of truth, these solemn words, contemplated mystically, as far as was possible for us, out of dim [?]. And to us who take pride in you, Mother of God, [grant] as the reward for this small [?] that we may have, more precious and more splendid than all treasures and costly wealth, your suppliant prayer to your Son, our Master and King and God and Lord. Through it, when we sin, we propitiate the Divine; when we do right, we draw it to be kinder to us. Because of it we consider weapons to be children's arrows, and spear and helmet and bow [?] remain useless and ineffective. And finally, through it every good thing is accomplished for Christians, including likeness to God. You have, beloved, the discourse on the mystery, even if it falls far short of what was hoped; at least it does not fall short of our eagerness [?]. A more mystical and loftier discourse you would seek from the Word himself, who emptied himself for your sake, took on the thickness of flesh, and out of love for humankind united you wholly to himself. It is not wrong to add: who became man, so that he might deify you wholly by [what he assumed?], and make the lower vanish in the higher, and raise you up with himself from the ground, and seat you upon the Father's thrones. Always be led up to him through a pure life and contemplation, living as a citizen of divine words and ways, seeing God as far as is possible. Hasten always toward him, so that he may become clearer to you through the illuminations of contemplation and the ascents of virtue, so that from both sides, I mean from action and contemplation, you may be complete and steadfast, attaining to the most perfect man

[?] was carried out from an unreasonable judgment. For who forced you to swear in the first place? What does the dancing of a frenzied girl have in common with the slaughter of a prophet? What share does anger have with merrymaking? If it was because of the oaths, as you yourself suppose, even so you should not have entrusted the verdict to drunkenness. For it was a time for festivity, not for killing a man. And the deed was thoroughly absurd and reckless. It called for a sober moment and a steady mind, since the harm concerned no ordinary matter. But if any of the evils in you had been hidden and gone unnoticed until then, you have exposed it against yourself, laying bare by murder the proof of your lawlessness. What need was there to lead in triumph the man who rebuked you and tried to stop you from committing adultery in secret? Because you love pleasure, you stand convicted, for you commit murder. You have thrown the order of the banquet into confusion, man. You chose to entertain your guests, and instead you preferred to grieve them. What are you doing, wretch? Instead of a dish, do you bring in this course, the head of the Baptizer? Instead of a mixing bowl, do you pour out such unmixed wine for your drinking companions? Is this the drink a king mixes for his counselors? Or do you not see how great an evil incontinence and the pursuit of pleasure are? Sober up a little, if you will, and understand that nothing so damages the inner man, or so feeds upon the outer man, as anger in the service of these things. You yoked your mind to them in abundance and enslaved the mind of your soul. Yet those wise in these matters define two most general passions among all the passions in us: anger and desire. Each of them gained mastery in you and, to your misfortune, reigned with a tyrant's impulse, not a private man's. Desire captured the citadel of your mind without siege engines, by the law of siege, and became as it were the guardian of your ungoverned soul. Anger enslaved you until it hurled you into the snare of Hades and into the furthest Charybdis of evils. Is this not the way of those who do [?] things? Or do you think that those who have been caught in this way will be examined by justice otherwise than in order to be punished? But let us listen again to the voice of the Gospels.

“For when Herod's birthday was being celebrated,” it says, “the daughter of Herodias danced in their midst, and pleased Herod.” Oh, what folly! A girl's dancing captured a king's good sense. Arms bent back, feet twisting and limbs [swaying] dissolved the king's firm resolve. Have you not heard of Alexander, son of Philip, when the daughters of Darius were brought to him for [?] ... [Note:] “Being in service to”: that is, to incontinence and love of pleasure [?] ... He also lacks the words “the inner man.”

Following the prologue, I think it right to set out, as far as I can, the theme of the present day, so that we may not go home from here incomplete and without fruit. That theme is the Baptist's boldness toward Herod, which the Gospel book, unrolled today, proclaims loudly. I mean that boldness which no blame could touch, the most entirely pure and unmixed boldness ever shown in creation. Its superiority was such that it made no distinction between a private person and a king. For the rebuke applies equally to both when the deed calls for the same penalty. But as befits a prophet of God, and why not, a zealot for his commands, he was to disregard the purple robe, the throne and the diadem, and all the things that puff up the vain with empty conceit, and instead to speak the truth boldly and reveal the authority of the law without any hesitation, because he did not want to make the freedom of the law look worthless. For how could the mediator between law and grace, the defender of the law, look on while the glory of the law was disregarded? And that the Master's Baptist was a defender of the law, who is so foolish as not to set this down as the first and chief of his achievements? What kind of zeal he had, and how fiercely it burned, the Gospel will show:

“At that time Herod the tetrarch heard the report about Jesus, and said to his servants: ‘This is John the Baptist; he has been raised from the dead, and that is why these powers are at work in him.’ For Herod had seized John and put him in prison because of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip. For John had been saying to him: ‘It is not lawful for you to have her.’ And though he wanted to kill him, he feared the crowd, because they regarded him as a prophet. But when Herod's birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced in their midst and pleased Herod, so that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she asked. Prompted by her mother, she said: ‘Give me here on a platter the head of John the Baptist.’ And the king was grieved. But because of his oaths and his fellow guests, he ordered it to be given. He sent and beheaded John in the prison. And his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother.”

Does he not seem to you a zealot, the most zealous of all zealots, since he did not give up the truth even in the face of slaughter, nor relax his zeal in the least, and this while contending against a king? Just imagine what it was to see a man clothed in camel's hair, with a leather belt around his waist, and a proud king with eyebrows raised high, seated on a lofty throne, tyrannized by the power of pleasures and driven by the rashness of anger to commit murder. [Note:] For [?]: Lipomano reads “of the enemy.”

Consider [?] to what [?] you were carried, rashly swearing [?] I say is a mark of a king [?] an unrestrained passion; having undergone it, you [?] accepted [?] as decided. Such [?] unbridled, and speech unguarded [?] judgment presiding over the reasonings [?] the mind not preventing it from doing [?] of the natural understanding. But [?] of lawlessness, the girl? [?] of adultery [?] Herod's hook; the snare on [?] slipping, he stumbled, and caught [?]. “She said,” it says, “to her mother: What [?]” “And she, having been prompted: ‘Give me here [?] the head of John the Baptist.’” [?] the evangelist [?] the truth everywhere [?]. For what does he say? “And Herodias [?] and wanted to kill him, and [?] for Herod feared John [?] a righteous and holy man; and hearing [?] he did many things, and heard him gladly.” [?] already pressing even before the oaths [?] the quarrelsome [?] against the prophet [?]. What [?] clearer than this testimony [?]? For the boldness and the [?] the rebuke of John against Herod [?] and the wrath nursed [?] deep within her for a long time, he brings before the eyes of the hearers. For this word “held [a grudge]” is [?] and indicative, since “he could not” also [?] has [?] Herod's [?] honor toward John; that [he held] him holy and righteous [?] hearing him he did many things, and gladly [?]. And if this [?] of the things above with those below [?] contains much difference within itself; and [?] the things [?] the ruler [?]. For the first [?] boldness [?] and rebukes [?] of the king [?] and him acting lawlessly [?] against his brother [?] plotting against the bed [?]. At the same time [?] holding [?] of God in reverence [?] as righteous and holy had a place [?]; but what follows is utterly unlike and incongruous [?], having nothing in any [?] of the former. For what reason, and why? [?] flushed with wine, to the lightness of drunkenness and [?] refuge, whence for the sake of a cold [?] [?] otherwise.

intercourse, [?] taking offense like a king. And the adulteress's dancing girl became something great to you, and your frenzy for her a pit at the edge of a cliff. “And the daughter of Herodias danced,” it says, “and pleased Herod, and he said: ‘Ask me whatever you wish, and I will give it to you.’ And he promised her with an oath to give her whatever she asked, up to half of his kingdom.” Very well: the girl pleased him then with her dancing. Perhaps something did have to be given to the girl by you, but something reasonable, not something extravagant; something to delight the guests, not something to grieve them. Surely not the head of a holy man and a prophet? “But because of his oaths and his fellow guests, he did not want to refuse her.” Alas for the grief! Alas for the hardness of heart, and for the senseless excuse! If she had asked you to give up the kingdom, how would you have dealt with your oaths to her? If she had demanded that her mother's eyes be gouged out, or ordered you to give up all intercourse with her mother, would you then have fulfilled what was asked? “But because of his oaths,” it says, “and his fellow guests, he did not want to refuse her.” For this phrase points to the inescapable force of necessity. What, then, would you have done if she had put forward one of the requests I mentioned? But it seems that “whoever commits sin is a slave of sin.” For whoever yokes his reason to pleasure becomes, without anyone seeing it, a slave of the passions; but when he uses the impulse of anger to serve them, he openly displays his disposition for all to see. [?] in the outcome of his conduct he appears to be what the passion that enslaved him wanted before the test, and anger did not cease until the [?] of pleasure had condemned the impassioned man. Do you see into what an excess of absurdity the utterance of your oaths slid? Alas, great is the hardening of the mind and the miscarriage of good sense, which gave birth to such stupidity. “Ask me whatever you wish, and I will give it to you, up to half of my kingdom.”

Are you so unguarded, so easygoing, that you set no limits to your reasonings, and do not see what you should not have accepted without examination? Consider to what a pitch of folly your rash oath carried you. To be carried away, I say, is not the mark of a king but the unrestrained passion of an unbridled tongue. Having fallen into it, you accepted what had not been decided as though it had been. Such is every unbridled mind and unguarded speech, when judgment of the good does not preside over the reasonings, and the mind does not stop one from doing the opposite, because the natural understanding has already been taken away. Herod, then, carried along so lightly and so wretchedly, has left behind a wretched memory for all time. And what of the girl of lawlessness, the bait of adultery, Herod's hook, the snare on which he slipped and stumbled, and, once caught, could not escape? “She said,” it says, “to her mother: ‘What shall I ask for?’ And she, having been prompted, said: ‘Give me here at once the head of John the Baptist.’” Do you see how the evangelist sets forth the truth everywhere? For what does he say? “Herodias held a grudge against him and wanted to kill him, but could not. For Herod feared John, knowing him to be a righteous and holy man; and when he heard him he did many things, and he heard him gladly.” Do you see that even before the oaths a quarrelsome hostility toward the prophet was already pressing upon that abominable woman? And what testimony could be clearer than this? For it presents both John's boldness and his zeal, shown in his rebuke of Herod, and it brings before the eyes of the hearers the wrath she had long nursed deep within her. This word “held a grudge” is at once [?] and indicative, since “she could not” also offers proof of Herod's reverent honor toward John: that he held him to be holy and righteous, and when he heard him he did many things, and heard him gladly. And even if this comparison of what came before with what came after contains a great difference within itself, and the things are not equal, since the ruler handled them differently [?], [let us consider it]. For the first things, the boldness, the zeal and the rebukes, struck at the king's folly and openly exposed him as acting lawlessly against his brother and plotting against his marriage bed. At the same time, his holding the prophet of God in reverence, as righteous and holy, still had a place for the time being. But what followed was utterly unlike and incongruous, and in no way comparable to what came before. For what reason, and why? Because, flushed with wine, he turned to the light and windy refuge of drunkenness, and so, for the sake of a cold [keeping of his oath?]

[?]… and out of shame before his fellow guests, he was in labor with a lawlessness greater than the unlawful union. It was as if he had acted out a drama of hypocrisy on a stage, thinking he could escape the eye that never forgets. How so? "For the king was grieved," it says, "but because of his oaths and those reclining at table with him, he did not wish to refuse her." What is more loathsome than this hypocrisy? What is more wretched than that keeping of an oath? He could have set the oaths aside under a more pious pretext and with a kingly resolve, but instead he completed evil with evil. "For he sent an executioner and ordered the head of John to be cut off and given to the girl." Do you see the excess of sluggishness and [?folly]? Would it not have been better to break an oath for a good end than to keep it for an evil one? Better to lie openly and, not [?] the prophet, to ask pardon for the oversight, than by keeping his word to be shown, rightly, the unjust murderer of a prophet, to store up a just judgment for himself, and to become a son of Gehenna? For if she had asked him to sin against God, to set up idols and pour out to them the blood of his subjects, and to sacrifice besides sons and daughters, mothers and brothers and wives, how would the fool have discharged his oaths in such a case? How would he have dared to fulfill them, when Judea, where he ruled badly as king while only a tetrarch, was a tributary of the Romans? But he, made a fool of in this way, was caught in the net of a wretched girl. And she, [?being] a tool found out for wickedness, and taking on herself the whole child-ruining mind of her mother, as though of a debtor…

…the head of the one whose right hand was sanctified by the One who sits at the right hand of the Father [?]. That head you pay out as the wage for an unlawful amusement, the head whose tongue stands crying out even now: "It is not lawful for you to have the wife of Philip your brother." This head you give on a platter to the girl, because she [?] your desire toward adultery and wounded your heart with her dancing. What are you doing, wretch? Do you lay down as law things that whoever does them acts lawlessly? Do you decree things that separate a man from God and by which justice is outraged? Where did you get this shameless and unlawful command? What impious law dictated it to you [?]? Away with it! Not of my God…

After the introduction, it is right to unfold, as far as we are able, the theme of the present day, so that we may not go home without profit or fruit from what is said here. That theme is the Baptist's boldness of speech toward Herod, which the Gospel book, opened today, proclaims aloud. I mean that boldness which no blame could touch, the purest and most unmixed boldness ever displayed in all creation. It so far surpassed others that it made no distinction between a private citizen and a king. For the rebuke is the same [?] for both when the deed carries the same penalty. But as befits a prophet of God, and what is more, a zealot for His commandments, he disdained the purple, the throne, the diadem, and everything that swells the empty puffed-up pride of the boastful. He spoke the truth boldly and, without any shrinking, revealed the authority of the law, since he did not want the law's freedom to be shown up as worthless. For how could the mediator of the law and of grace overlook the glory of the law and [?turn away from] the law? And that the Master's Baptist was a champion of the law, who is so foolish as not to place this first, as the chief of all his achievements? What kind of zeal he had, and how fiercely it was kindled, the Gospel will show: "At that time Herod the tetrarch heard the report about Jesus, and he said to his servants, 'This is John the Baptist; he has been raised from the dead, and that is why these powers are at work in him.' For Herod had seized John and put him in prison because of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip. For John had been telling him, 'It is not lawful for you to have her.' And though he wanted to kill him, he feared the crowd, because they held him to be a prophet. But when Herod's birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced before them and pleased Herod, so he promised with an oath to give her whatever she might ask. Prompted by her mother, she said, 'Give me here on a platter the head of John the Baptist.' And the king was grieved. Because of his oaths and those reclining with him, he ordered it to be given. He sent and had John beheaded in the prison. And his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother." Does this man not seem to you a zealot, the most zealous of all zealots, since he would not [?] give up the truth by keeping silent, nor relax any of his zeal, and that toward a king [?]? Consider what a thing it was to see a man [?] clothed in hair and girded with a leather belt, and opposite him a proud king, his brows raised high [?], seated on a lofty throne, tyrannized by the power of pleasures and driven to murder by the rashness of his anger. [?]

Consider how great the distance is between a private man and a king, between a hermit and a city-dweller who sways cities and countries. Or would you say that one of those who shone earlier under the law surpassed this man in zeal and was more fervent? Take, for example, that great one among the zealots, Phinehas, who ran his spear through the Midianite woman together with the Israelite. But the cases are not equal, nor was the opposition in similar circumstances. In that case, even if the defilement spread to many, the one against whom he raised his zeal was not one of the most eminent. Here it was a king. And what else is a king but one who carries the sentence of death on his tongue and, on any pretext, breathes murder against those under his hand? And what of that great zealot Elijah, it says, who drove a four-horsed chariot of fire and was lifted up above the earth, borne aloft on it; who put a bridle on heaven, holding back the rain, and brought on the earth a famine of three years, and who always cried, "I have been very zealous for the Lord"? How is it that he, unable to bear a woman's anger, embraced flight as his own hearth and the desert as a city? And what sort of woman was she? A lewd woman, mad for sacrifices, whose worship was idols, gods and demons, the objects of her adoration, with which and through which the thrice-wretched woman then made Israel sin. But up to this point our discourse, running along well, has shown John to be a zealot greater than those before him, inasmuch as they faced a death they could not foresee, while he had it plainly before his eyes. But perhaps some lovers of the feast will ask: why does the discourse want boldness and zeal to crown the all-holy head of the Baptist, like some costly and becoming ornament, as though perhaps some more glorious virtue were lacking, or some deed able to give dignity to the Forerunner of the Lord? And who was ever so full to overflowing with virtues as John, the great one we honor today? He alone of all those born of women was chosen as priest and baptizer of the one and first High Priest, who cleanses all by the Spirit and fire of baptism. The discourse had, beloved, many themes from John's achievements. But there is no leisure now to leave our subject and run off to others, since this is not the rule of an encomium. But I, yielding to the unattainable height of his qualities…

…my [?]." Are you so unguarded, so careless, that you set no measure on your reasonings and do not see what ought not to be accepted without examination? Consider to what folly your rash oath carried you. To be swept away in this way is not, I say, the mark of a king, but an uncontrolled weakness for loose talk. You yourself fell into it and accepted as decided what had not been decided. Such is every unbridled mind and every unguarded word: when the judgment of the good does not preside over the reasonings, and the mind does not prevent the opposite from being done, because natural good sense has been taken away beforehand. But Herod, carried away so lightly and so wretchedly, left behind a wretched memory for all time. And what of the girl of lawlessness, the bait of adultery, Herod's fishhook, the snare on which he slipped and stumbled, and, once caught, could not escape? "She said," it says, "to her mother, 'What shall I ask?' And she, prompted, said, 'Give me here at once the head of John the Baptist.'" Do you see how the evangelist holds forth the truth everywhere? For what does he say? "And Herodias held a grudge against him and wanted to kill him, but she could not. For Herod feared John, knowing him to be a righteous and holy man; and when he heard him he did many things, and he heard him gladly." Do you see that even before the oaths the quarrelsome intent against the prophet was already pressing upon that loathsome woman? And what testimony could be clearer than this? For it presents both John's boldness and his zeal through his rebuke of Herod, and it brings before the eyes of the hearers the wrath she had long been nursing deep within. This word "held a grudge" is at once [?expressive] and indicative, while "she could not" gives proof of Herod's reverent respect for John: he held him holy and righteous, and when he heard him he did many things, and he heard him gladly. Yet this comparison of the earlier with the later shows great difference within itself. The matters are not alike, since the ruler steered them in another direction. The first things, the boldness, the zeal and the rebukes, struck at the king's folly. They openly convicted him, before all else, of acting lawlessly against his brother and plotting against his marriage bed. At the same time, his reverence for the prophet before God, as a righteous and holy man, held its place for a while. But what followed was entirely unlike and incongruous, with nothing in any way comparable to what had gone before. For what reason, and why? Because, having become drunk, he turned aside to the light and windy bulwark of drunkenness, from which, for the sake of a frigid oath-keep[?]… [Mark 6:19–20]

…of Galilee. "And when the daughter of Herodias herself came in and danced, and pleased Herod and those reclining with him, the king said to the girl, 'Ask me whatever you wish, and I will give it to you, up to half of my kingdom.' So he promised with an oath to give her whatever she might ask. She went out and said to her mother, 'What shall I ask?' And she said, 'The head of John the Baptist.' At once she came in with haste to the king and made her request, saying, 'I want you to give me at once on a platter the head of John the Baptist.' And the king was deeply grieved, but because of his oaths and those reclining with him he did not wish to refuse her. Immediately he sent an executioner and ordered his head to be brought. He went and beheaded him in the prison, brought his head on a platter, and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother." O bitter birthday, and supper full of murder! This is the honor you kept for yourself; this is the delicacy you served at your birthday! Such is the banquet you prepared for yourself! Did you have to mix the supper for your guests with streams of blood? Is this how you showed kindness to your commanders [?] and your friends? Did you feel no shame before David, who was rebuked by Nathan and [?repented], putting away his sin rather than falling into despair? Nor did you respect the example of Saul, who was rebuked by the great Samuel before the whole [?assembly] of Israel, and who, though reproved, did nothing further out of reverence for the prophet. You have not noticed, wretch, that you have doubled Ahab's lawlessness against Naboth. He was caught overcome by desire for a vineyard, for lifeless land and wine-bearing plants; you, by adultery with a woman, by plotting against your brother's marriage bed, and, the last of all evils, by the murder of a prophet and Baptist, and this on a day of luxury and a birthday feast. Would that you had never been born, nor come into the light above the earth! Would that the seed from which you sprang [?] had perished, and the womb from which you came forth!
