Why [?] did you kill the prophet who declared the truth and rebuked you about what should not be done? You could have turned to the memory of your guilt and [?washed away] the pollution; or you could have directed your mind to the boldness of his rebukes and, with sober reasoning, prevailed by choosing the better. Instead you ran aground on the opposite, adding evil to evil rather than thrusting it away as you should have. If it was out of [?regard for] those [?] that you were driven to this [?], that is plain lack of education. For one ought to love, not murder, the one who rebukes, as Solomon thinks, so that you too may not hear: "They hated the one who rebukes in the gates, and abhorred a holy word." But if, clinging to the keeping of your oath, you preferred murder, as [?fleeing] the pit of perjury, you still ought, with a kingly mind and the [?balance] of reason, to have weighed the one against the other and come to the better lot, which for you, on the contr[ary]…

…these things, than of the legislation of Moses. Did you not hear the author of Proverbs saying, "Rescue those being led away to death, and redeem those being slain. If you say, 'I do not know this,' know that the Lord knows the hearts of all, and He will repay each according to his works"? Why do you gather fuel for yourself for the burning of eternal fire? "But," he says, "I do this because of my oaths and those reclining with me." Very well. And who forced you to make this promise in the first place? Who would accept you in any way at all, or give you even the slightest praise? For a promise made with an oath about things not yet known is improvident when it is uttered without judgment, because reason has not tested the matter on either side, weighing the good against the worse. Jephthah suffered this very thing before, that great and renowned one among the Judges. He made a vow without thinking and promised God something that, through his thoughtlessness, he could not foresee, for lack of sound judgment and of the mind's discernment about what ought to be done. You, then, having sworn to the girl, ought to have set out in advance something worthy of the dance, and not to have given up the Forerunner's head, which no wealth can equal, as the hire for an unlawful spectacle. For what precious or more elegant thing did you lack, being a king, to offer the dancer in return as the wage for her dance? But you wanted, by another route, to throw off the rebuke for your unlawful union, and so you chose to let the girl ask for that wage which, as you suppose, does away with the rebuke. And that wage was the head of the Baptist. You became his murderer, a killer of a prophet, unexpectedly but not unwillingly, caught in two outrages, adultery and murder, and bringing in the worst along with the worse. What is this great derangement? Who suggested to you that you should so offend God and commit murder in the hour of luxury? [?] You thought that by killing the Baptist you would kill the rebuke along with him. But he, though he dwells in a tomb and lies hidden under the earth, still sounds the rebuke in your ears none the less, crying out twice against your vanity on a double charge. You thought too that by his slaughter you would kindle your passion more fiercely, increase your frenzy, and inflame your pleasure…

And the true proof of this is that you did not at once stop your ears against that abominable demand, leap up immediately, protest at the dancer's unblinking [?shamelessness], and cry out with a great lament: "Alas, alas, if for so brief and [?] a delight I am to pay so great a wage, to which nothing [?]…" [?]

…is equal, nothing of equal weight among the treasures in palaces." For instead of sobering up and taking courage, as you should have, and refusing the request by answering her back, you did not stand up to the girl's request as a king, saying, "No, by the God who spoke through Moses, I will not give it; I will not pay such a wage for a worthless and passing spectacle. For the price of a harlot is barely that of a single loaf of bread," as the Proverb says. So your failure to refuse in the slightest, or even to show displeasure, was a sign of a mind willingly consenting. You should at once have raised your voice, lamented vehemently, and wailed in grief. Most easily you would then have sworn off the penalty of the oaths, and by offering a refusal in exchange you would have warded off the danger of perjury. How so? You could have set oath against oath and overturned the first with the second. A man unwilling to give up the blood of a Baptist and prophet for oaths of this kind, let alone to carry them out, would show himself sober and able to bear [?] a rebuke without anger. Conversely, a man who is not troubled enough to show a downcast face, or at the very least to put the matter off for consideration, would show that he had embraced the oaths eagerly. Being unable to see this, or, to speak more truly, unwilling, you declared at once and decisively that that head should be cut off by the sword, the head that to this day convicts you of the [?enormity] of your lawlessness. For you could have avoided swearing unguardedly and entrusting your oaths to drunkenness. You could have cast a grim and [?kingly] look at that shameless and bewitched girl, so that the quarrelsome creature, struck with fear at your glance, would shrink back, unable to see even what lay at her feet, let alone shamelessly demand such ill-omened things. Instead you did the opposite and lent your ear so readily [?] to the maenad, as though you were waiting for her to ask this and no other wage for the defilement. Thus the king of the Jews was taken captive; thus the frenzied folly of his mind was driven into Bacchic madness. To this madness the demon of drunkenness led him astray and wretchedly threw him over the cliff, persuading him to cut off that head which the hollows of the earth could not long bear to hide in their bosom [?]. Still quivering with blood, it was set before Herod on a platter like a dish, and he did not [?] when he saw it. But even cut off, the head cries out and will not keep silent. Still with boldness it convicts you of adultery: "It is not lawful for you," it shouts, "to have the wife of Philip your brother." So your wicked scheme was labored over in vain. Empty, too, was the counselor's plan, and futile the dancer's request. And you [?], as one who has perjured himself, stand condemned forever. "For transgressions

ensnare a man." And she, in addition to the pollution of adultery, took on the defilement of murder as well. "For a foolish woman," it says, "knows no shame, but meets [?] on the springboard of Hades." And the dancer, go-between for that lewd woman, who joined in the drunken outrage of her mother's murders, gained nothing more than the flame of Gehenna, where she justly pays the penalty. "The feet of folly lead those who keep company with her down with death into Hades, and her steps are not made firm." Such are the dramas of the lawless. This is the harvest that lust yields to its lovers; these are the wages that passionate incontinence in pleasures bestows on the licentious. Hear these things, you who are married and you who keep the unwedded life. Let us feast on the words of Proverbs, and let our ears be charmed by these instead. But what need is there to tell those who know what they cannot by nature be ignorant of? For we are all taught by God in Christ, according to the Apostle. Would that we too, this holy assembly gathered here, had been granted the same grace, so as not to need anyone to teach or rebuke us, but to be content with the example alone. Then we would flee every imitation of Herod's madness. We would neither, through some laxity, let our minds loose to the unrestrained impulses of passionate desires, nor have our reasoning stolen away by the smoothness of pleasures and be dragged into consent. For consent, in labor with the [?poison] of sin, gives birth to death as well. So that we may not suffer this, let us keep watch over ourselves, becoming all eye, closed by no drowsiness, so that the dragon may not slip in unnoticed and rob us of our treasure. Let us all together, then, take the author of Proverbs as our teacher today. He secures us with protective words and goes through in some detail the snares that women plot and lay for the simpler sort. He says: "Pay no heed to a worthless woman. For honey drips from the lips of a harlot, which for a time smooths your throat; but afterward you will find it more bitter than gall, and sharper than a two-edged sword." But so that the discourse may not seem [?] or burdensome, I will add a few things to what has been said, offering a reminder to those who know and no small safeguard to those who do not. "Drink," it says, "water from your own vessels, and from your own wells…" [?]

[…] earth. “Let the fountain of water be your own, and rejoice with the wife of your youth. For if you keep company with her in love, you will be greatly increased.” And again: “Do not spend much time with a strange woman, and do not be held in arms that are not your own. For the ways of a man are before the eyes of God.” “Give no sleep to your eyes, and no slumber to your eyelids, so that you may be saved like a gazelle from the snares and like a bird from the trap.” And again: “Do not let desire for beauty overcome you. Do not be caught by your eyes, or carried off by her eyelids. For a woman hunts the precious souls of men.” “Her house is the way to Hades, leading down to the chambers of death. But you, my son, listen to me: do not let your heart turn aside into her ways, and do not wander in her paths. For she has wounded many and cast them down [?], and those she has slain are beyond counting.” “Do not fix your eye on her. Leap away, and do not linger in the place, for that is how you would cross alien water. Keep away from alien water, and do not drink from an alien spring, so that you may live a long time and years of life may be added to you.”

These words are enough to bring the young to self-control. The word of Proverbs has given us ample security with them, and it speaks in support of the chaste tongue of that inspired man, the venerable Baptist, who has set this table before us today. His table is not stained red with blood. It does not serve up a freshly severed head as a dish, and it does not pour unmixed wine into the bowls along with gore. Those are the wages of Herod's lawlessness. With such things Herod entertains his banquet, and such are the drinks he mixes for his fellow guests. Our master of the feast does nothing of the kind. Far from it! He has entertained us with a supper of courage and self-control, and we have eaten our fill of its dishes and become better for it. We have crossed the great sea of John's banquet with Herod, and the breezes of John's prayers to God have brought us to a calm anchorage. So it is now time to slacken the sails and rest the oars of our speech inside the harbour. Yet I think it right (for sailors are accustomed to do this too) that we also, doing something holy, should weave a short address into the epilogue and crown the man with the flowers of Scripture. That is, if we should even call him a man, since he has been shown to be greater than all men born of women. For he is the one we shall find mentioned in many places of Scripture under many titles, if we go through it with the industry of the bee. The eminence of his deeds has given him many names, and by setting the fitting testimony beside each one, [I will show] the worth of the names […]
His first title, then, is Son: “Do not be afraid, Zechariah,” it says. “Behold, Elizabeth will bear

you a son, and many will rejoice at his birth.” “Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son.” Babe: “And when Elizabeth heard Mary's greeting, the babe leaped in her womb, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit.” “For behold,” she says, “when the sound of your greeting reached my ears, the babe in my womb leaped for joy.” Child: “And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High.” “And the child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the deserts,” and so on. Great: “He will be great before the Lord. He shall drink no wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb.” John: “On the eighth day they came to circumcise the child, and they were going to name him after his father, Zechariah. But his mother answered, ‘No; he shall be called John.’ And his father Zechariah asked for a writing tablet and wrote, ‘His name shall be John.’” Man: “There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.” Prophet: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. For all the prophets and the law prophesied until John.” Elijah: “And if you are willing to accept it, he is the Elijah who is to come.” “And he will go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah.” Teacher: “Tax collectors also came to be baptized, and they said to him,” and so on. Preparer: “For you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways.” Herald: “John came baptizing in the wilderness and proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. And he proclaimed: ‘After me comes one who is mightier than I,’” and so on. Voice: “‘Who are you, so that we may give an answer to those who sent us? What do you say about yourself?’ He said, ‘I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness.’” Baptist: “Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by him.” “John was baptizing, and everyone came and was baptized.” Confessor: “He confessed and did not deny it; he confessed, ‘I am not the Christ.’” Witness: “He was not the light, but came to bear witness to the light,” and so on. Delineator of the Trinity: “But he who sent me to baptize with water,” he says, “said to me, ‘The one on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.’ And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God.” Righteous and holy: “Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man.” Apostle: “You yourselves bear me witness that I said, ‘I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.’” Evangelist: “So with many [Luke 1:13, 14, 57; ibid. 41; Matt. 11:7, 15; … Luke … [?]]

other exhortations he preached the good news to the people.” Groomsman: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete.” Lamp: “He was the burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light.” Reprover of Herod: “For John had been telling him, ‘It is not lawful for you to have the wife of your brother Philip.’” “But Herod, reproved by him because of Herodias, shut him up in

These are the names by which John has been called, and with these he has been honoured. He earned the deeds that answer to each of these titles. He is that John than whom none greater has arisen among those born of women. He is truly the one of whom the great David sings, speaking as if in the person of God the Father [?]: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ, and upon him my holiness [?] will flourish.” He is that great Elijah: not the Tishbite, but the mediator between law and grace. Though second in time, he is the forerunner of Christ's first coming, and he went before him with the same inspiration and power as Elijah, as the angel foretold to Zechariah. He is the son [?] of Zechariah, whose blood cries out more loudly than Abel's. He is the one who leaped for joy in advance and recognized his own Master while still in the womb, before he came out into the light. Using his mother's tongue as his instrument, while he was still being carried in the womb, he announced the Child without a father, saying: “Why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” “He will turn the hearts of fathers to their children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous, to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.” He is the fruit of the promise, the good news of Gabriel, the shoot that sprang up past the age for it, the fruitful flower of the barren woman, the prophet born of a prophet, the citizen of the desert, the trainer of the world, the star of the Sun, the lamp of the Light, the soldier of the King, the groomsman of the Bridegroom, the servant of the Master, the voice of the Word. He is the priest of the one who is priest according to the order of Melchizedek, since he was found worthy to perform the sacred rite of his baptism. He heard the Father with his own ears, baptized the Son, and beheld the Spirit. He is the silence of the law, the mediator of grace, the crowning end of prophecy, the conclusion of the prophets, the herald of the kingdom, the forerunner of the truth, the door of repentance, the one who adorns virginity, the preparer of salvation, the lawgiver of chastity, the bridle of the lawless, the guide of the law-abiding. He is John the Great: the name given by God, the title written down from heaven by the voice of an archangel,

the voice that came from one who was silent. Through his father's loss of speech he took away the sterility of barrenness. With a speaking finger he pointed out the Lamb. He is the great boast of self-control, the one without flesh in a body, the pearl in the clay, the costly treasure in an earthen vessel. He brings the cutting of the axe against the fruitlessness of souls. He is the desert-loving turtledove of the Church, the mouth that is never silent, the voice that thunders everywhere, the voice of one crying in the wilderness: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.” His is the tongue that spoke the words of God, and even after his death his voice reproves Herod and proclaims the One who is coming, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” To him be glory and power to the ages of ages.

On the holy [?], blessed and all-renowned [?] apostle of Christ, Titus.

As I set out to take up the praises of an apostle, may the Spirit be present with me and grant me as much eloquence as I wish. For the Spirit is always ready to stand beside those who have chosen to speak through him, just as once, coming down from above as tongues, he descended and rested on each of Christ's disciples. May he be present, not measuring out his gift by the worth of my standing, but lavishing on us his infinitely multiplied grace in keeping with the greatness of his good and divine working toward us. And you who long to receive the outpouring of light that streams so generously from there, join me in praying for the same and say: “Lord, make it known to me, and I shall know, so that I may know when I ought to speak a word.” “And do not take the word of truth utterly out of my mouth.” So, when we consider the greatness of the task before us, we must by all means approach the Spirit in prayer. We must ask for more than we deserve, so that from him we may speak what is worthy, and so that the one we praise may not be insulted by our words. But you surely long to learn who it is that is now being praised. It is plainly the inspired Titus, the first foundation of the Church of the Cretans, the pillar of truth, the support of the faith, the bulwark of true doctrine. Titus is the never-silent trumpet of the gospel proclamation, the lofty echo of Paul's tongue, the rule of unerring knowledge. This great host has invited us today to the spiritual banquet of words. As dishes he has set before us the mysteries of unwritten wisdom, whether we should call them wonders or doctrines. As a surpassing bowl mixed with divine drink he offers the word that holds the divine teaching together, poured out, as it were, for all to share. That word is sharp, keener than any

two-edged sword, and pierces to the division of flesh and spirit, as I shall explain to those who love God a little later, by way of an epilogue. For now I will say what you will meanwhile be glad to hear and what it is fitting for me to say. The feast of a very great father has arrived. Come, then: like grateful children, let us bring our hymns to the father who loves his children, for we owe him this debt. Let this temple become a common ship for us all, on which we embark upon divine hymns. And may the Father of the Word grant us speech, guiding ours toward the discovery of the truth. Since I hold the rank of a father, it would be fitting for me, after roaming the spiritual meadows with all the industry of a bee, to present the man to you straight away, crowned in a holy manner with the sacred oracles. But my speech is afraid that it may run off the straight course from the starting line and go out of bounds. Then the din of the spectators would draw their gaze to other parts of the course and cut short their hopes, and those who urge on the rider of my speech would find their shouting idle and wasted. Still, even if my speech must fall far behind the man's worth (for that is what the law of encomium requires), I may yet use the saint's intercessions with God as reins to guide it, spur it to dash hard along the straight course, and bring it back again to the turning post. For whatever is within my power will surely be dear to him, since by nature he knows how to be modest and “associates with the lowly,” imitating Paul in this as well. Come, then, let us say as much as we have been permitted to say. Let no one blame us for setting our own speech against the abundance of the man's praises. We lack the power of eloquence, but out of longing for the saint we reach for things beyond our power. Where there is longing, all fear is plainly taken away, and where speech is free and bold, no trace of timidity remains. So we must by no means decline to say what is within our power, nor keep silent about what it is holy to proclaim, since the Spirit does not want these things buried in the depths of oblivion. He wants them to be revealed, at least in some modest way, to those who do not know them, for that is just, so that they may urge them eagerly on to zeal and imitation. Silence, then, does not seem to me necessary at present. And now my speech has reached the very heart of its purpose, the goal toward which and for the sake of which the whole of it set out. This great and celebrated Titus, then, was born of our own twelve-throned Crete,

which is honoured in a symbolic way with the apostolic number. Who he was at first, from what parents he was born, from what root the shoot sprang: I do not need to say these things. My present speech is not composed as the account of a life or according to the rules of history, but has been sketched in passing within the scope of an encomium. For as a rule, the speech of those who give encomia avoids the many-branched double courses of long narratives, so that none of the listeners will be worn out and find the speech cloying, weighed down by the tedium of long-windedness. Instead I will say what I know will profit both those gathered here and myself, who am offering you the spiritual banquet of words. I will begin my speech at the point where grace made him known to us.

This man disregarded birth, wealth and every kind of distinction, everything that held sway among the Greeks at that time and all the glory that surrounded the worshippers of idols. He plainly took no account of any of it and desired only one glory. He wanted to abandon all the polytheism and superstitious error of his fathers, to lay hold nobly, by an ineffable participation, of the divine wisdom of Jesus alone, which is ours, and to belong wholly to his Beloved and to the Christian portion. And so he did, for God called him and, by the Spirit who enlightens all, levelled for him the paths of truth toward the gospel proclamation. From then on he attached himself to the radiant lamp of the apostolic assembly. I mean Paul, who excelled lawfully under the law and graciously under grace. Titus became his follower and travelling companion, and by imitating Paul's zeal with an equal zeal he too proved to be a zealot. He was called a deserter of his ancestral law, but he cast off the empty, self-invented worship of pagan thinking and transferred his citizenship wholly and entirely to heaven.

But there is something that almost escaped me, and it is not right to pass it over. This transparent pearl of Christ, I mean this precious stone, is no less than the stone of Zerubbabel adorned with seven eyes, for he too adorned the crown of graces. He happened to have as a kinsman the proconsul of the country at that time, and to have relatives by descent whose first ancestors were Minos and Rhadamanthys, the sons of Zeus. Relying on his kinsman's power, and not at all afraid of anything he might have to suffer, he laid down the written Law for himself as a fine foundation for faith in Christ. For he came across the books of Moses and the whole Scripture of the Hebrews, and he devoted his mind to them with the greatest love of learning and was grounded in them completely. Thus in a short [?] [?]

[?] space of time he was so thoroughly trained in the learning of the Hebrews that everyone who had known him before supposed he was not the man of the day before, the one they had known from experience, but someone else like him, a Hebrew of Hebrews who had distinguished himself. For he was quick-witted, he had a fitting share of secular education, his power of speech was perfected, he knew how to express himself beautifully, and he understood things very readily. As he gave proof of himself and put others to the test, he was greatly admired and looked up to by everyone.

What does he do, and what does he contrive? He approaches his kinsman, wins him over with kind words, and persuades him to let him make the journey to Jerusalem quietly, as if to gather the fuller knowledge of the Jewish Scripture from its leading teachers and to collect it through diligent study. What, then, does this noble man and lover of true knowledge do? He reaches Judea very quickly, at the time when the proclamation of the Gospel had barely begun. Or, to put it more clearly [?], it was shortly after the grace of the divine Spirit, taking the form of tongues of fire, [had come upon] Christ's disciples. Through that grace they spoke in tongues that were foreign to them but native to the nations, so that the whole city was thrown into confusion and filled with amazement at the novelty of the sight and the strangeness of the wonder. Then, on that very day, as is said [?], this great man of God came upon the crowd of those gathered there, made his way in and mingled with them. Of these the book of Acts says: “There was a crowd of names gathered together, about a hundred and [?] twenty”; and all turned to the Lord. He became one of those who believed at that time, indeed the first of them, taught by the Holy Spirit, so that he made himself a firstfruits of the divine proclamation, a firstfruits of those made Christ's own by baptism. At once he joined Christ's [disciples], was formed by the timely word of the mystery, and became a disciple himself, their equal in honour and no less in worth and zeal.

Not much time passed in between. Paul, the great teacher of the Church, appeared: that Paul who travelled round the whole world with his preaching, from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum. Not yet having drawn near to God, he was making the journey to Damascus when, at midday, he was struck down [?] by the heavenly light. He hears a voice from above ringing around his ears and is found worthy of the manifestation of Jesus as God. Before baptism he receives the mysteries of baptism, and before adoption the grace of apostolic dignity and of the laying on of hands [?]. He is shown to be a chosen vessel, to carry [?]

my name [?] before nations and kings,” as the Spirit declares through the excellent Ananias. He became a trainer instead of a persecutor and a herald instead of a blasphemer. The inspired Titus, seeing him then with the keen sight of the spirit and perceiving the divine radiance of grace poured around him, gave himself wholly to the One who had called him, and to the herald who had appeared as if for that very purpose [?]. At once he left behind everything he had at hand, bade farewell to everything that deceives the senses, and went to him with a large company. At first he became one of Paul's familiar acquaintances, and before long his table-companion and tent-mate. As this wonderful man advanced, he became known to the God who had known him beforehand, and he was preserved for the super-eminent apostles by the purity of divine illumination [?]. From then on he became Paul's companion and fellow traveller in the proclamation of the Gospel.

My speech hesitates to tell what follows, since it is beyond our understanding and perhaps beyond what many could conceive. But I will turn to where my speech must be directed. Paul's care for him was such that he took him around everywhere and brought him along, as a very delightful catch, full of riches. From his earliest youth [?] Titus had everything that adorns one who lives in virtue and is led upward toward God. He was gentle, obliging, approachable and obedient. He was ready to be sent on a mission, useful in service and successful at reconciling people. He trained those who toiled and defended those who laboured for Christ, and he was quick to answer every call to what is good. But why should I speak of distant things, when I can bring Paul's own words into our midst and use them to show him to you now more distinctly, as if engraved in letters on a tablet? Writing once to the Corinthians, and describing the grace given him for preaching, at one point in his discourse Paul quietly praises this holy Titus in these words: “When a door was opened for me in the Lord for the gospel of Christ, I had no rest in my spirit, because I did not find my brother Titus.” You see how great and what kind of grace of the Spirit was poured upon him from the very foundations of his faith, so that he was even called Paul's brother, the comforter of his soul and

…refreshment? "For I had no rest in my spirit," he says, "because I did not find Titus my brother." Would you like me to show you another testimony that the great Apostle gave about him? "I am filled with comfort," he says; "I overflow with joy." How, and in what way? Tell me. "For he who comforts the lowly," he says, "comforted us by the coming of Titus; and not only by his coming, but also by the comfort with which he was comforted in you." Do you see how far his love went? Do you see the bond of one-mindedness, so that he counted that man's comfort as his own, and the joy over him as his own? Hear what he says when he writes to these same people again: "We rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by all of you. For if I have boasted to him at all about you, I was not put to shame. But just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true; and his affection for you is all the more abundant." And a little later: "But thanks be to God, who put the same earnest care for you into the heart of Titus. For he not only accepted our appeal, but being more earnest, he went to you of his own accord." Do you see how he testifies to his zeal everywhere? Do you see how he turns him this way and that, showering him with praises and raising him on high? On the one side: "If I have boasted at all to him, I was not put to shame," and: "Our boasting before Titus has proved true." On the other [?], the great zeal he had for the ministry of the Gentiles who had believed in Christ: "For being more earnest," he says, "he went of his own accord to

…let me show you Titus as Paul's partner and fellow worker, the glory of Christ and apostle of the Churches. Let Paul, the mouth of Christ, finish the wording of the discourse for me. [?] going through, by comparison, those whom he sent with him for the ministry entrusted to him: "As for Titus," he says, "he is my partner and fellow worker for you; as for our brothers, they are apostles of the Churches, the glory of Christ." Do you see the equal share in faith? Does it not seem marvellous to be ranked next to Paul [?], and to be his partner and fellow worker and be called so? And what kind of man was Paul? The one who soared up beyond the third heaven and [heard?] things that cannot be uttered to anyone, and who, before his departure, entered paradise in a way incomparably better than [?] ours. Of this man Titus is partner, fellow worker and travelling companion. And not only that, but also the glory of Christ and apostle of the Churches. See him, then, walking in the same spirit as Paul, and [?] his freedom from love of money attested. Hear, then, Paul's own words, plainly: "But be that as it may," he says,

"I did not burden you; but being crafty, I caught you by guile." What are you saying? Did you, being crafty, take by guile those whom you netted for Christ? "Yes," he says. "I practised the good deception, in imitation of Christ who tricked the enemy." For Christ too baited him with the covering of the flesh, [and caught him] on the hook of the Godhead [?], and as a screen. The word "crafty" we take to mean "wise." "Be that as it may," he says, "I did not burden you; but being crafty, I caught you by guile. Did I take advantage of you through any of those I sent to you? I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not walk in the same spirit? Did we not walk in the same footsteps?" Well done, truth! Well done indeed, Spirit, who joined these two heralds of Christ together so closely! Paul himself, then, the glory of Titus, has already set out his praise precisely and in advance, comparing that man's deeds with his own, and [?] has painted his portrait excellently and in fine colours. But you, O blessed Father, great boast and ornament of Crete, guide to the true tabernacle, to the mystical worship above and to divine things: receive from us this hymn of praise as a kind of Siren song, and, loving father that you are, gladly accept it, along with these words of mine, from one who wishes to stammer out your praise. For the lisping of children is dear to their fathers when they utter unaffected words from an artless mind. Yet what word could be given to one who has nothing fit for receiving the concise and all-embracing Word, except such as comes within the capacity of our weakness? And what word could praise you worthily, when you received your praise from above, from the Lord? We hear him proclaiming it clearly, at one point: "You are the salt of the earth"; "You are the light of the world"; "To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God"; and at another: "But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear. For I tell you that many prophets and kings longed to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it." What crown, then, shall we weave for you? From what words shall we gather flowers to set upon your all-holy head? Who is so foolish as to try to set his own words against the Master's? Even one single saying of his will be enough to complete your praise as it deserves. Which saying, and of what kind? The one we quoted a little earlier, which called you the light of the world, as men discipled by the first Light. For that is how we should understand it of those who went round through all creation with the Gospel, like the chariot of the sun. You are the salt of the Church, through which the bitter and briny waters of unbelief were sweetened, as you drove out barrenness with [?] fruitfulness, and what was undrinkable with what is drinkable. You are the citadel, set upon a mountain, of the Church's (ibid.; Matt.; Luke 10:23)

doctrines. You are the great achievement of Paul's labours, the fair tilled field, the [?] ornament of his boasts, the finest crown of his toils. You are the first offering of the homeland that raised you, [?] the sacred, favourable offering of Christ's unsacrificed flock, the august delight of the Church, the God-voiced tongue, the never-silent mouth of theology, the [?] flute of the apostles, the God-inscribed tablet of heavenly words, the God-speaking voice. You brought your [?] to the mixing bowl of the highest wisdom, drew in the divine Spirit and drew up the grace of miracles. You drank the life-giving draught from it, [drinking] in a more mystical sense "the cup of salvation" mixed with divine sanctification. You led the Church as a bride, bringing her as wedding gifts and dowry the offspring of Crete. You are the first chief shepherd and presiding bishop of the land that bore you: now calling together Christ's rational sheep with the spiritual shepherd's pipe, now leading them in and out from pasture, you guide them to the spiritual [pasture] of divine things. You are the burning lamp that cannot be hidden under a bushel, for it is not right that your light should be measured out [?], but [that it be set] on the high, golden-gleaming lampstand, I mean of the Church [?], so that you may shine in the world as luminaries, holding fast the word of life. You are the [?] mirror of virtues, the splendour of the apostles, the firstfruits of teachers, the foremost of priests, the shepherd of shepherds, the hunter of wolves and the champion of Christ's [?] flock. You are the God-planted branch of the Church's rational vine, ripening rational clusters of preaching. You are the choicest portion of Paul's planting, the [fruitful] field of his husbandry, the land watered by the mystical drops of divine words. And what shall I say, beloved, to [?] the discourse? With what words shall I crown that sacred, God-crowned head, revered by all? [?] I have nothing to offer for its praises: no power of words, no display of art, no [wealth] of thoughts, no experience of sophistic method [?], nothing else, not even a small [?], except this little funeral oration composed for him. But you, assembly of priests, [?] sealed company of holy Titus, receive me once more as I turn back to that discourse. I am fully persuaded [?] of Christ's flock. "Unsacrificed": the great and unsacrificed victim, so to speak. The great [?] sacred, favourable offering of Christ's unsacrificed flock [?] and the whole of the faithful

that you too will join in and rejoice with me. "For when the righteous man is praised, the peoples will rejoice," says the most wise Solomon. I think it right, then, to make the voice of all my own, and, as one of all on behalf of all, to set up for you in words this man, the rational statue of words, who has shown himself the teacher of the Churches throughout the earth. For this, this is the great Titus, travelling companion of the chosen vessel, his ardent partner in preaching the Gospel. Titus, the first adversary of the madness of idolatry and champion of Christ's divine wisdom; who was laid as a stone of stumbling against those who worship stones, and set before them Christ, the stone that became the head of the corner of the Church. Titus, the sheer seat and rock of faith, who firmly settled on Christ the rock those whose minds had turned to stone. Titus, the God-built bulwark of the Church of the Cretans, the unfailing help of those who come to him without hesitation, the comely forecourt of God's care for us, through whom we came to know the truth, gained life, received knowledge and were illumined with light. Titus, first in rank of the twelve sees of this land, the God-radiant heaven for our blindness, the bright sun of the Church's firmament, the torch-bearing star among the living lamps, who unerringly led those wandering in error to the unwavering paths of faith, and who lights up the whole world with the firm supports of truth. Titus, the eye of the Cherubim, the mouth of the Seraphim, the watchful eye, the sleepless eyelid of the mystical night watch. Titus, the invincible weapon, the sword burnished against enemies, the champion of his own children, the resource of the destitute, the food of the hungry, the shelter of the homeless, the cloak that covers the naked, the harbour that rescues those caught in the storm of the waves, the beacon of piety, the bright spark of divine doctrines, the living lamp of the Church, the pillar of the virtues, the breathing image of good deeds, the eloquent lyre of doctrines, the clear-voiced singer of divine songs, the never-silent harp which, with the [?] sealed company, as a chaste [?] of priests

plectrum of its sacred strokes, sets in order the passions of souls; the mystical mirror of faith, which dazzles the eyes of opponents with the reflected flashes of its rays. Titus, the great champion of the devout, the full armour of the faithful, the utter ruin of the enemy, the correction of those who think wrongly, the steady [?] of those who turn back, the physician of the sick, the rest of the weary, the release of prisoners, the comfort of those in distress, the relief of those in misfortune, the father of orphans, the protector of widows, the deliverer of captives, the host of those in foreign lands, the visitor of those in prison, the help of those in temptation. Titus, who became all things to all: easy of access to those who [approach him], quick to hear those who pray, [?] to suppliants; friendly, orderly, venerable, fair, gentle, meek, loving toward souls, mild, kind, apt to teach, gentle, self-controlled, true. Rightly does Paul, in adorning the true priest of Christ, fittingly honour him by calling him holy, guileless, and holding fast to every virtue. Such does the venerable Titus appear to us. For he gathered in himself the whole collection of divine achievements and became wholly and entirely of the Spirit, disregarding the body. Hence a [stream] of salvation springs from him, and a flood pours forth more abundant than the sand. From these I have just gathered the finest, like flowers, and I crown my discourse with them. For it is now time at last to fulfil my promise, and to join to it the epilogue of my words. So I lend him my voice and grant him my speech, and I become a small go-between in a great matter, spiritually handing over his [?] discourse to you, not with any elaborate, ornate chatter, but with true and unfeigned teaching alone, which I will strike up in due time, raising my voice on high. For today he uses my tongue and speaks with my voice: "My little children," he says, "for whom I am again in labour until Christ is formed in you" through perfection in practice. "Do not be children in your minds, but be infants in evil. Let no root of bitterness spring up and trouble you" and darken the upright mind. Let no shoot of sin sprout in your hearts. Let no cluster ripen [?] whose wine is the rage of dragons and the [venom] of asps. Let no one despise the Master's commandments of Christ, nor stop his ears like the [asp], so as not to hear the voice of [the charmer?]. Let no one, when it is possible to choose virtue and to pursue on earth the citizenship that is in heaven, choose vice [?] of earthly things [?], and wretchedly [prefer] a perishable life to the undefiled life. "Children, it is the last hour." Let us therefore prepare something for our departure, and provisions for the [journey]. Let us increase the [?] mina for ourselves. Let no one be so careless and so

slack as to put departing to Christ second to staying on and remaining bound up with clay. Christ calls us to the heavenly kingdom. The command is the Master's; let us take up a noble spirit. Strong is the one who calls; let us not be weak in purpose toward wealth beyond all thought, nor petty in our reckoning about the things we see. Why do we linger among visible things? Why do we neglect our ancestral hearth? Our city and homeland is Zion above, the mother city of the saints, the dwelling of the patriarchs, where there is no snake lying by the road to bite the heel and bar the entrance. Zion, whose towers are fixed upon the hands of the Lord; whose gates are carved, leading those who enter into the blessedness within; whose form and beauty are known to God who built it. The inheritance of the faithful is ageless life, ineffable light, the immortal kingdom, the reward of the good things stored up for the worthy, things neither seen by the eye nor grasped by the heart, which [?] has prepared for those who love him.

Let us not throw away the good fortune of these things, all of us who have been born through deifying baptism and have been shown to be children of God: of God, who loved us and gave as a ransom for us all his own Son, the only-begotten, one in nature and one in throne with him. Let us not set aside the gift of adoption. Let us not become slaves of sin when we have been set free in the Spirit. Let us not show ourselves [slaves] of pleasure, reaping insolence from surfeit; let us not open a door to the passions, from which the floods of death pour in upon us. Let us not halt our forward course, but always run, if somehow we may attain it, toward the prize of the upward call. It is good to forget what lies behind and strain toward what lies ahead. It is good to hear Christ saying: "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross and follow me." It is good to follow Christ as he journeys through the world: "Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." Christ commands; let us not resist. It is Christ who calls, and who does not listen? It is the voice of God that teaches: "I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life." And: "I have come into the world as light." What could be more akin to us than this light? For to leave the darkness and cling to the light truly makes the one who clings to the light a son of light. And how could this come about except by our despising all the gloomy sin that shoots at us in the moonless dark? And as for taking up the cross and following Christ, what clearer symbol could there be of dying daily,

whether strengthened by the hope of what is stored up or [hedged in] by fear of what is threatened? By the cross, beloved, you should properly understand death for Christ's sake; and if by Providence it should befall us, let us not refuse it. For if we die daily to sin by our own choice, and seem to have died wretchedly, how should we not be more blessed in choosing death for Christ? Let us die, then, that we may live. It is good to die with Christ, so that we may also live with him. And how does one die with Christ? By rising above the passions; by not betraying the truth out of any fear, nor pitiably giving up one's boldness toward God out of regard for friendship with men. This is how one contends for Christ; this is how one dies for him who died for us. And how does one inherit [?]? By leaving to the earth the things of the earth, which delight the eye for a little while and afterwards cause a longer pain. Let us leave behind, then, the pleasures of this world, so that we may inherit glory in the next. Let us give something of our life to God as well. Let us take him as a sharer in our life. Already the greater part of our life has gone by. We have lived for the flesh; let us live also for the Spirit. In a short span of time let us store up long ages for ourselves. What we give up is small compared with what we expect to receive. Nothing weighs as much as what is given. This is what this sacred interpreter of the Spirit [teaches] us. This is what Titus teaches: the great trumpet of the Church, resounding to all the ends of the earth round about, the [never-silent] instrument, the voice that thunders to all the world, which opened for us the floodgates of God's mercies, and which daily covers, like a deluge, the daily [uprisings] of our enemies. This is what Titus teaches us from the tomb by the Spirit, murmuring softly through us, lowly as we are. Let us then take to heart our teacher's lessons. Let us become disciples, not [?] of the gift. Let us show ourselves obedient, not disobedient, to the one who teaches us. Let us receive his word with reverence. Let us not move our lips in whispered pretences, but with unveiled face and uncovered gaze let us fix our eyes on the light of his words. Let us be initiated into the wisdom truly hidden from the ages, which none of the rulers of this age knew by partaking in an ascent of knowledge. And to put it briefly, let us become purely [?] of the Maker [?], leaving in ourselves no lump of the old and stinking leaven of sin. And this will come about [?] if we love one another; if we do good to those who hate us, disdaining to do evil; if we do not cure evil with evil; if we forgive one another our trespasses; if we remove all guile from our hearts; if every passage for envy and every channel for malice is shut; if anger [?] and wrath do not remain in us; if the pleasures of the passions [?]

and irrational desires, from which death comes, do not climb in through our windows; if we open our doors to every stranger; if we stretch out our hands in mercy; if we break our bread for the hungry; if we bring the naked and the homeless into our own houses; if we warm our shivering brothers; if we do not ignore the poor man when he cries out; if we do not pass by one who needs our kindness; if we hasten to the churches with fear and longing; if we offer God the firstfruits of our labours; if we offer God the sacrifices and prayers that please him; if we do not dig a pit for our brothers; if we do not let the sun go down on our anger, but are reconciled before evening with those who sin against us; if we love one another as Christ loved us and gave himself up to death as a ransom for us, despising the shame; if we bring our life to self-control and "put to death our members that are on earth: fornication, impurity, covetousness," and every pleasure, and that worst of vices, pride; if we hate the love of money, the midwife of all evils. "Who is wise and will understand this?" Who will undertake to keep these things and reap the fruit that comes from them? Truly blessed is such a man, in my eyes and in the eyes of every sound-minded person. For who will be able to harm him [?], when his mind is steeled by steadfastness in the good and fortified like a city by the secure rampart of the virtues? But you, children newly born from the blessed womb of Titus! For she [?] us in the manner of the Gospel [?]. Stand against all invisible enemies, putting on the full armour of his teaching. "Resist the devil, and he will flee from you." Be brave against the loathsome battle line of Satan, and count his blows as the arrows of infants. Stand with your loins girded with truth and your sides covered, carrying the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, through prayer and supplication. For bows and arrows and quiver, let us arm ourselves with the God-inspired oracles of Titus, the herald initiated into God's mysteries. For club and spear and sword, let us count our shepherd's intercessions with God on our behalf. He will stand in our place. He will draw up the battle line and shield us. For he will shatter the war being stirred up against you. He will bring down the haughtiness of the enemy. He will stand and make atonement, and turn away the wrath of the Lord. And may he turn away from us the cup of wrath that is in his hand, the bowl of staggering and the dregs of fury, and pour it out upon our enemies. And he will turn the destruction into a breeze, and into calm [?] in destruction. [?]

[?] …will turn the storm into a [?]. Yes, and this great vessel, the Church I mean, he will guide into the harbour of the divine will, so that it escapes every heaving sea and surge and lives the whole of its life in peace. “For who knows whether God will turn and repent of our evils?” For he does not seek our death, but that we should turn and live. He will bind up and heal, and there will be no one to harm or scourge us, nor will anyone snatch us out of his hand. Even if an enemy should attack us, he will be stoned. If he stretches out his spear and rages, his arrogance will be broken on it. If he brandishes his weapons, the sword will pierce his own heart, and the bow in his hand will be broken. For the Lord himself will fight for us. “He himself will come and save us. He will come and will not delay,” and all the Egyptians will see the mighty and great hand of God. “Let us flee,” they will say, “from the face of the Lord of the Christians, for the Lord fights for them.” He destroys the Egyptian Amalek and the race of Hagar, born of a slave mother, with utter ruin. I mean the enemies of the cross of Christ, “whose end is destruction.” The abyss will swallow them in the depths of the sea, and when they try to fight at sea, it will wrap them in its waves. This is our God. He will rout them by the tens of thousands, falling before a single pursuer, and will divide them as plunder, spoils and booty for the Romans. This is our God. May he crown with victories the emperors who share the crown and the throne, and preserve them [?] through long cycles of years. May he bring under their hand all the nations, the barbarians who delight in blood. For Titus, nursling of the Word and our bishop, will stand there as a merciful intercessor. And your renowned band of ten martyrs will stand there too, and by their own sufferings will make the Lord gracious, who is able to save from death. He will then accomplish everything that serves our salvation and the glory of his majesty.

[?] May these things come to pass without any delay at all, reach the full outcome of his goodness, and be fulfilled in deeds. For then our life too will be made smooth. Every word, deed and thought will be adorned by the divine laws of the Spirit, and we will live out a quiet and tranquil life, free from troubles. A little later, through virtue and contemplation, those who have advanced so far in their way of life will be given a share in the glory and the kingdom of the world to come. These, O father, O master of your suppliants and successors, unworthy as we are, these are the small offerings we bring you. They come from my small tongue and mind, which hold you dear and honour you above all. I offer them, the least among shepherds, who have been deemed worthy of this sacred throne and pulpit, how I do not know. And even if they are small and fall far short of what you deserve, they are at least no less than my warm affection for you. For you will receive them kindly, I know well, as a small funeral tribute. The more perfect and more glorious praise you will look for later, from him toward whom you always directed your zeal and your ever-moving longing. Now look down on us from above, O divine and sacred head, as you dance in the spirit around God the Trinity, stand by grace before the throne of grace, and are lit up in soul by the divine light. Intercede for us, that through you we may somehow be rescued from the wrath threatened against sluggards like me, from the passions that rise up against us and flare anew each day, and also from the malicious enemies who try to make war on us, both visibly and invisibly. May you calm the storm into a breeze for us, and may we attain the blessedness of that place. Then, sheltered there too beneath your wings, may we dwell with you in the tents where you yourself dwell, and, made pure, may we see clearly and purely the light that is in you, by the grace of him who called us with a holy calling into his marvellous light. To him belong all glory, honour and might, now and always and to the ages. Amen.
Encomium on the holy great martyr George. The commemorations of the holy martyrs are always splendid and worthy of all praise; but more praiseworthy, and

by far more remarkable than all the rest, is the one that has dawned [?] on us today. For the present commemoration of the martyr not only contains an imitation of the Lord’s passion, adorned with the contests of an athlete and made beautiful by the radiance of spring. It is also enriched with the brightness of the Lord’s [?] most exalted feasts themselves. It stands fixed between them like a moon between a pair of suns, each circling in its own course. Flashing with light from both, it illuminates the world with rays that imitate Christ. Shining before it in order, and rising with the most brilliant splendour of the season, is the universal and surpassingly radiant feast of feasts, which leads all the feasts. It rises together with this commemoration and follows close upon it, or is even joined to it. I mean the feast of the saving [?]… [?]

[?] …the dispensation of divine love and the evident kinship of divine things. In this way the one to whom witness was borne showed us his surpassing affection for the one who bore witness to him: he made him resemble himself not only [?], but also in the day of his passion. In the same way this feast leads the martyrs’ festivals of the year. It alone, after the feast of the Resurrection, presides over the brilliance of spring. Since the boundaries of this athlete’s festival are so delightful, it is fitting to go on and show its beauty as well. The beauty of a festival is either saving speech or godly action. For Greeks and barbarians, and all who were ruled by the error of idols, solemnity and festive joy meant serving the demons with every kind of indecency and excess. But for us, who have been given the trophy of the cross against death, it is the opposite: to put the demons to shame through every kind of contest. From this the dissipation of pleasures came to be hated as shameful, while the toil of the virtues and death for piety were preferred by the saints [?] as sweet. From this the error of idols was extinguished, and the multitudes of martyrs shone out. From this the things of earth have become heaven, adorned with the saints as with stars, and a festival lasting all day long fills the world. It honours their trophies and their relics and celebrates their contests. And by contests I mean those which the common enemy wickedly instigated. He was striving to carry off for himself, by way of the idols, the worship and the name that belong to God alone. But the God of all, Saviour and president of the games, in his love for humanity allowed them, wishing to show human nature victorious over the devil. So the devil, who sought to be worshipped as God by human beings, would be laughed at by them as a corpse trampled underfoot. At that time the darkness of idol-madness had been poured out over the whole world and had nearly filled even its uninhabited parts. Almost everyone was deserting to impiety. All of them had been handed over as captives to a lightless forgetfulness of the true God and had been shown to be prisoners of darkness and long night. They set great store by worshipping the demons, and, terrified by apparitions as if they were wonders, they grew more superstitious every day. The leaders and zealots of impiety, Diocletian and Magnentius [?], and their shield-bearers in each city, charged forward into impiety like swine and devoted themselves diligently to wickedness. “And there was no refusal in their death,” for “they walked on by the light of their fire”; “nor was there firmness in their scourge,” because God was patiently enduring it so that the righteous might be revealed, and so that not… [?] It leads the martyrs’ festivals [?]

…would human nature pass away unfulfilled, with the wheat cut down along with the tares. Then, then indeed, like a day-bringing star making piety shine brightly [?], this brilliant and renowned George appeared, sweet both in deed and in name. George showed the godly deed in his name, and in his deed the grace his name implies. He imitated Issachar and lovingly “desired the good” of divine husbandry. He loved laborious work and, as it is written, was himself shown to be “husbandry created by the Most High.” He was a farmer who toiled from his earliest youth and in due season rendered the fruit a hundredfold to the Master. With the plough of virtue he unswervingly cut a straight and sweet furrow of piety, and so he was shown to be fit for the kingdom of heaven. He sowed in tears and reaped in rejoicing. He cast the seed weeping and brought in the sheaves with joy. He is the well-tilled earth that has often drunk the rain of the Spirit falling upon it and bears a saving herb for those who gather it in faith. He is the most fragrant meadow where the flowers of piety have sprung up richly, from which unploughed honeycombs are harvested, whose sweetness heals the soul. He is the useful tree planted by the rivers of the Spirit, always flourishing and always bearing the ripe fruit of virtue for the spiritual cultivation of those who share in it faithfully. He is the fruitful branch of the true vine [?], whose vinedresser is the heavenly Father, who through him cultivates spiritual gladness for us, to heal the passions and renew soul and body. He is the spring of divine streams. Watered by it, a soul that had run to waste is cultivated and bears the fruit of faith, hope and love, a triad of virtues lovely to the Trinity. He is the cultivator of divine thoughts and the field of God, in whom the fruit of piety was cultivated and in whom multitudes of miracles are cultivated for all. For a name, too, knows how to proclaim God’s grace and human virtue, as we have learned in the case of Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Jacob, Moses, and many others. This is the man who was George in name and in deed. At that time he sprang up like a rose among thorns, and like a lily breathing the fragrance of piety, amid the… [?]

…filth of idolatry he blossomed. He was like a cypress among a thicket of brambles, like a fruitful olive in the desert, like a palm sweetening those in bitterness. He was like a full moon on the darkest night, like a beacon on a moonless night for those wandering on the sea of impiety, like a morning star amid gloomy clouds, like the sun flashing bright radiance through unbroken gloom. If you also ask where he came from and look for the good fortune of his birth, the facts cry out that he is a child of God and of the free Jerusalem above. “For as many as received him,” says the virgin disciple, “to them he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name.” Such was George, who proved his lineage by his deeds. But since you also long to learn of his earthly nobility: his homeland was the land of the Cappadocians, and he was raised in that of the Palestinians. He was a Christian from his forebears, young in age but grey in wisdom, upright in heart, and vigorous in both against impiety, this martyr of piety. From boyhood he distinguished himself in military exercises and trained thoroughly in courage for war. He was entrusted with the tribunate of a military unit, governed it as he should, and often showed valour in many actions. When he had built up a great deal of military experience and was reaching for a higher rank, he obtained a higher one. For he took the wealth he had inherited from his parents and went up to the man who was reigning at that time, and the same thing happened to him as to the son of Kish. Saul, looking for donkeys, found an earthly kingdom. George, looking for worldly rank, gained the kingdom of heaven, and what he gained along the way was greater than what he had set out for. When he arrived, he saw God insulted and demons being served, and this zealot for piety could not bear it. He thought of David saying, “I saw the senseless and wasted away,” and, “Zeal for you has consumed me, because my enemies have forgotten your words.” He remembered the Lord saying, “Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father in heaven.” [?] So, in his own reasoning, he hastened to seize the promise and to win God as one who would confess him in return, by confessing God. And since he was about to enter the narrow gate, he made sure that the weight of his wealth would not hinder him, and instead made his martyrdom stronger for himself…

…to use [?], as the Lord of the contest had once declared to the rich young man, saying, “If you wish to be perfect, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” What the first young man had neglected through sloth, the second fulfilled gladly. He put off the encumbrance of wealth, and with it bought, through the hands of the poor, the priceless pearl of the kingdom of heaven. In that kingdom he stored up for himself in advance the treasure that cannot be plundered, and he nailed his heart there completely. So he first destroyed the instigator of soul-destroying greed and snatched the first crown against him. He bound this crown on as provision for the road and as a token of a loftier victory. He covered himself with the prayers of the poor, trusting that through them he would add victory to victory. And so, confident as a lion, he took up his cross and leapt out to the war against impiety. For the wise man knew well that “by almsgiving and faithfulness sins are purged,” and sins are what stand in the way of victory. “Almsgiving delivers from death above all.” “Better than a mighty shield and better than a heavy spear, it will fight for you against the enemy,” says the son of Sirach. He anointed himself beforehand with this in practice, as athletes do, and went out boldly to the battle line. He put on no material armour, but the armour of the Holy Spirit which Paul [?] describes. For he girded his loins with truth and put on the breastplate of righteousness. He shod his feet with the readiness of the gospel of peace and put on the helmet of salvation. Above all, he took up the shield of faith, which quenches all the fiery arrows of the evil one, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. He fortified himself all round with this invisible and spiritual armour, since he was waging war not against flesh, but against the principalities, against the authorities, against the world rulers of darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness. He armed himself spiritually against spiritual foes, all but crying out the apostle’s saying: “Our

weapons are not fleshly, but mighty before God for the pulling down of strongholds.” At once, then, he called on the president of the games as his ally from above. He stirred up the anger that is natural to us, took up the zeal of the prophet Elijah, and made use of righteous wrath. “With the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left,” he advanced against injustice. There he found those who were emperors in name but were in reality ruled by impiety. They were wickedly using their power against the one who had granted it. In public they had set out a boundless variety and number of instruments of torture, not against wrongdoers but against the pious. Armed men of every tribe, nation and tongue stood in a circle around them, and they were making lawless speeches and threatening that anyone who named Christ would die without mercy, consumed by these instruments. Then, burning with the divine Spirit, “his reins trembled,” like those of that Maccabee, “and he let his anger rise as justice required.” Like a roaring lion, looking mighty and fierce, he cut their threats short and leapt into their midst. He loudly proclaimed himself a Christian and openly displayed the nobility of piety. O soul truly bearing God, conquered by divine love and wholly “beside itself for God”! O blessed voice! George, Christ’s aptly named husbandman, received its seeds from God and cultivated them well in his heart over a long time, then rendered it fully ripe to the Master in due season. The air was sanctified when it received that voice. Angels applauded from heaven, archangels acclaimed it, and all the Powers of the heavens rejoiced exceedingly. The God and Master of all accepted it, judged it right that his help should match George’s eagerness, and prepared for him the unfading crown of victory. The throng of the impious was astounded, and their general, the devil, received a mortal blow when he heard it. But the noble athlete persisted. In a clear, strong voice he confessed Christ as God, and those whom they worshipped [?]…

…he called demons. He declared that they were deceived and were making fools of others. He exposed them as slanderers [?] of gods that do not exist, and showed that they spoke shameful things rather than confessing God. He silenced the blasphemers and urged them to repent and acknowledge the one and only truly existing God. Finally, he kept repeating that saying of Scripture: “Let the gods who did not make heaven and earth perish.” But they used every kind of deceit and tested the athlete by every means. What did they not say, what did they not do? Sometimes they made their words softer than oil with flattery. At other times they shot at him with the naked darts of their threats. They pretended to praise his beauty and to admire his intelligence, his noble birth and his courage in war. They advised him to have pity on his youth and not madly prefer an untimely death to this sweet life. They offered him gifts of money and rank, and no ordinary ones. Then they announced every kind and number of tortures [?], and threatened further that his death would be long and more painful than any other if he refused their advice. But Christ’s soldier, firm and undaunted, had long been taught to obey God rather than men, and that nothing has greater force than obedience to God. In no way did he give way or cower. He exposed their treacherous flatteries by the severity of his rebukes and turned away from them. Their deceitful promises he despised as worthless and spat upon. Their impious counsels he repelled like a deadly poison. Their threats he laughed at, ready as he was to suffer anything. He urged them not to delay but to put him to the test at once and be convinced, crying out, “My love has been crucified.” In short, his enemies could not overcome him from any side. “Who shall separate me,” he said, “from the love of Christ? Will tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or… [?] Ignatius, discussing and writing to the Romans [?]

sword? For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor authorities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor any other creature will be able to separate me from the love of Christ.” “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” His struggle with his adversaries did not stop at words. He also opposed them with deeds, wisely and energetically at once. Like a mighty contestant, he showed his strength and courage not only by striking his opponents but also by bearing their blows firmly. He fought in body and in spirit, suffering in the one and striking back with the other. They tormented his body with whips, but he nobly overcame them by his endurance. It was they who were tortured, since they could not achieve what they wanted, rather than the man being scourged. Then they ordered the saint to be struck with a pike. But the pike bent back like lead, exposing their failure. Disappointed in their hope, they turned to another punishment and tried to subject the athlete to still more terrible penalties. In prison they laid a huge stone on his belly all night long, besides fastening his feet in the stocks, and added other punishments, as many and as terrible as they could. When the athlete was exhausted and nearly failing, they finally brought on the most violent of all. They put him on a wheel, thinking that this would break the noble man’s resolve. The great-souled man was bent and stretched around it at the loins like a scorpion, and nobly endured as the winding in the opposite direction squeezed the breath out of him. He was dislocated and broken in every limb, and his flesh was torn all round. At the same time his body was cut into many pieces by the points of the instruments fitted beneath it, and he reddened the instruments of torture with streams of blood. The blind men already reckoned him dead, and they left him lying in that posture [?], while they sang many hymns to their gods for this and…

But they were put to shame still more when, soon afterwards, they saw healthy the man they had supposed was among the dead. For Christ, the life of all, the true God and Saviour, released him at once from both the wounds and the instruments of torture, and utterly astounded the guards and drove them away. Longing again for mightier contests, the victor ran and appeared before the impious, proclaiming by deed and word the invincible power of Christ. It was truly a fearful and astonishing sight to see, one that strengthened the faithful and silenced the unbelievers alike. They, struck by the unexpected sight, and as if not

…was shown to be false. Although they had made sure of this by inquiry, and ought to have [?], they subjected the noble man to still worse constraints. They buried the pearl endowed with reason in quicklime as it was being slaked, or, better said, as it was being set ablaze. Here the marvel seems beyond belief to many. How could flesh, which by nature easily decays, survive even for a short time in such a violent, burning seethe of quicklime, and remain entirely unburnt and unharmed, down to the very hairs? Or how could a living creature whose natural life depends on breathing the thin air be hidden in a plastering substance [?], deprived of breath, and yet not be deprived of life? But suppose someone counters such reasoning by asking how Jonah, who lived three days in the belly of the whale, was drawn up unharmed; and how Jeremiah, who was buried in the pit of mire, was brought up without needing a tomb; and how the youths in the midst of the fiery furnace breathed fine air, so that not even the smell of fire was on them [?]; and how the God of great glory has worked so many astonishing wonders in every generation through his servants. That person would be all the quicker to agree with us in this case too, and in faith would say: Truly, “God is wonderful in his saints.” For nature, for all that exists, is whatever seems good to the Creator; and, “This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.” But words would fail me, and time even more, given how unskilled my speech is, if I wished to describe one by one and in detail every torture inflicted on the noble soldier of Christ, both in public and in prisons: their form and [?], and the unbearable pain that surpasses all words; the harshness, hardness and utter savagery of the torturers; the endurance and unyielding firmness of the athlete; and how at each torture the saying was fulfilled in him: “As dying, and behold, we live.” I would also have to describe the prayers he offered all night and all day during his contests. Some were supplications “to him who is able to save”; others gave thanks for the help he had received. Besides these came the sudden and complete overthrow of the so-called gods by the sign of the cross, and the wailing surrender of the demons themselves, who openly confessed that they were not gods, to the shame of those who senselessly worship them. Then there were the questions and replies exchanged in between, which were full of [?]. In addition came the [manifestations] by night and by day — (55) “With slaked quicklime”: Ἀσβέστῳ σβεννυμένῃ. [?]

that came to the martyr as a reward for his endurance: divine appearances and conversations, or rather, to put it as David does, helps, consolations and healings. Finding comfort in these, he readily forgot the toils already past and vigorously took on those that pressed on him next, as though he had, along with his soul, a [body?] of adamant [?]…

Anyone who wishes to learn everything in detail may get what he wants by reading the account of the martyrdom. From it he can be instructed, and be astonished at the overwhelming scale of the contests, the greatness of soul of the champion, the perfect justice of the victory and the fitting worth of the divine rewards. He can learn clearly, and marvel at, how those darkened in the depths of impiety craftily mixed the bitter with the sweet in their words. The martyr, by contrast, easily undid and overturned their clever and treacherous sophistries with the simple word of truth. With the firm and lofty wing of his mind he flew over their ambushes and hidden snares. By the strength of his endurance he mightily prevailed over their varied and grievous tortures, and he completed the course in the boots and the nails. At last he was handed over to the sword, and by bodily death he put the death of the soul to death. Shown victorious through his blood and crowned with the wreath of victory, he joyfully sent up in deed a hymn of triumph to the Giver of victory, saying: “Blessed be the Lord, who has not given us as prey to their teeth.” The diligent reader who studies such a narrative carefully will also learn that the martyr did not toil for himself alone. Through his own labours he brought about the salvation of a great many others, and he led many to finish the same course, pouring out their own blood to God. Among them were the generals Anatolius and Protoleon, who were struck with amazement at the works that shone out alongside his contest and emulated his courage. There was also Glycerius the [farmer?], who was freed from the senseless worship of idols by the wonder concerning the ox. The martyr snatched them, so to speak, from the very throat of the dragon, and brought them to his own Master as perfect and acceptable sacrifices. There were also very great and extraordinary miracles. Some were granted to the faithful who asked for them, falling like snowflakes. Others were requested without faith by his opponents, yet came to pass in deed through the martyr's prayer. Among these was a dead man who rose from a coff- [Note: perhaps “through” is missing.]

-in to refute the folly of those who had asked for the sign, and to bring them to knowledge of the truth, if only those who asked had eyes to see. Those very people refused to believe the outcome of the miracles and put their trust in apparitions [?], and so were caught once again. They had used up every instrument of torture and had grown weary in the face of the martyr's endurance. So, in the manner of the Jews, they turned to demanding signs that they supposed were impossible. When they were put to shame there too, since the miracles became the salvation of a great many who came to know the [true?] God through them, they could not counter the martyr's indescribable wonder-working. Nor could they bring themselves to turn back, because, as Isaiah says, they had been blinded and hardened in heart, ears and eyes. So of necessity they fell back on the deceit of their forefathers, thinking they could overturn the truth by sorcery. Accordingly they brought Athanasius forward, who thought very highly of his magic, more even than those in Egypt who were believed to oppose Moses. But before long here too the whole art of magic lay prostrate, as falsehood was conquered by truth. The magician's [defeat] here proved more profitable than it had been there. For those in Egypt recognised that it was the finger of God bringing about the overthrow of their [arts?], but they went no further than words. Athanasius, however, embraced the faith revealed to him through the deeds and even suffered death by the sword for it, a death in keeping with his name.
