I pass over naming each of the many others whom Christ's prize-winner guided to the same lot of contest. Among them, he caused even the empress Alexandra to display a virtue like that of Moses. There is need…

Encomium on our holy Father Nicholas, [archbishop?] of Myra in Lycia. Man of God and faithful servant, steward of the mysteries of Christ and man of desires of the Spirit: receive the discourse we offer you as a gift. Count it as grace for grace, in return for the wonderful and warm help you have shown us. We call you pillar and bulwark of the Church, and a luminary in the world…

…virtue has made you, and nothing good escaped you, best of shepherds and all-praised among high priests, Nicholas. For you laid up all the most precious virtues in your blessed soul, like translucent gems in a golden treasury, and so you became renowned among almost all [people?]. A lamp set on a high, gilded lampstand does not light up the ends of the earth as you do. Christ the true light once set you on the high-priestly throne, and there, as in a dark place, the lightless region of the world, you shine on all whom you shepherd, guiding them with your torch toward the light that knows no night. As from some lofty watchtower you cast the unerring radiance of spiritual knowledge not only on those near you but also on those far away. For the angelic way of life truly made you lofty. The purity and contemplation of your true union with the divine all but enabled you to fly above the vaults of heaven. From the same source came your many kinds of virtue, in which all of practical philosophy is gathered. Like a bee, you went round the lives of the saints and collected from them the first-fruits of the virtues. Which of the virtues of the saints did you not emulate, O Father? In whose footsteps among those who excelled did you not walk well? Or rather, which of those who lived virtuously did you rival without making yourself their equal? Abel the righteous was praised for his gifts; but you, most righteous Father, dedicated your whole self as a spiritual gift to God, who lacks nothing. Enoch hoped in the Lord; but you knew the clear proofs of the hopes laid up for us. Again, Enoch pleased God and was taken up; but you moved the whole mind of your soul from earth to heaven, and were wholly “beside yourself for God,” having exchanged the things that flow away for the things to come. Noah, being righteous, was accepted for his sacrifices, and in a wooden ark he saved the kinds of the animals when the flood covered the earth. But you offer the mystical services to God as spiritual victims and offerings. You show the Church of Christ to be another ark, which by your right handling of the word preserves those [rescued?] from heresy, like animals of every kind [?]. Abraham is admired for his hospitality and his love of God, and is called blessed for offering the son of the promise to God as an acceptable sacrifice that was never slain. But you receive Christ himself as your guest, eating him daily, and share the spiritual table with all who come. And you sacrifice neither a beloved son nor a sheep

offered in his place. Instead you offer your whole self to God continually as a whole burnt offering, and lay down your own soul for the sheep, as the Gospel teaches. Isaac is glorified for his righteousness. But you, like a rule of righteousness [present?] everywhere in the Spirit, restrain with great boldness those who wish to do wrong, appearing plainly in dreams even to sleeping kings. Jacob is celebrated for his simplicity of manner and [the number?] of his children. He saw a ladder reaching to heaven, which foreshadowed a greater mystery. But you, begetting patriarchs, shepherds and flocks for Christ the chief Shepherd, who entrusted the flock to you, did not fail. You “set ascents in your heart,” and, as if from step to step, were transformed from glory to glory, led up in contemplation from earth to heaven. Job was most [renowned?] for his innocence and his endurance in suffering. But you [?]… you were not shaken by the onslaughts of the heresies. You chose rather to let the waves dash against the tower than to let any of the treasure be plundered. Joseph was famed for chastity and for distributing grain. But you made your whole self an image of chastity and a store of grain for distribution to the province of the Lycians, and a school of your honey-sweet voice [?]. Moses is proclaimed for his meekness and for giving the law to the people, and Scripture records him as a god to Pharaoh and leader of Israel. But you, all-blessed Father, meek toward all but fearsome to sinners, gave the whole people the law to abstain from base deeds. The rebellions of the passions you sank, like another [Egyptian] host [?], beneath the sea of your achievements. David was noble, and overcame the arrogant Goliath with the full armour of the Spirit. You too are most mighty, routing every day the spiritual tyrant of souls and driving the heretical wolves, the robbers, away from the spiritual flock of Christ. So, by practical virtue, you [enrolled?] yourself in the list of the righteous and the prophets, most holy one. You emulated the boldness of one and the zeal of others, the meekness of one and the compassion of others, and the lofty life of others still. And not only these, but also the disciples of Christ, to whom grace and truth, drawing aside the shadowy veil of the observances of the Law, reveal [to us?] the mysteries of true worship in the Spirit. Accordingly, you yourself [became like them?]

in every way, and you were named the eye of the Church in your care for it, and a resounding trumpet. Now it is [fitting?] to quote truly that saying of Scripture: “The memory of the righteous is accompanied by praises.” And: “The righteous will be held in everlasting remembrance.” Most fittingly so, for when the righteous is praised, many peoples will rejoice. Who could rise to praises worthy of you, or hymn the greatness of the mighty works of your life, much-hymned Father? Whatever we might say of you, our speech falls far short of the truth. And if we tried to compare the achievements of others with yours, the examples would inevitably lag behind the realities. What then shall we call you? A farmer? The word will certainly be true if it is taken spiritually. For you tilled the spiritual fields of the whole province of the Lycians [?]. You cut out the thorns of unbelief and sowed the living word of piety, and you stored the harvest spiritually in the storehouses of souls, as in granaries. Shall we call you a master builder? We will not be lying. With the siege engine of your doctrines you pulled down the altars of idols and the shrines of foul demons. You raised up churches to Christ in every place, building holy and venerable precincts and temples of the martyrs. As a farmer you tended the newly planted spiritual vines and made them fruitful. As a wise master builder you set churches firmly on the foundation of faith, by the architecture of the Spirit. What then shall we call you? A soldier? Yes indeed. Like a heavy-armed commander campaigning against invisible enemies, you put on the full armour of the word, “having girded your loins with truth, put on the breastplate of righteousness, and shod your feet with the readiness of the gospel of peace.” So, beating off the assaults of the passions with the helmet of salvation, you stood like a rock, unmoved and unshaken, and repelled every counter-attack of the enemy. Using unshakeable hope as your shield, you meet those who dare to shoot at you and shoot back. Then nobly

defending your flock, you stand guard around it and [?] its opponents. Then, after closing ranks behind your shields, you [drew?] the sword of faith with your active right hand. With it you cut out by the root both Arius's living division and Sabellius's merging together. There were also those who dared to confuse or to divide the saving incarnation of Christ the true God, the One of the same blessed and venerable Trinity. There were others who did not rightly understand the indivisible [union?] of the natures that came together, each in its own way, in the one Christ and God. With one and the same [spear?], like that of Phinehas, you [pierced?] both groups together, though they erred in opposite directions, and so made atonement to the God of all on behalf of all. What then shall we call you? An angel? But you fell nothing short of the angels' freedom from the flesh. You were truly called bodiless while in the body, and to those who saw you, you were like some [heavenly?] man or earthly [angel?]. For you carried out an angelic flight: you appeared to the king in dreams; you struck terror into a man plotting murder for the next day; you chastened a raging right hand bent on slaughter with a scourge that left no wound, and checked its onrush; and you stood beside men who had done no wrong and ransomed them from death. Was this a more fitting [?] task than that of the angel who carried Habakkuk across from [Judea?] to Babylon, bringing Daniel his meal in the lions' den? [?] Shall I call you a helmsman? [?]

defending your flock, you stand guard around it and fight back [?] against its opponents. Then, after closing ranks behind your shields, with your active right hand [?]… [?]… of the lions. [?] We shall speak the truth. For you [steer?] those sailing across the great, broad sea, and those who are at sea [?] on land, with the tiller of your intercessions to God and the [?] of faith; [?] through the storm toward a [fair?] breeze [?], [bringing them?] to the harbour of [salvation?]. [?] This is clear from the things in which he himself plainly [?]… [?] like a [?], sometimes to the sailors [?]… [?] at that time your…

…these things the harbour of Andriace. Because they could not sail past it, you persuaded them [?] so that you might feed the starving people and rein in the fury of famine. [?] And with what were, as it were, three gold pieces, which, as the story goes, appeared from nowhere, you paid off the ship [?]. In the end it was impossible to [?] the protector and champion of the Lycian nation, Nicholas, angelic in manner and in deed. While you were still in the flesh, before you departed to Christ, you visited the afflicted in many ways. You helped those in need as quickly as possible, and rescued those who had fallen into murderous slaughter. What else does this show you to be, but one who had taken on the bodilessness of the angels and so worked wonders with ease? Who would not marvel at your long-suffering? Who would not be amazed at your gentleness and meekness besides, and at your peaceable [?] pleading? For, as they say, you were once visiting the branches of the true vine when you met Theognis of blessed memory, at one time bishop of the church of the Marcionites. A debate over Scripture arose, and you refuted him, until you turned the man [?] and brought him back to the [true?] view. Some very slight irritation may have arisen between you, and so you spoke aloud that gentle apostolic saying: “Come,” you said, “let us be reconciled, before the sun goes down on our anger.” Father of fathers, admirable lamp of the world, foundation of the Church, support of the faithful and [?], swiftest help of the wronged: now you shepherd us all the more, and cherish us more warmly, as you attend in purity upon God, the perfect and adorable Trinity. Around the Trinity you dance spiritually with the angelic ranks and watch over us from above. O divine and holy head, [adorned?] with apostolic gifts, do not hesitate to strengthen some and to arm others of us, O Father, interpreter of the Word and teacher [?] of things that cannot be spoken. There is one who shares your way of life and succeeds you in your holy conduct, long after you in time, but [your equal?] at once in grey hairs [?]. Make him strong in power and in the word of truth, together with your sons [?] and your descendants [?]. Embrace him above all with a father's tender affection, and with the spiritual javelins of your words drive away those who dare to attack the spiritual flock. Then he may keep safe and unafraid your little flock, which you yourself nourished: the priests of priestly order and the Christ-loving people, strengthened by the living and unerring doctrines of piety and by the greatness of your wonders. [?], inspired one; and so much [?] now that you draw nearer to God in greater purity, and from there shine all the more with the radiance of… — “you paid off”: as though by way of a pledge [?], says Metaphrastes: “Three [gold pieces?] to him [?]”

…[?] helps, you hold more plainly and more strikingly the shining of your radiant boldness before God. I call you blessed, city of Myra, metropolis of the Lycians, for the shepherd and protector you have received, one who loves his children so dearly! What a crown you have received upon your head, worthy of reverence and [?] of boasting! Who is this? Nicholas, who with divine joys [?] appears plainly to those in distress; the swiftest helper of the wronged; the most sacred ornament of priests; great in wonders and fearsome in signs; who rescues the innocent from dangers and chastens in dreams those who wish to do wrong. Blessed are you, then, among cities, for having nurtured such a guardian and enthroned him on your seats. “Under his [shelter?] we shall go, and in his shadow we shall live at rest,” as the sacred oracle says somewhere. With him you also have those who became champions of piety: I mean Crescens, Dioscorides and Nicocles, the three, shining with holiness and of one mind, belonging to the Trinity, whom that same Trinity honoured with the prizes of the kingdom that their victory deserved. Fittingly, then, you joined to them, in harmony, the head that is celebrated together with them, and worthily [crowned?] him. On the one hand, by the disposition of his will he nobly showed a contest equal to theirs. On the other hand, by his own labours he once again [emulated?] the martyrs, and by his zeal for them he is now joined with what befits them [?]. But come, all of you together today, most sacred assembly of faithful hearers, now that you have arrived at this church. Let us keep a holy and most festive feast, celebrating the most praiseworthy commemoration of our God-bearing Father. We do this bidding farewell to all worldly pomp and festivity and to deceptive adornments: everything that [?] the wretched [?] of Greek cleverness, and whatever [?] of the lower [?] and counterfeit [?] fleshly toys. For these are toys, fit only for laughter, and nothing is more wretched than they;

With rosebuds and sweet-smelling perfumes, made fragrant [?] by his works, let us crown the holy man with the spiritual flowers of song. These are the perfumes with which our holy father Nicholas loves to be honored. Feasts and festivals like these please him more than the showy processions that delight the wretched gods of the Greeks when the public honors them. And the threefold concord and harmony of the most noble champions adorns the feast with splendors that concern him. You are gathered with them, Nicholas, in the dwellings on high; you shine with them and dance with them in the spirit, seeing God as far as that is possible and being seen by him. So through their intercessions with God, and through your prayers, O Father, which God accepts, may we all be delivered from every heretical and demonic terror, from disease-bringing scourges, from everything in between, from the troubles in which people unexpectedly entangle us, and from all dangers together. May this come by the grace, mercy and love for humanity of Christ Jesus our Lord, who redeemed us with the precious blood of his life-giving side and freed us from the kingdom of error. With him all honor and glory, might and majesty belong to the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

On the blessed Patapius [?], and an account of some of his miracles. How splendid and spiritual this festival looks to me, and how unusual today's spectacle is! When I see such radiance, I cannot help marveling at how eagerly people of every rank have come running here together. The chosen among the clergy, the communities of monks, all that is modest and distinguished among the women, and the more sober of the mixed crowd have come to this holy church and hurry together to celebrate a radiant feast. But some lovers of feasts might ask why this crowd has gathered here and what kind of feast this is. My discourse will soon give them, here and now, an answer that matches their question.

We are holding this festival today [?] to honor the memory of the holy Patapius. It is he who has called everyone here now with a lofty proclamation. He sets himself before us like a lavish banquet and a heavenly table, and he offers his holy memory in place of food and spiritual delicacies. You were persuaded by him, beloved, and gathered here, and you have done very well. For the voice of the all-wise Paul lays down the law: "Obey your leaders and submit to them," and "Remember your leaders," along with everything that follows these words. You honor [?] their memory in your minds, and you define the perfect prize of that memory as the virtue of those who obey. So you have come without hesitation to the one who calls you. Since this is so, come, listen to me and hear this man's encomium, an account that reveals how he conducted his life. As far as I can, I am weaving a crown for that holy man, and I am far from passing over in silence anything that bears on his virtue. For you, who [?] the mysteries of the feast, I am making the festival as radiant as I can and bringing you great delight. Who, then, is this Patapius, and what kind of man was he? Why are we eager to offer him words of praise, and why have you been persuaded to come here and celebrate him? He was the citizen of the desert and the visitor of the inhabited world; an earthly angel and a heavenly man. He lived on earth as though in heaven and moved about heaven in the spirit, mystically, as though it were earth. He talked with people below and lived with the choirs above. He was clothed in a mortal body, yet his conduct confirmed the boundaries of the spiritual life. He was the last among ascetics and the greatest in virtues; untrained in speech, yet all-wise in understanding, "for Wisdom, the fashioner of all things, taught him." He was great in purity, distinguished in self-control, fervent in faith and awe-inspiring [?] in love. He lived in a city, yet never left the desert behind. He held within himself a most fervent, burning attachment to it, which set his inner self ablaze like fire and gave it no rest [?], and that noble man never wearied of doing what belonged to that life until the end. But oh, how am I to set the crown of praises before him? How shall I describe the splendor of his way of life? I am at a painful loss, beloved, a very great one. The wonders he performed through grace from above have a marvelous [?] that shakes my reasoning and makes it stand outside itself.

It forces my reasoning out of its proper bounds. Still, I will not hesitate to speak as far as my mind can reach. No one is condemned for failing to praise someone as he deserves, but failing to say what one is able to say deserves reproach. So I will keep my thought in proportion to my words and show my zeal for praise with all my strength and a fervent soul. I will break this discourse away from the ornamented trickery of the rhetoricians outside the faith. Instead I will show the beauty of the apostolic nobility that belongs to us the faithful, or piety, or truth, or wisdom, or whatever I should call it. And beyond these I will show the man's supreme virtue. For he too loved this plain, unadorned kind of speech, since he did not practice virtue in words but achieved its [?] in deed and action. He had been eager for this from his earliest childhood. So now too it is no great matter to fashion his praise from thought rather than from flowing, pouring speech. My friends and brothers, both those among us who are eminent in letters and those who say they have no share in them, you will surely forgive me if my praises do not keep to rhetorical order. They look only to the truth, and I aim to confirm it as far as possible from the man's achievements that can be seen and that are told. Anyone who wishes can see some of these in his miracles and others in stories about him. Helped by his prayers, and supported by the Word who is beyond being [?], who truly is, and who is united, beyond all nature [?] and knowledge, with the Father and the Spirit, in whom all the treasures of wisdom are stored, we will begin the praises. Our account will, of course, take in some of the things affirmed of him according to the flesh and according to knowledge [?]. But you too must join your efforts to my prayers and make God gracious to me, so that he may give me "a word when I open my mouth." Then I will not be judged to have attempted things beyond my worth [?], or to have brought nothing useful to the discourse of praise. For this does not depend on my weakness, where any form [of speech] is attached to worth [?]. It depends on the grace from above that gives each person what is fitting, "from which every good gift and every perfect gift comes down from above, from the Father of lights," among those who are worthy of the Spirit. [?] I will come to the beginning of the praises [?], finding a fine and especially swift ally for both parts [?]. [?] O holy and great common life [?], all of you who have tasted the life in Christ with the tip of a finger, and all of you who are eager to become its lovers, open wide the ears of your mind with eagerness. [?] Jonathan, 1 Samuel 14: "the tip of the staff" [?]

In what follows, the account concerns the glory and progress of the spirit, not of the flesh. The Lord [?] Word, then, the Wisdom and Power of the Spirit [?], is the cause of all things that exist. He governs and [?] this universe, and he is the substance, the deed and the will of the common salvation of all. He shows us the one way of virtue and cries out piercingly in the words of the Gospel: "Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and does it has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life." What is this word that the Word wants us not only to hear but also to do? He explains it to us himself elsewhere, saying: "Whoever wishes to come after me must deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me." And what does the cross signify? The mortification of the flesh; freedom from passion; forgetfulness of present things; the swiftest ascent to the life above; and, in short, an unstoppable longing for the final object of desire. People about to depart from this world care nothing for earthly things at the very moment when the parts of their being separate. In the same way, those who try to bear the cross of Christ ought to have no attachment [?] to earthly things. Instead, having put to death the mind of the flesh and taken every thought captive to Christ, they ought to run spiritually to the one who calls them, so that nothing hinders their ascent [?]. They should make their journey as if along a straight, well-trodden road until they reach release [?].

[?] increasing. Of these, I think, right-minded people prefer none other than the first, the one and only, which surpasses all things in every way, in definition and in its principle of nature and power. Every account of the truth knows it as virtue. By virtue we mean that which surpasses every mind. It exists in essence and in reason, in reality and not in imagination. It is the steward of good and very great gifts and the citadel of well-formed characters, habits and lives. In it is stored the sum of everything praiseworthy. It is the pure work, the possession and treasure that cannot be plundered, glory without limit and boundless renown. Without it no one can see God at all, and apart from it no one has been found worthy of crowns or glory. It glorified the Powers above, adorned the angels and made the archangels radiant. It set the apostles and prophets alight and crowned the martyrs. It made all who acquired it worthy of divine gifts and won them the kingdom of heaven. But how long will we go on describing its lovers while we pass over the wise Patapius, who both was and became its purest lover? While he lived, his whole life was virtue, and now that he has died, crowns of virtue are woven for him. Punishment for their sins awaits those who lived with vice, and in the same way a reward for their good deeds awaits the lovers of virtue when they depart. The memory of the virtuous is honored and revered forever among those who hold it dear. The memory of the wicked is sent down into the depths of oblivion, and from there the punishment of fire receives it forever. This great Patapius, then, a true servant of God, took virtue as the mother of his upbringing, his nurse and teacher at once, and drove on to the height of its knowledge. Virtue was to the beauty and brilliant comeliness of his life in Christ what colors are to painters. Painters skillfully color [?] the underlying sketch with them and turn the drawing into something like a living statue. They embellish the creature's forms with the varied beauty of their colors and show its features vividly. Besides this, virtue also kept the place of a mother for him, educating him by a mother's laws. Having given birth to him spiritually [?], she [fed him] mystical milk as if from a breast [?], and then, as solid food,

she set before him the knowledge of divine thoughts, which those "whose senses are [trained] to distinguish good from evil" are appointed to eat. As we said, virtue raised him and nourished him like a mother and trained him to keep vigil in divine meditations. She made his soul radiant, [?], and led it up to the heights. She made him a friend of God and prepared him to disregard present things. In short, she received him when he came into this world out of nothing, and she welcomed him again as her guest when he departed from it. She waits to bear witness to his excellence when the Judge declares to all their rewards according to their worth. But without noticing it I have digressed into these words and left aside what ought to have been said first. In doing so I have fared no better than people who try to fit the roof before the foundation. Yet, encouraged by your prayerful indulgence [?], I do not set much store by the order of my praises. We have no art in such matters, no skill in prologues, elaborations, conclusions, debates or anything of that kind by which we could bring the discourse to its end. Nevertheless, as far as our weakness in speaking allows, we will not tire of writing what is fitting about his homeland and the achievements of his life. We will write about how the man advanced to the height of philosophy according to Christ, and about anything else of that kind that has come down to us. Let others praise the refinement of parents, the fame of abundant wealth, the might [?] of power, and the [?] and distinction of family. Those who are eager to be praised for such things take pride in them and alone gape after them. They bring extraordinary harm, [and no] benefit.

But this noble man's homeland is the Jerusalem above, the mother of Peter and Paul. In him, let [?] of mind, the noblest action and contests without end be praised. Or rather, let these be passed over for now and honored in silence because of their dignity, kept for the proper time. But some curious and flesh-loving people, shameless and unblinking in their judgment, might make the man out to be without a city because I have kept silent in this way. To prevent that, [I will try]

to mention also his homeland here below, refuting their deliberately malicious quibbles. No one should find fault with this. Rather, let every lover of learning among you consider it and pay very careful attention to what is said. I will try, as far as I can, to show you lovers of beauty his twofold homeland by a kind of reciprocal demonstration and contrast. One homeland is from the earth and has its origin and its dissolution in the earth. The other is from heaven, eternal and without end. We will readily give the victory to one of the two as the better. They are not equal in weight or in honor, since they do not have the same working or the same grace. But let us return to our subject. Thebes gave birth to this Patapius, who is among the saints, according to the flesh, but the font, the common mother of us all, gave birth to him the second time. Egypt boasts of the first. It has the fruit-bearing Nile as its neighbor and borders on it, and it has a groveling, earthbound glory. The kingdom of God boasts of the second, the kindling of immortal life, of all wealth and glory. And this is very fitting. The one fattens and supplies [?] perishable food, while the other yields the lasting abundance of good things as its fruit. The one promises the glory of disgrace and a thickness of flesh, while the other promises unfailing glory and mystical contemplation. The one supplies gold and precious stones, while the other wins for those worthy of the Spirit the good things that have been prepared. Why say more? The one is Egypt and is called Egypt; the other is the font and is named the font. But Egypt gives birth to darkness and gloom, while the font is the midwife of immaterial light. Egypt is the nurse of sins, the font the supplier of righteous deeds. Egypt leads the way to death, the font leads by the hand to immortal life. Egypt is the maker of passions, the font the tutor of freedom from passion. Egypt is a place of grief, the font a storehouse of joy. Egypt is the dark dwelling of vice, the font the bright dwelling of virtue. As we said, this blessed man descended from Egypt according to the flesh, and from the font he was spiritually given his name according to the spirit. This seems to me well said. But I see that some of you, excited about present things, are not listening very closely to what is said, since we have said nothing elegant or clever about the blessed man's homeland. People who love this life like to have their ears piped to by the sophistical warbling of speeches. For them the musical games of evening revels and

the pompous amusements of the stage [?] seem something very great and useful. For their sake, now that I have reached this point in my discourse, I thought I would say a little about the land of Egypt. I am especially well supplied with sensible hearers who [love] the finest things, namely your charity. That way I will neither grieve them nor mislead you, for the one would be unkind and the other foolish. The present festival calls everyone together and hurries to gladden everyone on account of the one being praised. So let us move on to the account of his homeland. All of you know this Egypt, whether you have been there or have learned about it by hearsay. What kind of land was it, and how great? And what kind of place is Thebes? We know that their fame and their boasting are one and the same. There the soil is rich and the fields are fat and fruitful. There the cities are crowded and the countryside is green with grass. There are herds of horses and pastures for livestock, [flocks] of sheep, herds of cattle and droves of pigs. Everything there tends toward food and luxury and this life that is no life at all. River waters surround the mainland like a sea and water every place. For the Gihon, the one great river among the four said to be in Paradise, makes its way along courses whose source only its Creator knows. It descends from there and passes through to the Great Sea. Each year it rises in fertile floods, spreads out like a sea and turns the land into water.

It invites ships with countless cargoes [?] to sail, lets plows work among the sails, and bids water creatures herd together with land creatures, some of them grazing on grass and others feeding on flesh. What a wonder! Yesterday a deep-soiled field, today a deep, lake-like sea. Yesterday a home for beasts of burden and wild animals, today a lair for fish and swimming creatures. It was Egypt, plainly, that produced this young man for us. Egypt, the lavish provider of earthly luxury; the maker of splendid garments; the craftswoman of passions; the handmaid of pleasures; the source of clay and brickmaking; the supplier of meat and fleshpots. This land, which Scripture [?] calls darkness, flashed forth the one who chases darkness away. This workshop of idol-madness brought us the herald of [piety]. This dark lodging of the [demons?] produced the one who dances with the angels.

That is worth marveling at. For if godliness is an abomination to every ungodly person, how could Egypt, itself abominable, become the homeland of such a chosen vessel for us? How could it, being darkness, make a light rise that chases away the gloom? Yet this is very fitting, "for where sin increased, grace abounded all the more." Through the ineffable condescension of the only-begotten Son of God toward us, and his indescribable self-emptying that is beyond reason, all deceit and error were driven away, and the altars and the accursed idols vanished. Then Egypt was shaken and its handmade [idols] trembled. All the loathsome rites of the demons have been destroyed, and the whole earth was made holy. And the people "who sat in darkness and the shadow of death saw a great light," brighter than the sun, the light "that enlightens everyone coming into the world," Christ our God. To him be glory, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

[?] of our holy father Patapius. We have offered this Father the praise of an encomium as far as we were able. Now we thought it right to set out a most truthful account of his miracles, so that we may celebrate together with those who love God and love feasts, and say: "Truly the Lord is wonderful in his saints." Let no one doubt this, especially since the Lord himself says: "Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these." Such a person does not draw the benefit from his own power, but from my name and my calling, "for I am the one who works all things in all" by my sovereign authority. In this way the great Patapius, the man of God, left the gloom of Egypt and drew near to the light. He was crucified with Christ and lived the life of the bodiless powers in a mortal body. He was precious in soul and body. He longed for a life without possessions and became rich toward God, and he was found worthy of costly grace. He "received from God authority to tread on snakes and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy," and "to heal every disease and every sickness." So he too showed us in himself the marvels of the wonder-working God: grace without limit, a gushing spring, honey-flowing

On the healing of the blind man. Once a blind man, like the man born blind, came to this blessed one, crying out: "Servant of the Most High God, Patapius, heal my eyes! Open my blinded eyes and give light to me who am in darkness, if somehow through you the

…having seen how harmoniously the visible world is put together and having marvelled at its excellence, I may praise the Creator through his creatures." The blessed man looked at him. The young man's sight had been badly darkened until he was blind, but he had the faith that moves mountains. Patapius answered him: "Young man, why do you come to me asking for things beyond me? What excellence have you seen in me, my friend, that you ask me for this healing? Only the God of all [?] it, and he hands it out where, how and to whom he wills. Why did you not run to him? Why [?] leave the Creator and come to the creature? Why abandon the Master and run for refuge to the servant? Do you not know that all of us alike need his help? Do you not know that I too am a man, just as you are? Why then do you ask for what I cannot give? Why do you want me to heal a disease like this? Only he can grant its cure, he who long ago healed the blind man, as God." With these words the holy man gently tried to send the young man away and dismissed him with kind words. But the youth pressed him again. Like the blind man of old, he cried out loudly and begged: "Have mercy on me, Patapius, true servant of God! For God has given you this grace, and through you the true Light gives me the brightness of my eyes. Most blessed one, do not stain your boldness with hesitation. Do not put off the gift by delay, and do not [?] the sun with a cloud. See my affliction and grant me healing. Measure my faith and give me grace. Weigh my longing and heal my pain." What did the blessed man say then? "Do you have faith? Do you believe in God, who has the power? Do you believe in him who heals every disease and every infirmity?" And the youth said again: "I believe, Lord, and in that belief I come." Then Patapius said to him: "In the name of Jesus Christ, who healed the blind man, in whom you believed when you came here, you shall see the sun with nothing to hinder you." At once his eyes were opened and the young man was made whole. It was as if the pupils of his eyes had never been damaged and he had never suffered this affliction. When this astonishing healing had happened to him, those who saw it marvelled and sang praises to God. The young man who had received the healing went away glad and rejoicing. He praised God and glorified him who gives his saints such gifts against diseases. This was the holy man's first miracle, the firstfruits of his labours. Let us give fitting [?] to Christ, who gave it, and to the holy man, and then pass on to another miracle. On the healing of the man with dropsy. After that noble youth, then, let the story bring in the man who fell sick with dropsy and was granted healing [?]. He was one of those who lived in the imperial city. [?] he developed dropsy and, to his misfortune,

was in pain from the disease. He spent almost all his property on doctors, but in the end it did him no good at all. Then he hurried to the ineffable and [?]-giving love of Christ for humankind. He had first believed, and he had confirmed his faith by deeds. So he came to the blessed Patapius, showed him how serious his illness was and told him how sharp his pains were. The blessed man saw that the disease was pressing hard on him and had spread through his whole body. He did not use poultices or drugs, like those that Asclepiades, Hippocrates, Galen and their disciples use, which offer cold comfort to the sick. Instead he used prayer as his medicine and the cross as his instrument. He sealed the swollen belly with the sign of the cross. He mixed a tear with oil and laid it on as a plaster, saying: "In the name of Jesus Christ, who healed the man with dropsy, be healed of your affliction." As soon as he said this, the fluid blockages that bound the belly were loosed and the natural channels of discharge opened. The whole flood of trapped water poured out, and the foul-smelling fluids that had long collected around the bowels drained away. The man regained his strength, and the disease fled at the laying on of the saint's hands. He went away praising and blessing Christ, the God, Master and Saviour of all, who always gives his saints the power to heal and through them cures the diseases of the sick. Let us praise God with him, and then pass on to the holy man's third wonder. On the healing of the demoniac. A certain young man was driven by a malignant demon and had been held by it for a long time. Sometimes he was found naked or dressed in rags. Sometimes, wearing only a tunic, he was hurled down cliffs and into ditches. At other times he was driven into mountains, deserts and ravines and miserably tormented. At still other times he was dragged into rivers and seas and was in danger of dying a most pitiful death. That would have happened if the great Patapius had not stepped in first and healed the sufferer by the grace of the Spirit. How did it happen? The man who had the demon's spirit met the righteous man unexpectedly. He began to leap about, to cause an uproar by jumping and running around, to spit foam from his mouth, to roll his eyes and to try to frighten the holy man. Coming closer little by little, he cursed him, and the spirit cried out through him to the holy man: "O righteous Patapius! Why have you left the Thebaid and come here now? Why have you abandoned Egypt and taken over the imperial city? Why have you forsaken the desert and run up into the

inhabited world? Either drive me back to the place you fled from, or let me live here. Oh, woe from you, Nazarene! How long will you not leave us in peace? How long will you not stop making war on us? Ah, [?] I will leave my dwelling. If not, I will go into the [?]. For I can no longer bear being hunted by you. Wherever I go, I find that you have got there first. I cannot bear your power, Christ. I am not strong enough to wrestle with your servants. They wound me with a single weapon and drive me away with a single name, as clouds are driven off. I can no longer endure the torment. I am conquered, I am beaten, I withdraw from now on and will go into the deserts. I wore myself out looking for a dwelling, and when I found one I am driven out like a sojourner. Oh, oh, Nazarene! Great is your power and [?] your authority. Do what you will. For it is impossible for me to stay here." The evil spirit said these things and more to the blessed man, while it made the man leap about in violent convulsions. But Patapius, the servant of God, traced the sign of the cross in the air with his finger and spoke to it in a gentle voice: "Evil and unclean spirit, come out of this man, created in the image of his Creator. Come out and flee to the place where Christ condemned you with your [?] fellows. The Nazarene himself, whom you have confessed against your will to be Christ, has struck you with the cross through me and commanded you into exile. It is he who drives you out, wretched creature, and expels you against your will." When the righteous man had said this, the spirit [?] the young man and threw him down. It came out of his mouth like smoke and fled, rising up into the air like some [?]. And it began to [?] cry out to the holy man: "Truly you have not fooled me, Patapius. It is not you who are driving me out, but Christ, whom you serve. He has humbled me and stripped me bare, and it is in fear of him that I withdraw." The young man, as though coming to himself, got up quickly and fell at the holy man's feet. Weeping, he gave thanks and said: "I thank you, Patapius, servant of God Most High, because Christ, the physician of the sick, has healed me through you." The blessed man sealed the young man's forehead with his finger and sent him home rejoicing, praising and glorifying God, who freely gives all his saints the power to heal sufferings. On the healing of the woman suffering from [?]. Let us bring into our midst, then, the woman who had suffered for [?] years. She had put herself in the hands of doctors everywhere for a cure and spent all she had, but gained no relief from her disease. A cancer [?] in her breast at the nipple and had now [eaten away] almost the whole part, and the poor woman suffered the sharpest pains. Consumed by the disease and [?], she found no place of comfort. [?]

When she heard about the blessed man, she came running to him. She bowed her head at his feet and clasped his knees. Pleading tearfully and in great distress, she said: "Patapius, servant of the God of all, heal me, wretched as I am and without any help. Give me the remedy as a gift, for I have nothing left. I spent everything on doctors, and I took pain into my bosom rather than a cure. Remember the Lord, who says, 'You received freely; give freely.' Heal me, for I am suffering from two wounds, sickness and poverty. So I ask for a double return: a healing that cures me, and a gift that costs no money. For that is how he commands you to give the gift, and that is how he bids me receive it." The blessed man, as if moved with pity for her, answered: "If you believe in him who has the power, your longing will be fulfilled. If your faith and intention are sincere, you will be well and free of pain." She cried out loudly: "I come in faith, master. By faith I will receive healing. Let me not be turned away, wretched as I am, without healing for my sore. Let me not go home again still carrying the cancer, for I cannot bear the pains. I cannot endure the torments. It tears me to the depths of my heart, and the disease [?] my very soul. But I beg you, have mercy on me in my misery." He saw that the disease was tormenting her violently, and he told her to show him where the disease was. Then he laid his holy hand on her breast and made the sign of the cross where the cancer was. He said to her: "Woman, God, in whom you believed when you came to us, has accepted your faith and will reward it with healing of your disease. Your faith is bold and fervent, though the disease is grievous and hard to cure. But 'your faith has saved you; go in peace.'" And the woman went away with her breast healed and free of pain, glorifying God, who always gives his saints the power to heal. These are the miracles of St Patapius. These are the prizes of his labours. This is a partial account of the wonders he worked. With such rewards the Master honours his servants. "For whatever you ask of my Father in my name," he says, "he will give you." Such were the gifts God gave the righteous man in this present life. But the wonders after his departure from this world were so great and so many! People still sing and celebrate them to this day. Because this discourse is already long, I have decided not to mention them now. I would not want some to fall into disbelief because of the sheer number of miracles, which would not be good. So let us leave those wonders to be sung by human mouths, and known fully only to God, through whom they came about. Let us end our discourse here, after first saying a little about his departure to him.

This blessed man, then, did everything in his life wisely and in a way that pleased God. He proved himself a prudent householder and made himself wholly a vessel of God, ready for the passage from here to there. Then, receiving an unfading crown from God, he took up his dwelling in the eternal tabernacles. There he became the companion of the angels, joined the apostles in their dance and sat with them, and shared the journey of the saints. But this did not happen to him before that godly man had explained to the Fathers who lived in the monastery, both brothers and elders, the better things that lead to salvation. At that time they were all gloomy, downcast and grieving. They hung their heads and wished themselves dead. What laments they sang, and how many! "Why, Father," one of them said, "are you leaving us all and moving to a foreign and strange land? Why were we not taken first, and only then you, who love your children? But you have been [taken] from us without our knowing it. The precious treasure has been stolen. Who will make [us] rich from now on? [Who will] heal our diseases?" Some cried out like this. Others lamented in convulsions of grief. Still others wailed and mourned in other ways, and all comfort was banished. But that blessed and truly [?] man saw that he was already failing and ready to depart. [Looking] here and there with a gentle [eye], he said: "Do not weep for me, [?] children, and do not send off your [father] with laments. Rather [pray] from the depths [of your hearts] that I may find release from my faults and [?] toward the boundless light of the unapproachable [?], when I must stand before his fearful judgement seat. So do not weep, children, for I am going [?] to him who calls me. And you, [?] and fathers, take heed to yourselves and to [all] your flock. You know how I [conducted myself] among you, how I lived with you and how I [?]. I loved all as I love myself. [?] all. I made myself the slave of all, for the sake of him who commanded it." The blessed man [said] these things and others like them. At the same time he urged [?] the measure of age [?] and his own [?]. To the old he [gave advice] fitting for elders, [?] and likewise fitting advice to the young. He gave instructions to everyone as was [right], and [?] peace [?]. Then he handed over his [soul] into the hands of angels, to the glory and praise of [?]. [?] VARIANT READINGS [?] 'to him.' 'to the Fathers': marked with an asterisk, 'fathers' in place of 'elders'. [?]

who received him. The monks of the holy monastery gathered together and buried his precious and most sacred remains with honour and glory. They laid them in the church of the holy prophet John, the Forerunner and Baptist, in that same most holy Monastery of the Egyptians. They escorted him with psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, and they sent up glory and praise to him who has power over life and death. And we, beloved, praise God for all that has been told. We believe that this holy man dwells in the mansions of the righteous above. Let us set up our own trophy of victory over the passions and reach the harbour of freedom from passion. Let us bring with us the things in which God delights. Once we have reached it, may we attain perfect rest with those who are worthy, and the good things that have been promised, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ. With him be all glory, honour, might, greatness and majesty to the Father, together with the holy and life-giving Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

[?] [Account] setting forth the life of the blessed Patapius [?], as dictated by Andrew, archbishop. Everything that is truly divine and beneficial to people deserves to be believed. Such things are believed through hearing, as the divine oracle says, for hearing comes through the word. And the word, to put it simply, comes from a good intention, and through that intention a reward is stored up in heaven for those who are not found slothful. The word urges us on toward the ageless country, toward the enjoyment of good things and glory in God. So let us move our lips with great care and add this discourse as payment of a debt. Then not only may we receive a reward for [?], but even more for [?]. For this is why all these things are written down: so that by hearing such accounts, many may come to live a similar life,

as the prophet says somewhere, [?] truly such a thing. Since we have our life from him, let us not hesitate to show the way of life in truth, for he himself supplies us with this discourse. As for me, it is good to confess the sin I committed through disobedience, or rather to tell something marvellous to hear. I let hesitation become the constant companion of my mind, and I was openly rebuked as a slothful servant, so to speak, who wickedly hid his talent. I do not say this as though I were nothing, or unskilled in speech. I say it because [whoever] is present at good works, whether he sees them or hears of them, is regarded as hiding his talent if he keeps silent. But if he makes [the work] known through speech, he is justified and set free from condemnation, because he did not choose, like an envious servant, to hide the righteous deeds of God. So it seems to me, especially when someone has lived a virtuous life, that one should be willing to proclaim it. "Who will tell of the mighty deeds of the Lord," Scripture says, "or make all his praises heard?" Do you see that his praise becomes visible through telling? "Hear this, all you nations." [For what reason?] Because "The Lord has become king; he has clothed himself in majesty." That is, he has set us right toward himself and has put on altogether a beauty that was needed. That is why he says again, in another prophet: "Lift up your voice with strength." He bids us lift up our voice, because there is nothing [higher] than this, he says: to tell of his works. And the witness to this is the one who prophesied in [?]. For even if the awesome mystery of his dispensation is wondered at as something beyond belief, because all become worthy of such [?] love for humankind, and indeed [?] has come about, our nature has been shown [?]: the second from heaven, but the first again as from the

Let us now explain briefly the reason for this prologue, so that the defence I now offer does not make our discourse look worthless. He who glorifies those who glorify him in truth was also well pleased by this, through which reverence is fulfilled in his being glorified, as experience of the events has shown. A written memorial of the holy man was about to appear, by his good pleasure. My lowly self once came to the place where his precious body lies. Because he came from Egypt, it is said, the place (I mean) has kept that name in the monastery to this day: the man who truly believed in all the things of God. His memorial was being celebrated by the most devout women who live there, and I began to think the saint's name of no account. "Who is this man," I said, "who has appeared to us from Egypt, this Patapius [?]?" They offered me some encomia, [?] his words, and begged me to make his memorial more splendid by writing a Life of him, and to share in their joy. After the service they said, "He is worthy of your providing this for him. For divine miracles were displayed in him, and he has shown himself a luminary among us who love the memorials of the saints." But I thought their words worth nothing and kept insisting that they were nonsense. Again I said: "Who is this Patapius, some Egyptian, whom you admire so much?" That night I fell, as it were, into a trance. I saw a man of beautiful appearance, clothed in a garb befitting God. He shone like lightning, like an angel, in the habit of the monastic contemplative life. With him was a crowd of men in white, their faces turned toward him with joy. They appeared to my eyes as if each of them longed to come near him, so that I too wanted to move and stay with them. But again, because, he says, I was not known to him, I stayed motionless where I was, as though held back by shame. Then, somehow, I found myself in their midst, I do not know how. He pointed at me with his finger and showed me to them all, like a ruler bringing forward some enemy and condemning him

…reasonably. And the reasonableness of the rebuke was this: "Behold," he says, "my brothers, I have shown myself a lover to all of you, God surely being well pleased; but by this man I have been found reviled like one untimely born. Either he himself, as being surely superior to you, signifies this, slandering you also and appearing as a new Pharisee; or, not being [?] envy, he brings this upon himself, not having been moved by the supplications offered to him on my behalf by those who long for me, to bear witness to me in writing and offer it to God, in keeping with his most manly wisdom and name — a mind, I mean, made ready in him for blameless praise. That is why he has also become a worthy bishop of Crete, fitted by God with the pastoral staff over the rational sheep. He will undertake this by the power of the all-holy Spirit." As for me, my friends, I listened to these things with my mind, with trembling [?] and in great fear; and coming to myself and shaking off sleep, I offered praise to God. I pondered what this vision was: that the apparition was terrifying, certainly; but what the man's word, directed against me, might mean — unless it was surely that I had counted the man's way of life as nothing. For my ears were [?] full of the words the women were going to speak . . . . So, reckoning that this spiritual [vision?] was surely from God, and that the gift was from him on high, I was rekindled with longing, and made myself ready for the task, so that in writing I might hand on the elder's deeds to the faithful — having at first regarded what was told me as matter for disbelief, but afterward [recognizing] the great things revealed through him by God. Then, summoning the superior together with all the women who were with her in the ascetic life, I inquired of them precisely about the man's way of life, so that I might then begin to narrate it just as I had learned it, considering this: that God, who dwells in heaven, the God of all, will not let good things fail those who do good. But leaving aside the contemplation of his ascetic life in our account, let us readily proceed to the things that [?] bring it into view, narrating the first things from the last. "For better is the end of a word than its beginning." And let us recognize that when a pious life is displayed, even before a written account, [?] they enlighten the mind of us who live our lives in the world. It has also happened that this vigor of speech has come to us, perhaps because we are at a loss [?] most of the righteous man's achievements. And since the word runs ahead of his good labors like a burning lamp, it is impossible and not right, according to the Lord's saying, for it to be placed under a bed, but rather to be set upon [the lampstand?], Christ, so that everyone who believes in [?] may see the light; so it is first [?] the things of his life [?]. [Note:] In the Septuagint: "of a word."

…to leave aside, and so to go on in gladness to the things that bear witness to his life. For surely from this point these things too will be shown, as though found [?] beforehand. For there is no one who will not understand, from what is about to be heard, where these things come from, whence, and how they come to light. For light cannot have fellowship with darkness, nor a believer a share with an unbeliever, nor the temple of God agreement with idols — nor, to put it briefly, can God have [accord] with Beliar. For, as it is written, the rotten is crushed by the strong, and its end proves to be destruction. The things of the virtues, by contrast, firm and steadfast and well grounded, always endure, as the divine word shows; not being crushed by these things, they appear preserved by the word. But the things proper to wickedness "vanish like smoke," as it is written, and are revealed to be, as it were, of one substance with the unquenchable fire. For to those who do such things he says, "Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled." From here on, then, brothers, as though wishing to be rescued from fire through listening, let us strain the ears of our mind toward the man's surpassingly brilliant works, and, arriving at the light of knowledge, as Christ also teaches, let us hear what the Holy Spirit will speak among you. For through him [?] are spoken and come to utterance, as the apostolic letter teaches, so that we may fervently glorify the one who has given, and always gives, such authority, joining our voices with the Gospel, with God, to men. These syllables of praise, then, the aforementioned most holy bishop composed as words of fitting honor, words arranged with awe for the correction of those who wish to emulate the angelic life of our holy father Patapius. But [he did so] because the one who teaches knowledge to those who wait upon wisdom alone willed to clothe him with glory and honor. "For who has numbered the might of his majesty?" May he himself, who lives forever, grant us too a word in the opening of our mouth, so that we also may with longing hand on to the faithful the gifts of grace that came about after his death. Solomon the Preacher says, then: "The righteous, if he comes early to his end, will be at rest." And again he says: "The souls of the righteous are in the hand of the Lord." And a little after: "Their hope is full of immortality." Therefore I say, beloved, that the passage from here to there proves to be wealth and glory for the saints. For even if the earthly tent is laid down in the earth from which it was formed, yet it does not have what is spiritually akin to it cut off. For what is according to the image is preserved, and

…kinship with the immaterial powers, through virtue and [?] similar amendment of life. And that this is so, the body of Elisha will bear witness — how what was made of clay possesses living [energies] by the power of the Creator. And why need I speak of more of such operations, [?] which are worked by God in the saints, worthily, for the healing of men? Therefore, Word of the Father, who heal all, do not despise the wisdom of the poor man; but give me grace yourself, "for I am your servant and the son of your handmaid," to recount your gifts. For the demons will be afraid when they hear, and will enter into the chaos of the abyss, [give, I say, grace (?)] being driven out by them. This man, then, praiseworthy among the saints, having shone brightly in the monastery of the Egyptians [?] … and toil, [attaining?] the kingdom of heaven, was laid to rest in the tents of the saints [?], having worked graces of miracles. Now in those [times?] a certain girl, having renounced the tumults of worldly life, entered a convent and spent a short time there, not yet having been deemed worthy [of the habit?] of the perfect nuns. She, then, troubled by the wicked thoughts of the adversary [?] … [broke the?] bars and left the convent, and joined herself to prostitutes, and was yoked to the enemy of God, [?] shamefully the profligacy of her own body, her whole mind [turned] to foul pleasure and [?]. After much time had passed, [?] Jesus Christ, "who wills all to be saved," stirred up certain God-fearing men [and] women, and they urged her to withdraw from this stench. To put it briefly, by their exhortations they brought her and entrusted her to the [church?] of the spotless Virgin and Theotokos, which was [?] … And [he/she?] begins to guide [?] … there [?] a respectable man, and all who were leaders according to God [?]. These things being so, [?] turns [her] mind toward amendment [?] … of the adversary to [?] face [?] … of the compassionate [?]

…to them what is written: "My brothers," it says, "if anyone among you strays from the way of truth and someone turns him back, let him know that whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save a soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins." Having thus obtained this reward stored up in heaven, the aforementioned God-fearing people brought her little by little into the convent, wishing by gentle persuasion, as was fitting, to bring her in and confine her in the cell there — for the place was the old reclusory there, in which one woman lived in stillness — so that she would not run away again. So, coming together to her with godly visits, they did not cease admonishing her. Not long afterward she happened to fall ill. While she was still heavily weighed down by the disease and saw herself in despair, she asked the sisters, before she gave up her spirit, to put her too into the reclusory, so that she might be granted to die there. As she went on pleading at length, so that through this the flame kindled by the adversary might be quenched, the chief of the apostate powers sent to her some of his angels, turbulent and dark, crying out to her openly: "What is this you want to do, [?]? Turn back to us; you gain nothing." This went on for a considerable time, so that the woman lay speechless. The devout women in the convent, seeing these things, fell into despondency, and seeing the terrible collapse, they said among themselves: "Surely she will give up her soul shortly." And as the enemy of God went on wishing to net her and binding her tongue so that she could not give fitting praise to God, the nuns said: "Come, let us weep before the one who holds authority (for this is an end that meets us all), that she may give up her soul to God. And let us do what she asked." And they brought her into the reclusory. And while an all-night vigil was held from evening until morning, the prayer of this elder cut out the roots of the adversary and caused all his devices to be kept away from her. Appearing to her, he also gave her instructions, saying: "The physician of the soul's diseases grants amnesty for everything that has befallen you and consigns it to oblivion; wondrously you will have release from the evil phantoms. Therefore turn to Christ, the only refuge of those who have gone astray, and when you have come to your senses and regained your strength, send to the monastery of the Egyptians. For I am the servant of God Patapius, whom you now see speaking with you. And ask for some of the holy water provided there to the sick,

so that you too may enjoy the [gifts?] of God. Terrors will no longer come upon you; for the demons of the air that trouble you will be cast out." And Saint Patapius departed from her. And indeed, while this sacred vigil was being held, at the hour of the gospel words of our Lord Jesus Christ, she who had been seized in her natural members and whose tongue had been restrained — by the [power?] of the divine arm the demons, scourged by the elder's prayer, were driven away, and she cried out aloud: "God of Saint Patapius, help me!" And in that same hour she told everyone of the vision of this compassionate father. Hearing these things, they glorified God in fear, "who wills all to be saved" and not to stray from his knowledge, which moves to compunction. So the next day they went and received some of the holy water in faith. And partaking of it at once, she became well, and the tumult of the demons was driven away from her. This prayer of the elder, then, which reached the royal throne, did not let up until it had shaken her free from the envious one, like a captive. This prayer did not give up even after death, until it had set her free from the one who wronged us. This prayer did not grow weary until it had brought her a second time to Christ the Bridegroom. For the beginning of truly [evil?] things, and of whoring away from God, is to have been enslaved through weakness to the foul demons; for man came into being among the creatures of God without having the image rendered useless. For this reason, then, I, small in understanding, prayed concerning this, and set it down firmly. [Notes:] 37: "of the" is missing. 38: read "possessions."

…having obtained help, the aforementioned woman, in the stillness of one night, saw a table set out, placed opposite her; and one of those reclining at it said to her: "She is not worthy to taste." The voice she heard was known to her, as the one with which Saint Patapius had spoken to her before. When this voice had spoken, a second voice came in turn, from one of the women who were eating: "Yes, she will become worthy to taste from this table"; and she heard her say this. On waking, she realized that the first voice was that of the good teacher. And she asked again to be shut in further inside and lower down, so that she would have no freedom to receive what she needed from elsewhere, or to show herself to anyone, except only to the recluse who lived there with her — rightly condemning herself in this by reason. For this reason, then, beloved, those who fear God will find grace, and their lot is among the saints, and their reward is with the Lord, in whose eyes those who share in their commemorations find [favor]. For when the memorial of the saint was being celebrated now by those who had received it in faith and were awaiting with a pure heart the awe of the divine liturgy, after the vigil that night, they themselves saw the majesty of the Lord's glory. For when they had fallen asleep, as a first and divine gift, he appeared in a vision to the girl who bore the name Stoicheion [?], and speaking with this modest girl, he asked her with a smiling face: "Where is your portion with us today before the Lord?" As she looked closely, she saw someone else with him as well, both of them crowned with the monastic habit. The one walking in front held a lamp of light, in service to the second. When he had questioned the aforementioned modest and graceful girl, she, revering the man with great understanding, woke up; and at once she rose from her bed and told what she had seen to the godly-minded woman whom the holy father had sought out. When she learned it, she glorified God and was stretched still further in faith. What then, lovers of listening, [does it mean] that the saints come visiting in light? "Because," it says, "light is for the righteous always." [?] then must be reckoned as an excess, and of abundance, beloved: the saints show guidance to the worthy, to make good things dwell in them, I think, like water flowing into a house, for the enjoyment of eternal goods.

And we, O lovers of learning, rejoiced at all the things written by the aforementioned most holy bishop, even though he was unwilling. For the man was joined to the knowledge of the treasures of the Scriptures, and was trained by experience in the Attic dialect. Hence the things we wrote in the prologue would have been a ground of boasting for him, since the great father Patapius appeared to him in the vision. But the said man, reckoning [silence] a work of reverence, for this reason passed over these things — not unknowingly, but deliberately. I, however, reaching out toward the wealth of divine wisdom, have added this. For I directed my mind toward the corrector of all, that he might grant me to say worthily what is fitting. For I would not go to Plato, or Pythagoras, or Homer to learn the language, but to the guide of [wisdom?] and of the wise

…which you prepared from the beginning for our salvation. And who has known your counsel, unless you gave wisdom? "For the reasonings of mortals are timid, and our designs are precarious," as the lover of wisdom taught. For this reason you alone, coming down from heaven, showed us to be benefited, and took up our infirmities and bore our diseases; and [taught us] not to break one of your commandments, and taught us not to lose heart. And who will say, "What have you done?" to you who came into the world and saved the world? Or who will stand against your judgment, by which you have done great and unsearchable things? From these teachings, then, of the Savior, the Judge, the true God, beloved, let us open our mouth to the word of God, and let us not hide the glory of his majesty out of vainglory; but each one, if [?] — the said man reckoning this a work [?].

[?] of the Jordan [?]; who also, having come [?], proclaiming beforehand a new commandment, pointed out the Sun of righteousness to the offspring of vipers. That is why those who came to this baptism said to their neighbors: "Come, see a teaching such as none of the prophets proclaimed, nor did any commandment of the law enjoin." Have you seen him too, beloved, how he spoke exhortingly as he baptized? Have you seen Peter nailed to the cross, what delightful things he uttered? Have you seen Paul, how he exhorts Timothy and all the [?] to live their lives? Likewise Stephen too, the imitator of Christ the Savior, said while being persecuted [?]. But let our mind turn again to the teaching of Paul, since we have happily arrived at the fulfillment of what we were seeking. For he did not keep silent in admonishing the disorderly; he did not hesitate to console the fainthearted and to support them as weak; and he showed his imitators, as sharers in his teaching, how to be patient and at the same time not to lose heart in sound faith. For this is eternal life, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and might, with the all-holy Father and his life-giving Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen. (2) [?] so that the pleasant discourses [?] has been omitted. "What delightful things he uttered": several [manuscripts] have more: "An innumerable crowd came together, reviling Caesar, filled with anger, so that they wanted to [?] him. But Peter commanded them, saying: A few days ago, being urged by the [?], I was withdrawing, and I saw; and behold, I beheld my Lord Jesus Christ. And I worshiped him and said: Lord, where are you going? And he said to me: I am going away to Rome to be crucified again. And as I followed him, I returned [?] to Rome, and he said to me: Do not be afraid, for I am with you until I bring you into the house of my Father. Therefore [?], do not hinder my way; for my feet are already walking the heavenly road. So do not grieve, but rather rejoice with me, for today I obtain the fruits of my labors. And having said this he prayed thus: I thank you, good shepherd, that you have deemed me worthy of this hour. But I beg you: the sheep you entrusted to me, let them not feel my separation, since they have you, through whom I was able to shepherd this flock. And this [?] … [by which the greatest and] chief [apostle?] …"

On the Subject of the Publican and the Pharisee. The material of the Publican and the Pharisee is set before those who wish to hold fast to holy humility as a kind of preliminary exercise and a preparing of the way: humility, which lays hold of all the virtues, and in which the acquisition of the kingdom of heaven is truly established; and [it is set before them] so that they may keep away from God-hated arrogance, which turns a person aside from all the Christ-loving virtues. Who, then, will not emulate the Publican, his turning back and his repentance, and will not shake off the swollen pride of the Pharisee? For humility is joined to Christ, but arrogance to the [?] demon who is full of swollen pride. Arrogance made the first of the angels, whose name was Lucifer, wholly a devil. It drives Adam, the first father of the race, out of paradise. "And he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted the humble." "The Lord opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble." It brings down Pharaoh: "The fool has said in his heart, There is no God." It casts down Nebuchadnezzar: "For you shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve." And: "You shall not make any likeness." And if in the one the disease is cured, in the other the passion becomes a settled habit. Pride is truly a fever, stealing over the senses of the one in fever, a terrible frenzy [driving] toward a fall the

"For who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord? He who is innocent of hands and pure of heart, who has not taken up his soul in vain." Such was the vanity and haughtiness of Tyre, which, casting off the moisture of grace, [became] a parched land. For you know [?] this both by reason and by experience: the arrogant man does not ask for the perfecting grace of God; and for this reason he is parched and dry, lacking the vital warmth and the life-giving moisture. In this hollow [?] tree the night raven builds its nest, because

[?] … makes the Publican a herald of the Spirit; but arrogance makes the Pharisee an empty drum, [?], a melon, handsome outside but rotten and unlovely within. The Publican went up to the temple, and went up and [?]

…bodily and spiritually. The Pharisee went up into the temple bodily and spiritually. For the one went up in soul by going down through humility, while the other went down in soul by going up through pride. The one went up by the ascents of which David speaks, setting foot on the road that leads to paradise; the other went down, descending to Lucifer, the author of pride. The one went up, climbing and mounting toward the virtues; the other went down from the virtues and drew near to the vices. Many enter the temple, but few have a share in the temple, for they are not worthy of the house of God. The proud man does not abide in love, and according to John, whoever does not abide in love does not abide in God. But whoever abides in love abides in God, and God in him, and according to Paul he is a temple of God. Those in whom God is especially at work are the ones who truly enter the temple and sanctuary of God. And according to David, the leader of song, God enlightens only the infants and the little ones. "For where there is humility, there is also wisdom," according to Solomon: the wisdom of faith and the wisdom of action. The Pharisee lacked this wisdom. So, being a hypocrite, he gives thanks to God only in outward things, while inwardly he proves ungrateful to God. For he does not keep the commandment "You shall love your neighbor as yourself." The words "I thank you" were good, since the Pharisee did not credit the virtue to himself, as Nebuchadnezzar, Shemaiah and Peter supposed they could. Lucifer and Adam both fell into that kind of pride. Yet he was praying to have what he did not have, and even if he had had it, he lost it through pride. For even one who has it ought to confess that he does not have it and say, "I am an unprofitable servant," since "in your sight no one shall be justified…"

A person who is not humble truly casts off love, and a person who does not love looks down on others. Truly pride is the beginning of every kind of sin. Envy follows pride, and murder follows envy. Because of envy, Absalom looked on his father as an enemy and was driven to try to kill him. Truly the hidden wrongdoer is worse than the open one. He is not unlike the devil, who deceived the first-formed man through the serpent. That is why the open sinner is justified and the hidden one is condemned. The one has only wickedness, but the other has falsehood and deceit as well, and so he is driven far from the supreme truth. For it is through love that the elect are predestined, according to Peter in his Second Epistle, and Paul in the first chapter of Ephesians and the third of Colossians. Hostility, however, he rejects. The tax collector recognized his own sin and was justified, because he had come to be far from sin. So he lives, as Ezekiel says. [?] Life also accompanied David

too, as Nathan testified. The Pharisee did not recognize his own sin, and he comes to be far from life. Now, in the second place, consider the Gospel saying carefully: "Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector." They are an example and type of people who justify themselves and despise sinners. The Lord set the Pharisee as an example of the proud. He set the tax collector as an example of sinful people who offer their prayers and confessions with a contrite heart. In this way he teaches everyone to hate pride and to love humility. Through this parable Christ shows plainly that righteousness and virtue are great things and set a person near God. But when pride is added to them, they hurl that person down into the lowest abyss. This is what happened to the Pharisee. For this reason he was condemned and driven out to perdition. Injustice and sin are abominable and hateful, heavier than any evil, and they put a person far from God. Humility, however, through repentance and confession, justifies him, makes him worthy of salvation, and brings him near to God [?]. This is what the tax collector found, and for this reason he was justified and counted worthy of salvation. "The Pharisee stood and said to himself: God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men, robbers, unjust." Alas for pride! Through Isaiah the Lord treats it with contempt [?], as something that goes down to Egypt, puts its trust in Pharaoh and in the shadow of Egypt, and has its memory perish with a crash, as David the sacred psalmist says, rather than an everlasting [memory] [?]. Alas for the mouth that loves to revile! As the sixth chapter of Proverbs says: "I am not," he says, "like the rest of men, robbers, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector." Insolence appears to be the beginning of pride.
