The one who insults others and counts them as nothing regards some as poor, others as low-born, others as [?] and uneducated, and others as unjust and sinners. This insolence sweeps him along, and he thinks that he alone is wise, intelligent, [?] rich, powerful, righteous and superior to everyone. Insolence is the beginning of pride, and pride is the evil [fruit] of insolence [?]. For this reason the dreaded day of the Lord will take vengeance on everyone who is insolent and proud, for kindred sins are [punished] alike [?].
The Pharisee showed the self-exaltation and boastfulness he had both by his bearing and by the way he stood. At the beginning his words were grateful,

but everything else he said was filled with all boastfulness and pride. For he did not say, "You made me, Lord, and through your help I am free from all injustice and robbery and the other evils." "For what do you have," it says, "that you did not receive?" Instead, he reckoned that he had achieved all his good deeds by his own power. But let everyone be fully assured that without God's help he cannot accomplish anything good and has no strength to do it. "For without me," says Christ, "you can do nothing." And the Prophet says: "Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain." And the Apostle says: "It does not depend on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy." And: "Not I, but the grace of God that is with me." And: "It is God who works in us both to will and to act." That is why the tax collector was a garden drenched with spiritual waters, while the Pharisee was a leafless oak, as Isaiah and Solomon say. Although we have been honored with freedom of choice, without help from above we can still accomplish none of the brave deeds along the road of life. "For I know," it says, "that a person's way is not his own, and no one who walks can direct his own steps." So let us not credit ourselves with the trophies of our contests. Our part is only to choose the better thing and strive for it. It is God's part to bring the good desire and longing to fulfillment. Man has no power by nature; he receives it from grace, and only so can he say, "I can." Anything else is bragging and boasting: "For what do you have," it says, "that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?" "I fast twice a week; I give a tenth of everything I acquire." Since the Pharisee had accused the rest of men and the tax collector of being adulterers and robbers, he boasted of his fasting as a defense against the passion of adultery. Fornication comes from luxury, for satiety is the father of insolence, and fornication comes from surfeit. But the Pharisee, wasting his body away by fasting, boasted that he was far from such passions. The Pharisees fasted two days a week, Monday and Thursday. And against "robbers and unjust," the Pharisee said, "I give a tenth of everything I acquire." He boasted that he was so opposed to robbery and injustice that he even gave his own possessions to others. For the Hebrews gave "one tenth" of everything they had, and after that a third [tithe]. Taken together, the three tithes amounted to giving a third of their property. But they also offered firstfruits and firstborn, and many other things from what they owned [?]:

offerings for sins, offerings for purification, offerings at feasts, as well as the cancellation of debts, the release of slaves and interest-free loans. When all these are added up and reckoned together, a person [?] gives half his property. So he does nothing great when he is puffed up and boastful about it, especially since the Gospel says: "Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven." "But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, 'God, be merciful to me, the sinner.' I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but whoever humbles himself will be exalted." The tax collector, as he prayed, had no good works and could not list them as the Pharisee did. Instead he beat his breast and scourged his heart, and with great contrition and compunction he said, "God, be merciful to me, the sinner." That is why he finds the merciful Lord gracious and easily reconciled. For humility destroys all sins, while pride wipes out all the virtues, since it is greater and heavier than every sin and evil. It is better to sin and then turn back and be humbled than to do right and be puffed up. The tax collector stripped off his sins by accepting the Pharisee's accusation with meekness and patience. The Pharisee, by justifying himself and accusing the tax collector and the rest of men, fell from glory into the pit of dishonor. The tax collector returned from a disgraceful life and from sin to a blessed life and state, while the Pharisee was brought low from his swollen self-exaltation. Two things are required of all of us: to acknowledge our own sins and to forgive the sins of others. Whoever sees his own sins becomes more forgiving toward others. But whoever condemns others condemns himself and passes sentence on himself, even if he has acquired many virtues. Truly it is a great thing, brothers, not to condemn others but to condemn ourselves. Yet we let our own sins go and condemn others instead. We scrutinize others, not knowing that even if we are more righteous than everyone, we become liable once we condemn others. Then we deserve the same disgrace and punishment as the one we judge: "For with the judgment you pronounce," it says, "you will be judged." The fornicator transgresses a commandment, and so does the one who judges the fornicator. So both transgress a divine commandment, the fornicator and the judge alike. Let us instead turn the scrutiny [?] and

meddling we direct at others onto ourselves, beloved. When we see people sinning, let us keep our own sins before our eyes and count ours as worse than theirs. For those who sinned may well have repented in the very hour of their sin, while we always stay uncorrected, condemning and scrutinizing others. Lot lived in Sodom, yet he condemned no one and accused no one. For this reason he was justified and saved from the fire and from the utter destruction to which the Sodomites were condemned. So let us also humble ourselves, condemn ourselves and put ourselves to shame, so that we may escape condemnation and be exalted. Let us love humility. Through it the tax collector was justified and laid down the burden of his sins. Let us hate self-exaltation, for through it the Pharisee was condemned and lost the virtues he had. The Pharisee did a good thing in a way that was not good, and he has been condemned. The tax collector shook off his deeds that were not good in a good way, and he has been justified. For God looked on the tax collector's groaning, his contrition and the blows he struck on his breast. He accepted his "be merciful" and justified him, as he did Abel. But he loathed and rejected the sacrifices, virtues and good deeds of the Pharisee, as those of a braggart and a proud man. And he condemned him, as he did Cain the fratricide, because of this [?]

Let us learn, brothers, and be taught. Even if we accomplish great deeds, let us not be puffed up on their account. And if we become good, righteous, gentle, compassionate and merciful, let us still be humble and not have arrogance and boastfulness, so that we do not lose our labors and toils. "For when you have done all these things," says the Lord, "say, 'We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done.'" For it is a necessary and inescapable debt for us to offer to God, who is over all, the humility of servants, patience, submission, ready obedience, gratitude and thanksgiving. We must magnify and worship his all-holy will. We must not be stung by the reviling and insults of others, nor be vexed by trials, nor take it badly when we are reproached, since we reap much benefit from these things too. Let us learn and know, my brothers, the power, strength and help of humility. Let us learn the condemnation, loss and ruin that come from self-exaltation. It is the shadow of Behemoth in moist places and among the reeds, as Job says, a turning aside from the road of truth and from the light of righteousness. Repentance and confession are a great good, and so are contrition, tears, groans from the depths and compunction. Therefore I urge you: confess to God continually, and uncover your sins

to him. If we open our conscience and show him the wounds of our souls, and do not judge others, nor turn savage at our neighbors' insults, nor are grieved by their reproaches and injustices, then the Lord who loves mankind will be gracious to us. He will mix the medicines of his compassion and tender mercy, apply them, and heal us. Let us show our sins to the Master, who does not reproach but heals. Even if we keep silent, he knows everything. So let us tell our sins, brothers, and confess them sincerely to the Lord, so that we may gain his compassion. Let us lay our sins aside here, so that we may depart there clean and ready, and be brought by the just Judge into his endless and eternal kingdom. There may we inherit those future and [?] dwellings, and the delight and enjoyment that never run out. May we all attain them in Christ himself, our God, to whom be glory and might for ever and ever. Amen.

[?] Truly nothing in human affairs has stability or permanence. The glory and life of men are compared to an evening shadow and to withering grass. What is more paltry than a shadow? What is more perishable than grass? Yet our affairs are even more easily overthrown than these. Poverty and diseases, upheavals, sudden trials that come upon us on land and sea, ambushes laid by plotters, untimely deaths besides, and all that fences in this wretched span of life mark out how unstable the course of our life is. Has not disease often struck suddenly and destroyed people, and famine consumed them? Has not some unexpected collapse buried them, a wind hurled them over a cliff, or a chill passing unforeseen over the shoulder [?] brought about death? What is easier than for a man to die, even though we are puffed up by the image [of God] and lifted up as though we would never die? Well, then, does the one who says this speak: "Surely every living man is altogether vanity. He walks about as a mere image; surely he is disturbed in vain." And what is worse than this: "He heaps up treasure," it says, "and does not know for whom he will gather it." And how could he know, when he knows nothing of what comes after him? He does not know what is before his eyes, yet he has fancies about the future. What is in his [?]

hands he does not know, yet he passes judgment on what is unknown. He does not understand what lies at his feet, yet he speculates about things on high. He does not know what will happen to him shortly, yet he makes conjectures about eternal things. He is small and paltry, yet he dares to reach for the unattainable. Man: the most versatile and resourceful of instruments; the easily consumed lump of clay; the borderland between life and death; the intelligent compound and combination within matter; the rational product among sensible things; the statue not made by hands; the living image; the renowned creature; the finely drawn likeness; the godlike mirror; the boundary between things above and things below; the visible and intelligible structure; subject to corruption, yet indestructible. Man: the flower of a single day; the shadow that is easily passed over [?]; the grass that quickly withers; the prey that is easily caught; the slave who easily runs away; the creature that suffers much and is easily dissolved; clay, yet puffed up with great ideas; dust, yet gazing at the things above. This creature of many names, man, undergoes many changes that come upon him from outside, sometimes for the worse and sometimes for the better, and he has many deficiencies in each direction. For by losing the better things and receiving the worse in exchange, he fell of his own free choice, through passion, into a life of many sufferings. He was fashioned by God's hand and in his image after the rest of creation, and he was honored above creation. First, as a gift of grace, he was clothed in the garment [?] of immortality, and then he was dressed in the robe of incorruption. It was fitting that he, who had come to share in God's care, should be raised above all things that fall under the senses and should vie with all that transcend them. I mean that he did so through his kinship with both realms. And he received this magnificently and lavishly, in a way no one could imagine, for God's munificence shone out together with the work his own hand had fashioned. He had as his delight that life-giving place, paradise. There the blessedness that comes through freedom from passion was seen, and life in the company of angels. His dignity lay in being rational, intelligent, immortal and imperishable, since he shared in divine beauty, his image reproducing the likeness of its archetype. Besides all this, he had lordship over all living creatures together, whatever creeps on the earth, cuts through the air or swims through the waters. He also had lordship over the plants in paradise, except for one only, on which the first mark of the commandment was set. It was like a training ground set before him, so that through virtue he might reach perfection in the obedience of faith. In this way the godlike character of the image would have been kept unchanged, and the likeness that reproduced the original beauty would have stayed the same, never departing from its proper stability. But, alas! I cannot say how, but he was enticed by the demon as his counselor, through his leaning and inclination toward the things of sense, and he was utterly deprived. He was no longer celebrated as a citizen of paradise, nor did he glory as king over those beneath his hand. For how could someone who had become attached to the baser folly of the passions and had bowed to the irrational impulses of pleasure continue forever to share in such

greatness? He had once and for all made the whole free mind of his soul a slave to the mind of the flesh. Now, alas, he is pitied as a wanderer and as one who shares the wretched kinship of the beasts, not acclaimed as a king. He is altogether weighed down by grief, vexation, toil and a swarm of passions, for sin alone, and nothing else, is the cause of such things. What then? Is this not our condition now, and nothing more? "For man is born to toil." And grief plainly accompanies toil. "For in grief," it says, "you shall bear children." This is the first sentence passed against us. Then he is nursed, reared and brought up [?]. From then on come labors, sweat, griefs and despondency. "For in the sweat of your face," it says, "you shall eat your bread." This is the second sentence against us. "Thorns and thistles shall the earth bring forth for you." This is the third sentence. "Cursed is the ground in your works." This is the fourth sentence. "In grief you shall eat of it all the days of your life." This is the [fifth] sentence against us. "And you shall eat the grass of the field." This is the [sixth] sentence. "Until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for earth you are, and to earth you shall depart." This is the seventh sentence against us, and it signifies the sevenfold number of the present age. O bitter sentence, from which there is no escape and no way past! O voice whose bounds no one from the beginning of the ages has been able to resist! These things came from the bitter tasting of the tree and the ancient turning aside. These came from the serpent's counsel and the transgression of the commandment. These came from the first disobedience and the… [Job 5:7; Genesis 3:16; ibid. 19. Variant readings: another reading has "all have resisted the bounds" [?].]

[?] …the temptations, the poverty no one chooses, the deceits, the murders, the [?], the dissensions, the offences, the [?] in cities, at times shipwrecks on land and sea, at times piracy, and in short everything that fills the grief-laden life of human beings. These spring up for us from no other source than this, even if we seemed to devise countless subtle explanations.

What then? Is it not from this source that we are born "of the will of a man and of the will of the flesh", I mean our being brought forth "of blood"? And that we are born, live, die and are dissolved like irrational animals, and all this very cheaply and wretchedly? What [?] sprang up for us? Where does the flux and outflow of our constitution come from, and the causes by which youth and old age come upon our nature? And besides, being grieved and being pleased; groaning, being sick and being healthy, though [?] this lies precariously open to doubt, since plainly excess is a corruption of what is lacking, and having less than what is equal is a deviation and a loss. Where does the great revolution and flux of affairs that follow one another come from, if not from the cause I have named? Since this is so, and our lot is subject to so many evils, why do we not let go of what flows away and lay hold of what abides? Why do we not flee the final shame and hasten to run back to our ancient glory? Shall we not come to our senses from now on, brothers? Shall we not look up to heaven above, leaving the earth below with the things of the earth [?]? Shall we not bring back the kindred to its kin? Shall we not leave our earthly hearth, which is loosely bound and easily dissolved, and run back to our former way of life in paradise, by changing our purpose toward good counsel? Shall we not disdain all visible comeliness and join ourselves again to the things of heaven? Shall we not, even if we must suffer, renounce living irrationally and, having become rational, advance toward the image and the original likeness? Why do we make ourselves lowly, when we were made lofty? Why do we cling to visible things and so lose the things perceived by the mind? Why do we, who belong to the image, not honor what is according to the image? Why do we not revere our calling? Why do we set grace aside? Why do we make ourselves slaves of the passions, when we were fashioned free?

For it is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Among us there is no Jew, no Greek, no Scythian, no barbarian; there is no [male nor] female. We are all one in the Lord. By grace we have been saved. We have become sons of God, for he has given us power to become children of God. … God has sent forth the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, so that we are no longer slaves but sons, and heirs of God through Christ. Let us not, then, outrage our noble birth with cheap things. Let us not forget our homeland above and cling fast to this wretched life that sinks down below and has nothing more to it than corruption. Let us not prefer the present to the future, nor choose the perishable over the imperishable. Let us not, then, abandon heaven, which we might have as our dwelling, and make the earth our hearth along with those who dwell in tombs. Let us be sober from now on, brothers, and keep watch, shaking off the deep sleep of sloth; and, wiping the rheum from the eyes of the soul, let us know to whom we belong and where we come from. What, and of what kind, is our formation? How were we constituted together with a part, yet honored above the whole? Then let us apply ourselves to the things perceived by the senses [?], and, beyond the mind, to the things perceived by the intellect, and let us consider as far as we can who established all these things. Who is it that makes and fashions by his will alone? Who is it that fashions man from the earth and returns him to the earth? Who is it that [makes] darkness his hiding place, and covers the abyss of his judgments with cloud? Let [David] persuade you, O man, when he says: "Your knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is mighty, I cannot attain to it." And with good reason. For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? Who is it that gives the measures of life and fixes the times he foreknew before the body was put together? Who assigns to the human race its ways of life and its changes of age, cutting short the course of one and lengthening that of another? And before these things, who is it that fashions [?] and graciously forms the infant, and [?] the offspring, and sketches its form to fulfil a single beauty? Who carves the shape and models [?] and fits together [?] and assembles the parts, and fixes the organs, and articulates the positions of the limbs to suit the needs of the body [?] the shapes? And earlier still, who [?] the clay, and joins the dust to the spirit, and sets up a living statue? Who [turns] blood [into flesh?] and phlegm into bones, and, curdling the one and the other, brings them into a single marvellous compound? [Who], like a painter in the womb, sketches images, [?] qualities, and [?] depths, and [?] constitutes [?]? Who is it that stretches the sinews and [?] the muscles,

attaches membranes to the arteries, and fills the veins with blood? Who joins bone to bone and joint to joint, covers them with flesh, and magnificently clothes them with an outer covering? What tanner in the womb crafted the hide, smoothing so gently the visible surface of the skin with the hidden moisture of the flesh, then stretching it out entire, and so shaped it? Who is it that fashioned hearts, yoked the kidneys beneath them, and devised the arrangements of the entrails? Who is it that gives life and breath and all things? And earlier still, whose work is this great and all-harmonious world? How did heaven come to be the great and transparent covering of the whole? From where do some get the idea of giving it a spherical shape, turning obliquely like a wheel and rolled along aimlessly with the motion of the stars? And before these things, who constituted the pre-cosmic order of the powers above the world in ranks befitting angels? Who shaped their immaterial and fiery substances into myriads and thousands, giving form to what has no shape, and adorned them in manifold ways? Where do they get their fiery, luminous and winged nature, their lightness and airiness? [?] their keenness, their readiness and energy for service, their exceeding swiftness of flight and loftiness of course, and their being borne everywhere without toil, as the divine command directs? Whose contrivance is this diffused air, and the ethereal fire above it? How does the same air chill in one place and warm in another, the one by its natural moisture, the other by its nearness to the regions above? What weaver or embroiderer wove such a cloth, fitted to receive the rays of the sun? Of what craftsman is this most beautiful foundation that surrounds the earth? Who contrived it, setting it firm with nothing to hold it? On which of its foundations are its hidden outlets bound? Where does this great element, the sea, come from, and that vast and boundless water gathered into a single mass? Where do the manifold kinds of living creatures come from, those that fly above the earth, creep about on it, and swim upon the waters? How great is the power of the Maker of all things! Where do plants and kinds of plants come from, and tall and towering trees? Where do the kinds of seeds come from, and the pastures of cattle, and grassy lands, rose gardens and parks, the outflows of rivers, and caverns? Who is it that [?]

set heights for the mountains, and [?] the ridges, and broke open the necks of hills from beneath, and joined [?] smooth places, and spread out glens beneath them, and plains and ravines? Who is the father of the rain? Who has begotten the drops of dew? "Out of whose womb comes the ice?" says he who spoke to Job out of the whirlwind. Who has known the treasuries of hail? Who is it that creates the wind, makes the thunder firm, and [?] commands? Who sends lightnings for the rains and showers to water the earth, and commands the rivers to overflow? From what [ends of the earth] are the clouds brought up? From what treasuries does he bring out the winds? Who established all these things, who holds them in his hand? Who moves them, gives them life, steers and leads them by a nod alone? Who [set] sand as a boundary for the sea? Reined in by fear of whom is it restrained and tamed, held back and drawn away from its own [?], so that it does not pass its watery gates; but, as though bearing a fearful command at its mouth, it does not rise up against the neighboring land, but, stepping back upon itself, breathes out its foam, is [drawn back] to its shores with its spittle, and retreats, bearing the posture of a servant? Where do the countless kinds of creatures variously sown in it come from, among which every kind of [?] form is to be seen, scattered in manifold ways into species, parts and sizes, and leaving [?] the craftsman to marvel at a skill and understanding beyond the mind? But so as not to go through everything in detail (for an account of each of God's creatures, set out precisely for knowledge and [understanding], needs another occasion than the present), I think what has been said is enough, [?] to bring forward the manifest tokens of God's greatness; summing up the whole briefly, I will now take up the thread of my discourse. So then, to sum up: Who established all these things? Whom does everything serve? To whom is it bound? To whom does it yield? [Whose is] the strength? By whose nod is it led? Is it not his whose might is infinite and whose authority is eternal? At whose [command] is the soul separated from the body (for it is time now to touch on [our subject]), if not of him who long ago bound them together? Do not wonder if you hear of the separation of soul from body, knowing that the things under [?] are subject to change. For this belongs to matter and to [nature] in flux, from which bodies come, by which [?], and into which we are to be dissolved, undergoing the change into [?]. Since, then, we are wholly subject to ending and alteration,

[?] as he says who says: "What man is there who shall live and not see death?", and since we are all of yesterday, mortal and earthly, and returning to the earth, it is in vain that we are distressed over the dead, beating our breasts and distraught; and vain too to lament at their tombs those who have been dissolved and have returned to their own dust. If the shadow of change did not lie over the whole visible creation alike, mourning for the departed would be bearable for those who cannot bear their loss, since they would, as it were, be shut out, as far as one can see, from the most godlike re-formation laid up for us in better hopes. Such mourning is to be seen only among those who do not eagerly await the great and ineffable mystery of the common resurrection. For they do not know that human nature will then be counted worthy of a better and more honorable [state] than the rest of creation …

If, then, the resurrection is our hope, and what we await is renewal, not annihilation, nor a passing into non-being, let us not be grieved by those who have departed a little before us; nor let us weep more than is fitting over those who shared this life here as we do and have set out for the life there. How long shall we, the dead, bury the dead? Let us at last want to be living. How long the tears? How long the wailing, the lament, the outcry, the hair torn out, the hands [beaten], the clatter, the clapping, the shrieks, the tumult, the shouts, the groans, the ingratitude, the blasphemies, the self-mutilation all the way to the tomb, the lamentations before the burial, after the burial, in the marketplace, at home? What are you doing, O man? You see a dead man asleep, and you [blaspheme]? You stand before such a mystery, and you rise up against God? A deposit is being returned, and you go to court with the one who claims it? You pray, saying "Give him rest, Master," and you insult the Master? You escort your dead son, and you weep as though you yourself were not going to die? You see his end, and do you not expect your own? Remind yourself, O man, of who you are. Consider that, being mortal, you certainly begot a mortal who was bound to die. If you have had a beginning, you will plainly have an end too, since having been brought into being you will pass into corruption. Respect your nature, O man, which stands on the border between immortality and mortality. Reflect on the Lord's command. Consider the limit set by the Master's sentence, and do not refuse it, convicted as you are by it through the things you see every day tossed about at random and changing [?]; nor be aggrieved when you see a dead man carried off and passing to a better state.

For you know, you know that you yourself will follow him shortly, since no one among men has ever been able to escape this limit in the end. So when we could give thanks, let us not blaspheme our Benefactor; let us not insult the one who has taken to himself the one we long for. For the passage is not from better to worse, but from the corruptible to the incorruptible, and from things seen to things unseen, which are awaited only by those who have lived in virtue. He himself, then, has taken our loved one to himself, not hiding him in the earth but [receiving him] into the heavens and laying him up in places that he himself knows [?]. He himself sought back his own deposit and has received it; what he deposited he has claimed by his own authority. Who are you to plead your case against what pleases the Master? Who are you to judge him, or to go to trial against him? For he wishes to collect the debt now; he chooses not to extend the period of the term. Or does the maker of times not have authority over the times, to shorten them in one case and lengthen them in another? For how can we know the judgments of God and the abyss of his mysteries, by which some are short-lived and others long-lived; some die [young], others in old age; others even before their time; and others, before coming forth into the light—in Job's words, "those who have not seen the light"—are snatched away early? But let this not trouble us, nor let us complain because we see someone dead in the prime of life; rather, let us consider that he who lent each one his breath has called in the loan when he willed. Nor let us beat ourselves beyond measure with laments over the one who is [?] departing, lest we provoke to anger the one who gave the command. Let us not tear our tunics over him; let us not sprinkle ourselves with earth; let us not tear our flesh with our nails; let us not tear [our hair]; let us not disgrace our heads; let us not [?] tear [?]; let not our [?] be blasphemed; let us not become a laughingstock and a plaything to the children of the Greeks, and insult the beauty of the resurrection; let us not cheapen [?] of our nobility; let us look [?] to ourselves; let us know the power of the mystery; let us consider who we are and where we come from, and for whose sake [?], and where and how; and that not [he alone] now, but all of us shall travel [this road]. Why do we turn away from thanksgiving and rush into lament? Why do we not leave off mourning and turn to hymns? Be quiet a little, brothers, and listen to [these things]; be still and receive consolation; do not trouble the dead man. Fix your eyes on this spectacle, see what is being accomplished, and having seen it, be silent, and do not disturb our mystery. [See], brothers, the fearful thing [?] being accomplished: radiant angels, seeing [?] the astounding sight, coming from above, in choirs [?], clothed in white, having the appearance of light, breathing fire, bearing flame, hastening [?] swiftly [to claim] the deposit,

claiming it, and are we not ashamed? What are you doing, O man? The one lying here is beside himself, and are you not ashamed? The one lying here is beside himself, and you play? He is in agony, and you are raving? He is shaken, and do you not shudder? He is breathing out his soul, and are you not terrified? He is being judged, and are you not astounded? He is being called to account, and are you not numbed, expecting a like demand? He is amazed, seeing what he has never yet seen, and are you not afraid, and do you not draw back, brought to your senses? He is dying, and you snort with insolence? He is coming to his end, and you are in a frenzy? Hold back a little, O man. Let him depart in peace to where he has been called. Let him travel the road he has never yet travelled, from which he will not return, and which all of us alike shall travel, one at once, another a little later: to a land dark and gloomy, to a land of eternal darkness, where there is no light, nor any seeing of the life of mortals. There we too must certainly be, and experience it, like those who go down into the land of dust. But perhaps, hearing these things, you will say to me, beloved: What then? Is one not to weep for this reason, that the earth and a gloomy place receive the one who has gone before? And how shall I not rightly lament one who is led away to such a land, if one must think of such a state as a land? How shall I not wail and cry aloud, hearing that darkness is his dwelling and resting place? Do I have a heart of stone, that I should hear these things and not lament? For if even on hearing that he would be led into light I could not bring myself to let go of my grief, how shall I bear to keep silent when I hear that the one who until a little while ago lived with me now dwells in darkness? How shall I not mournfully bewail him whom I shall see no more? If only, when he left this sweet light, a place of light had received him, so that perhaps some small comfort might be offered to those who grieve! Ah, the absurd reversal of words, the folly, and the dimness of sight that so grips the mind, if one must say it! For was it not necessary that we, being mortal, should be subject to death? Ought we to appear greater than our own Master? If, then, he himself, being Lord and Master of all, the light of those in darkness and the life of all, chose to taste death and to show forth the descent into Hades, so that he might be made like us in all things except sin, and passed through the joyless region of Hades—the lightless one, I mean, full of moonless dark—for three days and nights, what is strange if we, who are sinners and already dead in our trespasses, as the great Apostle says, and subject to generation and corruption, should keep company with death and go down in the soul into the dark dwellings of Hades, where there is no light to see, nor any seeing of the life of mortals, as was said before? For are we above the Master, or better than the saints,

who [underwent] the same manner [of death] as we [?] what has been said, even if [their lot] was better than ours, inasmuch as they excelled in the abundance of virtue? Therefore we must not be aggrieved, but give thanks and pray, and be sober at all times, and not [?], when we hear of the dwelling in the dizzying darkness of Hades. But if they should have a share in that darkness which Scripture calls "outer", then we must beat our breasts and wail. Or rather, it is better to say, even then we should not beat ourselves or be distressed, but ask and [entreat] the Master to count them worthy of mercy at the judgments there, and with manifold kinds of prayer [beseech] the judge to be gracious to them [?] and a most gentle judge; not one who waits for entreaty from outside, but who urges himself to appear merciful and kindly to those being judged on the day of [judgment], when there is no one who dares to entreat him. Over such as these one should rather intensify the weeping, increase the lamentation, and [be drenched] with tears; but not over those who die in faith, grieving like pagans and [?]. And even this not without qualification, nor merely because they have departed before their time of sojourning with us, but only if they have departed having [gathered] for themselves none of the [prizes] of the glory there. Nor are they to be lamented because they have left this sweet sun; but if in this life they were not illumined in any way at all by the light of the Sun of righteousness, then we must be distraught and beat our breasts. Or rather, even here we must pray, both that they may obtain through pity the love of God for humankind, and that we ourselves may become better, being [chastened] by fear. Nor, if Hades is a dark dwelling of the dead, must we despair of those who [have gone] there; but if they did not bear the works of the night, nor were caught in the [snares] of sin, we should be of good cheer—not because they have escaped the hateful things of Hades, but because the light from above will receive them, by which our deeds are made manifest and discerned. And, as Scripture might say: "Weep for the dead, for the light has failed him"; [but] do not lament [?] much, for the light has not been quenched [?] from [?]

…passed from darkness into light. That intelligible light far surpasses our sensible light. Ours is followed by a twelve-hour night, the shadow that comes round the earth in its regular cycle, and it marks off a span of time. The other knows no darkness, no night, no unlit day, no cycle of time. It is bounded by no year, no age, no [?] and no interval. It shines forever on those who delight in its everlasting brightness, as the divine Scripture says somewhere: “Light is for the righteous always, but the name of the ungodly is put out.” The ungodly are those who have not walked by the light of God’s commandments through the dark place of this life. This is what Job meant when he said: “Who would set me back to the months of former days, in which God kept me unharmed, as when his lamp shone above my head?” The lamp is the light of the law. “When by his light I walked in darkness”: he clearly means the darkness of the present age, as the one who sings says: “Night is illumination in my delight. And the night shall be lit up as the day; as is its darkness, so also is its light.” God is light, as indeed he is, “and in him there is no darkness at all.” “In him we live and move and have our being,” and it is to him that we pass over. The souls of all of us, as rational beings, are in his hands. So the unreasonable objection raised about the darkness and the dark regions of Hades misses the mark, and so does the argument drawn from the contrary [?]. I have now briefly shown how souls pass in turn through Hades. So come, man, leave these matters aside and learn instead how our body breaks up. Do not search into the state of the soul after it leaves the body, for it is not for you or me to inquire into these things. Another is the one who knows them. If we cannot know the essence of the soul, how could we know its place of rest? We do not know its form, its shape or its size, how great or how large it is, or how it is bound to the vessel that carries it, by principles known only to God who joined them together. Since this is so, let us pass over the soul, that precious possession with its divine glory of the image, as something beyond our grasp. Let us occupy ourselves with this gross and tangible body, which is changed and overturned by the many changes of life, and fix our minds on it. Then you will learn, beloved, how lowly and earthbound our worthless nature is. It differs in nothing from the flowers of spring, so easily does it decay and wither as it breaks down into the things it was made of. Knowledge of this has some use and builds up those who listen to what is said with attention. So would you like me to show you how perishable the structure of our bodies is, and how it comes apart, and how cheap it is, differing in nothing from that of beasts?

Go a little way from here, and you will receive clear proof of my words. Walk slowly among the tombs outside the city, and report to me how what I say turns out. Peer into the tombs as through a window. Do not be revolted or recoil from what you see. You will see a sight that grieves, not one that delights. But stand there and look plainly, and let the loathsome decay of the dead bodies before you show me how wretched our arrogance is. Bear the stench for a little while, for it is ours and no one else’s. Endure bravely the smell of putrefaction rising from there and the [?] foul seepage. Bear the sight of the worms, hard to look upon, the decay smeared and heaped with gore. Look more closely, if you will, and tell them apart, if you can. Fit bone to bone, and with your own hands put back together, however you like, each of the loosened parts or limbs you can see. Try to work out, even roughly, whose these are and whose those are, who this one is and who that one is. Was this one or that one an old man or a youth when he died? Did one live in prosperity and the other in sorrow before ending his life? Was one short-lived and the other very long-lived? Did one live in glory and the other without it? Learn these things and look all around. See whether it is not full of great dejection and gloom for one who seemed to have beauty of form before [?]…

And why not? Is the sight not loathsome and full of disgust? Flesh dissolved, entrails and members, and the beauty of the body’s form, all rotting and running together? Each of us will be laid in a coffin and decay like them, and will be devoured as the same food for worms and dissolved. Understand what is being said, man. Look around at the tombs. See our bones, turn to yourself and weep. Groan deeply and long. Lament human worthlessness and the kind of end it has come to. Consider, and if you can, tell them apart and say: Who is the king, who the commoner? Who is the rich man, and who the poor? Who is the famous, and who the obscure? Who is the free man, and who the slave? Which is the soldier, which the general? Who is the righteous, and who the [?]? Who is the philosopher, and who the boor? Who is the [?], and who the barbarian? Who is the Roman? Who is the citizen, and who the countryman? Who is the Canaanite, and who the Jew? Who is the daughter who was born, and who the mother who bore her? Who is the father, who the son? But seeing only bare bones, you could not tell any of them apart, even if you said it ten thousand times, (Another reading: “stained.”)

even if you wrap yourself in all the learning of the scholarly disciplines. [?] In this way, perhaps, you will grasp how all the things of this world that flow and pass away in life go over into non-being. You may speak of wealth, rank, fading glory, power, dominion, beauty, strength, stature, noble birth, or anything else we count among the best or the worst things. All of it will suffer the same dissolution as our bones. Gold is taken from the mines, given over to the furnace and tested by fire, and it presents the goldsmiths with a [?] purer than itself. Silver is fired and purified like gold, and is made white. The blood of the murex dyes purple. The sea-mussel [?] nurtures the pearl. The emerald grows green out of the earth as a stone. The worm, as it feeds, produces silken fabric. The sea pinnas weave a strange thread and provide a twofold use. Then there are sea urchins, goats and bees. The urchins season a tasty dish of moist fare for us. The goats drip sweet milk from their udders: fresh, they provide us an impromptu drink, and curdled, they prepare a lasting food. Sheep too supply us with the same use, and both, yielding the wool shorn from their hair, furnish us with wonderful clothing. The bees fill the chambers of their hexagonal cells with honey, then leave the hives and abandon the combs, dripping with sweetness, to the harvesters. It is a work that bears the mark of wisdom, a precious piece of craftsmanship by a lowly winged creature, a discovery for life’s needs, gathered by nature’s artistry in industrious flights. In short, all the things that make up our life, the most useful and most pleasant, and whatever beauty is lavishly joined to them, suffer the same corruption as everything subject to change, and are dissolved in the same way. Our condition differs from theirs only in this: it has been honoured with the resurrection, and with the renewal [?] putting on the royal [?], he clothed himself in our nature [?] the admired pearl stone. [?] Purple shellfish are produced, and a great multitude of oysters and other creatures. One is peculiar, which they call [?], and from it came the pearl stone. [?] dyed in the Spirit from the immaculate and virginal blood, royally [?]…

…conformed to God by [?] of the resurrection, it receives deification by grace. [?] From this, beloved, you can be still more certain how uncertain our fortunes are. Would you like me to show you a worthlessness even more dishonourable than this disgrace? Take, first, an image of how unstably we are turned about: I mean the daily revolving and changing of affairs. You see, perhaps, that our affairs never stay the same but change from day to day. Some are turned unsteadily up and down, others are jumbled together in confusion, and nothing at all is firm and secure. Believe me, for I describe our condition truly, and take the clear proof from what happens every day. See what our affairs are like now. Yesterday a man sat enthroned on a gold-inlaid seat, his brows raised, stirring up intolerable trouble, surrounded by many ranks of attendants. Today he lies at the tomb, carried on a bier, wretched and pitiable, led away a corpse to the grave. A crowd surrounds him, he is mourned, torches and candles light his way, and shortly afterwards everyone abandons him. A friend of the dead is a friend only as far as the tomb. Yesterday he was acclaimed, today he is pitied. Yesterday he was puffed up with power, today he is gripped by sickness. Yesterday in the city, today on a bed. A little while ago he was feared, today he stinks. Yesterday he was handsome, today he is to be shunned. Today great, tomorrow blackened. Yesterday in a house, today in a tomb. Yesterday perfumed, today reeking, swarming with worms and smelling of rot. Do you see what disgrace our apparent glory has come to? Do you see how extreme the change is, and how glory and fortune vary and alter? Do you know where our affairs are heading? Tell me: where is the [?]? Where is the boasting? Where are the gold-bridled horses, the splendid ornaments of precious Indian stones, the golden necklaces? Where are those who ran beside him and went before him, the bodyguards who frightened and threw everyone into confusion? Where are the dominions, the powers, the council chambers, the proclamations, the brave deeds in war? Are they not all ashes? Are they not all earth and dust, and [?] more worthless still? Where are all these things? Gone. Where is all that glory, where is the use of it? Perished. Where are so-and-so and so-and-so, who yesterday were held up as a great pride above everyone and towered over the many with the weight of their power? Where is our friend so-and-so? He has fallen asleep. Where is this man’s wife, that woman’s daughter, this man’s son? They have passed away, one a little while ago, another long ago, one in a foreign land, another in his homeland, one beneath the sea, another taken by wild beasts. Fittingly, then, the saying of Ecclesiastes will apply to these things. (Another reading: “lamented with dirges.”)

[?] gold-bridled horses [?] tell me: where is the boasting? Where are the gold-bridled horses? [?] splendid ornaments [?] the splendid ornaments of precious Indian stones [?] golden necklaces, those who ran beside [?] those who went before [?] and threw into confusion [?] Are they not all earth and dust? [?] brave deeds? Are they not all ashes? Are they not all earth and dust? [?] Where are all these things? Gone. [?] more worthless? Where are all these things? [?] Perished. [?] Where is all that glory, where is the use of it? Perished. [?] who yesterday were great above everyone [?] so-and-so and so-and-so, who yesterday were held up as a great pride above everyone [?] towering over the many with the weight of their power? Where is our friend so-and-so? He has fallen asleep. And where is this man’s wife, and that woman’s daughter [?] this man’s wife, and that woman’s daughter, and [?] They have passed away. One a little while ago [?] one in a foreign land, another in [?] one in a foreign land, another [?] one beneath the sea [?] one beneath the sea, another [?] Fittingly, then, the saying of Ecclesiastes will apply to these things [?] Fittingly, then, the saying of Ecclesiastes will apply to these things

who said: “Vanity of vanities; all is vanity and a chasing after wind.” To quote that most divine man again: “All came from the dust, and all return to the dust. What befalls the beast befalls men; as the one dies, so dies the other, and man has no advantage over the beast. And who has seen the spirit of man, whether it goes upward, and the spirit of the beast, whether it goes down to the earth?” If this is so, then our toil is in vain, and so are the luxury of wealth and the comfort of passing things, which rests on uncertainty. And if you like, I will take up the discourse here for a little and show you that the whole course of life differs in nothing from a madness that goes round in circles. Hear, then, what Ecclesiastes sets before us, depicting our condition as in an image through his own example: “I, Ecclesiastes,” he says, “was king over Israel in Jerusalem. And I gave my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom concerning all that is done under heaven; for God has given the sons of men an evil distraction to be distracted by. And I saw all the works that are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and a chasing after wind.” And again: “Behold, I grew great and added wisdom beyond all who were before me in Jerusalem. And I gave my heart to know wisdom and knowledge. [And my heart saw much wisdom and knowledge,] parables and understanding. I knew that this too is a chasing after wind; for in much wisdom is much knowledge, and he who adds knowledge adds pain.” And: “I said of laughter, ‘Madness,’ and of mirth, ‘What does this do?’” And a little later: “I made my works great,” he says. “I built myself houses, I planted myself vineyards, I made myself gardens and orchards, and planted in them every fruit-bearing tree. I made myself pools of water, to water

from them a forest of growing trees. I acquired [?] … in my toil that I toiled to do. And behold, all is vanity and a chasing after wind.” Do you see what worthlessness our life comes to? Have you seen what misery so great a glory brings our pride to? So hold back, man, from complacency about these things, and do not long to be pampered by things that exist today but will not exist tomorrow. Do not mourn the one who has died, who has left behind the vanity of all things and exchanged what flows away for what endures. I will turn back to him in my discourse. Do you pity his youth? Rather pity yourself, grown old and with nothing virtuous achieved even to these grey hairs. “Alas,” someone says, “the boy was young and had not yet reached his prime. He did not even enjoy this sweetest light, but was led away without tasting, as one might say, the good things of life.” But in this way he stood before the Creator. [?]

not only had her hands stretched out to the spindle, but had already extended them to every kind of virtue? She nurtured her children and loved them, kept her household very well throughout her life, helped widows, gave shelter to strangers, aided the poor, and accomplished every good thing. But since she was mortal, she had to taste death, for the same end is set before all. Come then, be persuaded by me. I call on all of you who have listened diligently to my words, and I think that all of you have soundly grasped the truth of these counsels. Let us raise one common voice and with hymns of thanksgiving praise the divine and blessed lordship, divinity and sovereignty of the impassible nature, singing: Blessed is he who alone is eternal, who alone has no successor, who alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light. To him be glory, honour and eternal might, to all the ages of ages.

ON THE VENERATION OF THE HOLY ICONS. Nothing in Christianity is unproven or [?]. The very use of the holy icons comes from ancient tradition, and we have trustworthy examples that support the case for icons. The first is the venerable image of our Lord Jesus Christ sent to Abgar the toparch in [?]. It is an imprint of his bodily features and falls in no way short of a painting in colours. The second is the image of Mary, who bore him without seed, in Lydda, which is called Diospolis,

an image not made by hands, which shows on very clean panels the three-cubit figure of the Mother of God. It has been venerated from the times of the apostles until now in the church built by them [?] on the western side. It is depicted as perfectly as if by a painter’s hand: the purple, I mean, and the garments, the hands and the face and the whole rendering of her appearance. These can still be seen preserved even now. They say that Julian, that apostate and hater of Christ, learned about this image and had it examined by sending [?] Hebrews. When he was assured of the truth, he marvelled at it, but did nothing at all against it. They also say that this church was built while the Mother of God was still alive in the flesh. The apostles went up to Sion, where she lived, and said to her: “Where have you been, Lady? We have built you a house in Lydda.” She answered them: “I too was there with you, and I am there now.” At that word they went down to Lydda, went round the church, and found, just as she had said, her whole figure imprinted in her own likeness. This ancient [?] has prevailed among the local people from of old until now

[third] example. All who lived at that time have said that Luke the apostle and evangelist painted with his own hands both the incarnate Christ himself and his immaculate Mother, and that Rome possesses their images, to its own glory. They also say that these images are carefully preserved in Jerusalem. Moreover, the Jew Josephus likewise relates that the Lord was seen with eyebrows meeting, fine eyes and a long face, slightly stooping and of good stature, just as he appeared, evidently, while living among men. He gives in the same way the form of the Mother of God as it is seen now, which some also call the [image] of the Romans. [?] Peter and John, staying in Lydda, called Diospolis, eighteen miles from Jerusalem, built a house of prayer in the [?] of the Lord and of the Mother of God…

OF SAINT ANDREW OF CRETE, THE JERUSALEMITE: SELECT CANONS AND TRIODIA. DECEMBER 9. THE CONCEPTION OF SAINT ANNE, ANCESTRESS OF GOD. The canon, a composition of the lord Andrew. Ode 1. Tone 1. “A song of victory.” Today we celebrate your conception, godly-minded Anne, for you have conceived her who contained the One whom nothing can contain, and you have been set free from the bonds of barrenness.
Glorious Anne now conceives the pure one, who conceived the bodiless Lord [?]. And she is about to bear the one who is about to bear him in the flesh.
Ode 3. “Let my heart be established.” “If you grant me fruit of the womb,” Anne cried to the Lord, “I shall be magnified, and I will dedicate it to you.” Therefore she conceives the [?]

[?] they offered a supplication to the Giver of all things. He heard their prayer and granted them the true gate of life, whose holy Conception let us honour. Ode 4. “Foreseeing in the Spirit.” “O divine message! O strange words! Shall I too conceive?” When an angel was sent to her, Anne was astonished and cried aloud: “Glory to my God, who works wonders.” “Rejoice with me, all you tribes of Israel! I have conceived in my womb the new heaven, from which the star of salvation will shortly rise, Jesus the giver of light,” Anne cried out with joy. God heard Anne’s groans, and the Lord heeded her prayer. He scattered the cloud of childlessness and wondrously made the light of fruitfulness shine on her. So she conceives the only pure one.

Virgin Mother of God, undefiled tabernacle, I am defiled by sins: cleanse me now with the most pure drops of your compassion, and give me a helping hand, so that I may cry: Glory to you, pure one, glorified by God. Ode 5. “Your peace.” Anne, sprung from the root of David and Jesse, now begins to bring forth the divine rod, which put forth the mystical flower, Christ the creator of all. “The peoples will see that I have become a mother,” Anne cries out, “and they will marvel. For behold, I am with child, as it pleased him who loosed the bonds of my barrenness.” How blessed is the house of David, from which you have come forth! [?] The daughters of Matthan of [the line of] Solo[mon]…

We know you as cloud and paradise, yes, as gate of light [?], as table and fleece, and as the jar that holds the manna within, the sweetness for the world, pure Virgin Mother. Ode 6. Heirmos: "The prophet Jonah." How is she contained in a womb, she who contained God? How is she born, she who gave birth to Christ in the flesh? And how is she [nursed?], she who nursed the Creator with milk? God has heard your prayer and has now given you a most fruitful offspring today, all-praised Joachim and Anna. When Anna conceived the pure dove in her womb, she was filled with spiritual joy, truly [?] bringing songs of thanksgiving to God. [?] Theotokion. Storms of thoughts, onslaughts of passions and the deep of sins toss my wretched soul like a tempest: help me, holy Lady. Kontakion. Tone 4. Heirmos: "You have appeared today." Today the whole world celebrates the conception of Anna, which was brought about by God; for she conceived the one who conceived the Word beyond reason. Oikos. "You who once, in [Abraham's?] deepest old age, by your care and promise [gave] a son, the great Isaac; you who opened the barren womb of Hannah, Almighty, mother of Samuel your [prophet?]: look now upon me also [?], fulfil my requests and accept my prayers," cried the chaste Anna, barren as she was, in [her prayers?]. And the Benefactor heard her, and so with joy she conceived the Virgin who conceived the Word beyond reason.

Our Lord and God wished to prepare for himself a living temple and a holy house to dwell in. So he sent his angel to the righteous Joachim and Anna, from whom he willed that his mother according to the flesh should come forth, and announced in advance the conception by the childless and barren woman, to confirm the birth of the Virgin. Thus the holy Virgin Mary was conceived and born. She was not born, as some say, at seven months, or without a man; she was born after nine full months, and though by a promise, yet from the union and seed of a man. But from the holy Virgin Mary our Lord Jesus Christ was born ineffably and inexplicably, as he alone knows, without the desires of the flesh, being perfect God; and from her he took perfectly all that belongs to the economy in the flesh, just as he also fashioned and formed human nature in the beginning. We therefore celebrate this day as holding the memory of the oracles given by the angel, who announced the good news of the holy conception of the pure Mother of God. Bringing these to fulfilment, God, who brought all things into being out of nothing, roused the barren womb to bear fruit; and her who had grown old in childlessness he wondrously made the mother of a child. He granted this as a worthy end to the righteous petition of the righteous: a daughter from whom he himself, God bearing flesh, was to come forth for the regeneration of all. For he was pleased that the chaste parents should bear a daughter, who would be Mother of God and mediator for humankind, she who before the ages had been foreordained and chosen out of all generations to be born. This synaxis is celebrated in the venerable house of the Theotokos, which is in [?] near the most holy church. Ode 7. Heirmos: "The youths in the furnace." Anna besought the Master of all that she might escape the reproach of childlessness; and the Compassionate One, hearing her voice, gave her as fruit the one who would conceive him, as he was well pleased to do. The royal purple begins to be woven in your womb, Anna; and God, the King of all, will wear it and be seen by mortals, and will humble the enemies who war against us. You conceived in your womb, Anna, the fragrant myrrh, she who wondrously received the Myrrh of life, the Master, who has filled our minds with fragrance by the breaths of grace. As one of the Trinity we glorify you, Christ: for, made flesh from a Virgin without change, you endured all things as a man, not departing from the Father's nature, Jesus, though you were united to us. Ode 8. Heirmos: "Him at whom the angels tremble." "Behold, I receive in my womb the queen whom David foretold," Anna cries out, "and I shall bear the protection of all the faithful, her who is to [bear] Christ the King

September 8. The Nativity of our most holy Lady the Theotokos. Canon of Kyr Andrew [?]. Ode 1, plagal tone 4. Heirmos: "To him who crushed." Three without beginning I glorify, three holy ones I hymn; three coeternal in one essence I proclaim. For one God is glorified in Father, Son and Spirit.

Who has seen a child whom no father sowed, nourished with milk? Or where has a Virgin Mother been seen? Truly both are beyond understanding, pure Mother of God. Ode 3. Heirmos: "My heart is established." Blessed is your heart, chaste Anna; for you conceived the [fountain?] of virginity, her who without seed bore the [Maker?] of creation and Redeemer, Jesus. Brought up in the Holy of Holies, spotless Virgin Theotokos, you were shown higher than creation, for you conceived the Creator in the flesh.

[?] Spotless Theotokos, you bore for humankind the Prince of Life, and were revealed as the treasure of our life and the gate of the unapproachable light. Kathisma, plagal tone 4. "You have heard my prayer, Lord," let Anna say, "giving me today the fruit of the promise, her who was foreordained out of all generations and all women as your pure and spotless Mother." The world rejoices with you today, God-minded Anna; for you have brought to flower the mother of its Redeemer, the rod of power that sprang from the root of David, bearing for us the flower, Christ.

I glorify you, Trinity without beginning, undivided in [essence?], crying out with the Cherubim with my tongue of clay: Holy, holy is he who is and abides for ever, the one eternal God. Both now. Theotokion. Spotless one, the prophecies of those who spoke of God have been fulfilled, who faithfully call you tabernacle and gate and spiritual mountain, bush, and the rod of Aaron that blossomed. Dance, barren women and mothers! [?] Anna, you surpass mothers [?] until a daughter is born to you. On the eighth Anna brings forth to the light the Mother of God. Her father Joachim drew his lineage from the royal tribe. Though, as a lover of God and a rich man, he offered double gifts to God, he was nevertheless reproached for his childlessness. Stung to the heart at this, he on the mountain, and his wife Anna in the garden, besought God with tears; and God granted them a holy fruit of the womb, the all-holy Theotokos. So that we may also see Anna's descent on both sides, I shall relate it exactly. Twenty-third from the line of David and Solomon is found Matthan, who married Mary of the tribe of Judah and begot Jacob, the father of the carpenter, and three daughters, Mary, Sobe and Anna. Mary bore Salome the midwife; Sobe bore Elizabeth; and Anna bore the Theotokos. So the Theotokos is the granddaughter of Matthan and of Mary his wife, while Elizabeth and Salome are nieces of Anna and cousins of the Theotokos. By her intercessions, Christ God, have mercy on us. Ode 7. Heirmos: "The furnace of the Chaldeans." [Hymn] of Andrew of Jerusalem for the Annunciation, March 25. Today is the good news of joy, a virginal festival; things below are joined to things above; Adam is renewed; Eve is freed from her first sorrow; and the tabernacle of our substance, through the deification of the lump of clay that was assumed, has become a temple of God. O mystery! The manner of the self-emptying is unknown; the manner of the conception is ineffable. An angel ministers to the wonder; a virgin womb receives the Son; the Holy Spirit is sent down; the Father is well pleased from on high; and the exchange is carried out by common will. In him and through him we are saved, so in harmony with Gabriel let us cry to the Virgin: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you, from whom came salvation, Christ our God, who took our nature and led it back to himself." Entreat him that our souls may be saved. On the Thursday of the fifth week [the bell?] is sounded at the [?] hour of the night. When we have gathered in the church, the blessing is given by the [priest?]; [we sing] the Alleluia and the Trinitarian hymns of the tone, as is customary, and we recite the appointed kathisma of the Psalter. Then we say the kathismata of [?], and read the life of the holy Mary of Egypt [?]. Then [?] we begin the Great Canon, and with a contrite heart and [?] we make [prostrations?] at each [troparion?].

Where shall I begin to lament the deeds of my wretched life? What beginning shall I make, O Christ, for this present lament? But since you are compassionate, grant me forgiveness of my transgressions. Come, wretched soul, with your flesh, confess to the Creator of all; turn away henceforth from your former folly, and offer God tears in repentance. I rivalled the first-formed Adam in transgression, and I know that I have been stripped of God and of the eternal kingdom and delight because of my sins.

In place of the Eve of the senses, an Eve of the mind has risen up within me: the passionate thought in the flesh, showing me sweet things, yet ever tasting of the bitter draught. Following in the bloodguilt of Cain, I have by my own choice become a murderer of my soul's conscience, giving life to the flesh and waging war against the soul with my wicked deeds. I declare to you, Savior, the sins I have committed, and the wounds of my soul and body, which murderous thoughts within have inflicted on me like robbers.
